Russia’s military expenditure reached an estimated $190 billion in 2025, approximately 7.5 percent of gross domestic product according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute. Market-rate comparisons understate the domestic purchasing power of Russian spending because salaries, ammunition, fuel and locally produced equipment cost less inside Russia than comparable systems in Western economies.

NATO’s resource advantage remains immense. In 2025, all allies met or exceeded the previous benchmark of spending at least 2 percent of GDP on defence. European allies and Canada collectively invested more than $574 billion when measured in constant 2021 prices. Total alliance expenditure exceeded $1.4 trillion.

At the 2025 Hague Summit, allies committed to spending 5 percent of GDP annually on defence and security-related requirements by 2035. At least 3.5 percent is intended for core military needs, while up to 1.5 percent can support infrastructure, resilience, civil preparedness, networks, innovation and industrial capacity.

If fully implemented, the commitment will widen NATO’s advantage. It could produce larger ammunition stockpiles, hardened infrastructure, more deployable forces and stronger European capacity. If treated as an accounting exercise, it may generate impressive budgets without correcting readiness gaps.

The strategic balance can be summarised across five levels:

  • Global conventional power: NATO holds a decisive advantage.
  • Regional land war near Russia: The balance is far more contested, especially during the opening weeks.
  • Air and maritime warfare: NATO possesses superior aggregate capability, provided bases and reinforcement routes remain operational.
  • Industrial endurance: NATO has greater latent capacity, while Russia currently demonstrates stronger wartime mobilisation in selected categories.
  • Nuclear escalation: Neither side can achieve meaningful victory without risking catastrophic destruction.

The most dangerous misconception is that NATO’s economic superiority makes Russian aggression irrational and therefore impossible. Putin’s government does not need to defeat the entire alliance. It could seek to seize limited territory, fracture allied decision-making, threaten nuclear escalation and present NATO leaders with a choice between accepting a fait accompli or widening the war.

The opposite misconception is that Russia’s battlefield adaptation makes it capable of conquering Europe. Russia has struggled for years to subdue Ukraine, a country with fewer resources than NATO and no independent nuclear deterrent. A united alliance entering a conventional war with full American participation would impose military pressure Russia could not sustainably match.

NATO is stronger than Russia. Russia may still be locally stronger than the NATO forces available at the place and time where Moscow chooses to create a crisis.

Deterrence depends on eliminating that difference. NATO must possess sufficient forward strength, rapid reinforcement, integrated air defence, long-range fires and political cohesion to deny Russia a short-war opportunity. Its goal is not to prepare for the conquest of Russia. It is to make aggression against allied territory visibly unwinnable from the first hour.

Background

The Cold War Military Balance

NATO was established in 1949 to deter Soviet expansion and bind North American power to the defence of Western Europe. Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty declared that an armed attack against one member would be considered an attack against all.

The Soviet-led Warsaw Pact maintained enormous conventional forces across Central and Eastern Europe. NATO relied on forward-deployed divisions, reinforcement from North America, tactical nuclear weapons and the strategic nuclear forces of the United States, Britain and France.

The alliance’s central problem was geographic. Soviet and Warsaw Pact forces could concentrate close to the inner-German border, while American reinforcements had to cross the Atlantic. NATO sought to deter a rapid offensive through a combination of conventional defence and nuclear escalation.

The Soviet Union’s collapse removed the immediate threat. The Warsaw Pact dissolved, Russian forces withdrew from much of Eastern Europe and NATO members reduced defence budgets. Large armoured formations disappeared. Ammunition stockpiles contracted. Mobilisation infrastructure deteriorated.

NATO shifted toward crisis-management operations in the Balkans, Afghanistan and Libya. European forces became smaller, professional and optimised for expeditionary deployments rather than industrial-scale territorial warfare.

Russia underwent its own collapse. Military salaries went unpaid, equipment deteriorated and the Chechen wars exposed severe operational weaknesses. Putin’s government later invested in reform, readiness, precision weapons and nuclear modernisation.

NATO Enlargement

Former Warsaw Pact members and Soviet republics joined NATO because they feared renewed Russian domination. Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary entered in 1999. The Baltic states joined in 2004, placing Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania inside the alliance.

Moscow portrayed enlargement as a strategic encirclement. NATO argued that membership was a sovereign choice and that the alliance remained defensive. The disagreement became one of the defining disputes in post-Cold War European security.

Russia’s 2014 annexation of Crimea and intervention in eastern Ukraine ended any remaining assumption that Moscow accepted the territorial settlement created after the Soviet collapse. NATO responded with sanctions, rotational deployments and multinational battlegroups on its eastern flank.

Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 transformed the alliance. Finland joined NATO in April 2023, adding a highly capable military and more than 1,300 kilometres of border with Russia. Sweden entered in March 2024, strengthening the defence of the Baltic Sea, Arctic approaches and Scandinavia.

NATO now has 32 members. The accession of Finland and Sweden was a strategic defeat for Moscow. Russia sought to prevent NATO’s expansion but instead pushed two historically non-aligned European states into the alliance.

Russia’s Military Reforms

Russia’s armed forces underwent major reforms after poor performance in the 2008 war against Georgia. Moscow reduced hollow formations, improved readiness, professionalised selected units and created brigade-based structures intended for rapid deployment.

Russia invested heavily in long-range precision weapons, air defence, electronic warfare, submarines and nuclear delivery systems. The 2015 intervention in Syria showcased air power, cruise missiles and expeditionary logistics.

The Syrian campaign also encouraged excessive confidence. Operations took place against opponents without advanced air power, layered air defence or long-range strike. Russia’s military leadership drew lessons that did not fully prepare it for a large conventional war against Ukraine.

The 2022 invasion revealed failures in planning, intelligence, logistics, command and combined-arms execution. Russian columns advanced without adequate protection or sustainment. Airborne assaults failed to deliver strategic collapse. Ukrainian resistance and Western support forced Moscow into a prolonged attritional war.

Russia adapted. It mobilised personnel, constructed defensive lines, expanded drone use and integrated reconnaissance with artillery. The military became less elegant but more experienced in the realities of high-intensity warfare.

The Ukraine War as a Strategic Laboratory

Ukraine has become the central reference point for any NATO–Russia comparison. It has demonstrated the continuing importance of artillery, mines, trenches and manpower while revealing the transformative effect of drones, satellite intelligence, electronic warfare and precision weapons.

Neither Russia nor Ukraine achieved sustained air superiority. Dense air defences forced aircraft to operate cautiously and increased reliance on stand-off weapons, glide bombs and unmanned systems.

Commercial technology became militarised at extraordinary speed. Small drones identified targets, corrected artillery fire, dropped explosives and attacked vehicles. First-person-view drones turned exposed movement into a lethal activity.

Electronic warfare disrupted navigation and communications. Both sides adapted frequencies, autonomous guidance and fibre-optic control systems. The innovation cycle compressed from years to weeks.

Russia’s missile and drone attacks targeted Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, ports and cities. Ukraine used Western missiles, domestically produced drones and covert action to strike Russian command centres, airfields, oil facilities and naval assets.

The war demonstrated that modern conflict is simultaneously industrial and digital. States require millions of shells and inexpensive drones alongside satellites, algorithms and precision missiles.

Current Situation

NATO’s Strategic Posture

NATO’s 2022 Strategic Concept identifies Russia as the most significant and direct threat to allied security. The alliance has shifted from reassurance toward forward defence.

Multinational battlegroups are deployed in Bulgaria, Estonia, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Romania and Slovakia. Plans exist to expand selected battlegroups toward brigade strength. Germany is establishing a permanent armoured brigade in Lithuania, intended to reach full operational capability in 2027.

NATO has adopted regional defence plans covering the High North and Atlantic, Central Europe and the Mediterranean. These plans connect force requirements with specific operational scenarios and national capability targets.

The alliance’s New Force Model is designed to provide larger numbers of high-readiness forces, with approximately 300,000 troops envisaged at higher readiness levels. The value of this framework depends on whether units possess equipment, ammunition, transport and political authorisation for deployment.

Finland and Sweden improve the northern balance. Finland brings a large trained reserve, extensive artillery, hardened infrastructure and experience operating in Arctic conditions. Sweden provides advanced aircraft, submarines, naval forces and control of Gotland, a strategically located Baltic Sea island.

The Nordic region is no longer divided between NATO members and non-aligned states. Norway, Denmark, Finland and Sweden can coordinate defence across the Arctic, Baltic and North Atlantic approaches.

Russia’s Wartime Force

Russia’s military is larger on paper than it was before the invasion, though quality varies sharply. Contract soldiers, mobilised personnel, conscripts, volunteers and irregular formations coexist within a complex force.

Putin’s decree authorising 1.5 million active personnel reflects Russia’s effort to replace losses, sustain the Ukrainian front and create formations for other strategic directions. Recruitment relies heavily on financial incentives and regional quotas.

Russia has avoided another politically disruptive nationwide mobilisation on the scale of September 2022 by offering substantial signing bonuses and recruiting from economically disadvantaged regions. This model is expensive but has provided manpower without placing equal pressure on Moscow and St Petersburg.

Combat experience is now distributed widely across the Russian military. Officers and soldiers have learned to operate under drone observation, artillery threat and electronic attack. Experience has been purchased through severe casualties and does not erase deficiencies in training or leadership.

Russia continues to retrieve older tanks and armoured vehicles from storage. Refurbished Soviet-era systems supplement new production. This preserves mass but reduces average fleet quality as the best pre-war equipment is lost or consumed.

Russian air power retains modern Su-35, Su-34 and Su-30 aircraft, long-range bombers and large missile inventories. The Aerospace Forces have not achieved decisive air superiority over Ukraine, but they have improved their use of glide bombs and stand-off weapons.

Russia’s navy remains a potent nuclear and submarine force despite serious Black Sea losses. The Northern Fleet protects ballistic-missile submarines and operates advanced attack submarines. The Black Sea Fleet has been pushed away from portions of its traditional operating area by Ukrainian missiles and maritime drones.

Defence Spending

NATO’s financial advantage is overwhelming. Alliance spending exceeded $1.4 trillion in 2025. The United States remained the largest contributor, while European allies and Canada collectively spent more than $574 billion in constant 2021 prices.

Every ally met or exceeded the previous 2 percent benchmark in 2025. The distribution remains uneven because the largest economies contribute the greatest absolute sums while frontline states often spend the highest shares of GDP.

Poland has become one of the most ambitious military spenders, acquiring American Abrams tanks, South Korean K2 tanks and K9 artillery, F-35 aircraft, attack helicopters, air defence and rocket systems. The Baltic states and Nordic members have also expanded defence expenditure.

Germany’s Zeitenwende increased spending and created a €100 billion special fund, while later fiscal reforms opened greater borrowing space for security. Britain and France remain Europe’s leading nuclear and expeditionary powers.

Russia’s estimated $190 billion expenditure in 2025 is much smaller in dollar terms, but the figure represents approximately 7.5 percent of GDP and a far larger share of government expenditure than most NATO states commit.

Comparisons at market exchange rates exaggerate NATO’s advantage in domestically produced matériel. Russia pays personnel in roubles and produces many tanks, shells and missiles locally. Purchasing-power comparisons narrow the gap, though they do not remove NATO’s technological and economic superiority.

NATO’s 2035 commitment to spend 3.5 percent of GDP on core defence and up to 1.5 percent on security-related requirements could transform the balance. Europe’s combined economy is vastly larger than Russia’s. A sustained rearmament programme would eventually outproduce Moscow across most categories.

Military Personnel

NATO’s combined active-duty forces number several million personnel, with the United States, Turkey, Poland, France, Germany, Italy, Britain and other allies maintaining significant militaries. Reserve systems add millions more in varying states of readiness.

Aggregate personnel figures conceal critical differences. Many European militaries have struggled with recruitment, retention and understrength units. Reserve mobilisation systems range from Finland’s highly developed model to countries with limited recent experience.

Russia’s authorised 1.5 million active personnel should not be interpreted as 1.5 million deployable combat troops. The total includes command, support, training, naval, aerospace and strategic forces. Recruitment targets may not be fully achieved.

Russia nevertheless has a clear advantage in willingness to generate and expend manpower for the current war. Its political system can impose costs that would create greater controversy in most NATO democracies.

NATO’s advantage lies in population and economic depth. Its weakness is political mobilisation. The alliance can generate far larger forces if governments and societies accept the requirement, but mobilisation may begin only after a crisis.

Land Forces

Russia retains one of the world’s largest land-warfare establishments. Its ground forces possess tanks, infantry fighting vehicles, artillery, ballistic missiles, air defence, electronic warfare and engineering units designed for continental operations.

Losses in Ukraine have reduced the proportion of modern equipment. Many elite formations suffered severe attrition. Yet Russia continues to field mass through refurbishment, new production and organisational expansion.

Russian doctrine places heavy emphasis on artillery, long-range fires and integrated air defence. Iskander ballistic and cruise missiles can target airfields, headquarters and logistics nodes. Tornado and Smerch rocket systems provide area and precision effects. Lancet and other loitering munitions threaten artillery and vehicles.

NATO land forces vary widely. The United States fields advanced armoured brigades with strong logistics, aviation and intelligence. Poland is rapidly expanding heavy forces. Turkey maintains a large army. Finland brings artillery and reserves suited to territorial defence.

Britain, France and Germany possess high-quality formations but have faced readiness and scale limitations. Smaller allies contribute specialised units and territorial defence.

In a fully mobilised war, NATO could assemble a larger and more technologically advanced land force. During the opening phase of a Baltic crisis, Russia might achieve local superiority if NATO reinforcement is delayed.

The central land-warfare question is therefore not total tank numbers. It is whether allied brigades can arrive with ammunition, air defence, engineering support, fuel and command networks before Russia secures operational objectives.

Artillery and Ammunition

Russia holds a major advantage in current artillery consumption and production culture. Its forces have fired enormous quantities of shells in Ukraine, relying on domestic production, stored Soviet stocks and supplies from North Korea.

Estimates of exact annual production vary, but Russia has expanded output far beyond pre-war levels. Its economy and labour system have been reorganised to support sustained military demand.

NATO countries entered the war with limited ammunition stockpiles and production lines designed for peacetime orders. European governments pledged expansion, but new factories, explosives production and skilled labour require time.

The United States and Europe possess the capital and technology to surpass Russian output. The gap lies in urgency, contracting and industrial coordination. Companies will not build capacity without predictable long-term orders.

Artillery comparisons must also consider accuracy and targeting. NATO systems often deliver greater precision, range and sensor integration. Russia compensates through volume, drones and acceptance of high expenditure.

A major war would require both quality and quantity. Precision missiles cannot replace every artillery shell, and massed unguided fire cannot substitute for accurate deep strike.

Air Power

NATO’s strongest conventional advantage lies in aerospace power. The alliance operates thousands of combat aircraft, including F-35, F-22, Rafale, Eurofighter Typhoon, F-16, F-15, Gripen and other platforms.

The United States contributes stealth aircraft, strategic bombers, aerial refuelling, airborne early warning, electronic attack, suppression of enemy air defences and space-based intelligence. European members add advanced fighters, cruise missiles and specialised capabilities.

Russia fields capable aircraft and some highly advanced missiles. Its S-300 and S-400 families create formidable air-defence zones. Russian aircraft can employ long-range air-to-air missiles, anti-radiation weapons and glide bombs.

NATO would seek to degrade Russian air defences through stealth, electronic warfare, cyber operations, decoys and stand-off weapons. This would be difficult and costly. Russia’s integrated air-defence network is denser than any Western air force has faced in recent combat.

NATO’s numerical superiority would matter only if air bases remained usable. Russian missiles would target runways, fuel storage, aircraft shelters, command centres and ports. European dispersal and hardened infrastructure remain uneven.

American refuelling aircraft and intelligence platforms are powerful but vulnerable high-value assets. Russia would attempt to disrupt them through long-range missiles, cyberattack and attacks on supporting bases.

If NATO preserved command, basing and logistics, it would likely establish air superiority over time. It should not assume immediate freedom of action.

Air and Missile Defence

Russia possesses extensive ground-based air defence. S-400, S-300, Buk, Tor and Pantsir systems provide overlapping layers, though performance depends on crews, radar coverage, network integrity and ammunition.

Ukraine has destroyed or suppressed Russian systems, demonstrating that they are not invulnerable. Russia has also adapted through mobility, decoys and electronic protection.

NATO’s air defence is less dense across much of Europe because allies relied on aircraft and assumed limited missile threats after the Cold War. Patriot, SAMP/T, NASAMS, IRIS-T and other systems are expanding but remain insufficient to defend every military and civilian target.

The European Sky Shield Initiative seeks to improve procurement and integration. Poland, Germany, the Nordic states and frontline allies are investing heavily in layered defence.

Missile-defence economics create a shared problem. Russia can launch drones costing far less than advanced interceptors. NATO requires low-cost counter-drone systems, guns, electronic warfare, hardened facilities and rapid repair alongside expensive missile defences.

Naval Power

NATO possesses overwhelming aggregate naval superiority. The United States operates carrier strike groups, nuclear attack submarines, ballistic-missile submarines, amphibious forces and global logistics. Britain, France, Italy, Spain and Turkey add carriers or aviation-capable ships, submarines and surface combatants.

Norway, Germany, Sweden and other allies contribute advanced submarines optimised for northern and Baltic waters. NATO maritime patrol aircraft provide extensive anti-submarine capability.

Russia cannot contest NATO across the Atlantic and Mediterranean simultaneously. Its surface fleet is smaller, and several ships are ageing. The Black Sea Fleet’s losses exposed vulnerability to missiles and unmanned boats.

Russia remains dangerous beneath the surface. Its nuclear-powered submarines can threaten reinforcement routes, carrier groups and undersea infrastructure. The Northern Fleet protects Russia’s strategic submarine bastions and operates near the Greenland–Iceland–United Kingdom gap.

Russian long-range anti-ship missiles can threaten ports and naval formations. Mines, submarines and sabotage could complicate the movement of American forces across the Atlantic.

The naval contest would therefore involve protection of reinforcement rather than a simple fleet battle. NATO must secure ports, shipping, undersea cables and sea lanes while containing Russian submarines.

Drones and Electronic Warfare

Russia possesses greater recent experience operating drones and electronic warfare at industrial scale. Reconnaissance drones observe the front continuously. First-person-view systems attack vehicles and personnel. Lancet loitering munitions target artillery and air defence.

Russia has also imported Iranian-designed Shahed drones and developed domestic variants for long-range attacks. These weapons impose pressure on Ukrainian air defence and energy infrastructure.

NATO members possess more advanced unmanned technologies in many categories, but few have employed them at the intensity seen in Ukraine. Procurement systems often produce expensive platforms in small numbers.

The alliance must combine high-end intelligence drones with millions of inexpensive, replaceable systems. Software updates, autonomous navigation and electronic protection are as important as airframe production.

Russia’s electronic-warfare capability can jam navigation, communications and drone links. NATO’s dependence on data networks creates powerful advantages but also vulnerabilities. Forces must train to operate with degraded communications and disrupted satellite navigation.

Cyber and Space

NATO benefits from the United States’ satellite architecture, global communications, navigation and intelligence systems. Commercial companies add imagery, connectivity and data analysis.

Russia possesses cyber, electronic and counter-space capabilities designed to disrupt these advantages. It can target satellites, ground stations, undersea cables, telecommunications and civilian infrastructure.

A NATO–Russia war would likely begin in cyberspace and the electromagnetic spectrum before public confirmation of conventional attack. Railways, ports, banks, energy grids and government networks would become targets.

NATO’s distributed commercial and national systems provide resilience, but civil infrastructure is unevenly protected. Russia’s more centralised systems may be easier to control during war yet vulnerable to sophisticated penetration.

Nuclear Forces

Nuclear weapons make a direct NATO–Russia war fundamentally different from the conflict in Ukraine. Russia and the United States possess the world’s largest nuclear arsenals. Britain and France maintain independent nuclear forces.

Open-source estimates in 2025 placed Russia’s total inventory at roughly 5,400 nuclear warheads across deployed, stored and retired categories. The precise number changes as weapons are retired, dismantled or modernised.

The United States maintains a comparable strategic arsenal and deploys gravity bombs in Europe under NATO nuclear-sharing arrangements. Britain operates submarine-launched ballistic missiles. France maintains submarine and air-launched nuclear forces.

Russia’s doctrine allows nuclear use in circumstances where the state perceives severe conventional or strategic threats. Moscow has repeatedly used nuclear signalling during the Ukraine war.

NATO’s nuclear posture aims to deter aggression and coercion. Any nuclear use against the alliance would fundamentally alter the conflict, but NATO deliberately avoids detailing the exact form of response.

Neither side possesses a reliable path to nuclear victory. Missile defences cannot neutralise a large strategic strike. Command systems would operate under extreme uncertainty, creating danger of misinterpretation and accidental escalation.

Strategic Analysis

Why Aggregate Comparisons Mislead

Adding every NATO tank, aircraft and soldier creates a total that Russia cannot match. Yet NATO is a political and military alliance, not a unitary state. Forces remain under national control until governments authorise their use.

Some allied forces are committed to national territories or other missions. American forces must also consider the Indo-Pacific, Middle East and global responsibilities. Turkey’s strategic priorities differ from those of Estonia. Spain’s geography creates different requirements from Poland’s.

Russia has a unified command system and can concentrate resources rapidly. Its authoritarian government can conceal planning, suppress dissent and impose mobilisation costs.

NATO’s political process is slower but produces durable legitimacy when consensus exists. An unambiguous attack on allied territory would likely strengthen unity. A deniable, ambiguous or limited operation could create debate over attribution and response.

Geography and the Opening War

Russia’s most plausible conventional challenge lies on NATO’s eastern flank. The Baltic states are geographically exposed and possess limited strategic depth. They connect to the rest of allied territory through the Suwałki corridor between Poland and Lithuania.

Finland’s accession complicates Russian planning by extending the frontier and placing allied territory near the Kola Peninsula and St Petersburg. Sweden improves access to the Baltic and defence of reinforcement routes.

Kaliningrad contains missiles, air defence and military infrastructure capable of threatening Poland, Lithuania and the Baltic Sea. Belarus provides Russia with additional depth and access.

NATO’s objective is to prevent Russia from achieving a rapid territorial seizure. Forward forces must be strong enough to deny easy movement, preserve airfields and receive reinforcement.

The United States Factor

With full American participation, NATO possesses decisive advantages in air power, intelligence, logistics and nuclear deterrence. Without the United States, European NATO members would remain economically stronger than Russia but would face serious capability gaps.

Europe depends heavily on American strategic transport, aerial refuelling, satellite intelligence, missile defence, electronic warfare and long-range strike. European forces could defend themselves, but a rapid transition away from American support would be dangerous.

Donald Trump’s return to the White House intensified burden-sharing pressure. The Hague spending commitment reflects European recognition that American engagement cannot be treated as politically cost-free.

Russia will attempt to separate Washington from Europe. Deterrence therefore depends as much on political signalling as hardware.

Industrial Endurance

NATO’s combined industrial potential exceeds Russia’s by a vast margin. The alliance includes leading aerospace, electronics, shipbuilding and automotive economies.

Russia currently converts a greater share of available resources into immediate war production. Its procurement is less constrained by peacetime efficiency, environmental review or dispersed national requirements.

NATO’s defence industry remains fragmented. European states operate multiple tank, fighter, missile and artillery programmes. National workshare politics complicates common procurement.

The alliance must move from annual purchasing toward multi-year production commitments. Industrial capacity is a form of deterrence only when adversaries believe it can generate weapons before a war is decided.

Combat Experience

Russia’s armed forces possess recent experience in large-scale war. This includes tactical adaptation, battlefield engineering, casualty replacement and operation under persistent surveillance.

NATO forces have extensive professional experience from Afghanistan, Iraq, the Balkans and counterterrorism missions. These campaigns produced strong small-unit skills, joint air operations and expeditionary logistics but did not replicate the conditions of the Ukrainian front.

Ukraine’s forces hold the deepest relevant experience. NATO training and doctrine should absorb Ukrainian lessons without assuming every feature of that war will transfer directly to alliance defence.

Political Will

Russia’s greatest strategic hope is not defeating NATO’s combined military. It is convincing some allies that defending another member is too costly or escalatory.

NATO’s Article 5 is powerful because it transforms a local conflict into an alliance-wide calculation. Its credibility rests on visible forces, exercises, plans and public commitment.

Russia uses nuclear threats, disinformation, energy pressure and political influence to weaken cohesion. NATO must defend the political space in which military decisions are made.

Global Impact

Ukraine

Ukraine is degrading Russian military capacity while also revealing and accelerating Russian adaptation. Continued Western support affects the future NATO–Russia balance.

If Ukraine remains sovereign and capable, Russia must commit forces to a long frontier and cannot easily redirect its entire military toward NATO. If Moscow subordinates Ukraine, it gains territory, resources, infrastructure and a more advantageous position against Poland, Slovakia, Hungary and Romania.

China

China benefits when American attention and resources are concentrated in Europe. Beijing also studies Russian and Ukrainian operations for lessons relevant to Taiwan and high-technology war.

Russia depends increasingly on Chinese trade, electronics and diplomatic support. Beijing does not want Russian defeat, but it also avoids a formal obligation to fight NATO.

A simultaneous crisis in Europe and around Taiwan would stress American forces and allied ammunition stocks. NATO’s ability to defend Europe with a stronger European pillar directly affects the Indo-Pacific balance.

Global Chanakya’s China, Xi Jinping, Taiwan, QUAD, AUKUS and South China Sea pages should be linked to this two-theatre challenge.

India

India has longstanding defence ties with Russia and expanding strategic cooperation with the United States and Europe. A NATO–Russia conflict would place New Delhi under severe pressure.

Russian arms deliveries and spare parts could be disrupted. Energy markets would become volatile. India would seek strategic autonomy while resisting demands to align fully with either side.

A weakened Russia could become more dependent on China, an outcome contrary to Indian interests. New Delhi benefits from a stable multipolar balance in which Moscow retains strategic independence from Beijing.

The Middle East

A European war would divert American and European air defence, naval assets and munitions from the Middle East. Iran and regional armed groups could interpret the distraction as an opportunity.

Russia’s influence in Syria and relationships with Iran would interact with the European theatre. Energy producers in the Gulf would gain leverage as European demand increased.

The Global Economy

A direct NATO–Russia war would disrupt energy, grain, shipping, aviation and financial markets. The Baltic and Black seas could become combat zones. Cyberattacks could affect global banks and communications.

European infrastructure would face sabotage and missile threats. Insurance costs would rise. Trade routes would shift, and states would impose emergency controls on strategic goods.

The economic consequences would exceed those of the Ukraine war because NATO territory and Russian strategic assets would be directly involved.

Risk Assessment

Risk One: Baltic Fait Accompli

Russia could attempt a limited territorial seizure before NATO reinforcement arrives, betting that nuclear threats and political division would prevent reversal.

Probability: Low to medium.

Impact: Extreme.

Risk Two: Ukraine War Spillover

A missile strike, aircraft incident or attack on logistics inside NATO territory could trigger escalation.

Probability: Medium.

Impact: Very high.

Risk Three: Nuclear Escalation

Conventional attacks on command systems, early-warning radars or dual-capable forces could be interpreted as preparation for nuclear disarmament.

Probability: Low.

Impact: Catastrophic.

Risk Four: American Political Retrenchment

Reduced American commitment could create a temporary deterrence gap before Europe develops replacement capabilities.

Probability: Medium.

Impact: Very high.

Risk Five: Ammunition Exhaustion

A prolonged war could consume air-defence interceptors, precision missiles and artillery shells faster than NATO production replaces them.

Probability: Medium to high.

Impact: High.

Risk Six: Hybrid Attack Below Article 5

Russia may use cyberattacks, sabotage, migration pressure, maritime incidents and deniable violence to avoid triggering a unified response.

Probability: High.

Impact: Medium to high.

Risk Seven: Russian Miscalculation

Moscow could mistake alliance debate for an absence of resolve, as it underestimated Ukrainian resistance and Western support in 2022.

Probability: Medium.

Impact: Extreme.

Future Scenarios

Scenario Analysis One: Successful Deterrence

NATO implements the Hague commitment, expands ammunition production and deploys credible forces on the eastern flank. Europe assumes greater responsibility while the United States remains engaged.

Russia concludes that aggression cannot achieve rapid gains. Competition continues through espionage, cyberattack and political influence, but direct war is avoided.

Scenario Analysis Two: Limited Baltic War

Russia creates a crisis involving Baltic territory, supported by cyberattacks, sabotage and nuclear threats. NATO activates defence plans and reinforces Poland and the Baltic region.

The outcome depends on airfield survival, the Suwałki corridor, maritime access and the speed of American deployment. Even a limited conflict carries severe escalation risk.

Scenario Analysis Three: European NATO Without Immediate U.S. Support

Washington delays direct participation while providing intelligence and matériel. European allies must contain Russia with their own land, air and naval forces.

Europe possesses sufficient economic and military potential but faces shortages in strategic enablers. Poland, Germany, France, Britain and the Nordic states become central to the response.

Scenario Analysis Four: Russian Exhaustion

The Ukraine war, sanctions, demographics and equipment losses weaken Russia’s ability to sustain military expansion. Moscow retains nuclear power but reduces conventional ambitions.

NATO maintains deterrence while pursuing selective arms-control and risk-reduction measures. This outcome would not produce friendship, but it could reduce immediate war danger.

Scenario Analysis Five: Dual Crisis with China

Russia pressures NATO as China escalates around Taiwan. The United States must divide aircraft, submarines, air defence and political attention between theatres.

European readiness becomes decisive. If Europe can contain Russia, Washington retains greater freedom in the Indo-Pacific. If not, allied strategy faces severe strain.

Intelligence Forecast

Russia will remain NATO’s principal direct military threat through the early 2030s, regardless of the eventual outcome in Ukraine.

Moscow will rebuild land forces, prioritise missiles, drones, electronic warfare and air defence, and preserve a large nuclear arsenal. Quantity will recover faster than quality.

NATO defence expenditure will continue rising, but capability delivery will lag budgets because factories, personnel and infrastructure require time.

Poland, Finland, Sweden, Germany and the Baltic states will drive eastern-flank readiness. Britain and France will remain essential nuclear and expeditionary powers.

The United States will remain indispensable during the late 2020s, particularly for intelligence, air power, strategic transport and nuclear deterrence.

European ammunition and missile production will expand through multi-year contracts. Fragmentation and national industrial competition will slow standardisation.

Drones, counter-drone systems and electronic warfare will receive accelerated investment. NATO will increasingly treat inexpensive unmanned systems as consumable ammunition.

Russia will intensify hybrid operations against logistics, defence companies, undersea infrastructure and political institutions.

The Arctic and Baltic regions will become more militarised following Finnish and Swedish accession. Submarine activity and infrastructure protection will gain priority.

Nuclear signalling will remain central to Russian strategy. NATO will strengthen exercises, command resilience and nuclear consultation while avoiding unnecessary doctrinal instability.

A deliberate Russian attack on NATO remains less likely than continued war in Ukraine or hybrid pressure. The probability will rise if Moscow perceives declining American commitment, weak European readiness or political division.

Final Strategic Takeaway

NATO possesses the economic scale, technology, population and military resources to defeat Russia in a conventional contest. That conclusion is strategically relevant but operationally incomplete.

Russia does not need to match every allied aircraft or ship. It needs to create local superiority, move faster than NATO’s political process and convince alliance leaders that reversing aggression would risk nuclear war.

The Ukraine conflict has weakened Russia and hardened it. Moscow has lost equipment and experienced personnel while learning how to fight a prolonged industrial war. NATO has gained warning time and battlefield knowledge but has not yet completed the transformation from peacetime forces to credible territorial defence.

The alliance’s greatest advantages are American aerospace power, maritime dominance, advanced intelligence and vast economic capacity. Its greatest vulnerabilities are political fragmentation, limited European stockpiles, slow mobilisation and dependence on a small number of reinforcement routes.

Russia’s greatest advantages are geographic concentration, centralised decision-making, artillery mass, wartime production and tolerance for casualties. Its greatest vulnerabilities are a smaller economy, technological dependence, severe battlefield losses, weaker naval and aerospace depth, and the danger of fighting a coalition it cannot outproduce.

Nuclear weapons prevent either side from treating war as a normal contest. A conventional campaign could escalate through attacks on early-warning systems, command networks or dual-capable forces. Military superiority cannot remove that danger.

The purpose of NATO rearmament is therefore not to prepare an invasion of Russia. It is to deny Moscow any belief that limited aggression could remain limited, profitable or politically survivable.

The Hague spending commitment can make that deterrent credible if it produces brigades, interceptors, shells, hardened bases, protected infrastructure and industrial surge capacity. Percentages without readiness will not stop a war.

The final balance is clear. NATO is stronger. Russia is closer, mobilised and willing to test the meaning of that strength. Peace will depend on whether the alliance can place sufficient capability at the decisive geography before a crisis begins—and whether both sides preserve enough communication to prevent conventional rivalry from crossing the nuclear threshold.

title: India’s Defence Modernization Roadmap: Building Power for a Two-Front Era
content:
India’s Defence Modernization Roadmap: Building Power for a Two-Front Era

Executive Summary

India’s military modernization is entering its most demanding phase since the nuclear tests of 1998. The country is no longer preparing primarily for a limited conventional war with Pakistan. It must now deter a nuclear-armed Pakistan, manage a militarized Line of Actual Control with China, protect an expanding maritime sphere in the Indian Ocean, defend space and cyber infrastructure, and sustain the industrial foundations of prolonged high-technology conflict.

The strategic environment has shifted faster than India’s inherited force structure. China’s military transformation has produced long-range precision weapons, integrated air defence, fifth-generation aircraft, a rapidly expanding navy, counter-space systems and theatre-level joint commands. Pakistan remains conventionally weaker than India but retains nuclear weapons, Chinese equipment, ballistic and cruise missiles, armed drones, and a long history of supporting cross-border terrorism.

The possibility of coordinated pressure from China and Pakistan is no longer treated as an abstract planning exercise. Their defence relationship includes the JF-17 combat aircraft, submarines, air-defence systems, unmanned platforms, satellites and intelligence cooperation. The China–Pakistan Economic Corridor also gives Beijing a deeper strategic stake in Pakistan and access to infrastructure extending toward the Arabian Sea.

India’s response combines military acquisition with institutional and industrial reform. Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government has expanded capital expenditure, reserved a large share of procurement for domestic companies, corporatized the former Ordnance Factory Board, promoted private-sector participation and used Positive Indigenisation Lists to reduce selected imports. The Defence Acquisition Procedure 2020, Innovations for Defence Excellence and the Technology Development Fund seek to connect the armed forces with start-ups, universities and private manufacturers.

The Union Budget for 2026–27 allocated ₹7.85 lakh crore to the Ministry of Defence, a 15.19 percent increase over the previous year’s budget estimate. More than ₹2.19 lakh crore was assigned under the capital head, including approximately ₹1.85 lakh crore for capital acquisition. Around 75 percent of the acquisition budget—₹1.39 lakh crore—was reserved for domestic industry. The Defence Research and Development Organisation received ₹29,100.25 crore.

These figures mark a serious expansion of resources, but the budget also exposes structural pressure. Defence pensions exceed ₹1.71 lakh crore. Salaries, allowances, maintenance and operational expenditure consume another large share. India must simultaneously fund current readiness, support a large standing military, replace ageing systems and invest in emerging technology.

The modernization roadmap rests on six operational pillars:

  • Restructuring the armed forces for joint theatre warfare.
  • Restoring combat-aircraft strength and developing an indigenous aerospace ecosystem.
  • Building a sea-control and sea-denial force for the Indian Ocean.
  • Expanding precision strike, air defence, drone and counter-drone capabilities.
  • Securing India’s nuclear deterrent, space architecture and military networks.
  • Creating an industrial base capable of sustained production during war.

The Indian Army is moving toward lighter, more mobile and technologically networked formations, especially along the Himalayan frontier. The Navy is commissioning indigenous destroyers, frigates and submarines while developing carrier aviation, nuclear-powered platforms and long-range maritime surveillance. The Air Force is attempting to manage declining squadron strength while inducting the Tejas, upgrading the Su-30MKI fleet, integrating Rafale fighters and supporting development of the Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft.

India has also acquired 31 MQ-9B remotely piloted aircraft from the United States and signed a 2025 agreement with France for 26 Rafale Marine aircraft. Indigenous programmes include the Tejas Mk1A and Mk2, AMCA, Zorawar light tank, Pinaka rocket system, Akash air defence, BrahMos cruise missile, Project Kusha, indigenous artillery and a growing family of unmanned platforms.

Modernization is nevertheless constrained by delay. The Tejas Mk1A schedule has been affected by engine-supply and integration problems. Project 75(I) for conventional submarines has moved slowly. Theatre-command reform remains politically and institutionally sensitive. India still depends on foreign suppliers for aero engines, certain sensors, submarine technologies, high-end electronics and specialised materials.

The central danger is not that India lacks programmes. It is that too many programmes mature late, in small numbers or without the joint command, logistics and data architecture required to convert platforms into combat power.

India’s defence challenge is no longer the absence of ambition. It is the conversion of ambition into scale, speed, interoperability and wartime endurance.

The roadmap through the 2030s must therefore prioritise operational outcomes rather than procurement symbolism. India needs combat-ready squadrons, deployable brigades, submarine availability, protected satellites, large ammunition reserves, resilient supply chains and commanders capable of combining all domains in real time.

Background

From Continental Defence to Multi-Domain Competition

India’s military institutions were shaped by the experience of partition, the wars of 1947–48, 1962, 1965 and 1971, the Kargil conflict of 1999, and decades of cross-border terrorism. The country developed a large manpower-intensive military designed to defend long land borders and respond to conflict with Pakistan.

The 1962 war with China left a lasting strategic scar. India expanded mountain formations and border infrastructure, but for decades the Chinese frontier remained relatively quiet compared with the Line of Control with Pakistan. New Delhi assumed that political agreements and confidence-building mechanisms would prevent local disputes from escalating into sustained military confrontation.

That assumption weakened through repeated standoffs at Depsang, Chumar and Doklam. It collapsed after the 2020 Galwan Valley clash, in which Indian and Chinese soldiers were killed during brutal hand-to-hand fighting. Both countries subsequently deployed large forces, artillery, armour, air defence and aircraft across the Himalayan theatre.

The border crisis transformed India’s planning. The People’s Liberation Army was no longer a distant long-term benchmark. It had become an immediate operational competitor capable of mobilising forces through modern roads, railways, airfields and logistics hubs on the Tibetan plateau.

Pakistan remained active throughout this shift. Its military preserved a force posture centred on India while expanding tactical nuclear capabilities, cruise missiles, drones and Chinese-supplied aircraft. Terrorist organisations operating from Pakistani territory continued to create the risk of rapid escalation.

India’s maritime environment changed at the same time. China established its first overseas military base in Djibouti, expanded access to ports across the Indian Ocean and deployed submarines and survey vessels into waters close to India. Chinese investment in Gwadar, Hambantota and other infrastructure generated concern about dual-use logistics and long-term naval access.

India therefore moved from a primarily continental security model toward a multi-domain framework. The Army still requires mass and readiness along two disputed borders, but the Navy must monitor an ocean spanning the Strait of Hormuz, the approaches to the Malacca Strait and the eastern coast of Africa. The Air Force must support both theatres while defending national airspace, strategic infrastructure and nuclear forces.

The Legacy of Import Dependence

India’s armed forces historically relied on foreign platforms from a diverse range of suppliers. The Soviet Union and later Russia supplied combat aircraft, tanks, submarines, helicopters, missiles and warships. France provided Mirage fighters, submarines and other systems. Israel became a major source of drones, radars, sensors, precision weapons and air-defence technology. The United States emerged as an important supplier of transport aircraft, maritime patrol aircraft, helicopters and unmanned systems.

This diversification reduced dependence on any single power but created logistical complexity. Different fleets require separate maintenance chains, weapons, training systems and software environments. Wartime availability can depend on foreign spare parts, export approvals and geopolitical conditions.

Russia’s war against Ukraine exposed the vulnerability of legacy supply chains. Russia remains a significant Indian defence partner and continues to support systems such as the Su-30MKI, T-90, S-400 and BrahMos. Yet Russian industry faces wartime demand, sanctions and production constraints. India cannot assume that every component will remain available during a simultaneous Asian crisis.

Western systems also create dependencies. The Tejas Mk1A relies on the American GE F404 engine. Delays in engine deliveries affected aircraft production. The next generation of Indian fighters will require access to advanced propulsion, materials, electronic warfare and manufacturing technologies that no foreign partner will transfer without limits.

Self-reliance does not mean producing every bolt domestically. It means ensuring that India can operate, repair, replenish and upgrade critical systems during sustained conflict without depending on the political permission of another state.

The Kargil Reform Process

The 1999 Kargil conflict exposed serious weaknesses in intelligence coordination, surveillance and joint operations. The Kargil Review Committee and subsequent Group of Ministers recommended changes to national-security management.

Several reforms followed, but the creation of a Chief of Defence Staff took two decades. General Bipin Rawat became India’s first CDS in 2020 and headed the newly established Department of Military Affairs. The position was designed to promote jointness, prioritise procurement and restructure the armed forces into integrated theatre commands.

General Rawat’s death in a helicopter crash in December 2021 interrupted the process. General Anil Chauhan became CDS in 2022 and continued work on joint structures. The services have since developed common logistics nodes, joint doctrines and plans for reorganised theatre commands.

Full implementation has remained slower than originally expected. The Army, Navy and Air Force differ over command boundaries, control of scarce air assets, force-generation responsibilities and the relationship between service chiefs and theatre commanders.

The debate is legitimate. India should not copy the American or Chinese command model mechanically. Its system must reflect geography, civil-military arrangements, nuclear command, available assets and the distinct demands of continental and maritime warfare. Yet delay also carries a cost. China already operates through theatre commands, including the Western Theatre Command responsible for the Indian frontier.

Aatmanirbhar Bharat and Industrial Reform

The Modi government made defence manufacturing a central component of Aatmanirbhar Bharat. The policy aims to reduce imports, retain expenditure inside India, create skilled employment, expand exports and build strategic autonomy.

The Defence Acquisition Procedure 2020 prioritised Indian design and production through procurement categories favouring domestic content. Positive Indigenisation Lists identified systems and components that would no longer be imported after specified dates. The SRIJAN portal connected domestic suppliers with requirements previously met from abroad.

The former Ordnance Factory Board was corporatized into seven defence public-sector companies in 2021. The reform sought to improve accountability, efficiency, cost control and responsiveness to users. Private firms including Tata Advanced Systems, Larsen and Toubro, Bharat Forge, Mahindra Defence and Adani Defence expanded their role alongside Hindustan Aeronautics Limited, Bharat Electronics Limited, Bharat Dynamics Limited and other public enterprises.

Defence production rose to approximately ₹1.78 lakh crore in financial year 2025–26. Exports reached a record ₹38,424 crore, up 62.66 percent from ₹23,622 crore in the previous year. Public-sector companies contributed ₹21,071 crore, while private firms contributed ₹17,353 crore. Indian defence products reached more than 80 countries.

The export increase demonstrates improving industrial capacity, but export value alone does not prove technological independence. India exports components, protective equipment, patrol vessels, artillery systems, radars, missiles and aerospace structures while continuing to import several high-end technologies. The next stage must move from manufacturing participation to design authority and control of critical intellectual property.

Current Situation

The 2026–27 Defence Budget

The ₹7.85 lakh crore allocation for 2026–27 is the largest assigned to any central government ministry. It accounts for 14.67 percent of total central expenditure and represents a major nominal increase from the previous year.

Approximately 27.95 percent of the defence allocation is assigned to capital expenditure. Revenue spending on operational sustenance accounts for another significant share, while pay, allowances and pensions together consume almost half the budget.

The capital allocation of more than ₹2.19 lakh crore is 21.84 percent higher than the 2025–26 budget estimate. Approximately ₹1.85 lakh crore is earmarked for acquisitions, allowing the services to finance aircraft, warships, submarines, drones, weapons and communications systems.

The domestic procurement reservation of ₹1.39 lakh crore creates a large guaranteed market for Indian manufacturers. Predictability matters because companies will not invest in production lines, research and skilled labour without confidence that orders will continue beyond a single contract.

DRDO’s ₹29,100.25 crore allocation supports laboratories, prototypes and advanced research. Around 25 percent of the defence research budget has been opened to industry, start-ups and academia. By March 2026, iDEX had engaged 676 start-ups, micro, small and medium enterprises and innovators, with 551 design-and-development contracts signed.

The budget is moving in the correct direction, but India’s economic scale must be considered. Defence expenditure remains below the levels that a simultaneous land, maritime, air, cyber and space competition with China could eventually demand. New Delhi must avoid measuring readiness only through year-on-year budget growth.

Operation Sindoor and the New Combat Environment

The April 2025 terrorist attack at Pahalgam killed 26 people and triggered another India–Pakistan crisis. India launched Operation Sindoor in May, striking what it described as terrorist infrastructure in Pakistan and Pakistan-administered territory. Pakistan retaliated, and the confrontation expanded into drone, missile, artillery and air operations before military action ceased on 10 May.

The episode offered a compressed view of modern South Asian conflict. Unmanned systems, electronic warfare, long-range precision weapons, air defence, satellite information and information operations became central. Both sides attempted to control escalation while demonstrating the capacity to strike beyond the immediate border.

Public claims concerning aircraft losses and the performance of individual systems were heavily contested. Strategic analysis should avoid turning wartime narratives into verified technical conclusions. The broader lesson is more durable: future India–Pakistan conflict will not resemble the massed land campaigns of 1965 or 1971.

India requires persistent surveillance, distributed air defence, protected command networks, accurate battle-damage assessment and the ability to launch calibrated strikes without exposing high-value aircraft unnecessarily. Cheap drones can reveal radar positions, saturate defences or impose disproportionate interceptor costs.

Operation Sindoor also demonstrated that Chinese-origin systems in Pakistani service are now operational factors rather than export-market abstractions. India must prepare to face Chinese sensors, aircraft, air-defence systems, weapons and data links through Pakistan even in a conflict where China is not a declared participant.

The Northern Border

India and China reached arrangements for disengagement at several friction points, but the broader military competition along the Line of Actual Control remains. The infrastructure and force levels created after 2020 will not disappear quickly.

India accelerated roads, tunnels, bridges, ammunition storage and advanced landing grounds. The Border Roads Organisation received ₹7,394 crore in capital funding for 2026–27. Projects such as the Atal Tunnel, Sela Tunnel and expanded frontier roads improve mobility, reinforcement and civilian connectivity.

Infrastructure narrows the historical advantage enjoyed by China on the Tibetan plateau, but roads alone cannot solve the Himalayan challenge. India requires resilient logistics, high-altitude artillery, helicopters, drones, air defence, secure communications and forces acclimatised for prolonged deployment.

The Zorawar light-tank programme emerged from the requirement for mobile armoured firepower at high altitude. Developed by DRDO with Larsen and Toubro, the platform is designed to be lighter and more deployable than India’s T-90 and Arjun tanks. Trials and protection requirements will determine its induction schedule.

The Army is also expanding surveillance and precision fires through drones, loitering munitions, Pinaka rockets, BrahMos missiles and modern artillery. The challenge is integrating these systems into a network capable of locating, prioritising and striking targets before they relocate.

Army Modernization

The Indian Army remains one of the world’s largest standing land forces. Its modernization must balance high-altitude confrontation with China, conventional deterrence against Pakistan, counterterrorism, internal security assistance and United Nations deployments.

Its artillery renewal has advanced after decades of delay. The M777 lightweight howitzer supports mountain operations. The K9 Vajra-T provides tracked firepower. The indigenous Dhanush and Advanced Towed Artillery Gun System expand domestic production. Pinaka provides increasingly long-range rocket artillery.

The strategic direction should be clear: artillery must evolve from an area-fire arm into a sensor-linked precision-strike network. Counter-battery radars, drones, satellite imagery and ground sensors should feed firing units through secure digital command systems.

Armoured-force modernization presents a different problem. The T-72 fleet is ageing, while the T-90 remains central to India’s mechanised force. The Arjun Mk1A adds an indigenous heavy platform but has faced weight, logistics and fleet-standardisation concerns. The Future Ready Combat Vehicle programme is intended to replace older tanks over time.

Infantry modernization includes the AK-203 rifle, SIG716 rifles, body armour, night-vision systems, communications and battlefield-management tools. Progress has been uneven because India must equip a very large force. Elite units can receive advanced equipment quickly, but modernization must reach ordinary battalions to alter battlefield performance.

The Army’s Agnipath recruitment model seeks to create a younger force and reduce long-term pension pressure by inducting personnel known as Agniveers for limited service, with a portion retained. The scheme has generated political debate over experience, cohesion, post-service employment and the appropriate balance between short-service and career personnel.

Financial logic cannot be the sole criterion. Military manpower policy must be judged by combat effectiveness, technical specialisation, unit cohesion and mobilisation capacity. Modern weapons often require years of training. Cyber, air-defence, intelligence, engineering and maintenance roles cannot be treated as interchangeable short-term labour.

Air-Power Modernization

The Indian Air Force faces the sharpest near-term capability gap. Its authorised strength has traditionally been described as 42 fighter squadrons, but actual strength has remained significantly lower. The retirement of ageing MiG-21 aircraft intensified pressure.

The fighter fleet includes Su-30MKI aircraft, Rafales, Mirage 2000s, MiG-29s, Jaguars and Tejas variants. Each contributes different capabilities, but fleet diversity complicates logistics and weapons integration.

The Su-30MKI will remain the numerical backbone. Planned upgrades are expected to improve radars, electronic warfare, weapons, mission computers and survivability. The aircraft’s range and payload make it valuable for air superiority, maritime operations and long-range strike.

The 36 Rafales acquired from France provide advanced sensors, electronic warfare and precision weapons. Their performance and commonality influenced the Navy’s decision to acquire 26 Rafale Marine aircraft for carrier operations under a 2025 agreement valued at approximately $7.4 billion.

The Tejas programme is strategically indispensable because India cannot sustain a large combat fleet through imported aircraft alone. The Tejas Mk1A includes an active electronically scanned array radar, improved electronic warfare and greater maintainability. The Air Force ordered 83 aircraft, and additional numbers are intended to replace retiring fighters.

Production delays exposed India’s dependence on imported GE F404 engines and the limited tolerance built into the supply chain. HAL must expand output, but engine availability, certification, software integration and supplier quality all influence delivery.

The Tejas Mk2 is intended to become a larger medium-weight fighter capable of replacing Mirage 2000, Jaguar and MiG-29 fleets. The Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft is planned as a fifth-generation stealth platform. In May 2025, Defence Minister Rajnath Singh approved an AMCA execution model allowing participation by public and private industry through competitive partnership.

The decision is strategically sound. India cannot allow a single company to carry the entire combat-aircraft ecosystem. Private firms need real design, integration and manufacturing responsibility rather than peripheral work packages.

AMCA timelines must remain realistic. Stealth shaping, internal weapons bays, advanced flight controls, sensor fusion, low-observable materials and propulsion integration make fifth-generation aircraft exceptionally difficult. The first version may rely on a foreign engine before a more powerful indigenous or jointly developed engine becomes available.

India must avoid waiting for a perfect future platform while current squadron strength declines. The roadmap needs three parallel tracks:

  • Accelerated Tejas Mk1A production and Su-30MKI upgrades.
  • Timely Tejas Mk2 development and a bridging multirole acquisition if required.
  • Protected long-term funding for AMCA, engines and unmanned combat aircraft.

Air power also depends on force multipliers. India needs more airborne early-warning aircraft, aerial refuellers, electronic-intelligence systems and long-range stand-off weapons. Fighter numbers alone do not determine air superiority.

Air and Missile Defence

India faces threats ranging from small drones and cruise missiles to ballistic missiles and combat aircraft. No single system can defend such a spectrum.

The S-400 provides long-range engagement capacity and contributes to area defence against aircraft and selected missile threats. Indigenous Akash systems cover shorter ranges, while the Medium Range Surface-to-Air Missile developed with Israel adds another layer.

India’s ballistic-missile defence programme and Project Kusha are intended to strengthen protection against high-altitude and long-range threats. The Integrated Air Command and Control System connects sensors and weapons across the country.

The lesson from Ukraine, the Red Sea and the Iran–Israel wars is that interceptor economics matter. An advanced missile should not be used against every low-cost drone. India requires guns, electronic warfare, directed-energy research, low-cost interceptors and mobile counter-drone systems beneath its more expensive air-defence layers.

Air bases, ammunition depots, nuclear command facilities, ports, data centres, refineries and political centres cannot all receive equal protection. Strategic prioritisation, dispersal, hardened shelters, deception and rapid repair are essential.

Naval Modernization and the Indian Ocean

The Indian Navy is the service through which India can exert influence beyond its immediate borders. The Indian Ocean carries energy supplies, container traffic and undersea communications connecting the Middle East, Africa, Europe and Asia. India’s geography gives it a central position astride these routes.

The Navy operates the aircraft carriers INS Vikramaditya and INS Vikrant. Vikrant’s indigenous construction was a major industrial achievement, demonstrating India’s ability to design and build a complex capital ship.

The Rafale Marine acquisition will provide a modern carrier fighter while India develops the Twin Engine Deck Based Fighter. Carrier aviation gives India mobile air power, surveillance and fleet defence. Yet carriers are expensive and vulnerable without escorts, submarines, airborne early warning and robust logistics.

India’s surface fleet is being renewed through Visakhapatnam-class destroyers, Nilgiri-class frigates, Kamorta-class anti-submarine corvettes and other indigenous vessels. Indian shipyards have developed meaningful design and construction capability, with progressively higher domestic content.

The submarine arm remains a critical concern. Six Kalvari-class submarines built under Project 75 improved capability, but older Kilo and Shishumar-class boats face ageing pressures. Project 75(I), intended to acquire six conventional submarines with air-independent propulsion and substantial domestic participation, has been delayed by complex requirements and negotiations.

China’s expanding submarine fleet makes delay increasingly expensive. India needs conventional submarines for operations in the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal, nuclear attack submarines for endurance and escort missions, and ballistic-missile submarines for strategic deterrence.

The government approved progress toward indigenous nuclear-powered attack submarines, a programme that will require sustained investment in reactor design, quieting, sensors and weapons. These boats would provide high endurance for monitoring Chinese deployments and protecting carrier and deterrent forces.

The nuclear-powered ballistic-missile submarines INS Arihant and INS Arighaat strengthen India’s sea-based deterrent. Survivable submarine-launched missiles reduce the risk that an adversary could neutralise India’s nuclear forces in a first strike.

Maritime-domain awareness is expanding through P-8I aircraft, MH-60R helicopters, satellites, coastal radars, information-sharing agreements and the planned MQ-9B SeaGuardian fleet. The Information Fusion Centre–Indian Ocean Region supports cooperation with partner states.

The Andaman and Nicobar Command has exceptional strategic value. The islands sit near the western approaches to the Malacca Strait. Airfields, surveillance systems, missiles and logistics infrastructure there can monitor traffic between the Pacific and Indian oceans.

India should strengthen the islands without assuming that geography creates an automatic blockade capability. Sustained operations would require hardened bases, fuel, air defence, submarines, aircraft and protection against long-range Chinese missiles.

Drones, Autonomy and Electronic Warfare

Unmanned systems have moved from specialised tools to mass battlefield assets. Ukraine demonstrated the value of commercial quadcopters, first-person-view attack drones, maritime drones and long-range one-way systems. Operation Sindoor reinforced the relevance of drones and counter-drone defences in South Asia.

India’s acquisition of 31 MQ-9B aircraft provides long-endurance surveillance and precision-strike capacity across land and maritime theatres. The fleet is divided among the three services and improves coverage of the Indian Ocean and frontier regions.

Imported high-end drones should complement, not displace, indigenous development. India needs expendable systems that can be produced in thousands, not merely exquisite platforms available in small numbers. Swarming drones, loitering munitions, autonomous underwater vehicles and collaborative combat aircraft will shape future force design.

Electronic warfare is equally important. Drones depend on communications, navigation and data links that can be jammed or deceived. Forces must operate under degraded satellite navigation and contested electromagnetic conditions.

The modernization roadmap should treat software, artificial intelligence and electronic warfare as weapons rather than support services. Procurement systems built around physical platforms are poorly suited to capabilities that require constant updates.

Space, Cyber and Information Warfare

India’s military relies increasingly on satellites for communication, navigation, surveillance, missile warning and maritime awareness. The Defence Space Agency and Defence Cyber Agency were established to coordinate activity beyond traditional service boundaries.

Mission Shakti in 2019 demonstrated an anti-satellite capability. The test signalled that India could threaten space assets if deterrence failed. Yet destructive anti-satellite weapons create debris and may be less useful than reversible electronic or cyber effects.

China possesses a broad counter-space programme including direct-ascent missiles, jamming, cyber capabilities and rendezvous systems. Pakistan benefits from Chinese satellite services. India must assume that its military satellites will be targeted during major conflict.

Resilience requires proliferated satellites, rapid launch, protected communications, ground-station redundancy and the ability to operate when space support is degraded. Private Indian space companies can contribute launch systems, imagery, communications and satellite manufacturing.

Cyber warfare will target power grids, railways, financial systems, telecommunications and military networks. Defence cannot be isolated from national infrastructure. Cooperation among the armed forces, intelligence agencies, civilian ministries and private operators is essential.

Information warfare also shapes crisis control. False claims, manipulated imagery and selective disclosure can compress political decision time. India needs credible communication, rapid declassification procedures and disciplined public messaging. Propaganda should not replace accurate battle-damage assessment.

Nuclear Modernization

India’s declared nuclear doctrine rests on credible minimum deterrence and no first use, with massive retaliation promised following a nuclear attack. The doctrine also reserves a response option to major chemical or biological attack.

China and Pakistan create different deterrence problems. China possesses a much larger and expanding nuclear arsenal with intercontinental systems, ballistic-missile submarines and sophisticated command networks. Pakistan maintains a smaller arsenal oriented primarily toward India and includes short-range systems intended to deter conventional operations.

India is modernizing land, air and sea-based nuclear forces. The Agni missile family provides ranges covering regional and wider strategic targets. The 2024 Mission Divyastra test demonstrated multiple independently targetable re-entry vehicle technology on the Agni-V platform.

MIRVs can strengthen penetration and complicate missile defence, but they also create pressure on command, surveillance and stockpile management. India must maintain strict civilian control, secure communications and reliable early warning.

The sea-based deterrent requires more than submarines and missiles. It needs quiet patrol areas, secure communication with national leadership, trained crews and protection from enemy anti-submarine warfare. As Chinese naval activity expands in the Indian Ocean, preserving SSBN survivability will become more demanding.

India should preserve doctrinal clarity while modernizing delivery systems. Ambiguity can support deterrence in some contexts, but uncontrolled speculation about abandoning no first use may create instability without generating additional capability.

Strategic Analysis

The Two-Front Problem

A simultaneous full-scale war with China and Pakistan remains unlikely, but coordinated coercion is plausible. Pakistan could increase pressure along the Line of Control or activate terrorist networks during an India–China crisis. China could provide intelligence, equipment and diplomatic support without formally entering a Pakistan-led confrontation.

India should therefore plan for a primary front and an opportunistic secondary front rather than assuming two identical conventional wars. The required force posture emphasises mobility, reserves, air power, long-range fires and joint intelligence.

China is the pacing challenge because it possesses the greater economic, technological and military capacity. Pakistan remains the more frequent trigger because terrorism and short-warning crises create pressure for rapid retaliation.

This combination is dangerous. India must maintain sufficient force against Pakistan without allowing the western front to absorb resources required for long-term competition with China.

Joint Theatre Commands

Theatre commands should integrate Army, Navy and Air Force assets under commanders responsible for defined operational areas. Potential structures have included northern, western and maritime commands, supported by functional organisations for air defence, logistics, cyber and space.

The Air Force has legitimate concerns about fragmenting scarce aircraft among geographic commands. Air power is inherently flexible and may need to shift rapidly between fronts. The solution is not to preserve service silos but to design a joint allocation system that retains central flexibility while giving theatre commanders access to required effects.

Theatre reform must separate force generation from force employment. Service headquarters should recruit, train, equip and sustain forces. Theatre commanders should plan and conduct operations using assigned capabilities.

India also needs an integrated planning process connecting political objectives with military campaigns. Jointness is not achieved by changing reporting lines alone. Common data standards, communications, logistics and doctrine matter more than organisational diagrams.

The Procurement Trap

Indian defence procurement has often produced long competitions, changing requirements, legal disputes and small orders. By the time a system is contracted, technology may have evolved and costs may have increased.

The armed forces sometimes seek the best available global specifications while domestic industry requires stable, achievable requirements. Repeated changes create delay and discourage investment. Conversely, accepting immature systems solely because they are indigenous can reduce operational readiness.

A better model would use spiral development. The services should induct viable systems in blocks, provide feedback and fund upgrades. This approach builds production capacity while technology matures.

India must also order at meaningful scale. Production lines become efficient only when manufacturers can spread investment across sustained demand. Small purchases increase unit costs and make exports difficult.

The Aero-Engine Constraint

Combat-aircraft propulsion is India’s most serious technological dependency. The Kaveri programme did not produce an engine suitable for the original Tejas requirement, though its technologies continue to support other applications.

Foreign partnership is necessary, but co-production should not be confused with design sovereignty. India needs knowledge of hot-section materials, single-crystal blades, coatings, combustion, testing and digital engine control.

Engine development requires decades of sustained funding and tolerance for failure. The government should treat it as national infrastructure comparable to the nuclear and space programmes. Without propulsion autonomy, every future fighter, unmanned combat aircraft and cruise missile programme remains exposed.

War Reserves and Industrial Mobilisation

Modern conflict consumes missiles, shells, drones and spare parts at rates far above peacetime planning. India cannot assume that foreign suppliers will replenish stocks during a crisis involving China.

War-wastage reserves should be connected to surge-production contracts. Companies need pre-negotiated arrangements for expanding output, access to materials and protected electricity and transport.

Critical production should be geographically distributed. Concentrated factories are vulnerable to missile or cyberattack. Secure data, alternative suppliers and repair capacity matter as much as headline manufacturing figures.
