India’s pharmaceutical, automotive, electronics and software sectors provide a broad industrial foundation. Defence planners must learn how to mobilise civilian capacity without waiting for war.

Quality, Accountability and User Confidence

Self-reliance will fail if the armed forces view indigenous equipment as politically protected from criticism. Soldiers, sailors and aircrew must be able to report defects honestly. Manufacturers must be accountable for delivery, maintenance and reliability.

At the same time, the services must accept responsibility for supporting domestic systems through early difficulties. No major military-industrial power achieved autonomy by importing whenever local development encountered setbacks.

The correct relationship is demanding partnership: realistic specifications, transparent trials, firm schedules, assured orders and continuous improvement.

Global Impact

China and the Indo-Pacific Balance

India’s modernization forces China to allocate attention and resources to its western frontier and the Indian Ocean. A capable India complicates Beijing’s ability to concentrate exclusively on Taiwan, the South China Sea and the western Pacific.

India does not seek a formal alliance against China. Its strategic autonomy remains central. Yet cooperation through the QUAD with the United States, Japan and Australia improves maritime awareness, logistics, exercises and diplomatic coordination.

AUKUS affects India indirectly by strengthening allied undersea and technological capacity in the Indo-Pacific. New Delhi will not join the pact, but it can benefit from a regional balance that limits unilateral Chinese dominance.

Global Chanakya’s China, Xi Jinping, Taiwan, South China Sea, QUAD and AUKUS pages provide the wider strategic environment in which India’s military choices must be understood.

Pakistan

Indian modernization will push Pakistan toward deeper reliance on China, nuclear deterrence, drones, missiles and asymmetric warfare. Islamabad cannot match India platform for platform without imposing severe economic costs.

Pakistan will seek capabilities that bypass Indian conventional strength. These include tactical nuclear weapons, long-range precision missiles, submarines, cyber operations and support for deniable armed groups.

India must avoid creating a strategy in which every terrorist attack automatically produces an escalatory sequence controlled by the adversary. Intelligence, covert action, financial pressure, border security and calibrated military force should remain part of a wider toolkit.

Russia

Russia will remain a significant partner because of legacy fleets, BrahMos cooperation, nuclear-submarine experience and strategic history. India is unlikely to abandon Russian systems abruptly.

New Delhi will nevertheless diversify. The war in Ukraine and Russia’s growing relationship with China reduce the wisdom of excessive dependence. India’s objective should be to preserve useful cooperation while acquiring source access, localisation and alternative supply chains.

Global Chanakya’s Russia and Vladimir Putin intelligence pages should be linked to analysis of India’s procurement diversification and the future of the Russia–India strategic relationship.

The United States

India–U.S. defence relations have expanded through the LEMOA logistics agreement, COMCASA communications framework and BECA geospatial accord. India operates American-origin P-8I aircraft, C-17 and C-130J transports, Apache helicopters, Chinooks and MH-60R naval helicopters, with MQ-9B aircraft to follow.

Cooperation provides access to advanced systems, exercises and intelligence. It also creates exposure to American export controls and political conditions. India will resist alliance obligations and preserve independent policy toward Russia, Iran and other partners.

Washington views India as a critical balancing power in the Indo-Pacific. New Delhi views the United States as an essential technology and security partner but not a treaty guarantor.

France and Israel

France is one of India’s most trusted defence partners. Cooperation spans Rafale aircraft, Scorpene submarines, space, maritime security and potential engine technology. France’s Indo-Pacific territories and preference for strategic autonomy align with Indian thinking.

Israel provides drones, radars, missiles, electronic warfare and agricultural and technological cooperation. The relationship is operationally valuable because Israeli companies have often adapted systems quickly to Indian requirements.

India will preserve these partnerships while pressing for greater local production and technology access.

Defence Exports and Global South Diplomacy

The BrahMos export to the Philippines marked a major breakthrough. The system gives Manila a coastal anti-ship capability relevant to pressure in the South China Sea. India has also exported artillery, patrol platforms, radars, protective equipment and components.

Defence exports strengthen diplomacy when they include training, maintenance and long-term support. They can deepen India’s relationships across Southeast Asia, Africa, the Middle East and Latin America.

Export success will depend on reliability, financing, after-sales service and production capacity. India cannot build credibility if domestic orders consume all available output or deliveries are delayed.

Risk Assessment

Risk One: Capability Arrives Too Late

China’s military modernization is already mature in several domains. Delays to fighters, submarines, engines and theatre commands could leave India with a dangerous capability gap during the late 2020s.

Probability: High.

Impact: Very high.

Risk Two: Budget Growth Without Combat Power

Higher allocations may be absorbed by pensions, salaries, inflation and delayed contracts. Expenditure can rise without producing proportional readiness.

Probability: Medium to high.

Impact: High.

Risk Three: Two-Front Coercion

China and Pakistan may coordinate political, intelligence or military pressure during a crisis without launching simultaneous full-scale wars.

Probability: Medium.

Impact: Very high.

Risk Four: Foreign Technology Denial

Sanctions, export controls, war or supply-chain disruption could affect engines, electronics, spares and specialised materials.

Probability: Medium.

Impact: High.

Risk Five: Drone Saturation

Low-cost drones could overwhelm expensive air-defence systems and expose command posts, artillery and logistics.

Probability: High.

Impact: High.

Risk Six: Organisational Resistance

Service competition may dilute theatre-command reform and preserve separate procurement, communications and logistics structures.

Probability: Medium to high.

Impact: High.

Risk Seven: Industrial Concentration

Excessive dependence on a small number of public or private companies could create bottlenecks and reduce competitive pressure.

Probability: Medium.

Impact: Medium to high.

Risk Eight: Nuclear Escalation

A conventional India–Pakistan conflict could cross nuclear thresholds through misperception, attacks on dual-use systems or fear of pre-emption.

Probability: Low to medium.

Impact: Extreme.

Future Scenarios

Scenario Analysis One: Integrated Indigenous Power by 2035

India operationalises theatre commands, accelerates Tejas production, fields Tejas Mk2 and begins AMCA induction. The Navy expands submarine numbers and commissions indigenous nuclear attack submarines. Drone and space networks connect forces across both fronts.

Domestic companies control key sensors, weapons, software and maintenance. Defence exports grow alongside wartime production capacity. India becomes capable of denying China easy military gains while preserving escalation dominance against Pakistan.

Scenario Analysis Two: Selective Modernization

India inducts advanced platforms but in insufficient numbers. Elite formations become highly capable while much of the force remains dependent on ageing equipment and fragmented networks.

The Navy and missile forces progress, but fighter strength and submarine availability remain below requirements. India can manage limited crises but faces strain during prolonged two-front pressure.

This is the most plausible trajectory without deeper procurement and organisational reform.

Scenario Analysis Three: Emergency Import Cycle

Delays create an urgent capability gap. India launches large foreign purchases of fighters, drones, submarines and air-defence systems. Readiness improves quickly, but domestic programmes lose orders and strategic dependence persists.

This scenario may be operationally necessary in selected areas, but repeated emergency imports would undermine the industrial roadmap.

Scenario Analysis Four: Himalayan Crisis

A new Line of Actual Control confrontation expands beyond local patrol clashes. Both sides employ drones, electronic warfare, artillery and cyber operations. Pakistan increases pressure along the western front.

India’s infrastructure and precision fires perform better than in 2020, but airlift, ammunition and integrated command become decisive. The crisis accelerates theatre-command reform and domestic production.

Scenario Analysis Five: Indian Ocean Competition

Chinese naval deployments become permanent, supported by logistics access across the region. India responds with submarines, maritime aircraft, long-range missiles and partnerships through the QUAD and Indian Ocean states.

The Andaman and Nicobar Islands become a major surveillance and denial hub. Undersea competition emerges as the central test of Indian maritime power.

Intelligence Forecast

India’s defence budget will remain on an upward trajectory, with capital acquisition and domestic procurement receiving political priority. Fiscal pressure from pensions and personnel costs will continue driving manpower reform.

Theatre commands are likely to progress through phased implementation rather than a single dramatic reorganisation. Joint logistics, communications and planning will mature before every command relationship is settled.

The Air Force will remain the most stressed service through the late 2020s. Tejas Mk1A production, engine deliveries and Su-30MKI upgrades will be watched as indicators of whether the squadron decline can be stabilised.

AMCA will remain protected as a national strategic programme, but operational induction is unlikely to solve immediate fighter shortages. Engine development will become a defining test of India’s technological autonomy.

The Navy will continue receiving the largest proportional benefits from indigenous design and shipbuilding. Submarine numbers, rather than surface-ship launches alone, will determine the credibility of maritime modernization.

India will accelerate procurement of drones, loitering munitions, electronic warfare and counter-unmanned systems after lessons from Operation Sindoor and other contemporary conflicts.

Long-range precision fires will expand across the services. BrahMos variants, Pinaka rockets, Pralay missiles and air-launched weapons will support a doctrine of calibrated conventional response.

Defence cooperation with the United States, France and Israel will deepen, while Russian-origin fleets will remain operationally significant. India will pursue diversification without formal alliance dependence.

Defence exports will continue growing, though the extraordinary 2025–26 rate may not repeat every year. Missiles, artillery, radars, naval platforms and aerospace components offer the strongest prospects.

The nuclear submarine programme will receive sustained funding because sea-based deterrence and Chinese naval activity converge as strategic priorities.

China will remain the principal long-term benchmark. Pakistan will remain the most likely source of sudden military crisis. India’s roadmap will be judged by whether it can prepare for one without becoming vulnerable to the other.

Final Strategic Takeaway

India is not modernizing for prestige. It is modernizing because the military balance around it is becoming less forgiving.

China possesses greater industrial scale, a larger defence budget and an increasingly mature system of joint warfare. Pakistan combines nuclear weapons, Chinese technology and asymmetric strategy. The Indian Ocean is no longer protected by distance. Space, cyber networks and civilian infrastructure have become part of the battlefield.

New Delhi has responded with higher expenditure, indigenous production, missile development, naval expansion and closer partnerships. The direction is credible. The pace remains uneven.

The strongest programmes share common features: stable political support, clear operational demand, sustained orders and close cooperation among users, scientists and manufacturers. India’s missile and naval achievements show what is possible. Delays in fighters, engines and submarines show what happens when responsibility is fragmented and timelines slip.

A successful roadmap must resist two temptations. The first is import dependence disguised as rapid modernization. The second is self-reliance reduced to slogans while the armed forces wait for usable capability.

India requires a disciplined middle path: indigenous design where sovereignty is essential, foreign partnership where technology gaps are real, and emergency imports only where delay creates unacceptable operational risk.

By 2035, success should be measured through outcomes. The Air Force should possess sufficient modern squadrons and force multipliers. The Army should field networked formations with long-range precision fires and resilient logistics. The Navy should maintain credible submarine, carrier and maritime-surveillance forces. All three services should operate through shared command systems supported by protected space and cyber infrastructure.

Industry should be able to produce ammunition, missiles, drones, sensors and spare parts at wartime rates. Nuclear forces should remain survivable, secure and under unquestioned civilian control. India’s external partnerships should multiply national power without limiting strategic autonomy.

The ₹7.85 lakh crore defence allocation creates opportunity, not assurance. Money becomes deterrence only when it produces trained personnel, available equipment, stocked magazines, secure networks and commanders who can integrate them under pressure.

India’s defence modernization will succeed when an adversary no longer sees a gap between what New Delhi announces, what Indian industry promises and what the armed forces can deploy. That is the standard for a country seeking to remain sovereign in a two-front, multi-domain and increasingly unforgiving strategic era.

title: China's Naval Expansion: The Fleet That Is Reshaping the Pacific
content:
China's Naval Expansion: The Fleet That Is Reshaping the Pacific

In November 2025, President Xi Jinping stood on the deck of China's newest aircraft carrier, the Fujian, at the Sanya naval base on Hainan Island as the ship was formally commissioned into the People's Liberation Army Navy. The symbolism was deliberate and unmistakable. The Fujian — the world's first catapult-equipped carrier outside the United States — is the third aircraft carrier China has commissioned in thirteen years. Xi's personal attendance at the ceremony was a statement: this is not a procurement milestone, it is a declaration of national strategic ambition.

The United States Navy has spent eight decades as the uncontested dominant force in the Pacific. What is happening in China's shipyards right now — across carriers, destroyers, submarines, and amphibious assault ships simultaneously — represents the most serious challenge to that dominance since Japan's naval rearmament in the 1930s. The PLAN launched and commissioned at least twenty-one major combatants in 2025 alone, totaling a quarter-million tons of new warships in a single year. The submarine force is transitioning from conventionally powered to nuclear-dominated ahead of schedule. Nine aircraft carriers are planned by 2035. A presumed nuclear-powered carrier, designated Type 004, is under construction at Dalian. And the United States, watching all of this with increasing alarm, unveiled a May 2026 shipbuilding plan targeting a fleet of over 450 vessels specifically to counter what its own defense planners describe as the coming "decade of maximum danger" in the Pacific.

This is the story of the most consequential naval expansion of the twenty-first century — and why it matters for every country that depends on Pacific maritime order.

Executive Summary

The People's Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) has undergone the most rapid and comprehensive naval modernization of any power since the post-World War II American fleet demobilization reversed itself during the Cold War buildup. From a coastal defense force of aging Soviet-derived vessels in the early 2000s, the PLAN has transformed into the world's largest navy by hull count — exceeding 370 warships and submarines — including three operational aircraft carriers, ten Type 055 guided-missile cruisers, the world's largest fleet of modern frigates and destroyers, and a submarine force in the midst of a structural transition toward nuclear-powered predominance.

China's naval strategy has evolved through a clearly defined progression, from "near seas defense" covering the Yellow Sea, East China Sea, and South China Sea to an operational doctrine now explicitly described as "Near Seas Defense, Far Seas Protection" — combining robust defensive capability in its immediate maritime environment with a growing capacity to conduct sustained naval operations far beyond the First and Second Island Chains, toward the Indian Ocean, the western Pacific, and eventually global blue-water presence. The 7 percent increase in PLA defense spending announced at the March 2026 National People's Congress — the fifth consecutive annual increase and an acceleration from four preceding years of 6 percent growth — ensures this trajectory will continue at pace through the remainder of the decade.

The strategic logic driving this expansion operates on three distinct levels simultaneously: deterring US military intervention in a Taiwan contingency through anti-access/area-denial (A2/AD) capability sufficient to hold carrier strike groups at risk; projecting power throughout the broader Indo-Pacific to protect China's economic arteries and overseas interests; and, at the longest time horizon, displacing the United States as the dominant maritime power in Asia — an objective Xi Jinping has characterized as essential to the "great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation" by 2049.

Background: From Coastal Defense to Blue-Water Ambition

Understanding the scale and speed of China's naval transformation requires understanding what it replaced. As recently as the late 1990s, the PLAN was, by the assessment of virtually every external naval analysis, a coastal and near-coastal defense force built around second-generation Soviet designs, aging Romeo-class submarines, and surface combatants with limited blue-water endurance. The 1996 Taiwan Strait Crisis — when the United States deployed two carrier battle groups toward Taiwan in response to Chinese missile tests, and the PLAN could do essentially nothing to contest them — constituted a humiliation that Beijing's leadership absorbed as a foundational strategic lesson: naval power determines the credible limits of sovereignty in the modern era, and China had none in the waters that mattered most.

The response was systematic and patient. China's defense budget began growing at double-digit rates through the 2000s, with naval modernization receiving sustained prioritization. The acquisition of Varyag — an incomplete Soviet carrier hull purchased from Ukraine ostensibly for conversion into a floating casino — became the Liaoning, commissioned in 2012, giving the PLAN its first aircraft carrier. From that initial, Soviet-heritage platform, China proceeded with a domestic carrier development program of remarkable pace: Shandong commissioned in 2019, Fujian in November 2025, with a probable fourth carrier under construction. The speed of this progression — three carriers in thirteen years, beginning from a standing start with no previous carrier tradition — is without modern parallel.

Simultaneously, China's shipbuilding industrial capacity became the critical enabler that no Western assessment should underestimate. China now builds more commercial shipping tonnage annually than the rest of the world combined, and that industrial infrastructure — skilled labor, yard capacity, steel production, electronics manufacturing — translates directly into naval shipbuilding capability. When analysts observe that China commissioned twenty-one major combatants in 2025 alone, they should understand that this output reflects an industrial scale that no Western nation currently approaches in naval construction, with the partial exception of the United States when it mobilizes its full production capacity, which it historically does only in wartime.

Current Situation

The Carrier Fleet: Entering a Three-Carrier Era With More on the Way

The November 5, 2025, commissioning of the Fujian (Type 003) at Sanya's Yulin naval base, with Xi Jinping personally presiding, formally established China as the world's second-largest carrier operator. Three carriers in service, but the more consequential story lies in what the Fujian represents technologically and what comes next.

The Fujian is the world's first carrier outside the United States to be equipped with electromagnetic catapult launch systems (EMALS). This is not an incremental upgrade — it is a transformation of naval aviation capability. EMALS allows aircraft to launch at heavier weights and with less structural stress than steam catapults or ski-jump ramps, meaning the Fujian can deploy the J-35 stealth fighter in carrier configuration (a substantially heavier aircraft than the J-15 currently flying from the earlier carriers), the KJ-600 airborne early warning and control aircraft for organic fleet air battle management, and potentially unmanned combat aerial vehicles given the Type 076 amphibious assault ship's demonstrated UCAV integration. The combination of EMALS and stealth carrier aviation makes Fujian genuinely comparable, in individual aircraft capability if not yet in air wing experience and operational integration, to the US Ford-class carrier concept.

Since commissioning, Fujian has conducted extensive shakedown operations including a transit from the South China Sea to Yuchi naval base in the Northern Theater Command's Yellow Sea area — operationally significant because it demonstrated multi-theater deployment flexibility — arriving there in December 2025 alongside the Liaoning. Meanwhile, satellite imagery analysis has confirmed what naval watchers have long speculated: a new hull under construction at Dalian shipyard, designated by analysts as Type 004, features dimensions, structural characteristics, and construction pace that point unmistakably toward a nuclear-powered aircraft carrier. Nuclear propulsion would eliminate the refueling constraints that limit conventionally powered carriers and dramatically extend the operational range and endurance of China's carrier strike group capability. The Pentagon's December 2025 annual China military power report explicitly confirmed China plans nine aircraft carriers by 2035, establishing what would be a global naval aviation footprint that challenges — though does not yet equal — the eleven-carrier US fleet.

The Submarine Revolution: Nuclear Transition Ahead of Schedule

If the carrier expansion represents China's most visible naval statement, the submarine force's nuclear transition may be the more strategically significant development. On March 1, 2026, Rear Admiral Michael Brookes, commander of the Office of Naval Intelligence, testified before the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission that China's submarine force is projected to reach approximately 70 submarines by 2027 — through the addition of six nuclear-powered guided-missile submarines, three smaller-class nuclear-powered attack submarines, and two ballistic missile submarines, while simultaneously retiring older vessels. By 2035, that fleet is projected to reach approximately 80 submarines, with up to half nuclear-powered, representing what Brookes characterized as "a significant strategic shift" from China's previous prioritization of diesel-electric construction.

The key new classes driving this transformation deserve individual attention:

  • Type 093B Shang III SSGN: The PLAN's current most capable operational attack submarine, according to Brookes' direct testimony. Equipped with pump-jet propulsors for reduced acoustic signature — a significant acoustic quieting improvement over earlier Chinese submarines — and a vertical launch system capable of firing anti-ship and land-attack cruise missiles including the YJ-20 hypersonic anti-ship missile tested in December 2025. At least six of eight expected Shang III hulls have been launched since 2022, with more entering service. Brookes described both the Type 093B and the Type 095 as "formidable, incorporating advanced technologies that challenge the U.S. Navy's longstanding undersea dominance."
  • Type 095 SSGN: A newly revealed class of nuclear-powered guided-missile attack submarine incorporating advanced technologies that ONI assesses represents "significant advances in capabilities, posing a multi-faceted threat to the United States and its interests in the Indo-Pacific." The Type 095's specifications remain significantly classified, but its appearance alongside the Type 093B in Brookes' testimony underscores how rapidly China is fielding new nuclear submarine capability.
  • Type 094A Jin-class SSBN: Six Jin-class ballistic missile submarines currently in service represent China's first credible sea-based nuclear deterrent, each carrying up to 12 JL-2 or JL-3 submarine-launched ballistic missiles. The JL-3's range, estimated at approximately 10,000 kilometers, enables patrols from home waters to strike continental US targets, providing genuine survivable second-strike capability that China did not possess as recently as a decade ago.
  • Type 096 SSBN: The next-generation ballistic missile submarine expected to begin construction in the near term, armed with a longer-range successor SLBM and designed to operate concurrently with the Jin class through the 2030s and 2040s. The Type 096 represents China's transition to a genuinely sophisticated sea-based nuclear deterrent triad leg comparable in concept, if not yet in scale, to the US Ohio-class SSBN force.
  • Type 041 Zhou-class: A smaller-class nuclear-powered attack submarine configured for regional missions, alongside the more intriguing Type 041 experimental variant incorporating air-independent propulsion with a micro-nuclear reactor — a hybrid propulsion approach representing genuine technological innovation without parallel in other navies.

ONI's assessment that by the early 2040s the PLAN could transition to an all-nuclear submarine force — and that by then the submarine force "may credibly challenge US regional maritime dominance, complicating crisis response, power projection and allied defense" — represents perhaps the most significant long-term assessment in the entire China military power debate. US undersea dominance has been the most reliable and least-questioned asymmetric advantage Washington holds over Beijing; the current trajectory suggests that advantage, while substantial today, is narrowing on a clearly visible timeline.

The Surface Combatant Fleet: Quantity Meeting Quality

Surface fleet modernization has proceeded on a scale that makes the carrier program look almost modest by comparison. The PLAN now fields more major surface combatants than any other navy in the world, and the quality gap with Western navies has closed dramatically from the position of a decade ago.

The Type 055 Renhai-class guided-missile destroyer — which the US Navy classifies internally as a cruiser given its 13,000-ton displacement and 112-cell vertical launch system, comparable in role and lethality to the US Ticonderoga-class cruiser — now stands at ten commissioned vessels, with four more under construction at two shipyards. Each Fleet command now includes Type 055s following the commissioning of the ninth and tenth vessels (Dongguan and Anqing) in May 2025 and their assignment to the East Sea Fleet, making the PLAN's most capable and lethal surface combatants available in all three operational theaters simultaneously. The Type 055's combat capability advanced further in December 2025 when the Wuxi conducted the first confirmed launch of a YJ-20 hypersonic anti-ship missile from a surface ship — integrating hypersonic strike capability directly into the surface fleet for the first time.

The Type 052D Luyang III destroyer production line — 7,500-ton guided-missile destroyers that represent a significant capability step above comparable contemporaries from many Western navies — now approaches forty total hulls commissioned, with additional units under construction. The Type 052DM, the latest variant, saw eight commissioned in 2025 alone, with a ninth in early 2026. The Type 054B frigate, commissioned in 2025 as the first new-generation stealth frigate, represents the beginning of the next frigate modernization wave, with the existing Type 054A family spanning more than forty hulls across four variants.

Amphibious Power: The Taiwan-Specific Capability

No dimension of PLAN expansion carries more direct Taiwan contingency relevance than the amphibious assault fleet, and here too the 2025-2026 period has produced significant milestones. The fourth Type 075 Hainan-class large deck amphibious assault ship, Hubei, was commissioned in August 2025. The Type 075 at 35,000 tons carries a large complement of helicopters and marine infantry, designed specifically for the kind of combined arms amphibious operation that a Taiwan scenario would require at scale.

More significant still is the Type 076 Sichuan, which began sea trials on November 14, 2025 — a vessel Naval News describes as a "large catapult-equipped amphibious assault carrier" of over 40,000 tons displacement, featuring not just helicopter operations but electromagnetic catapult launch capability for both manned aircraft and unmanned combat aerial vehicles. Six apparent UCAV mockups were observed aboard during sea trials. The Type 076 effectively creates a hybrid carrier-amphibious assault ship that can project both air power and marine infantry, a capability with no direct equivalent in any current US amphibious platform and one specifically designed to support the kind of combined amphibious and air operations that a forcible Taiwan Strait crossing would demand. Commissioning is projected for early 2027 given the complexity of the new systems involved.

Alongside the big-deck amphibious platforms, the PLAN has developed and deployed the Shuiqiao-class landing platform utility barge — a relocatable pier system that can transfer heavy equipment from ship to shore without established port facilities, directly addressing one of the fundamental logistical challenges of any amphibious operation against a defended coastline. The Pentagon's 2025 China military power report explicitly cited this development as evidence that China is testing and refining the essential components of a Taiwan amphibious operation in granular operational detail.

The Maritime Gray Zone: Coast Guard and Maritime Militia

The PLAN's conventional warship expansion operates alongside, and is often directly enabled by, China's Coast Guard — assessed by the US Department of Defense as the largest maritime law enforcement fleet in the world — and the Maritime Militia, a force of fishing vessels, survey ships, and other civilian-flagged assets that carry out Beijing's maritime coercion policy under a veneer of non-military activity. In the South China Sea, at the Senkaku Islands, and across disputed territorial waters, it is these gray zone forces that conduct the daily friction operations designed to assert and gradually consolidate Chinese maritime claims, with the PLAN operating over the horizon as the credible threat making compliance more rational than resistance for smaller regional states.

This gray zone architecture gives China a graduated toolkit for maritime coercion that runs from fishing boat harassment through coast guard water cannon and vessel ramming all the way to PLAN destroyer deployment — allowing Beijing to incrementally impose costs and control without crossing the threshold of military action that would clearly invoke alliance obligations or justify symmetric military responses.

Strategic Analysis

The Anti-Access/Area-Denial Architecture

China's naval expansion cannot be understood in isolation from the broader anti-access/area-denial (A2/AD) architecture within which the PLAN operates. The navy is one layer of a multi-domain system specifically designed to prevent the United States from intervening effectively in a Taiwan or South China Sea contingency. The DF-21D "carrier killer" anti-ship ballistic missile and the DF-26 dual-capable intermediate-range ballistic missile, both operated by the PLA Rocket Force rather than the PLAN, hold US carrier strike groups at risk at ranges far beyond China's maritime horizon. The vast YJ-series anti-ship cruise missile inventory deployed across surface ships, submarines, and shore-based platforms provides multiple overlapping engagement envelopes. Air defense coverage from S-400 systems and indigenous HQ-9B extends far beyond China's coastline.

The PLAN's role within this architecture is not to defeat the US Navy in a classical fleet engagement — that remains a mismatch given the US Navy's current overall capability advantage — but to complicate, delay, and raise the cost of any US military intervention sufficiently that political decision-makers in Washington calculate that the cost of intervention exceeds the benefit of Taiwan's defense. This "fait accompli" strategy — seize Taiwan faster than the US can respond effectively — depends critically on the PLAN's ability to initially protect an invasion force against US submarine and air attack while the Rocket Force's missiles hold US carrier groups at bay.

Far Seas Protection and Global Power Projection

Beyond the near-seas A2/AD mission, the PLAN's expanding blue-water capability reflects genuine strategic ambition for global power projection. China's 46th Naval Escort Task Force has maintained a continuous presence in the Gulf of Aden for anti-piracy escort operations since 2008 — a mission that has functioned as a consistent blue-water operational training opportunity while providing political cover for the capability development it sustains. Chinese naval vessels have deployed to the Indian Ocean, the South Pacific, the Mediterranean, and most recently near Australia and east of the International Date Line, extending operational familiarity with distant waters that would have been unrealistic even a decade ago.

China's pursuit of overseas naval logistics access points — in Djibouti, where a formal base was established in 2017, and through negotiated access arrangements in Cambodia, Myanmar, and potentially through port agreements in the Pacific Islands — reflects the infrastructure dimension of this far-seas capability development. Xi Jinping's Belt and Road Initiative, viewed through a strategic naval lens, is partially a project of securing the port access and maritime logistics infrastructure that a truly global navy requires.

The 2027 Deadline and Taiwan

Xi Jinping's widely reported instruction to the PLA to be capable of seizing Taiwan by force by 2027 provides the organizing timeline for virtually every aspect of current PLAN development. The Pentagon's most recent annual report assesses that the PLA has already tested essential components of multiple Taiwan invasion options, including amphibious assault exercises, firepower strike campaigns targeting sea and land objectives, and maritime blockade simulations. The Type 076's catapult-equipped UCAV integration, the Shuiqiao landing barges, the ongoing expansion of submarine capability specifically aimed at contesting US undersea superiority, and the nine-carrier fleet trajectory — all of these cohere as elements of a force specifically optimized for the Taiwan contingency, even as Chinese officials consistently deny any offensive intent.

The 2027 deadline does not mean Xi has decided to invade Taiwan in 2027. It means he has directed the PLA to achieve the military capability to do so successfully by that date, giving him a credible option should political circumstances make it strategically attractive. The distinction matters enormously: capability without intent creates strategic ambiguity that itself shapes other actors' decisions, regardless of whether the option is ever exercised.

The Shipbuilding Industrial Comparison

The most structurally important asymmetry between China and the United States in the naval competition is not any individual platform or weapon system — it is industrial capacity. China builds more commercial shipping annually than any other country by a substantial margin, and its naval shipyards are operating at production rates the US defense industrial base simply cannot currently replicate. The May 2026 US Navy Shipbuilding Plan targeting a 450-vessel fleet reflects not just strategic ambition but a recognition that industrial mobilization — expanding shipyard capacity, training workers, securing supply chains — is the genuine long-term constraint on US naval power. Twenty-one major Chinese combatants commissioned in a single year (2025) versus the US Navy's challenged production of even a handful of vessels annually in most recent years represents a production rate differential that aggregate defense budgets alone cannot explain or resolve without fundamental industrial policy change.

Global Impact

Japan and the Indo-Pacific Alliance Response

Japan's response to PLAN expansion has been the most consequential allied reaction, given its geographic position, the East China Sea disputes over the Senkaku Islands, and the historical sensitivities around Japanese remilitarization. The doubling of Japan's defense budget to 2 percent of GDP — now translated into actual procurement of F-35Bs, Type 12 anti-ship missile upgrades with extended range, and counterstrike capability development — reflects Tokyo's assessment that PLAN carrier exercises transiting near Japanese territorial waters and deploying toward the Pacific represent a genuine security challenge requiring response. Japan's December 2025 experience of China's Liaoning carrier operating near its waters amid tensions over Tokyo's statements about possible Taiwan military intervention signals that PLAN operational presence is already reshaping Japan's immediate security environment.

India and the Indian Ocean Contest

For India, China's naval expansion creates a dual challenge: growing PLAN presence in what New Delhi views as its strategic maritime domain — the Indian Ocean — combined with the military pressure that a PLA capable of two-front operations along India's land borders while simultaneously projecting naval power in the Indian Ocean would represent. India's response includes accelerating INS Vikrant's operational integration, advancing the INS Vishal large carrier project, expanding its submarine fleet including the Arihant-class SSBNs, and deepening maritime intelligence and surveillance cooperation with the United States, France, Australia, and Japan through bilateral and QUAD frameworks. The Indian Ocean's strategic centrality to China's energy and trade supply lines — the so-called "Malacca Dilemma" — simultaneously gives India leverage over Chinese vulnerability that a stronger Indian naval presence can exploit.

The AUKUS Submarine Response

The AUKUS agreement's nuclear-powered submarine technology transfer to Australia — providing Canberra with an eventual fleet of SSN-AUKUS class submarines capable of sustained operations throughout the Indo-Pacific — represents the most direct counter-measure any state has yet committed to against PLAN submarine expansion. A submarine-capable Australia operating in partnership with the US and UK undersea forces meaningfully complicates China's ability to achieve the undersea dominance in the Indo-Pacific that Brookes' testimony suggests is the PLAN's long-term objective. Whether AUKUS's timeline — with Australian SSNs not expected before the mid-2030s at the earliest — is fast enough to matter in the critical 2027-2035 window is the genuine strategic uncertainty surrounding the program.

The US Carrier Fleet Paradox

The PLAN's A2/AD architecture specifically targets US carrier strike groups as the primary instruments of American power projection — and US carrier strike groups remain genuinely, substantially more capable in individual platform terms than any existing Chinese counterpart. The paradox is that this capability advantage may be of limited operational value if Chinese missiles, submarines, and air defenses can hold carriers at risk at ranges beyond which carrier aviation can effectively operate. The US Navy's May 2026 450-ship fleet plan, with its emphasis on distributed lethality, Virginia-class submarines, autonomous surface and undersea systems, and the new nuclear-powered battleship concept, reflects an adaptation away from carrier-centric power projection toward a more distributed, resilient model specifically in recognition of the A2/AD threat that PLAN expansion embodies.

Risk Assessment

  • High-probability risk: Continued PLAN expansion toward nine carrier groups by 2035, with the Type 004 nuclear carrier confirming its identity through increasingly visible construction progress at Dalian, raising the strategic stakes in the Taiwan Strait and broader Pacific fundamentally.
  • High-probability risk: PLAN submarine force reaching approximately 70 hulls by 2027 with growing nuclear-powered proportion, narrowing the US undersea advantage in the Western Pacific and complicating any US Navy attempt to contest a PLAN blockade of Taiwan in the early-to-mid 2030s.
  • High-probability risk: Continued gray zone operations by coast guard and maritime militia around Taiwan, in the South China Sea, and near the Senkakus, with the PLAN's growing conventional superiority in the near-seas making those operations progressively harder to resist through conventional naval presence.
  • Moderate-probability risk: A Taiwan contingency triggering a conflict before the US Navy's 450-ship plan can materially improve American fleet mass, forcing the US to contest a PLAN military operation with a fleet whose quantitative and certain qualitative gaps have not yet been addressed.
  • Moderate-probability risk: PLAN blue-water presence extending into the South Pacific, near Australian waters, and east of the International Date Line, requiring additional allied response commitments that strain coalition bandwidth and resources.
  • Lower-probability, high-impact risk: Chinese submarine force achieving the acoustic quieting and capability levels necessary to seriously contest US undersea dominance in the Pacific in the 2035-2040 timeframe, eliminating what US defense planners currently regard as one of the most critical asymmetric advantages available against China.

Future Scenarios

Scenario Analysis — the following are illustrative projections based on current development trajectories, not confirmed outcomes.

Scenario One: Managed Competition with Deterrence Stability (Most Likely)

China continues PLAN expansion at current pace, reaching six carriers and approximately 70 submarines by 2027-2030, while the United States begins implementing its 450-ship fleet plan, Japanese defense spending reaches 3 percent of GDP, and AUKUS submarine timelines accelerate modestly. The result is a higher-tension but deterrence-stable Pacific in which neither side has decisive military advantage in the Taiwan Strait, preserving the current ambiguous status quo through continued mutual deterrence — neither comfortable nor crisis-prone, but manageable if political leadership on both sides prioritizes crisis management over confrontation signaling.

Scenario Two: PLAN Achieves Regional Superiority Window Before US Counter-Build

Chinese carrier and submarine expansion proceeds at or above current pace, while US shipbuilding plan faces congressional funding constraints and industrial capacity bottlenecks. Between approximately 2028 and 2035, the PLAN achieves a genuine regional naval superiority window in the near-seas A2/AD zone — not global naval supremacy, but sufficient localized advantage that a Taiwan military contingency becomes operationally credible. This window, whether or not China chooses to act militarily, fundamentally reshapes the diplomatic calculus of every Pacific state regarding accommodation with Beijing versus alignment with Washington.

Scenario Three: Conflict in the Taiwan Strait

A Taiwan contingency — triggered by either a Chinese decision to act on the 2027 capability deadline or a crisis arising from Taipei's political trajectory toward formal independence — brings the PLAN's expanded capabilities into direct confrontation with US and allied naval forces. Even a successful Chinese military operation would likely entail severe military losses given US submarine advantage, long-range strike capability, and the combat experience differential between the two navies. The scenario most catastrophic for global stability is one where China miscalculates US willingness to intervene militarily, or where the US miscalculates China's political resolve — a risk that grows as PLAN capability narrows the gap that once made the outcome of any such confrontation unambiguous.

Scenario Four: Negotiated Maritime Framework

US-China diplomatic engagement — building on back-channel military-to-military communication — produces a framework agreement managing Taiwan Strait operations, South China Sea navigation rights, and strategic submarine patrols in ways that reduce acute crisis risk without resolving the underlying sovereignty disputes. This scenario requires political will from both leaderships that is not currently visible, but remains the only scenario in which PLAN expansion and US counter-build do not eventually produce a crisis whose outcome is determined by who blinked first.

Intelligence Forecast

First, the PLAN's trajectory — twenty-one major combatants commissioned in 2025, a 7 percent 2026 defense budget increase, a nuclear carrier under construction, and a submarine nuclear transition ahead of schedule — will continue through the remainder of the decade regardless of US diplomatic or economic pressure, because it reflects strategic decisions made and resourced at the highest levels of Chinese state power for the preceding decade.

Second, the Taiwan contingency window of concern to US defense planners — roughly 2027 to 2035, before US counter-build and AUKUS submarine programs materially shift the balance — will intensify rather than recede as PLAN capability milestones are achieved. The political decision to use that capability, however, remains Xi Jinping's personal choice, and is therefore as much a function of political timing, domestic legitimacy calculations, and global economic conditions as of military readiness.

Third, the submarine competition is the least visible and most strategically consequential dimension of the entire PLAN expansion, and the Brookes testimony's projection of potential PLAN challenge to US undersea dominance by the early 2040s should be treated as the critical long-term planning horizon around which US naval investment decisions — particularly the Virginia-class submarine production rate and the AUKUS SSN transfer timeline — need to be urgently evaluated.

Fourth, the gray zone maritime coercion toolkit — coast guard, maritime militia, PLAN over the horizon — will continue functioning as China's primary instrument for incrementally reshaping the South China Sea and East China Sea status quo, regardless of any specific developments in the more conspicuous carrier and submarine programs, because its effectiveness is calibrated precisely to remain below the response thresholds that would trigger formal military counter-measures.

Final Strategic Takeaway

There is a temptation, when examining the PLAN's expansion in aggregated statistics — hull counts, tonnage commissioned, carrier numbers — to treat this as a military-technical competition analyzable through the same lens as any Cold War-era arms race. That framing misses something essential. What China is building is not just a navy. It is the physical expression of a political project: Xi Jinping's determination to ensure that the scenario that humiliated China in 1996 — two US carrier groups operating unchallenged in waters China considers its own — can never happen again, and that by 2049, China's sovereign territory and strategic interests are defended by military power that no external actor can credibly challenge.

The honest assessment of where this leads is not comfortable for anyone. A Pacific in which China fields nine carrier groups, a predominantly nuclear-powered submarine force approaching the US in capability, and a hypersonic anti-ship arsenal that holds surface fleets at risk across the First Island Chain is a Pacific where the rules governing Taiwan's status, South China Sea navigation rights, and the credibility of US alliance commitments across the Indo-Pacific are all potentially renegotiated by the facts of military power rather than by treaty and diplomatic consensus.

Every government in Asia is already calculating what that Pacific looks like and positioning itself accordingly — Japan rearming at historic pace, Australia accelerating its AUKUS commitment, India deepening its Quad engagement, smaller South China Sea states hedging between Beijing's proximity and Washington's guarantees. The PLAN's expansion is not just China's story. It is the defining structural fact of Indo-Pacific geopolitics for the next generation, and every strategic decision made by every major power in the region will be made in its shadow.

title: Hypersonic Weapons Race: Who's Winning and What's at Stake
content:
Hypersonic Weapons Race: Who's Winning and What's at Stake

Speed has always mattered in warfare. But there is a threshold beyond which speed stops being an advantage and becomes something categorically different — a problem that existing defenses simply cannot solve. That threshold is Mach 5, five times the speed of sound, roughly 6,200 kilometers per hour. Above it, a missile covers the distance from London to Moscow in under fifteen minutes. It can maneuver unpredictably at that speed, flying at altitudes that traditional air defenses were not designed to track. And when it arrives, most intercept systems cannot react in time, even if they see it coming.

This is why the global hypersonic weapons race is not a technical curiosity for defense industry analysts. It is a fundamental challenge to the deterrence architecture that has prevented great-power war for eighty years — an architecture built, at its core, on the assumption that no adversary can strike with enough speed and precision to destroy your retaliatory capability before you can respond. If that assumption breaks, the logic of deterrence breaks with it. Every major military power knows this, which is why Russia, China, the United States, India, France, Japan, Australia, and a growing list of second-tier actors are investing billions in hypersonic weapon development with an urgency that has not been seen in a technology race since the original space race of the 1960s. This report explains what is actually happening, who is actually ahead, and why it matters for the global strategic balance of 2026 and beyond.

Executive Summary

The global hypersonic weapons race has entered its most consequential phase in 2026. Three of the world's major military powers have moved beyond development into actual combat deployment — Russia has used the Oreshnik intermediate-range ballistic missile against Ukraine on three separate occasions, including a May 24, 2026, strike on Bila Tserkva as part of a mass attack involving 600 drones and 90 missiles. China has fielded what analysts now characterize as the world's most advanced operational hypersonic arsenal, showcasing the CJ-1000 and YJ-19 scramjet-powered hypersonic cruise missiles at its September 2025 Victory Day parade alongside the already-operational DF-17 hypersonic glide vehicle — representing the first time any country has demonstrated operational land-based scramjet propulsion. The United States, despite decades of foundational research and the world's largest aggregate defense research and development budget, remains in a genuine catch-up position in terms of fielded systems, with its most advanced programs either still in late-stage testing or just entering early deployment.

The asymmetry is stark and acknowledged at the highest levels of American defense planning. The Pentagon requested $3.9 billion for hypersonic weapons research and development in FY2026 — a significant but notably reduced figure from $6.9 billion in FY2025, reflecting budget pressures even as the strategic urgency intensifies. Meanwhile, an Atlantic Council study by former senior US defense and nuclear officials characterized America's hypersonic gap with Russia and China as creating genuine "battlefield asymmetry," urging an overhaul of production capacity and accelerated deployment timelines.

Layered on top of the technical race is a profound strategic challenge: existing arms control frameworks were not designed with hypersonic weapons in mind, the systems blur conventional and nuclear capability in ways that create dangerous ambiguity under pressure, and the compressed decision timelines they impose could fundamentally alter crisis escalation dynamics in ways that the current generation of political leadership has not yet fully reckoned with.

Background: What Makes Hypersonic Weapons Different

To understand why hypersonic weapons have triggered such a concentrated global arms race, it helps to understand what makes them genuinely different from the ballistic and cruise missiles that have been central to military arsenals since the 1950s.

Ballistic missiles travel along a predictable, high-altitude arc — launching steeply upward, exiting the atmosphere, and descending at hypersonic speeds toward their target. Their trajectories, precisely because they follow predictable physics, can be calculated and tracked by early warning radar systems, giving some window of intercept opportunity. Traditional cruise missiles fly low and slow — typically below Mach 1 — relying on stealth and terrain-following to evade radar rather than speed to outrun it.

Hypersonic weapons combine the worst attributes of both from a defender's perspective. They travel at Mach 5 or faster, compressing reaction time dramatically, but unlike a ballistic missile they do not follow a predictable arc. They maneuver within the atmosphere, changing altitude and trajectory during flight in ways that defeat intercept calculations built for fixed-trajectory systems. They typically fly at altitudes between 20 and 100 kilometers — higher than a cruise missile but lower than a ballistic missile on its descent arc — precisely the altitude regime where existing radar networks have gaps and where existing intercept systems, designed either for lower-altitude cruise missiles or higher-altitude ballistic missile warheads, have the poorest coverage.

Two distinct technical approaches have emerged as the primary development paths:

  • Hypersonic Glide Vehicles (HGVs): Launched on a ballistic rocket to altitude, then released to glide and maneuver at hypersonic speeds within the upper atmosphere toward their target. Examples include Russia's Avangard, China's DF-ZF (mounted on the DF-17), and the US Long-Range Hypersonic Weapon (Dark Eagle) and Conventional Prompt Strike (CPS). HGVs represent the more mature, more widely fielded technology path.
  • Hypersonic Cruise Missiles (HCMs): Powered throughout their flight by air-breathing scramjet engines — engines that use atmospheric oxygen rather than on-board oxidizer, functioning at speeds where conventional jet engines cannot operate. Scramjet propulsion is significantly more technically difficult than HGV boost-glide, but enables sustained, powered hypersonic flight rather than an unpowered glide, and theoretically allows for greater range and maneuverability. China's CJ-1000 and Russia's 3M22 Zircon are the current operational examples.

The defining strategic consequence of both approaches is the same: existing missile defense systems — Patriot batteries, Terminal High-Altitude Area Defense (THAAD), Aegis ship-based intercept systems — are poorly optimized for hypersonic threats due to their speed, low-altitude flight path, and maneuverability. This is not a matter of insufficient investment in existing defense architectures; it is a fundamental technical mismatch between systems designed for different threat profiles and a genuinely new class of offensive weapon.

Current Situation

China: The Hypersonic Superpower

China's hypersonic weapons program has advanced further and faster than most Western analysts predicted even five years ago, and the September 2025 Victory Day parade in Beijing was the most significant public demonstration of that acceleration to date. China revealed, publicly and simultaneously, two systems that represent the current global frontier in scramjet propulsion: the CJ-1000, a road-mobile land-based hypersonic cruise missile powered by a scramjet engine — the world's first and, as of early 2026, only such operational system in land-based configuration — and the YJ-19, a ship-launched hypersonic cruise missile with similar air-breathing propulsion. The parade also showcased the YJ-17 and newer variants with hypersonic glide and scramjet features designed specifically for anti-ship roles against aircraft carrier groups.

An analysis published in the February 2026 edition of the Chinese defense journal Shipborne Weapons made the strategic implications explicit: scramjet engines represent a technically superior development path compared to glide vehicles, and China's operational fielding of the CJ-1000 and YJ-19 represents a lead over the United States — which has no operational scramjet-powered hypersonic missile — that is genuinely strategic rather than merely developmental. The South China Morning Post coverage of this analysis, published February 2026, assessed that China has "overtaken the US in hypersonic defence" specifically in the scramjet domain.

China's hypersonic portfolio extends well beyond scramjet systems. The DF-17 medium-range ballistic missile, designed specifically to carry the DF-ZF hypersonic glide vehicle, has been in operational service since at least 2020 and represents the world's first operational road-mobile ballistic missile with a dedicated hypersonic glide vehicle payload. Its estimated range of 1,800 to 2,500 kilometers places the entire First Island Chain — including Taiwan, US bases in Japan and Guam, and much of the South China Sea — within strike range. The larger DF-ZF glide vehicle, carried on the DF-41 ICBM, extends hypersonic strike capability to intercontinental ranges. The recently demonstrated YJ-20 hypersonic anti-ship missile, filmed launching from a Type 055 destroyer, extends the same maneuverability and speed to carrier-killing naval missions.

The US commander of Strategic Command's March 2026 congressional testimony, which confirmed China has surpassed 600 nuclear warheads, also addressed the hypersonic-nuclear integration question: China's rapidly expanding Rocket Force hypersonic inventory includes systems that can carry either conventional or nuclear warheads, creating a dangerous ambiguity — an adversary detecting an incoming Chinese hypersonic missile cannot immediately determine whether it carries a conventional or nuclear payload, compressing decision time and raising escalation risk in any crisis scenario involving Chinese hypersonic strikes.

Russia: Deployed, Demonstrated, But Partially Oversold

Russia presents the most operationally experienced hypersonic power in 2026, by virtue of having actually used its systems in combat — repeatedly, against Ukraine. But honest intelligence assessment requires separating Russia's genuine capability from the considerably larger capability that Kremlin messaging has attempted to project through selective disclosure and strategic ambiguity.

The most important current system is the Oreshnik, an intermediate-range ballistic missile carrying multiple independently targetable reentry vehicles (MIRVs), used in combat three times against Ukraine: first on November 21, 2024, against Dnipro in what was the first combat use of a MIRV-capable weapon in history; secondly on January 9, 2026, against an infrastructure facility in Lviv; and most recently on May 24, 2026, against Bila Tserkva as part of a mass attack that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky had pre-warned was imminent based on European and US intelligence, with Russia's defense ministry publicly confirming the Oreshnik's use. The missile's MIRV payload — six warheads each reportedly carrying six sub-munitions — makes it significantly harder to intercept than a single-warhead system. President Putin characterized it as traveling "like a meteorite, impossible to stop."

The intelligence picture on Oreshnik, however, requires qualification. CSIS's Missile Threat assessment characterizes it as a modified RS-26 Rubezh IRBM rather than a genuinely novel system. Nonproliferation expert Dr. Jeffrey Lewis has stated none of the technology is novel — it is "a series of old technologies put together in a new way." A University of Oslo defense expert suggested it incorporates no more than ten percent new components. Ukraine's assessments of the January 2026 Lviv strike indicated the warheads carried inert payloads, leading US experts to describe it as "an expensive way to deliver not that much destruction." Russia is assessed to possess only a limited number of Oreshnik units, making sustained operational use against Ukraine logistically challenging. The cost per launch is estimated in the tens of millions of dollars per missile.

Where Russia's hypersonic portfolio is genuinely impressive is in the older, more established systems. The Kinzhal air-launched hypersonic ballistic missile, carried by MiG-31K interceptors, has been used extensively against Ukraine and represents genuine operational capability — albeit subject to the same debate about whether a fast ballistic missile's reentry vehicle technically constitutes "hypersonic" in the sense distinct from traditional ballistic missiles. The Avangard boost-glide vehicle, carried on SS-19 Stiletto and RS-28 Sarmat ICBMs, is perhaps Russia's most technically credible hypersonic system for strategic deterrence purposes — a genuine boost-glide vehicle claimed to maneuver at Mach 20-plus during descent, making it effectively uninterceptable by any currently deployed missile defense system. The Zircon (3M22) ship-launched hypersonic cruise missile, powered by a scramjet engine and capable of engaging both land and naval targets, is in serial production and has been tested from surface ships and submarines. Russia is manufacturing close to 2,500 high-precision missiles annually across cruise, ballistic, and hypersonic classes according to Ukrainian military intelligence assessments, reflecting an impressive production ramp despite economic sanctions.

Putin confirmed in 2025-2026 that Oreshnik is entering mass production, with Russia having deployed the system to Belarus — with Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko claiming Belarus will host ten Oreshnik missiles, deployed at what satellite imagery identified as a former airbase site near Krichev. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas characterized this deployment explicitly as "meant as a warning to Europe and to the US." Germany's defense budget response — €108.2 billion in 2026 spending, representing a historic increase, with the European Defence Fund including €168 million specifically for hypersonic countermeasures and endoatmospheric interception capabilities — reflects how seriously the Oreshnik's deployment has been received in European capitals.

United States: The Catch-Up Race

The United States has spent more on hypersonic weapons research and development over the past decade than any other nation, and it originated much of the foundational science underlying the field. Its current position — trailing China in fielded scramjet systems and Russia in combat-deployed hypersonic operational experience — is the product of a specific set of choices rather than fundamental technological incapacity: the post-2001 pivot toward counterterrorism-oriented defense spending, inconsistent funding for long-duration high-speed weapons programs, strict safety and reliability requirements that slow the development-to-deployment transition relative to adversaries willing to field less mature systems faster, and — critically — a chronic bottleneck in hypersonic testing infrastructure, with only a handful of facilities capable of testing systems at true hypersonic speeds limiting how quickly programs can be iterated and refined.

The current US hypersonic portfolio comprises four primary programs in varying stages of development and early deployment:

  • Long-Range Hypersonic Weapon (LRHW / Dark Eagle): The Army's primary program, carrying a Common Hypersonic Glide Body (C-HGB) shared with the Navy's Conventional Prompt Strike system. Dark Eagle has made recent progress including a successful test, and senior officials have praised its development pace as "remarkable" for a five-year program timeline. It is still projected to field in 2026 but remains delayed from earlier targets.
  • Conventional Prompt Strike (CPS): The Navy's program, using the same C-HGB glide body as Dark Eagle but launched from surface ships and eventually from submarines. CPS achieved a successful end-to-end test using a cold-gas sea-based launch in a breakthrough described as "the first of its kind," with surface-ship deployment targeted for 2027 and submarine deployment in the early 2030s.
  • Air-Launched Rapid Response Weapon (ARRW): The Air Force's air-launched hypersonic glide vehicle, carried by B-52H bombers. ARRW was shelved following test setbacks before being revived, with $387 million allocated in FY2026 to begin procurement — reflecting the Pentagon's reassessment that multiple hypersonic weapon types are needed for different mission sets.
  • Hypersonic Attack Cruise Missile (HACM): The Air Force's scramjet-powered hypersonic cruise missile, representing the closest American equivalent to China's CJ-1000. HACM is experiencing significant cost overruns — approximately $2 billion to date — and schedule delays, though some test reductions may reduce expenditure going forward.

On the defensive side, the US has taken concrete steps to address its current interceptor gap. The Missile Defense Agency awarded approximately $475 million in additional funding to Northrop Grumman to accelerate the Glide Phase Interceptor (GPI), designed specifically to engage hypersonic glide vehicles during their most predictable flight phase, pushing initial operational capability forward into the early 2030s. The Pentagon has also procured upgraded AN/TPY-2 radars with Gallium Nitride arrays and improved computing to better detect and track hypersonic threats. And President Trump's administration has moved toward developing and prototyping the ambitious "Golden Dome" missile defense initiative — a multi-tiered intercept architecture combining space, midcourse, high-altitude, and terminal intercept layers against ballistic and hypersonic threats, at an estimated cost in the range of $175 billion, though technical and fiscal challenges remain substantial.

India, Japan, France, Australia: The Second-Tier Accelerants

Beyond the three primary competitors, a growing cohort of second-tier powers is accelerating hypersonic development with strategic urgency, reflecting how comprehensively the technology has reshaped threat perceptions worldwide.

India has made the most substantial progress among this group. The Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) has conducted multiple successful hypersonic glide vehicle tests, and the Hypersonic Technology Demonstrator Vehicle (HSTDV) program has validated scramjet engine technology at relevant speeds and altitudes. India's hypersonic program is driven by dual imperatives — the growing Chinese threat along the Line of Actual Control and the need for credible second-strike deterrence capability in its nuclear posture — and benefits from the scientific and industrial base that India's broader missile program, including Agni-V development, has built over decades.

Japan has taken hypersonic development more seriously than at any point since the postwar constitution's defensive posture constraints. Japan is developing both Hypersonic Guided Missiles (HGM) and Hyper Velocity Gliding Projectile (HVGP) systems under the Japan Ground Self-Defense Force's emerging counterstrike doctrine. Funding for these programs has accelerated under Japan's doubled defense budget, with operational capability targeted in the late 2020s to early 2030s.

France has tested its ASN4G hypersonic missile concept — intended as a successor to the ASMP-A nuclear air-launched cruise missile — with the Hypersonica Munich startup working on modular hypersonic architecture development at dramatically reduced cost and development timeline compared to traditional state procurement. The European Defence Fund's €168 million 2026 allocation for hypersonic countermeasures reflects broader European institutional acknowledgment that the continent needs indigenous capability in both offensive and defensive hypersonics.

Australia, through the AUKUS partnership, is collaborating with the United States and United Kingdom on hypersonic strike programs, with the Southern Cross Integrated Flight Research Experiment (SCIFiRE) program representing a joint US-Australian scramjet hypersonic cruise missile development initiative that is more advanced than most open-source reporting captures.

Strategic Analysis

Why Scramjet Leadership Matters More Than HGV Count

The most analytically important distinction in the current hypersonic race is between hypersonic glide vehicles — which have been the primary development focus for Russia and the United States — and scramjet-powered hypersonic cruise missiles, in which China has now established a demonstrable lead. The distinction matters for three reasons. First, scramjet propulsion enables sustained powered hypersonic flight rather than a glide from initial altitude, meaning range and terminal maneuverability are less constrained by energy bleed during the glide phase. Second, scramjet missiles can fly at lower, flatter trajectories for extended periods, potentially making them even harder to detect and engage than HGVs whose relatively predictable glide paths give defenders slightly more intercept geometry to work with. Third, operational scramjet propulsion is technically harder — there is a reason the United States, despite enormous investment in the HACM program, has not yet fielded an operational scramjet weapon while China has now apparently done so on two separate platforms simultaneously.

The Nuclear-Conventional Ambiguity Problem

The most strategically dangerous dimension of the hypersonic race is not the offensive capability itself but the ambiguity it creates between conventional and nuclear attack. Both Russia's Kinzhal and Oreshnik, and China's DF-17 and various HCM systems, can carry either conventional or nuclear warheads. An adversary detecting an incoming hypersonic missile cannot know, in the compressed decision window available, whether it carries conventional high explosives or a nuclear warhead — and the consequence of that uncertainty, under the pressure of a genuine crisis, could be escalatory responses calibrated for the worst case.

This dynamic has been explicitly identified by STRATCOM officials as one of the most serious emerging strategic stability challenges, and it is not addressed by any existing arms control framework. The New START treaty, which expired in 2026 without extension, did not cover hypersonic delivery systems. The INF Treaty, which covered ground-launched missiles in the 1,000-5,500 kilometer range that would include several hypersonic systems, was abandoned by both the United States and Russia in 2019. There is currently no multilateral framework of any kind that addresses hypersonic weapons, and the technical characteristics of these systems — dual-capable, ambiguous payload, extremely compressed decision time — may make them harder to include in traditional arms control verification regimes than earlier generations of strategic weapons.

The Decision Timeline Compression

A hypersonic glide vehicle launched from eastern China can reach US bases in Japan or Guam in approximately fifteen to thirty minutes. A Kinzhal launched from a MiG-31K operating at maximum intercept altitude over Russia can strike targets in much of Europe in ten minutes or less. An Oreshnik fired from Belarus can reach any capital in central or western Europe in a matter of minutes. The compressed decision timelines these systems impose on political leadership during a crisis fundamentally alter the crisis management calculus that has underpinned nuclear deterrence for seven decades — the deliberate, negotiated back-and-forth of the Cuban Missile Crisis or the careful de-escalation of earlier US-Soviet crises becomes considerably harder when the window between first warning and required decision shrinks from hours to minutes.

Global Impact

Carrier Strike Group Vulnerability

Aircraft carrier strike groups have been the foundation of US forward power projection and extended deterrence for eight decades. China's explicit development of anti-ship hypersonic systems — the YJ-17, YJ-19, and YJ-20 operating from surface ships and submarines, the DF-21D "carrier killer" ballistic missile system, and now hypersonic glide vehicles capable of terminal maneuvering against moving targets — represents the most serious challenge to carrier viability since anti-ship missile technology first emerged in the 1960s. A carrier group operating within the First Island Chain in a Taiwan contingency now faces a threat environment no existing defensive architecture was designed to manage comprehensively.

NATO's Eastern Flank and European Security

Russia's Oreshnik deployment to Belarus, combined with the existing Iskander tactical ballistic missile deployments in Kaliningrad and the longer-range Kinzhal capability, means that essentially every NATO member in eastern and central Europe now sits within the effective range of Russian hypersonic-capable systems. Germany's historic defense spending increase and the EU's €168 million specifically allocated for hypersonic countermeasures in 2026 reflect the degree to which the Oreshnik has concentrated European strategic attention on a capability gap that cannot be addressed through the existing Patriot and THAAD architecture alone.

Deterrence Architecture Under Stress

The combination of compressed decision timelines, nuclear-conventional ambiguity, and current intercept inadequacy creates a deterrence environment that is genuinely more unstable than the one that existed before hypersonic weapons became operationally significant. Deterrence theory assumes that an adversary's rational calculation of costs and benefits, combined with the survivability of retaliatory forces, prevents first strikes. Hypersonic weapons challenge each component of that formula: they compress the time available for rational deliberation, they create ambiguity about whether a first strike is nuclear or conventional (and therefore what response it warrants), and they raise questions about whether existing retaliatory forces — particularly time-critical command and control nodes — are survivable against hypersonic precision.

Risk Assessment

  • High-probability risk: Continued US hypersonic development delays relative to China and Russia extending the current battlefield asymmetry into the late 2020s, given documented testing bottlenecks, cost overruns, and the FY2026 reduction in overall hypersonic R&D funding from $6.9 billion to $3.9 billion.
  • High-probability risk: Russia continuing to use Oreshnik against Ukraine in high-profile strikes where escalatory signaling value justifies the substantial per-unit cost, particularly in response to major Ukrainian long-range strikes on Russian territory with Western-supplied systems.
  • High-probability risk: China accelerating DF-17 and naval hypersonic deployments in the East and South China Seas specifically to complicate US carrier strike group operations in any Taiwan contingency.
  • Moderate-probability risk: A crisis scenario in which an adversary's detection of an incoming hypersonic missile generates ambiguity about nuclear or conventional payload, creating escalation pressure that existing crisis communication protocols are inadequate to manage.
  • Moderate-probability risk: India or another second-tier power successfully testing an operational scramjet hypersonic missile, further proliferating the technology to a growing number of actors without any arms control architecture in place to manage the resulting strategic environment.
  • Lower-probability, high-impact risk: The emergence of a successful, deployable hypersonic intercept capability — the Glide Phase Interceptor achieving earlier-than-projected operational capability, or a "Golden Dome" breakthrough — triggering a reactive arms race in which adversaries respond to improved defenses by fielding larger, more complex, and harder-to-intercept hypersonic attack salvos.

Future Scenarios

Scenario Analysis — the following are illustrative projections based on current development trajectories, not confirmed outcomes.

Scenario One: Layered Hypersonic Parity by 2030

The United States successfully accelerates Dark Eagle fielding, Conventional Prompt Strike achieves surface-ship deployment by 2027 as projected, and ARRW procurement produces a usable air-launched inventory by 2028. The Glide Phase Interceptor achieves initial operational capability in the early 2030s as now targeted. The strategic outcome is not US dominance but rough three-way hypersonic parity among the major powers, combined with the beginning of a counter-hypersonic capability — a more stable, if more complex, deterrence environment than the current asymmetry.

Scenario Two: Chinese Scramjet Supremacy Reshapes Indo-Pacific Balance

The CJ-1000 and YJ-19 prove operationally superior to any existing or near-term US intercept capability, and China deploys them in sufficient numbers to credibly threaten US carrier strike groups across the entire First Island Chain operating area.
