  • The fragile ceasefire will likely continue experiencing periodic violations without complete collapse into renewed full-scale war, consistent with the pattern established since March, as both governments retain genuine, if limited, interest in avoiding the economic and military costs sustained full conflict imposes.
  • China will likely continue its active mediation role, leveraging its substantial economic interests in both countries and its concern about instability spillover toward Central Asia and Xinjiang to sustain diplomatic pressure toward de-escalation.
  • ISKP will likely continue exploiting the reduced counterterrorism coordination between Pakistan and Afghan Taliban forces, rebuilding operational capacity and potentially conducting additional attacks that further complicate the broader regional security environment.
  • Pakistan's domestic political pressure to demonstrate decisive action against the TTP will likely persist, given the group's continued attack capacity inside Pakistani territory, sustaining underlying pressure toward renewed military escalation regardless of diplomatic efforts.
  • The Afghan Taliban government's internal political coherence regarding TTP relations will likely remain genuinely constrained by the ethnic and ideological kinship factors this analysis identifies, limiting Kabul's practical capacity to deliver the kind of decisive crackdown Pakistani demands require, regardless of diplomatic commitments made during ceasefire negotiations.

Final Strategic Takeaway

The Pakistan-Afghanistan conflict of 2026 represents far more than a border dispute escalating beyond its previous bounds — it represents the definitive, public collapse of a strategic doctrine Pakistan's military establishment spent over two decades constructing and defending. The "strategic depth" framework that justified sustained Pakistani support for the Afghan Taliban movement, premised on the assumption that ideological and historical ties would translate into a cooperative, pliable government in Kabul, has instead produced a neighboring state whose ruling movement's own internal coherence and legitimacy depend substantially on maintaining solidarity with ideological kin that Pakistan now needs suppressed — kin who share the Taliban's own ethnic composition, religious framework, and revolutionary lineage in ways that make genuine, sustained crackdown extraordinarily difficult regardless of the diplomatic and military pressure Islamabad applies.

This structural reality explains why conventional diplomatic and military pressure, however substantial — destroyed corps headquarters, captured border posts, sustained airstrike campaigns reaching the Afghan capital itself — has not produced the kind of decisive resolution either government's stated objectives require. Pakistan cannot bomb its way to genuine Afghan Taliban willingness to move decisively against the TTP when that willingness is constrained by factors more fundamental than battlefield damage assessment. The Afghan Taliban, meanwhile, cannot indefinitely sustain a conflict against a conventionally superior neighbor without genuine economic and humanitarian costs that an already fragile, internationally isolated government can ill afford, particularly given Afghanistan's continued dependence on cross-border trade through Pakistan that the conflict has substantially disrupted.

What this suggests for the conflict's longer-term trajectory is a genuinely difficult equilibrium: neither side possesses the capacity to impose a decisive, lasting resolution on the other, yet neither side's underlying grievances — Pakistani security demands regarding TTP sanctuary, Afghan sovereignty concerns regarding cross-border strikes, and the unresolved Durand Line dispute underlying both — show genuine signs of resolution through the current cycle of conflict and mediated de-escalation. The most realistic expectation, consistent with the available evidence and the structural factors this analysis has identified, is continued instability: periodic ceasefires, periodic violations, sustained humanitarian costs, and a regional security environment that, as ISKP's documented exploitation of the resulting vacuum illustrates, generates dangerous second-order consequences extending well beyond the immediate bilateral relationship that initially seemed, however imperfectly, manageable before February 2026's collapse into open war.

Global Chanakya Intelligence Assessment: Pakistan's strategic depth doctrine has produced its own negation — a Taliban government too ideologically entangled with its Pakistani offshoot to suppress it, and a Pakistani state too threatened by that offshoot to tolerate the entanglement. Until this fundamental contradiction is resolved, no ceasefire brokered by Beijing, Ankara, Doha, or Riyadh will hold for long.

title: Red Sea Crisis: The Chokepoint Reshaping World Trade
content:
Red Sea Crisis: The Chokepoint Reshaping World Trade

Somewhere off the coast of South Africa right now, container ships carrying goods bound from Shanghai to Rotterdam are sailing four thousand extra miles around the Cape of Good Hope — a detour their owners never planned for, burning fuel their budgets never accounted for, on a route that exists for one reason: a relatively small, lightly resourced armed movement in one of the world's poorest countries decided, in November 2023, that it could hold global commerce hostage. Two and a half years later, even with Houthi attacks formally paused since the October 2025 Gaza ceasefire, that detour has not ended. The ships have not gone back.

This is the part of the Red Sea crisis that rarely makes headlines anymore but matters more than almost anything else happening in global trade right now: a crisis that was supposed to be temporary has become structural. Insurance markets, shipping conglomerates, and the entire architecture of Asia-Europe and Asia-US East Coast trade have quietly rebuilt themselves around the assumption that the Red Sea is not coming back to normal — not this year, and quite possibly not for several more. This report examines why that reality matters far beyond shipping industry trade publications, and what it tells us about the future of global trade security in an era when chokepoints, not great-power navies, increasingly determine the flow of world commerce.

Executive Summary

The Red Sea crisis began in November 2023, when Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi movement began attacking commercial and naval vessels transiting the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, framing the campaign as solidarity with Palestinians amid the Gaza war. What followed was one of the most consequential disruptions to global maritime trade in decades: a corridor carrying roughly 12 to 15 percent of global trade volume, including nearly a third of all Asia-Europe container traffic, was rendered sufficiently dangerous that the vast majority of global shipping abandoned it entirely in favor of the much longer Cape of Good Hope route around southern Africa.

Houthi attacks paused following the October 2025 Gaza ceasefire, with the group confirming the halt in a November 2025 letter to Hamas's al-Qassam Brigades and releasing the captured crew of the Greek-operated MV Eternity C in early December. Attack frequency collapsed accordingly — from roughly 150 recorded Houthi attacks on commercial vessels in 2024 to just seven in all of 2025. Yet shipping traffic through the Suez Canal and Bab el-Mandeb Strait has not meaningfully recovered. As of mid-2026, daily traffic through the strait remains significantly below pre-crisis levels, the vast majority of major carriers continue routing Asia-Europe and Asia-US East Coast services around the Cape of Good Hope by default, and the Bab el-Mandeb sits at a persistent "moderate threat" classification under multinational maritime security advisories.

The crisis has been further complicated, rather than resolved, by the broader 2026 Iran war. Following the February 28 US-Israeli strikes on Iran, the Houthis threatened renewed Red Sea escalation and on March 28 launched a ballistic missile directly at Israel, joining the broader regional conflict. Though no confirmed attacks on commercial shipping have occurred since the Gaza ceasefire, the Houthis have explicitly warned that closure of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait remains "likely" should the conflict against Iran significantly escalate or should Gulf Arab states formally join the war — a live, standing threat that the Soufan Center's 2026 forecast characterizes as making renewed attacks "almost certain" if the underlying Gaza or Iran ceasefires collapse. With global shipping capacity still absorbing the equivalent of 1.3 to 1.8 million TEU due to longer routings, and industry consensus now projecting Cape diversions to continue through at least 2027, the Red Sea crisis stands as a defining case study in how a non-state actor can permanently reshape the architecture of global trade.

Background

The Red Sea connects the Mediterranean to the Indian Ocean via two critical chokepoints: the Suez Canal at its northern end, and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait — a narrow passage between Yemen and the Horn of Africa — at its southern approach. Together, these two chokepoints have historically carried between 12 and 15 percent of total global trade volume and roughly 30 percent of all container shipping traffic moving between Asia and Europe, making the corridor one of a handful of genuinely indispensable arteries in the global trading system, alongside the Strait of Hormuz, the Strait of Malacca, and the Panama Canal.

The Houthi movement, formally known as Ansar Allah, has controlled Yemen's capital Sana'a and the bulk of the country's Red Sea coastline, including the strategic port of Hodeidah, since 2014, when it ousted the internationally recognized government in a campaign that triggered Saudi Arabia's intervention and the broader Yemeni civil war that Global Chanakya has analyzed extensively elsewhere. For nearly a decade, the Houthis' conflict remained primarily domestic and regional in character, centered on the contest for control of Yemen itself rather than any direct confrontation with global shipping or Israel.

That changed within weeks of Hamas's October 7, 2023, attack on Israel and the resulting Gaza war. The Houthis, framing their actions as solidarity with the Palestinian cause and leveraging their geographic position astride the Bab el-Mandeb, began launching missile, drone, and naval mine attacks against vessels they characterized as linked to Israel, beginning November 19, 2023. By February 2024, the group had attacked forty vessels. The campaign rapidly expanded beyond strictly Israeli-linked shipping to encompass American, British, and eventually a far broader range of commercial vessels regardless of ownership or flag, transforming what began as a targeted political statement into an indiscriminate threat to global maritime commerce.

The international response was swift but only partially effective. The United States organized Operation Prosperity Guardian in December 2023, a multinational naval coalition intended to secure Red Sea shipping lanes, while the European Union separately launched Operation Aspides. The US and UK conducted direct airstrikes against Houthi military positions inside Yemen beginning in January 2024. Despite this substantial multinational military investment, the operations achieved only limited deterrent effect — the Houthis retained both the operational capability and political will to continue attacks, illustrating a structural truth about asymmetric maritime threats that has shaped strategic thinking ever since: deterrence works best against actors with centralized, valuable assets and clear cost-benefit calculations, and the Houthis, operating a fragmented, dispersed, low-cost weapons system with high tolerance for risk and enormous symbolic payoff from each successful strike, simply did not fit that model.

The financial and trade impact during the crisis's initial, most acute phase was staggering. The Russell Group estimated that goods worth approximately $1 trillion were disrupted by Houthi attacks between October 2023 and May 2024 alone. Suez Canal traffic, which had handled 2,068 ship transits in November 2023, collapsed to just 877 by October 2024 — a decline of more than 57 percent. World Bank analysis found container ship transits through the canal plummeted by 90 percent between December 2023 and March 2024 specifically, the crisis's most acute window.

Current Situation

The Pause That Wasn't a Return

The most important, and most frequently misunderstood, fact about the Red Sea crisis in 2026 is the gap between attack frequency and actual shipping recovery. Houthi attacks on commercial vessels effectively stopped following the October 10, 2025, Gaza ceasefire — ACLED data recorded just seven Houthi attacks on commercial shipping across all of 2025, a dramatic collapse from the roughly 150 attacks recorded in 2024. The Houthis confirmed this operational pause in an undated letter to Hamas's al-Qassam Brigades, published in November 2025, while explicitly conditioning the pause on continued Israeli adherence to the Gaza ceasefire. On December 3, 2025, the group released the eleven captive crew members of the Greek-owned Eternity C cargo vessel, a further tangible de-escalation signal.

Despite this dramatic attack reduction, global shipping has not meaningfully returned to the Red Sea route. As of the April 2026 multinational maritime security advisory, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait remained classified at a "moderate threat" level, and daily traffic through the strait as of May 2026 remained significantly below pre-crisis levels. The vast majority of major container carriers continue defaulting to Cape of Good Hope routing for Asia-Europe and Asia-US East Coast services, with only occasional, exception-based Suez transits offered during extended periods of confirmed reduced attack frequency — a posture industry analysts characterize as "watchful waiting" rather than genuine confidence in the route's restored security.

This persistence reflects a structural reality about how shipping and insurance markets respond to security risk: once major carriers and insurers have absorbed the fixed costs of rerouting — additional vessel deployment, revised scheduling, renegotiated charter agreements increasingly written with Cape routing assumptions built directly into their terms — the threshold for returning to a previously dangerous route rises considerably higher than the threshold that originally triggered the diversion. Carriers are weighing the option value of cautious, gradual Suez return against the proven reliability and now-normalized cost structure of Cape routing, and for most major operators, that calculation currently still favors continued avoidance.

The 2026 Iran War Complication

Just as the maritime industry was cautiously contemplating what a genuine return to Red Sea normalcy might look like, the broader regional security picture deteriorated sharply. Following the February 28, 2026, joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran — which killed Iran's Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei — the Houthis threatened to escalate and resume Red Sea attacks in direct response. On March 28, they followed through on part of that threat, launching a ballistic missile directly at Israel and formally joining the broader 2026 Iran war, marking their first direct strike on Israeli territory since the war's earlier phases.

Critically, the Houthis explicitly tied their maritime threat to the war's broader trajectory, warning that closure of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait was "likely" if the conflict against Iran and Lebanon escalated sharply, or if Gulf Arab states formally joined the war against Tehran. This represents a meaningfully more aggressive threat posture than the group's earlier, narrower framing around Israeli-linked or Gaza-conflict-specific targeting — a genuine strait closure threat, rather than selective vessel targeting, would represent an entirely different order of disruption to global shipping, given that even partial, selective targeting during 2024 was sufficient to drive the vast majority of global container traffic away from the route entirely.

Following the eventual ceasefire in the broader Iran war, Houthi leader Abdul-Malik al-Houthi characterized the outcome as a "great victory" for Iran and the broader "Axis of Resistance," while explicitly warning of further attacks depending on how the situation develops going forward — language that leaves the door deliberately open to renewed escalation rather than signaling any genuine, durable de-escalation commitment. The US responded to this heightened threat environment by deploying the aircraft carrier USS Gerald R. Ford to the Red Sea in March 2026, reinforcing the multinational naval presence even amid the formal attack pause.

The Economics of Permanent Disruption

The financial architecture of global shipping has now adapted substantially to treat Red Sea avoidance as the durable baseline rather than a temporary emergency measure. Current 2026 data illustrates the scale: Asia-Europe freight rates remain 25 to 40 percent above pre-crisis levels, while Asia-US East Coast routing — which typically transited via Suez and the Atlantic as the shortest available path — now runs 15 to 25 percent higher with 8 to 12 additional transit days, even as Pacific-routed Asia-US West Coast trade remains largely unaffected given its geographic independence from the Red Sea corridor entirely.

The capacity impact extends well beyond routes that physically touch the Red Sea. An estimated 5 to 7 percent of total global container fleet capacity — equivalent to roughly 1.3 to 1.8 million TEU — remains absorbed simply by the additional sailing days the Cape of Good Hope route requires compared to the Suez alternative. Because the global container fleet operates as a genuinely interconnected system, this absorption cascades: carriers have redeployed vessels from less profitable routes including intra-Asia, Latin America, and Africa services toward the more lucrative but now longer Asia-Europe and Asia-US lanes, meaning even shipping routes with no direct physical connection to the Red Sea experience tighter capacity and correspondingly higher rates as a downstream consequence.

New vessel deliveries — an estimated 3.2 million TEU currently on order across the global container shipping industry — are expected to gradually help absorb this capacity strain, with industry analysts projecting potential rate easing by mid-2027 as new tonnage enters service. Until then, the structural capacity squeeze the crisis has created persists as a meaningful, ongoing drag on global shipping economics independent of whether Houthi attacks themselves resume.

New Regulatory Architecture

The crisis has also produced lasting regulatory change extending beyond the immediate security situation. New mandatory amendments to SOLAS Chapter V took effect January 1, 2026, requiring immediate notification of containers lost at sea or observed floating adrift — a direct regulatory response to the elevated risk of cargo loss associated with Cape of Good Hope routing, which exposes vessels to considerably harsher weather conditions and rougher seas than the comparatively sheltered Red Sea-Suez corridor. This represents a quiet but meaningful illustration of how the crisis has reshaped not just trade routes but the underlying international regulatory framework governing global shipping safety.

Sanctions Evasion and the Russia-China Dimension

A notable and strategically significant detail emerging through 2026 monitoring involves documented allegations that the Houthis have provided effective safe passage guarantees for Russian and Chinese-affiliated vessels transiting the Red Sea even during the crisis's most acute phases, according to US Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control. This dimension adds a further layer of geopolitical complexity to the crisis: rather than functioning as an indiscriminate threat to all global shipping, Houthi targeting has, at least in part, reflected a selective political logic aligned with the broader Russia-China-Iran axis, raising questions about coordination or tacit understanding between the Houthis and these external powers regarding which commercial interests merit protection from attack.

Strategic Analysis

The Houthi Demonstration Effect

The Red Sea crisis's most enduring strategic lesson extends well beyond Yemen or the immediate Gaza-Iran conflict context: it has demonstrated, conclusively and in real time, that a relatively under-resourced non-state actor controlling a strip of coastline adjacent to a critical maritime chokepoint can impose costs on the global trading system disproportionate to any conventional measure of its military or economic power. The Houthis did not need to sink a large number of ships, nor did they need to defeat any element of the multinational naval coalition arrayed against them. They needed only to demonstrate sufficient capability and willingness to create persistent uncertainty — uncertainty that insurance markets, inherently risk-averse, translated into elevated premiums sufficient to make Cape of Good Hope routing the more economically rational choice for the large majority of carriers, even during periods of relatively low actual attack frequency.

This demonstration effect carries implications well beyond the Red Sea itself. Naval planners and strategists across multiple theaters — including in the Indo-Pacific, where the same fundamental logic applies to scenarios involving the Strait of Malacca, the South China Sea, and Taiwan Strait — are studying the Houthi case closely as a template for how asymmetric, land-based missile and drone capability can achieve meaningful sea-denial effects against vastly superior conventional naval forces, without requiring anything resembling parity in traditional military terms.

The Limits of Naval Deterrence Against Asymmetric Threats

Operation Prosperity Guardian and Operation Aspides represented substantial, sustained multinational military commitments, yet neither achieved the kind of decisive deterrent effect that conventional naval doctrine would predict against a comparably resourced adversary. This gap between military investment and strategic outcome reflects a structural mismatch: deterrence theory assumes a rational actor weighing centralized, valuable assets against potential retaliatory costs, but the Houthis operate a fundamentally different model — dispersed, mobile, low-cost weapons systems controlled by an organization whose political legitimacy and domestic support, particularly amid the broader Gaza war context, was actively enhanced rather than diminished by continued defiance of Western and Israeli military pressure.

The practical lesson for naval and maritime security planners is sobering: protecting a chokepoint of this scale against a determined, asymmetric, land-based threat requires either a fundamentally different security architecture than traditional naval escort and interdiction models provide, or acceptance that some baseline level of elevated risk and cost will persist indefinitely regardless of military commitment, absent an underlying political resolution to the conflict driving the threat in the first place.

Egypt's Acute Economic Exposure

Among all the countries affected by the Red Sea crisis, Egypt bears a uniquely concentrated and severe economic burden. Suez Canal transit revenue represents one of Egypt's most significant sources of foreign currency earnings, and the crisis-driven collapse in canal traffic — sustained now for well over two years — has directly compounded Egypt's broader economic vulnerabilities, including its substantial external debt burden and currency pressures. Unlike the diffuse, globally distributed cost burden the crisis imposes on shipping companies and consumers worldwide, Egypt's exposure is concentrated, structural, and directly tied to a single critical revenue stream that shows no near-term sign of recovering to pre-crisis levels.

Uneven Global Economic Impact

The crisis has exposed what regional analysts have termed a genuine paradox of globalization: the same interconnected trading system that delivers efficiency gains during normal operation also amplifies vulnerability when disrupted, and that amplified vulnerability falls unevenly across the global economy. Wealthy shipping companies and major economies have generally been able to absorb elevated costs through higher freight rates passed incrementally through to consumers. Poorer nations more directly dependent on imports — including many East African and Middle Eastern economies whose own trade and commodity export volumes have been directly impacted — face considerably sharper, less easily absorbed consequences, compounding pre-existing economic vulnerabilities in ways that have received comparatively little international attention relative to the crisis's impact on major shipping conglomerates and developed-economy consumer prices.

Global Impact

Inflationary Pressure and Consumer Prices

The crisis's persistent elevation of shipping costs — Asia-Europe rates remaining 25 to 40 percent above pre-crisis baselines well over two years into the disruption — represents a sustained, structural contributor to global goods price inflation, particularly across categories dependent on Asia-Europe and Asia-US East Coast supply chains including electronics, automotive components, and certain agricultural and consumer goods categories. While shipping cost pass-through to final consumer prices typically operates with a meaningful lag and represents only one of many inflationary inputs, the sustained, multi-year nature of this particular disruption means its cumulative inflationary contribution has likely compounded more significantly than initial 2024 assessments anticipated, given how persistently carriers have maintained Cape routing even amid attack pauses.

Supply Chain Resilience as Permanent Strategic Priority

The crisis has fundamentally and likely permanently altered how major corporations and governments approach supply chain risk planning. Industries built around just-in-time manufacturing principles — particularly automotive and electronics sectors most exposed to Asia-Europe shipping lanes — have been forced to build structural resilience assuming continued Red Sea disruption as a baseline operating condition, rather than treating the crisis as a temporary anomaly to wait out. This represents a broader, lasting shift in global supply chain strategic thinking: chokepoint risk, rather than being treated as a low-probability tail risk requiring minimal contingency planning, has become a first-order strategic planning consideration for any business with meaningful exposure to Asia-Europe or broader intercontinental shipping lanes.

A Template for Future Chokepoint Crises

The Red Sea crisis's demonstrated dynamics — a relatively limited military and political actor achieving outsized global economic disruption through sustained threat to a critical maritime chokepoint — carries direct relevance for how policymakers and naval strategists assess risk across other globally significant chokepoints, including the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has long maintained comparable asymmetric disruption capability, and the Strait of Malacca and South China Sea, where China's own anti-access/area-denial military doctrine draws on related strategic principles. The Red Sea crisis functions, whether intentionally or not, as a real-world demonstration of exactly how such disruption campaigns unfold in practice, providing both potential adversaries and defenders with a detailed operational case study.

Alternative Corridor Development

The sustained Red Sea disruption has accelerated interest in alternative connectivity corridors that reduce dependence on the Suez-Bab el-Mandeb route entirely. This dynamic directly intersects with developments Global Chanakya has tracked separately, including India's continued investment in the International North-South Transport Corridor and growing interest in the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor framework, as well as the broader Middle Corridor connectivity architecture linking Central Asia, the Caucasus, and Europe that the Armenia-Azerbaijan peace process has helped advance. While none of these alternatives can fully substitute for the Suez Canal's core function connecting Asian manufacturing hubs to European and North American markets, the crisis has measurably increased the strategic premium attached to corridor diversification across the global trading system.

Risk Assessment

High-Probability Risks

  • Continued suppressed Suez/Red Sea traffic through 2026: Given persistent carrier risk aversion, elevated insurance premiums, and the absence of any confirmed durable security guarantee, continued below-normal Red Sea shipping traffic through the remainder of 2026 is highly likely regardless of further attack developments.
  • Continued elevated freight rates and consumer cost pass-through: Given the sustained capacity absorption from longer routings, continued elevated Asia-Europe and Asia-US East Coast freight rates, with corresponding gradual consumer price pass-through, remains highly probable through at least 2027.
  • Continued Houthi conditional threats tied to regional conflict status: Given the demonstrated pattern of explicit Houthi threat escalation tied directly to Gaza ceasefire status and the broader Iran war trajectory, continued conditional threat rhetoric is highly likely to persist as a standing feature of the situation.

Moderate-Probability Risks

  • Resumption of attacks on commercial shipping: Given the Soufan Center's explicit "almost certain" assessment conditional on Gaza ceasefire collapse, and the inherently fragile nature of that ceasefire alongside Hamas's continued refusal to disarm under the Trump administration's peace plan, a moderate-to-high probability risk exists of renewed Houthi attacks on commercial vessels within the coming twelve months.
  • Formal Bab el-Mandeb closure threat materializing: Given explicit Houthi statements conditioning strait closure on broader Iran war escalation or Gulf Arab state involvement, a moderate-probability risk exists of this threat materializing into actual closure attempts should the broader regional conflict reignite at scale.
  • Gradual, partial carrier return to Suez routing: Given continued industry "watchful waiting" posture and the substantial cost savings the Suez route offers when judged safe, a moderate-probability risk (from a security-risk perspective) or opportunity (from a normalization perspective) exists of gradual, partial carrier return during sustained low-attack-frequency periods, potentially followed by renewed disruption if security conditions deteriorate again.

Lower-Probability but High-Impact Risks

  • Full, sustained Bab el-Mandeb closure: While explicitly threatened under specific escalation conditions, a genuine, sustained full closure of the strait — as opposed to selective, intermittent vessel targeting — remains a lower-probability outcome given the severity of international response such an action would likely trigger, though it represents a uniquely high-impact scenario given the strait's centrality to global trade flows.
  • Broader regional conflict drawing Gulf Arab states directly into the war: Despite Houthi threats conditioning further maritime escalation on this scenario, direct Gulf Arab state military involvement in the broader Iran conflict remains a lower-probability outcome given the demonstrated preference among Gulf states for de-escalation and economic diversification over direct military confrontation.
  • Permanent structural shift away from Suez Canal centrality: While alternative corridor development continues accelerating, a genuine, permanent structural displacement of the Suez Canal's centrality to global Asia-Europe trade remains a lower-probability outcome given the canal's fundamental geographic efficiency advantage, which persists even amid the current security-driven avoidance.

Future Scenarios

Scenario Analysis — the following projections are illustrative simulations based on current trajectories, not confirmed events.

Scenario One: Prolonged Cautious Stalemate (Most Likely)

Houthi attacks remain paused or highly intermittent through the remainder of 2026, contingent on continued Gaza ceasefire adherence and the broader Iran conflict remaining de-escalated, but the vast majority of global shipping continues defaulting to Cape of Good Hope routing given persistent insurance market caution and the absence of any formal, internationally verified security guarantee. Gradual, partial carrier testing of Suez routing occurs with lower-value cargo, but full normalization remains incomplete through 2027, consistent with industry's own 18-to-24-month estimated timeline from confirmed security stabilization to full service restoration.

Scenario Two: Renewed Escalation and Crisis Reintensification

Either the Gaza ceasefire collapses or the broader Iran-Israel-US conflict reignites at meaningful scale, triggering the Houthis to resume systematic attacks on commercial shipping and potentially move toward the explicitly threatened Bab el-Mandeb closure scenario. This would represent a return to or exceeding the crisis's original 2024 intensity, with corresponding renewed collapse in Suez traffic, sharp freight rate spikes, and intensified international military response, likely including expanded US and allied naval operations.

Scenario Three: Genuine De-escalation and Gradual Normalization

Sustained Gaza ceasefire durability, combined with continued broader regional de-escalation in the Iran-Israel dynamic and potentially renewed diplomatic engagement specifically addressing Houthi maritime security guarantees, produces genuine, verified security improvement sufficient for insurance markets to meaningfully reduce war-risk premiums. Carriers gradually restore Suez service frequency over an extended 18-to-24-month timeline, achieving substantial though likely not complete normalization by late 2027, consistent with industry's most optimistic documented projections.

Scenario Four: Permanent Bifurcation

Regardless of security trajectory, the global shipping industry's accumulated structural adaptations — long-term charter agreements incorporating Cape routing assumptions, redeployed fleet allocations, and a more general "lessons learned" risk-aversion culture around Red Sea exposure — produce a permanent bifurcation in global shipping patterns, with a meaningful and durable share of traffic continuing Cape routing indefinitely even after substantial security improvement, given that the option value of route diversification itself has become a permanent feature of carrier risk management strategy following this crisis.

Intelligence Forecast

Based on current trajectories, Global Chanakya's assessment for the next twelve to eighteen months centers on four core judgments.

First, the Gaza ceasefire's durability — not any independent Yemen-specific development — will remain the single most important variable determining whether Red Sea shipping attacks resume, given the Houthis' explicit, repeated conditioning of their maritime campaign on the broader Gaza conflict's status.

Second, even in scenarios of continued attack pause, genuine shipping normalization will likely remain incomplete through 2027, given the structural, multi-year adaptations the industry has already made and the inherently asymmetric risk calculation facing carriers and insurers weighing modest cost savings against catastrophic tail-risk exposure.

Third, the broader Iran-Israel-US conflict trajectory will continue functioning as a meaningful overlay risk on top of the Gaza-specific dynamic, given the Houthis' demonstrated willingness to activate as a forward platform for Iran's broader regional confrontation independent of the original Gaza-solidarity framing that initiated the crisis.

Fourth, structural shipping industry adaptations — fleet redeployment, alternative corridor investment, and revised risk management frameworks — will likely persist as durable features of global trade architecture regardless of how the underlying security situation eventually resolves, representing one of the crisis's most consequential and least reversible long-term legacies.

Final Strategic Takeaway

The Red Sea crisis will likely be remembered, in retrospect, less as a story about Yemen or even about the broader Gaza-Iran-Israel conflict that triggered it, and more as the defining case study of the early 2020s for how thoroughly a single, geographically concentrated, asymmetric threat can reshape the architecture of global trade — not temporarily, but in ways that persist well beyond the immediate security trigger itself. Two and a half years after the first Houthi missile struck a commercial vessel in the Red Sea, attack frequency has collapsed to a fraction of its peak, and yet global shipping has not gone home.

That gap between reduced threat and persistent disruption is the single most important fact about this crisis, and it carries a sobering lesson for how the global trading system should think about chokepoint security going forward: once confidence in a critical artery's safety is broken, restoring it takes considerably longer, and requires considerably more verified certainty, than breaking it ever did.

For policymakers, shipping executives, and strategic planners across the Indo-Pacific, Middle East, and beyond, the Red Sea crisis offers a clear, uncomfortable template: a determined, asymmetric actor controlling the right strip of coastline can impose costs on the global economy that persist for years, regardless of how much conventional military force is arrayed against them, and regardless of how quickly the original triggering conflict eventually de-escalates. Whether the Bab el-Mandeb genuinely returns to normalcy by 2027, or whether this crisis settles into a permanent, structural feature of how global trade routes itself, will depend less on Yemen's internal politics than on whether the broader Middle East — Gaza, Iran, Israel, and the entire fragile architecture connecting them — finally finds a stability it has not achieved in over two years of trying.

title: Hezbollah vs Israel: What Comes After the 2026 War
content:
Hezbollah vs Israel: What Comes After the 2026 War

Lebanon has just lived through the most destructive chapter of its conflict with Israel since the 2006 war — and in some respects, the most destructive since 1982. Between March and June 2026, what began as a retaliatory missile barrage following the killing of Iran's Supreme Leader spiraled into a five-division Israeli ground invasion, the demolition of bridges across the Litani River, a single day of bombing that Lebanese officials now call "Black Wednesday," and a death toll that climbed past four thousand. A ceasefire now technically holds. Direct Israel-Lebanon negotiations, the first since 1983, are underway in Washington. And yet the single question that triggered this entire war — what happens to Hezbollah's weapons — remains as unresolved today as it was when the fighting started.

This is the genuine state of the Hezbollah-Israel conflict heading into the second half of 2026: not a frozen rivalry awaiting some future flashpoint, but an active, still-smoldering war whose underlying dispute has outlasted three ceasefires, two governments' disarmament plans, and a regional war against Hezbollah's own patron. Understanding where this goes next requires understanding exactly how fragile the current calm actually is.

Executive Summary

The Hezbollah-Israel conflict, rooted in Hezbollah's 1982 founding as an Iran-backed resistance movement against Israel's occupation of southern Lebanon, has cycled through several escalation phases since October 2023, when Hezbollah began firing on Israel in declared solidarity with Hamas. A year of cross-border exchanges culminated in Israel's October 2024 invasion of southern Lebanon and the assassination of longtime Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah, followed by a November 2024 US- and France-brokered ceasefire under which Lebanon's government committed to disarming Hezbollah south of the Litani River and handing the area to the Lebanese Armed Forces (LAF).

That ceasefire never fully held. Israel conducted more than 10,000 strikes against Lebanon in the year that followed, citing continued Hezbollah rearmament, while Hezbollah rebuilt portions of its military infrastructure despite Lebanon's September 2025 disarmament plan and the LAF's January 2026 announcement that it had achieved a "state monopoly on arms" south of the Litani. The fragile equilibrium collapsed entirely following the February 28, 2026, joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran, which killed Iran's Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei. Hezbollah, declaring solidarity with its principal patron, launched its first sustained rocket and drone barrage against Israel in over a year. Israel responded with an air campaign and, from March 16, a full ground invasion deploying five divisions — the most significant Israeli military operation in Lebanon since 1982.

The resulting war killed more than four thousand people in Lebanon and displaced over a million — roughly one in five Lebanese — before a US-brokered ceasefire, renewed and extended by President Donald Trump, took hold in mid-June 2026. Israeli forces remain deployed in southern Lebanon. Direct Israel-Lebanon negotiations, described as historic given they represent the first formal bilateral talks since the failed 1983 May 17 Agreement, are underway in Washington, centered on the unresolved core dispute: Israel's demand for complete Hezbollah disarmament as a precondition for any lasting peace, against Hezbollah's refusal to surrender weapons while Israeli troops remain on Lebanese soil. With Lebanon's parliamentary elections looming, the window for resolving this standoff before it potentially reignites into renewed conflict is widely assessed as narrow.

Background

Hezbollah emerged in 1982 amid Israel's invasion and subsequent eighteen-year occupation of southern Lebanon, organized and trained with direct support from Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and built around an explicit ideological commitment to armed resistance against Israel, allegiance to Iran's supreme leader, and the eventual establishment of an Islamic government — though in practice the group evolved into Lebanon's most powerful political and military actor within a fragile multi-confessional state, blending social service provision, electoral participation, and a parallel, Iran-backed military structure that for decades operated independently of and more capably than Lebanon's own national army.

Israel's 2000 withdrawal from southern Lebanon did not end the conflict; it merely changed its character into one of periodic, lower-intensity confrontation, most significantly the devastating 2006 Lebanon War, which ended in a UN-brokered ceasefire under Security Council Resolution 1701 that called for Hezbollah's disarmament south of the Litani River — a provision that, like its 2024 successor, was never genuinely implemented. Hezbollah used the subsequent years to dramatically expand its arsenal, reportedly accumulating well over 100,000 rockets and missiles at its pre-2023 peak, while also deploying fighters to Syria from 2011 onward in support of Bashar al-Assad's government during the Syrian civil war — an intervention that built genuine combat experience but also generated significant domestic Lebanese and broader Arab criticism.

The current conflict cycle began the day after Hamas's October 7, 2023, attack on Israel, when Hezbollah opened a so-called "support front," firing rockets and artillery into northern Israel in declared solidarity with Gaza. A year of escalating cross-border exchanges, displacing tens of thousands of civilians on both sides of the border, culminated in September 2024 with one of Israel's most significant intelligence and military operations against the group: the simultaneous detonation of thousands of Hezbollah communication devices, followed by the assassination of Hezbollah's longtime secretary-general Hassan Nasrallah and much of the group's senior military leadership, alongside the destruction of significant portions of its missile infrastructure. Israel's subsequent October 2024 ground invasion of southern Lebanon inflicted further heavy losses before a US- and France-brokered ceasefire took effect November 27, 2024.

That ceasefire's core terms — Israeli withdrawal from Lebanese territory, Hezbollah's relocation north of the Litani River, a mutual halt to attacks, and deployment of the LAF to assume security responsibility in the south — were honored only partially and asymmetrically. The United Nations documented over 10,000 Israeli air and ground attacks into Lebanon during the year following the ceasefire, which Israel justified as necessary strikes against continued Hezbollah rearmament efforts, killing more than 370 people according to Lebanese authorities even as Israel maintained the ceasefire was formally in effect. Hezbollah, for its part, worked to rebuild its military infrastructure in violation of the agreement's spirit, while consistently rejecting calls to disarm north of the Litani, arguing the ceasefire's disarmament provisions applied exclusively to the area south of the river.

Current Situation

The 2026 War: From Retaliation to Invasion

The fragile November 2024 ceasefire collapsed entirely in early 2026, triggered by events far beyond Lebanon's own borders. On February 28, 2026, the United States and Israel launched a joint military campaign against Iran, killing Iran's Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei in the opening strikes — an extraordinary escalation against Hezbollah's principal regional patron and the architect of the broader "Axis of Resistance" network the group belongs to. Hezbollah's secretary-general Naim Qassem, who had assumed leadership following Nasrallah's 2024 assassination, vowed retaliation, declaring the group would not abandon "the field of honor and resistance," and Hezbollah launched its first sustained missile and drone barrage against Israel in over a year, striking an Israeli military site in Haifa among other targets.

Israel's response was immediate and overwhelming. A sustained air campaign across Lebanon began within days, and on March 16, 2026, Israeli ground forces invaded southern Lebanon, eventually deploying five full divisions — a scale of commitment representing Israel's most significant military operation inside Lebanese territory since the 1982 invasion. Hezbollah responded with what remained of its missile and drone capability, firing as many as 2,000 rockets into Israel over the following weeks even as its degraded post-2024 arsenal limited the campaign's scale compared to the group's pre-2023 capability. Israel destroyed the main bridges crossing the Litani River specifically to sever southern Lebanon from resupply and reinforcement from the north, while Israeli forces fought a sustained battle for control of the southern town of Bint Jbeil, a historic Hezbollah stronghold.

The war's human cost mounted rapidly and severely. More than 4,000 people were killed in Lebanon from Israeli strikes, and over one million people — more than twenty percent of Lebanon's total population — were displaced. The single most devastating episode came on April 8, 2026, a day Lebanese officials have since labeled "Black Wednesday," when Israel conducted its heaviest strikes of the entire war, killing more than 350 people in attacks that drew international condemnation from the UN, EU, UK, and France. UN human rights officials raised explicit questions about international law violations given strikes on civilian commercial districts without prior warning, while documented patterns across the campaign — including high child casualty figures and widespread displacement — have prompted broader characterizations of potential war crimes by multiple monitoring organizations.

The Fragile Ceasefire and Historic Direct Talks

A US-brokered ceasefire took effect April 16, 2026, subsequently extended by President Trump even as Israeli forces remained deployed in southern Lebanon and sporadic exchanges of fire continued. A further agreement reached June 3, 2026, renewed the ceasefire and established so-called "pilot zones" — though Hezbollah rejected the specific Washington-negotiated deal the following day, demanding instead a comprehensive ceasefire paired with complete Israeli withdrawal from Lebanese territory. Lebanese Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri, a longtime power broker between Hezbollah and the Lebanese state, proposed a simultaneous withdrawal of both Hezbollah and Israeli forces from south of the Litani combined with a full ceasefire — a framework that has not yet been formally accepted by either side.

The broader regional context shifted further on June 7, when an Israeli strike in southern Beirut killed two people; Iran, citing this strike alongside an ongoing US naval blockade, launched missiles toward Israel, prompting renewed Israeli strikes on Iranian territory. On June 15, Pakistan announced that the US and Iran had agreed to cease all military operations, including specifically in Lebanon, formally ending the broader 2026 Iran war — though Israel stated explicitly that it would maintain its forces inside Lebanese territory regardless of this broader regional de-escalation.

Despite this turbulent backdrop, a genuinely historic diplomatic development has emerged: direct, formal bilateral negotiations between Israel and Lebanon, the first since the failed May 17, 1983, agreement collapsed under Syrian and domestic Lebanese pressure decades ago. These talks, opened under US mediation, are addressing border demarcation and the framework for a comprehensive security agreement — representing a genuine, if fragile, diplomatic breakthrough even as the conflict's core underlying dispute remains entirely unresolved.

The Disarmament Standoff

Hezbollah's disarmament — the issue that has overshadowed every ceasefire negotiation since November 2024 — remains the central, unresolved fault line. Lebanon's government, under President Joseph Aoun and Prime Minister Nawaf Salam, adopted a five-phase disarmament plan on September 5, 2025, beginning with the area south of the Litani River and proceeding progressively north and east. The Lebanese Armed Forces achieved a genuine, if contested, milestone on January 8, 2026, announcing it had established a "state monopoly on arms" south of the Litani in an "effective and tangible way" — a significant achievement representing the first time in roughly four decades that the LAF, rather than Hezbollah, held primary security control over this historically contested territory, with deployments exceeding 9,000 soldiers.

Lebanon's government subsequently announced in February 2026 that completing phase two — disarming Hezbollah's arsenals between the Litani and Awali Rivers — would require at least four additional months, extendable depending on available capabilities and the severity of continued Israeli attacks. Hezbollah's leadership, including both Qassem and Deputy Head of the Political Council Mahmoud Qamati, has consistently and explicitly rejected this entire framework, with Qassem characterizing the disarmament focus as a "grave sin" that serves Israeli aggression's goals, and warning that any attempt to forcibly confront Hezbollah would mean "no life" for Lebanon.

The eruption of full-scale war in March 2026 effectively froze the disarmament process entirely. Military and political analysts now widely agree that disarmament cannot meaningfully proceed amid active fighting, for both practical and political reasons: Hezbollah's elite Radwan Force units have been directly engaging Israeli troops on Lebanese territory throughout the war, and the LAF's task of accessing Hezbollah's remaining weapons caches — concentrated, according to Lebanese military sources, in deep, difficult-to-access valleys north of the Litani River, precisely the area phase two was meant to address — has become considerably more dangerous given continued Israeli strikes in those same areas, including strikes that have killed Lebanese soldiers even during the nominal ceasefire period.

A Lebanese analyst closely associated with Hezbollah, Qassem Kassir, articulated the structural problem starkly: with Israeli ground troops continuing to occupy positions inside Lebanese territory, "no one can implement the government's decision" to enforce Hezbollah's disarmament, because any continued Israeli occupation risks generating renewed armed resistance — whether from Hezbollah itself or potentially from other groups should Hezbollah actually disarm, leaving a vacuum.

The Domestic Lebanese Calculus

Beyond the military and diplomatic dimensions, recent survey research from King's College London's Cross-Border Conflict Evidence research program reveals a more complex domestic Lebanese picture than simple sectarian loyalty would suggest. Opposition to Hezbollah's disarmament runs remarkably high — above 70 percent — specifically within Hezbollah's southern Lebanon and Bekaa Valley strongholds, but the research found this opposition is driven less by straightforward security calculations about Israeli threat than by a deeper, more corrosive grievance: a fundamental loss of trust in the Lebanese state's capacity and willingness to protect or serve these communities, regardless of the disarmament question's specific merits.

This finding carries significant strategic implications. It suggests that purely military or economic pressure campaigns aimed at forcing Hezbollah's disarmament are unlikely to succeed on their own, because the underlying resistance is rooted in genuine state-legitimacy grievances rather than simple material dependence on Hezbollah's parallel social service network. As one Beirut resident interviewed for the research put it, articulating a demand for reciprocal legitimacy: a state that wishes to impose disarmament must first demonstrate it has "given me my rights" — electricity, services, basic governance functions — before it can credibly demand Hezbollah's communities surrender their primary source of both services and deterrent security.

Strategic Analysis

Israel's Calculated but Incomplete Victory

From a purely military standpoint, Israel has achieved substantial, even historic, degradation of Hezbollah's capability across the cumulative campaigns since October 2023: the elimination of Nasrallah and much of the group's senior military leadership, destruction of significant missile infrastructure, the pager and communications device operation that crippled internal coordination, and now a further round of intensive strikes and ground operations during the 2026 war. Hezbollah's capacity to threaten Israel has unquestionably been reduced from its pre-2023 peak.

Yet Israel's challenge, as Jerusalem Post analysis has bluntly noted, has never primarily been military degradation capacity — it has been the considerably harder task of shaping the political order that follows military success, an area where Israel's historical track record in Lebanon, dating to the strategic failures following its 1982 intervention, has been genuinely poor. The risk Israel now faces is repeating that exact historical pattern: achieving overwhelming tactical military success against Hezbollah while failing to translate that success into a durable political settlement that prevents the group's eventual military reconstitution, as occurred repeatedly following previous rounds of conflict including 2006.

Hezbollah's Survival Strategy: Strategic Patience Over Capitulation

Hezbollah's calculated refusal to disarm, even amid severe military degradation and the loss of its primary regional patron's supreme leader, reflects a coherent strategic logic rather than mere ideological intransigence. The group's leadership appears to be betting that Israel's continued military presence in southern Lebanon — which Israel has maintained even amid the ceasefire, retaining control of five strategic border posts — provides sufficient ongoing justification for continued "resistance" framing to sustain both internal Hezbollah cohesion and broader Shiite community support, even as that same continued occupation simultaneously undermines the Lebanese government's capacity to credibly demand Hezbollah's disarmament as a sovereign, rather than externally imposed, decision.

This is a genuinely difficult bind for all parties involved. Hezbollah's position effectively holds Lebanon's broader stability hostage to Israeli withdrawal terms Israel has shown no clear willingness to fully meet, while Israel's continued partial occupation provides Hezbollah with precisely the narrative ammunition needed to resist the very disarmament process that occupation is nominally meant to incentivize.

Iran's Diminished but Persistent Patronage

The killing of Iran's Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei in the February 2026 strikes represents an extraordinary, unprecedented blow to the broader Iranian regional axis Hezbollah belongs to — arguably the single most significant decapitation strike against Iran's leadership structure in the Islamic Republic's history. Hezbollah's immediate decision to resume attacks on Israel specifically in solidarity with this loss, despite having maintained relative restraint for over a year previously even amid continued Israeli strikes, illustrates how deeply embedded Hezbollah's strategic identity remains within the broader Iranian-led resistance axis, regardless of the group's own severely degraded independent military capacity.

This raises a genuinely important structural question for the conflict's future trajectory: with Iran's own leadership structure now in flux following Khamenei's death and the broader 2026 war's devastating impact on Iranian military and nuclear infrastructure, Hezbollah's capacity to receive sustained resupply, financing, and strategic direction from Tehran faces meaningfully greater uncertainty than at any point in the group's history — a structural vulnerability that could shape Hezbollah's longer-term trajectory more decisively than any specific Lebanese domestic political development.

The Election Deadline

Lebanon's May 2026 parliamentary elections — repeatedly cited by Israeli and American analysts as a critical near-term deadline — represent a genuine inflection point for the entire disarmament project's political viability. Should Hezbollah and its allied parties perform strongly despite the group's military degradation and the devastating costs the 2026 war imposed on precisely the communities that form its electoral base, the disarmament process could lose whatever fragile domestic political momentum it has accumulated, given that continued progress fundamentally depends on the Lebanese government being perceived as pursuing genuine national sovereignty rather than functioning as an instrument of Israeli or American pressure.

Global Impact

A Template for Israel's Multi-Front Doctrine

The 2026 Lebanon war, conducted in direct conjunction with the broader US-Israeli strikes on Iran, illustrates an increasingly explicit Israeli strategic doctrine: treating Iran's regional proxy network — Hezbollah, the Houthis, Iraqi militias, and historically Hamas — not as separate, independently manageable threats, but as components of a single integrated adversary system whose various nodes can and should be struck in coordinated fashion when conditions allow. This doctrine, visible across Global Chanakya's parallel coverage of Yemen's Houthi dynamics and the broader Iran confrontation, represents a meaningful evolution in how Israel approaches its security environment, with significant implications for how future regional escalations are likely to unfold.

UNIFIL's Termination and the Peacekeeping Vacuum

The UN Security Council's September 2025 decision to terminate UNIFIL — the UN peacekeeping mission that had maintained a presence in southern Lebanon for decades — under direct pressure from Israel and the United States, with its mandate set to formally end no later than 2027, removes a long-standing, if imperfect, international buffering mechanism precisely as the security situation has deteriorated into outright war. This termination reflects broader skepticism, particularly within the Trump administration, about the value of long-running UN peacekeeping deployments that have failed to prevent recurring conflict, but it also removes independent international monitoring capacity at precisely the moment verification of ceasefire compliance and disarmament progress has become most critical.

Lebanon's Economic and Banking Collapse

Lebanon's underlying economic fragility — rooted in its collapsed banking sector, which has destroyed public trust and fostered a dollarized cash economy that both facilitates corruption and sustains parallel financial institutions like Hezbollah-linked exchange houses such as al-Qard al-Hassan — represents a critical, underappreciated dimension of the broader disarmament challenge. International policy analysts have specifically identified addressing this informal financial infrastructure, alongside providing credible government alternatives for Shiite communities currently dependent on Hezbollah-run institutions, as essential complements to any military or political disarmament strategy; Lebanon's parliament approved a $250 million World Bank reconstruction loan in December 2025 as an initial, if clearly insufficient, step in this direction.

Implications for the Broader Axis of Resistance

Hezbollah's trajectory carries direct relevance for understanding the broader trajectory of Iran's regional proxy network following the devastating 2026 war against Iran itself. Hezbollah's continued, if severely degraded, defiance — refusing disarmament even amid catastrophic losses and its patron's decapitation — illustrates the resilience embedded in these movements' ideological and organizational structures, a resilience that mirrors patterns Global Chanakya has separately documented regarding the Houthis' continued operational capability despite years of Saudi, American, and Israeli military pressure.

Risk Assessment

High-Probability Risks

  • Continued ceasefire violations short of full war resumption: Given the documented pattern of over 10,000 Israeli strikes during the previous ceasefire period and continued exchanges even after the April and June 2026 ceasefire agreements, further sporadic violations and localized strikes are highly likely to continue.
  • Continued stalled disarmament north of the Litani: Given the practical and political obstacles documented by Lebanese military sources, genuine progress on phase two of the disarmament plan — covering the area between the Litani and Awali Rivers — is highly unlikely to proceed meaningfully in the near term absent a fundamental shift in the security situation.
  • Continued Israeli occupation of border positions: Given Israel's explicit statements regarding maintaining forces in Lebanon despite the broader Iran war's conclusion, continued Israeli retention of strategic border positions inside Lebanese territory remains highly probable for the foreseeable future.

Moderate-Probability Risks

  • Renewed large-scale escalation before Lebanon's elections: Given the high stakes both sides attach to the electoral outcome and the fragility of the current ceasefire architecture, a moderate-probability risk exists of renewed significant escalation in the run-up to Lebanon's parliamentary elections, potentially involving either preemptive Israeli strikes aimed at degrading Hezbollah's electoral position or Hezbollah-initiated attacks aimed at demonstrating continued relevance to its base.
  • Strong Hezbollah-aligned electoral performance derailing disarmament: Given documented opposition to disarmament exceeding 70 percent within Hezbollah's core constituencies, a moderate-probability risk exists of an electoral outcome that effectively ends the current disarmament process's political viability.
  • Iranian resupply attempts triggering renewed strikes: Given Hezbollah's demonstrated rearmament pattern following the 2024 ceasefire, a moderate-probability risk exists of renewed Iranian resupply efforts — however constrained by Iran's own post-war degradation — triggering further significant Israeli preemptive strikes.

Lower-Probability but High-Impact Risks

  • Full Lebanese state collapse or civil conflict: While forced disarmament carries genuine risk of triggering conflict with Hezbollah's Shia community base or fracturing the LAF itself, given the army's own significant Shiite composition, a complete Lebanese state collapse or internal civil conflict remains a lower-probability outcome given the LAF's demonstrated institutional cohesion through the current crisis.
  • Comprehensive Israel-Lebanon peace agreement: Despite the genuinely historic nature of current direct talks, a comprehensive, formal peace agreement resolving border demarcation, security arrangements, and the disarmament question simultaneously remains a lower-probability near-term outcome given the depth of unresolved core disputes, though it represents a meaningfully higher-probability outcome than at almost any prior point in the conflict's history.
  • Hezbollah's complete organizational collapse: Despite severe military and leadership losses, Hezbollah's demonstrated organizational resilience, continued political representation, and deep social service infrastructure make complete organizational collapse a lower-probability outcome compared to continued, if diminished, persistence as a weakened but still functioning political and residual military actor.

Future Scenarios

Scenario Analysis — the following projections are illustrative simulations based on current trajectories, not confirmed events.

Scenario One: Frozen Conflict with Periodic Flare-Ups (Most Likely)

The current ceasefire holds in a degraded, frequently-violated form, with Israel retaining its remaining border positions and continuing periodic strikes against perceived Hezbollah rearmament efforts, while disarmament north of the Litani remains effectively frozen absent a fundamental political breakthrough. Direct Israel-Lebanon talks continue at a technical level, producing incremental progress on border demarcation without resolving the core disarmament dispute. Lebanon's May elections proceed with Hezbollah-aligned parties retaining meaningful, if somewhat reduced, parliamentary representation, sufficient to block any forced disarmament timeline.

Scenario Two: Comprehensive Settlement

Building on the historic direct talks framework, sustained US mediation produces a genuine comprehensive agreement: full Israeli withdrawal from remaining Lebanese border positions, paired with verified Hezbollah disarmament north of the Litani conducted under Lebanese Armed Forces authority with international monitoring support, alongside formal border demarcation resolving longstanding disputed points. This would represent a genuinely historic breakthrough, though it requires both sides accepting politically costly concessions — Israeli withdrawal without complete verified disarmament guarantees, and Hezbollah accepting disarmament without unconditional Israeli withdrawal guaranteed in advance.

Scenario Three: Renewed Major War

Continued Hezbollah rearmament efforts, however constrained by degraded Iranian support capacity, combined with continued Israeli strikes and occupation, eventually trigger a third major war cycle within the current decade — potentially even more devastating than the 2026 conflict given Hezbollah's accumulated grievances and Israel's demonstrated willingness to escalate to five-division ground operations. This scenario would likely further devastate Lebanon's already fragile economy and statehood while testing whether Hezbollah retains sufficient organizational and military coherence to mount meaningful resistance after the cumulative losses of 2024 and 2026.

Scenario Four: Hezbollah's Political Transformation

Sustained military pressure, Iranian patron degradation, and genuine Lebanese government investment in alternative governance and economic infrastructure for Shiite communities gradually shift Hezbollah's trajectory toward a more conventional political party model, progressively shedding military capability in exchange for guaranteed political representation and resourcing — a slow-motion transformation more likely to unfold over years rather than months, but one increasingly discussed by Lebanese and international analysts as the most sustainable long-term resolution to the underlying dispute.

Intelligence Forecast

Based on current trajectories, Global Chanakya's assessment for the next twelve to eighteen months centers on four core judgments.

First, Lebanon's May 2026 elections will function as the single most consequential near-term variable shaping the disarmament process's political viability, with a strong Hezbollah-aligned electoral performance likely to effectively stall further progress regardless of continued international pressure.

Second, Israel's continued retention of border positions inside Lebanese territory will remain the primary structural obstacle to genuine disarmament progress, given the well-documented dynamic whereby continued occupation undermines the Lebanese government's capacity to present disarmament as a sovereign rather than externally-imposed decision.

Third, Hezbollah's capacity for sustained reconstitution will depend significantly on Iran's own post-war recovery trajectory following the unprecedented loss of its Supreme Leader and broader military degradation, making Iran's internal succession and strategic recovery process — a topic Global Chanakya will continue tracking separately — a critical, somewhat external variable shaping Hezbollah's longer-term capability.

Fourth, the historic direct Israel-Lebanon negotiations represent a genuine structural shift with potential long-term significance extending beyond the immediate disarmament dispute, but near-term comprehensive resolution remains unlikely given the depth of unresolved core issues and the domestic political constraints facing both governments.

Final Strategic Takeaway

The Hezbollah-Israel conflict has reached a genuinely unusual moment: a militarily devastated Hezbollah, a regionally weakened Iran, an Israel demonstrating unprecedented willingness to invade Lebanon at scale, and yet — despite all of this — no closer to a durable resolution of the conflict's core dispute than at any point in the past two decades. Military force has degraded Hezbollah's capability dramatically. It has not, and likely cannot on its own, resolve the underlying political and sovereignty questions that have allowed Hezbollah to persist as Lebanon's most powerful non-state actor for over four decades.

The uncomfortable truth animating this entire conflict is that disarmament was never purely a military problem requiring purely a military solution — it is fundamentally a question of whether the Lebanese state can become legitimate and capable enough, in the eyes of its own Shiite citizens, to credibly claim a monopoly on force that Hezbollah has held for four decades.

Israel can continue striking, continue occupying, and continue degrading Hezbollah's military infrastructure indefinitely, but absent genuine investment in Lebanese state capacity, economic recovery, and the kind of reciprocal legitimacy King's College London's research identified as the actual driver of disarmament resistance, each cycle of conflict risks simply resetting the clock rather than resolving anything. The historic direct talks now underway in Washington represent the most promising diplomatic opening this conflict has seen in over four decades — but promising openings have come before, in 1983 and at multiple points since, only to collapse under the weight of exactly the dynamics still visible today: an occupied population resistant to disarming under occupation, a state too weak to fill the vacuum disarmament would create, and external patrons on both sides whose interests do not always align neatly with genuine Lebanese stability. Watch Lebanon's May elections, watch Israel's border posts, and watch Iran's post-Khamenei trajectory. Those three variables, more than any single battlefield development, will determine whether 2026's devastating war becomes the conflict's final chapter or merely its latest one.

title: Sahel Crisis 2026: Africa's Expanding Jihadist War
content:
Sahel Crisis 2026: Africa's Expanding Jihadist War

There is a region on this planet right now where jihadist groups control more territory than at any point since the Islamic State's territorial peak in Iraq and Syria, where capital cities have faced fuel blockades and coordinated assaults on their own military headquarters, and where the world's most active terrorism theater operates with almost no sustained Western military presence and minimal global media coverage. That region is the Sahel — the semi-arid belt stretching across Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger — and in 2026, after more than a decade of French intervention, UN peacekeeping, military coups, and a wholesale pivot to Russian security partnership, the insurgency these states were supposed to defeat is winning.

The numbers alone should command global attention: nearly 9,400 deaths from security incidents across the central Sahel in 2025 alone, a capital city's military command structure attacked in broad daylight, an international airport stormed by militants, and a UN assessment that the Sahel now accounts for the largest share of terrorism-related deaths anywhere on earth. This report examines why the Sahel crisis deserves to be understood not as a regional counterinsurgency problem, but as a strategic case study in state collapse, great-power realignment, and the limits of military-first approaches to ungoverned space — with implications that already extend from West Africa's Atlantic coast to Europe's migration crisis and the broader contest between Western and Russian influence across the continent.

Executive Summary

The Sahel crisis centers on a sustained, expanding jihadist insurgency across Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger, driven principally by two rival groups: Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM), the dominant al-Qaeda-affiliated coalition, and the Islamic State Sahel Province (ISSP), its rival and occasional battlefield competitor. Both groups have expanded dramatically in territorial control, operational sophistication, and geographic reach since military juntas seized power in all three core Sahelian states between 2020 and 2023, expelled French and UN forces, and pivoted toward Russian security partnership through the Wagner Group and its successor, Africa Corps.

That pivot has not worked. Security outcomes have deteriorated sharply since the juntas took power, with jihadist territorial control and attack frequency rising across rural Mali, northern Burkina Faso, and the Mali-Niger-Burkina Faso tri-border area. The crisis reached a genuine inflection point on April 25, 2026, when a coordinated JNIM offensive — notably executed in tactical alliance with the Tuareg separatist Azawad Liberation Front (FLA), an unusual convergence between jihadist and ethno-nationalist actors — struck multiple targets across Mali simultaneously, including the capital Bamako, nearby Kati, the northern strongholds of Gao and Kidal, and the central city of Séveré, killing Mali's Defense Minister Sadio Camara among other senior officials. The attacks exposed severe Malian military intelligence failures and confirmed what regional analysts have warned for months: Mali now faces genuine risk of territorial fragmentation.

Niger and Burkina Faso face parallel deterioration. Niger declared a "general mobilization" in December 2025 granting sweeping powers to requisition civilians and resources, after ISSP staged an unprecedented attack on Niamey's international airport in February 2026. Burkina Faso's junta has moved to dissolve all political parties, mirroring a similar move by Niger's General Abdourahamane Tiani, who launched a five-year transition mandate in March 2026. Both JNIM and ISSP have meanwhile begun pushing south toward the Gulf of Guinea, with deadly attacks now reaching Benin, Togo, and Côte d'Ivoire — a southward expansion that threatens to transform a central Sahelian insurgency into a continent-spanning West African security crisis.

Background

The Sahel crisis traces its modern origins to two compounding shocks roughly contemporaneous in the early 2010s. The 2011 NATO-backed overthrow of Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi triggered Libya's collapse into prolonged civil conflict, flooding the wider Sahara-Sahel region with weapons looted from Libyan military stockpiles and fighters — including Tuareg mercenaries who had served in Gaddafi's forces — who returned to northern Mali heavily armed and radicalized. This influx directly enabled the 2012 Tuareg separatist uprising in northern Mali, which jihadist groups including al-Qaeda in the Islamic Maghreb (AQIM) rapidly exploited and ultimately hijacked, seizing control of major northern Malian cities including Timbuktu and Gao before a French-led military intervention, Operation Serval, pushed them back in early 2013.

France's subsequent, larger Operation Barkhane, launched in 2014, represented a sustained, multi-year counterinsurgency commitment across the wider Sahel, eventually involving thousands of French troops alongside UN peacekeeping forces (MINUSMA) and various international partners. Despite this substantial investment, the insurgency not only persisted but expanded, spreading from Mali into Burkina Faso by 2015 and Niger by 2017, as jihadist groups exploited chronic governance weaknesses, ethnic tensions, and popular grievances against both insurgents and the often heavy-handed, abuse-prone counterinsurgency operations conducted by national militaries and their foreign partners.

In March 2017, several Mali-based jihadist factions merged to form Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM), pledging formal allegiance to al-Qaeda and explicitly setting a goal of unifying Islamist insurgencies across Mali while confronting the French-led international coalition. A rival force, the Islamic State Sahel Province (ISSP), emerged from a separate lineage rooted in the tri-border area between Mali, Niger, and Burkina Faso, competing with — and periodically fighting directly against — JNIM even as both groups expanded their respective territorial footprints across the region.

The decisive political rupture came through a wave of military coups: Mali in August 2020 and again in May 2021, Burkina Faso in January and September 2022, and Niger in July 2023. Each coup was driven substantially by popular frustration with civilian governments' failure to contain the jihadist insurgency despite years of French and international support, and each brought to power military juntas who built their legitimacy explicitly around anti-French, sovereigntist nationalism.
