All three governments subsequently expelled French forces — France's presence in Chad, its last regional foothold, ended in late 2024 when N'Djamena itself ordered French troops to leave — and the United States lost its drone bases and special operations presence in Niger in 2024, closing a critical regional intelligence and counterterrorism hub. In their place, all three juntas invited Russian security support, first through the Wagner Group beginning with Mali in late 2021, and subsequently through Wagner's rebranded successor, Africa Corps, following Yevgeny Prigozhin's August 2023 death.

The three juntas formalized their political and security realignment by founding the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) in October 2023, a mutual defense pact that has since evolved into the foundation for full withdrawal from the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) — the regional bloc that had imposed sanctions on the juntas and threatened military intervention in Niger's case — formalizing a genuine geopolitical bloc realignment away from the traditional West African regional order.

Current Situation

Mali: The April 25 Inflection Point

Mali's security trajectory reached a genuinely alarming new threshold on April 25, 2026, when JNIM, operating in tactical coordination with the Tuareg separatist Azawad Liberation Front (FLA), launched coordinated attacks against military and government installations across multiple Malian cities simultaneously — Bamako and nearby Kati, the northern strongholds of Gao and Kidal, and the central city of Séveré. The attacks killed Mali's Defense Minister Sadio Camara, whose state funeral was held in Bamako on April 30, alongside other senior military and government officials.

What makes this assault strategically significant extends well beyond its scale. The collaboration between JNIM, a Salafi-jihadist movement seeking sharia-based governance, and the FLA, a secular Tuareg ethno-nationalist movement seeking autonomy or independence for northern Mali's Azawad region, represents a genuinely unusual convergence between historically contradictory ideological projects. Regional analysts describe this as a pragmatic alliance of convenience against a shared adversary — Mali's military junta — rather than genuine ideological alignment, but the practical military effect is the same regardless of motive: a more coordinated, more capable opposition to the Malian state than either actor could mount independently.

The attack's aftermath has confirmed what analysts had warned for months. The assault exposed severe Malian military intelligence failures and what the Stimson Center has bluntly characterized as the incompetence of Malian Armed Forces in countering the insurgency. Mali now faces genuine, serious risk of territorial fragmentation as militant groups continue expanding territorial control while state authority correspondingly weakens. Violence has spread into Mali's southwest, a region historically more insulated from the worst fighting, while populations in Timbuktu, Gao, Mopti, and Ménaka continue facing recurrent attacks, abductions, and forced resource extraction by armed groups.

Compounding the military crisis, JNIM has waged sustained economic warfare against the Malian state, most dramatically through a months-long fuel and transport blockade on Bamako that began in September 2025, alongside a sweeping embargo imposed on the cities of Kayes and Nioro du Sahel as part of coordinated offensives spanning multiple regions. Mali's government negotiated a hostage release deal with JNIM intended to produce a pause in attacks on fuel convoys through at least May 2026 — itself a remarkable indicator of how far the balance of leverage has shifted, with a sovereign government negotiating directly with the jihadist movement besieging its own capital.

Niger: General Mobilization and Direct Capital Attacks

Niger's security situation has deteriorated with particular severity in the southwest Tillabéri region, which ACLED data identifies as the deadliest region across the entire Central Sahel in 2025, driven primarily by ISSP, followed by Nigerien military operations themselves, then JNIM. Suspected militants killed over fifty civilians across two major attacks in early 2026 alone, and the pattern of civilian targeting in the region has reached levels serious enough that Nigerien military drone strikes intended to counter the insurgency have themselves killed scores of civilians — strikes independent monitors assess likely amount to war crimes.

The Nigerien military's response has been to escalate dramatically. In December 2025, the government declared a "general mobilization," granting sweeping powers to requisition civilians and resources for reinforced counterinsurgency operations — an extraordinary measure reflecting the severity of the threat assessment driving Niamey's response. Despite this mobilization, ISSP achieved what represents one of the insurgency's most symbolically significant operations to date: in February 2026, the group launched an unprecedented, high-profile attack directly on Niamey's international airport, demonstrating a capability to strike at the heart of the capital's critical infrastructure that would have seemed implausible even a year earlier. A subsequent March attack targeted Tahoua Airport, reinforcing the pattern of ISSP specifically prioritizing high-value infrastructure targets as part of a deliberate strategy of economic warfare and symbolic state delegitimization.

Politically, Niger's junta under General Abdourahamane Tiani has moved to fully consolidate power, dissolving all political parties in late March 2026 and launching a formal five-year transition mandate — a move that closes off any near-term pathway back toward civilian governance while the security situation continues deteriorating.

Burkina Faso: Coordinated Offensives and Political Closure

Burkina Faso has experienced what ACLED describes as a particularly sharp escalation in JNIM operational reach. In February 2026, JNIM launched a week-long series of coordinated attacks across eastern and northern Burkina Faso, demonstrating mobility and operational sophistication across large swathes of territory that underscore the group's growing capacity to operate at scale rather than through isolated, localized strikes. JNIM's military approach increasingly combines swarming assaults using motorcycle and vehicle-borne assault squads, armed drones, and suicide car bombs — a tactical evolution that proved effective enough in 2025 to overrun multiple provincial capitals.

Burkina Faso's domestic counterinsurgency apparatus, centered on the Volunteers for the Defense of the Homeland (VDP) civilian defense force that had been central to junta leader Ibrahim Traoré's mobilization strategy, has suffered heavy losses and has been pushed into a largely defensive posture, significantly limiting the state's capacity to hold or reclaim contested territory. Politically, Burkina Faso's junta followed Niger's pattern almost precisely, announcing measures to dissolve all political parties in late January 2026 — a near-simultaneous consolidation of authoritarian control across both states that reflects a shared junta playbook: framing political closure as a necessary wartime measure even as the underlying security situation continues to worsen rather than improve.

The Drone Warfare Escalation

One of the most significant tactical developments reshaping the conflict's character is the rapid proliferation of armed drone use by both JNIM and ISSP. JNIM's use of armed drones rose from fewer than ten recorded strikes in 2024 to approximately eighty in 2025 — an eightfold increase in a single year that illustrates how quickly low-cost, commercially-derived drone technology has been weaponized and integrated into jihadist operational doctrine across the region. While drones remain a relatively small component of these groups' broader tactical repertoire compared to ground assaults and vehicle-borne attacks, their low cost, adaptability, and the practical difficulty of countering them with the limited air-defense capability available to Sahelian state militaries make them an increasingly serious and growing threat to military, civilian, and economic targets alike — directly mirroring the same drone-proliferation dynamic Global Chanakya has documented separately in Sudan's civil war.

The Russian Security Partnership's Limited Returns

Perhaps the most consequential strategic finding to emerge from the past two years of Sahelian security policy is the demonstrable failure of the Wagner-to-Africa Corps security partnership to deliver the outcomes juntas promised when they expelled French and Western forces in its favor. Africa Corps deployments, typically involving between 1,000 and 2,000 personnel per country, have provided presidential guard services, counterinsurgency support, and national force training — but multiple independent assessments confirm that jihadist territorial control and attack frequency have increased, not decreased, since the juntas took power and pivoted toward Russian partnership.

Africa Corps' more limited operational scope compared to Wagner's earlier, more expansive deployment has left large areas effectively unprotected, with the partnership's practical role increasingly narrowing toward securing fuel convoys and key supply routes — as seen in southern Mali, where Africa Corps support helped erode JNIM's Bamako blockade momentum toward the end of 2025 — rather than the broader territorial reconquest and counterinsurgency success the juntas had promised their populations as justification for the French expulsion.

Strategic Analysis

The Sovereignty Paradox

The Sahelian juntas built their domestic legitimacy almost entirely around a sovereigntist narrative: that French and Western military presence had failed to defeat the insurgency while perpetuating neo-colonial economic and political relationships, and that genuine African-led, Russian-partnered security solutions would succeed where Western intervention had not. This narrative carried genuine popular resonance — anti-French sentiment across the region was real and substantially grounded in legitimate grievances about the limited security returns from a decade of French military presence.

The strategic problem is that the empirical record since the juntas' consolidation directly contradicts their core promise. Security outcomes have deteriorated, not improved, across every meaningful metric: territorial control, attack frequency, civilian casualties, and economic disruption have all worsened since the French and UN withdrawal. This creates a genuine legitimacy paradox for the juntas: their founding justification was security delivery, and on that specific metric, they have demonstrably failed more comprehensively than the civilian governments and French partnership they replaced — yet having eliminated competitive political processes through party dissolution and extended transition mandates, none of the three governments currently faces any meaningful electoral accountability mechanism for this failure.

JNIM's Strategic Patience Versus ISSP's Aggressive Expansion

The two dominant jihadist actors pursue meaningfully different strategic approaches, a distinction with significant implications for how the conflict evolves. JNIM has demonstrated a degree of strategic patience and territorial governance sophistication — operating actual governance structures in controlled areas, including tax collection and sharia enforcement, suggesting a long-term state-building orientation rather than purely destructive insurgency. JNIM's leadership has reportedly expressed internal concern about expanding too rapidly beyond the core Sahel, fearing this could dilute organizational cohesion — even as individual commanders and rank-and-file fighters favor continued southward expansion given its recruitment and material benefits.

ISSP, by contrast, has pursued a more aggressively destructive approach, including documented mass atrocities against civilians used explicitly to assert territorial control in contested areas, alongside high-profile, symbolically loaded attacks against critical infrastructure like the Niamey and Tahoua airport assaults. This divergence reflects the two groups' different ideological lineages and strategic theories of victory: JNIM's al-Qaeda-aligned approach favoring gradual territorial and population control through hybrid coercion and governance, ISSP's Islamic State-aligned approach favoring more immediate, spectacular demonstrations of capability and willingness to use extreme violence.

The Southward Expansion Dilemma

JNIM's calculated, if internally contested, push toward coastal West Africa — with deadly attacks now documented in Benin, Côte d'Ivoire, and Togo since 2019, and Benin specifically recording nearly 70 percent more fatalities through the first eleven months of 2025 compared to the same period in 2024 — represents one of the most consequential strategic developments shaping the conflict's likely future trajectory. For JNIM, southward expansion offers genuine strategic value: access to new recruitment pools, fresh extortion and taxation revenue streams, and demonstration of the movement's continued momentum to both supporters and rivals.

For the coastal states themselves — Benin, Togo, Côte d'Ivoire, and Ghana — this expansion represents an entirely new category of security threat for governments with comparatively stronger institutional capacity than the central Sahelian juntas, but with far less accumulated counterinsurgency experience and infrastructure. Western security partners, having lost their primary Sahelian footholds, have explicitly pivoted toward an "over-the-horizon" approach prioritizing counterterrorism partnerships with these coastal states specifically to prevent jihadist expansion from consolidating into a second, even more difficult-to-reverse territorial foothold along the Gulf of Guinea.

The Humanitarian Funding Collapse

The Sahel crisis has been directly and severely compounded by sharp reductions in international humanitarian funding precisely as needs have intensified. World Food Programme officials have explicitly attributed deepening hunger and malnutrition across the region to reduced 2025 funding levels, warning that as needs outpace available resources, the risk of young people falling into desperation — and, implicitly, into recruitment by armed groups offering economic alternatives — correspondingly rises. In Mali specifically, reduced food rations have driven a 64 percent increase in famine conditions in some areas, with roughly 1.5 million vulnerable Malians facing acute food crisis risk, while Niger has been formally identified among countries facing a 2026 hunger alert.

Global Impact

Europe's Migration Pressure Valve

The Sahel functions as a critical transit corridor for migration flows toward Europe, with displaced populations and economic migrants moving through Mali, Niger, and onward through Libya toward Mediterranean crossing points — the same route documented by UNICEF as the primary pathway for unaccompanied minors arriving in Lampedusa, Italy. Continued Sahelian state fragmentation and the more than three million people already internally displaced across the central Sahel — with Burkina Faso alone hosting over two million IDPs — represents a sustained, likely growing source of migration pressure toward Europe, directly intersecting with European domestic political debates over migration policy that have reshaped electoral politics across the continent.

Russia's Africa Strategy Under Strain

The Sahel represents one of Russia's most prominent post-Wagner Africa Corps engagements, and the demonstrable failure of this security partnership to deliver improved outcomes carries broader implications for Moscow's wider African influence strategy at a moment when Russia is simultaneously expanding engagement elsewhere on the continent, including the new foothold reportedly being established in Madagascar. A sustained pattern of Russian security partnerships failing to deliver tangible counterinsurgency results, even as they succeed in displacing Western influence and securing access to regional resources and political alignment, raises genuine questions about the durability and ultimate strategic value of Moscow's broader African security-partnership model — questions other African governments considering similar partnerships are likely watching closely.

A Global Terrorism Epicenter

The Sahel's emergence as the world's most active center of jihadist violence — with the region driving the largest share of global terrorism-related deaths according to UN assessments — represents a structural shift in the global geography of Islamist militancy away from its earlier Middle Eastern and South Asian centers of gravity. This carries direct relevance for global counterterrorism strategy and resource allocation, as international attention and funding have historically lagged significantly behind the Sahel's actual threat severity compared to better-resourced and higher-profile theaters elsewhere.

Critical Mineral and Resource Implications

Mali, Niger, and the broader Sahel region hold significant mineral resources, including uranium reserves critical to global nuclear fuel supply chains and gold deposits that have become both a target of jihadist economic warfare and, in some documented cases, a direct funding source for armed groups through taxation and extortion of mining operations. Continued instability across this resource-rich but increasingly ungoverned territory carries direct implications for global critical mineral supply chain security, an increasingly prominent strategic concern given broader great-power competition over resource access.

Risk Assessment

High-Probability Risks

  • Continued Mali territorial fragmentation: Given the scale and coordination demonstrated in the April 25 attacks and the documented JNIM-FLA tactical alignment, continued erosion of Malian state territorial control is highly likely absent a fundamental shift in counterinsurgency approach or external support.
  • Continued southward jihadist expansion: Given JNIM's demonstrated strategic interest and documented attack pattern in Benin, Togo, and Côte d'Ivoire, continued expansion pressure into coastal West African states is highly probable through 2026 and beyond.
  • Worsening humanitarian conditions: Given chronic underfunding and continued insecurity disrupting agricultural production and aid access, further deterioration in food security and displacement figures across the central Sahel is highly likely.

Moderate-Probability Risks

  • Successful jihadist seizure of a major Sahelian city: Given the demonstrated capability shown in recent coordinated offensives and the weakening state of national militaries, a moderate-probability risk exists of JNIM or ISSP achieving sustained control of a significant population center beyond the smaller towns already affected.
  • Coastal state security crisis: Given accelerating attack frequency in Benin and the broader Gulf of Guinea border region, a moderate-probability risk exists of a serious security deterioration in one or more coastal states within the next twelve to eighteen months.
  • Further junta political instability: Given the gap between security promises and actual outcomes, a moderate-probability risk exists of internal military or popular unrest within one of the three core junta governments, with potential regional domino effects given the AES's interlinked political and security architecture.

Lower-Probability but High-Impact Risks

  • Complete state collapse in Mali, Burkina Faso, or Niger: While territorial fragmentation is increasingly likely, complete formal state collapse remains a lower-probability outcome given continued Africa Corps support and the juntas' demonstrated capacity to retain control of key urban centers and supply routes even amid broader rural territorial loss.
  • Direct AES-ECOWAS military confrontation: Despite the formal political rupture between the AES bloc and ECOWAS, direct military confrontation between the two blocs remains a lower-probability outcome given the absence of clear strategic benefit for either side and ECOWAS's demonstrated preference for continued mediation efforts.
  • JNIM-ISSP merger or formal ceasefire: Given the two groups' demonstrated rivalry and periodic direct conflict, a formal merger or sustained ceasefire between them remains unlikely, though continued tactical "outbidding" dynamics could still produce escalating violence even without direct cooperation.

Future Scenarios

Scenario Analysis — the following projections are illustrative simulations based on current trajectories, not confirmed events.

Scenario One: Continued Gradual Fragmentation (Most Likely)

The three core Sahelian juntas retain formal control of capital cities and major urban centers, supported by continued Africa Corps logistical and aerial assistance, while jihadist groups continue expanding control over rural areas, transit routes, and smaller population centers. JNIM and ISSP continue their southward expansion pressure into coastal states without yet achieving comparable territorial consolidation there. This scenario essentially extends the current trajectory: formal state sovereignty persisting in name while practical territorial control and population security continue eroding.

Scenario Two: Major Urban Center Falls

Continued JNIM or ISSP operational escalation, building on the demonstrated capability shown in the April 2026 Mali attacks and the Niamey airport assault, achieves sustained control of a significant Sahelian city beyond current contested towns — a development that would represent a genuine strategic inflection point, likely triggering renewed international attention, potential emergency external intervention discussions, and significant regional destabilization given the symbolic and practical importance of urban centers to state legitimacy claims.

Scenario Three: Coastal Crisis Triggers Renewed International Engagement

Accelerating jihadist expansion into Benin, Togo, or Côte d'Ivoire produces a security crisis serious enough to overcome these states' historical reluctance toward heavy international security partnership, triggering renewed, more substantial Western counterterrorism engagement focused specifically on preventing the coastal corridor's consolidation — potentially including expanded US, French, or other Western special operations and intelligence support explicitly structured to avoid the "boots on the ground" framing that proved politically toxic in the central Sahel.

Scenario Four: Negotiated Local Accommodation

Building on the precedent of Mali's hostage-release and fuel-convoy negotiation with JNIM, one or more Sahelian governments pursue more extensive negotiated accommodation with JNIM specifically — given its demonstrated governance orientation and relative strategic patience compared to ISSP — potentially including localized ceasefire arrangements or informal territorial accommodation in exchange for reduced attacks on critical infrastructure and population centers, even without formal political legitimacy being extended to the group.

Intelligence Forecast

Based on current trajectories, Global Chanakya's assessment for the next twelve to eighteen months centers on four core judgments.

First, Mali's trajectory following the April 25 attacks represents the single most important near-term indicator for the broader region, given the demonstrated JNIM-FLA tactical coordination and the exposed weaknesses in Malian military intelligence and counterinsurgency capacity — continued deterioration here is likely to set the broader regional tone more than developments in Niger or Burkina Faso individually.

Second, the Russia-Africa Corps security partnership will continue delivering limited, primarily defensive results — securing key supply routes and urban centers rather than achieving genuine counterinsurgency reversal — meaning the fundamental security trajectory across all three core states is unlikely to improve meaningfully absent a substantial strategic shift in approach.

Third, southward jihadist expansion into coastal West Africa will continue accelerating, making the Benin-Niger-Nigeria and broader Gulf of Guinea borderlands an increasingly critical region to monitor independently of the core Sahelian crisis, with genuine potential to reshape the conflict's geographic center of gravity over the coming several years.

Fourth, humanitarian conditions will continue deteriorating absent a substantial funding and access breakthrough, with continued risk that worsening food insecurity and displacement directly feed further jihadist recruitment, creating a self-reinforcing cycle between humanitarian collapse and security deterioration that neither military nor humanitarian interventions alone are likely to break.

Final Strategic Takeaway

The Sahel crisis offers one of the clearest contemporary illustrations of how a security narrative — French withdrawal as liberation, Russian partnership as solution, military rule as necessary wartime governance — can persist politically even as the empirical reality it claims to address grows demonstrably worse. The juntas that seized power across Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger promised their populations security their predecessors could not deliver. More than four years into that experiment, jihadist groups control more territory, conduct more sophisticated and far-reaching attacks, and pose a more severe threat to state survival than at any point during the French-led intervention era these juntas replaced.

What makes the Sahel crisis particularly dangerous in 2026 is not any single battlefield development, but the structural convergence of multiple reinforcing failures at once: military approaches that have not worked, political systems that have eliminated their own accountability mechanisms, humanitarian funding that has collapsed precisely when need has peaked, and jihadist groups sophisticated enough to exploit every one of these gaps simultaneously.

For the international community, the Sahel represents an uncomfortable test of whether sustained engagement with a region this volatile, this resource-significant, and this consequential for both European migration pressure and the broader global terrorism landscape can be maintained without falling into either the failed heavy-footprint interventionism of the Barkhane era or the current pattern of strategic neglect that has allowed this crisis to compound largely outside sustained global attention. Coastal West Africa is now the place to watch most closely — not because the central Sahel crisis is resolved, but because where JNIM and ISSP choose to push next will determine whether this remains a regional catastrophe or becomes a genuinely continental one.

title: Ethiopia-Tigray: The Horn of Africa's Next War?
content:
Ethiopia-Tigray: The Horn of Africa's Next War?

Four years ago, the guns in northern Ethiopia fell silent. The Pretoria Agreement, signed in November 2022, ended a war that had killed an estimated 600,000 people and displaced millions — a toll that placed it among the deadliest conflicts of the twenty-first century, fought almost entirely outside the world's sustained attention. The peace that followed was always fragile, built on disarmament provisions never fully honored, displaced populations never fully returned, and a power-sharing arrangement that satisfied no one completely. But it held, for a while.

It is no longer holding cleanly. In 2026, Ethiopia finds itself watching the same fault lines that produced the Tigray war reopen simultaneously: a fractured Tigrayan political leadership locked in its own internal power struggle, a federal government in Addis Ababa extending interim administrative rule by decree rather than elections, Eritrean forces reportedly visible again near the border for the first time in years, and a prime minister whose escalating rhetoric about reclaiming Red Sea access has begun to look, to a growing number of regional analysts, less like aspiration and more like preparation. This report examines why Ethiopia-Tigray tensions deserve to be understood not as a closed chapter, but as one of the most dangerous live fault lines in the Horn of Africa.

Executive Summary

The Tigray war that ran from November 2020 to November 2022 formally ended with the African Union-mediated Pretoria Agreement, which established an interim regional administration to govern Tigray pending elections and committed all parties to disarmament, the withdrawal of Amhara militia and Eritrean forces from occupied Tigrayan territory, and the return of displaced populations. Implementation has been incomplete on virtually every count. As of 2026, Amhara militias continue occupying significant portions of Western Tigray in defiance of the agreement, Eritrean troops remain present in parts of northern Tigray, and hundreds of thousands of displaced Tigrayans have not returned home.

Compounding this incomplete peace is a serious internal fracture within Tigrayan politics itself. In March 2025, a hardline faction of the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), led by party chairman Debretsion Gebremichael, executed what amounted to an internal coup, ousting the more conciliatory interim administration head Getachew Reda — who had signed the Pretoria Agreement and was viewed by hardliners as having capitulated — and installing the more confrontational Tadesse Worede in his place. The federal government responded by stripping the TPLF of its legal status as a political party in May 2025, leaving Tigray's dominant political force operating entirely outside formal Ethiopian institutional recognition even as it controls the region's de facto administration and reconstituted military command structure, the Tigray Defense Forces.

Layered onto this internal Tigrayan crisis is a deteriorating Ethiopia-Eritrea relationship driven substantially by Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's increasingly explicit demand for Red Sea maritime access, framed as "a matter of survival" and focused specifically on Eritrea's port of Assab — territory Ethiopia lost when Eritrea gained independence in 1993. With Ethiopia's national elections scheduled for June 2026, fears persist that elections cannot credibly proceed in Tigray given its unresolved political status, and that a politically pressured Abiy could find Red Sea nationalism, or a renewed confrontation with Tigrayan or Eritrean adversaries, strategically useful as a unifying cause precisely when his domestic position is most vulnerable.

Background

To understand why Tigray remains so combustible, it helps to remember how central the TPLF was to modern Ethiopian state formation. The Tigray People's Liberation Front, founded as an armed insurgency against the Derg military junta in the 1970s, became the dominant force within the Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF) coalition that took power in 1991. For the following twenty-seven years, under the leadership of Meles Zenawi until his 2012 death and his successors thereafter, Tigrayan political and military elites occupied a disproportionate share of Ethiopia's security, intelligence, and economic leadership — a dominance that generated deep resentment among Ethiopia's larger Oromo and Amhara populations, ultimately fueling the protest movement that brought Abiy Ahmed to power in 2018.

Abiy's rise ended nearly three decades of TPLF political dominance virtually overnight. His subsequent dissolution of the EPRDF's ethnic-federal party structure into a unified Prosperity Party in December 2019 — a move the TPLF refused to join, viewing it correctly as designed to permanently dilute their influence — set Tigray's leadership on a collision course with Addis Ababa. Tigray's defiant September 2020 regional elections, held against federal orders during the COVID-19 pandemic, escalated tensions further, and in November 2020, Tigrayan forces' attack on the Ethiopian National Defense Force's Northern Command headquarters in Mekelle triggered the war.

What followed was catastrophic by almost any measure. Federal forces, supported directly by Eritrean troops under President Isaias Afwerki — Tigray's historic regional rival, given Eritrea's own war of independence and subsequent 1998-2000 border war with Ethiopia — and by Amhara regional militias seeking to reclaim contested territory, fought a brutal two-year campaign against the Tigray Defense Forces. Documented atrocities included systematic sexual violence used as a weapon of war, with surveys finding roughly one in ten Tigrayan women subjected to sexual violence during the conflict, alongside engineered famine conditions and ethnic-targeted violence that UN investigators and human rights organizations characterized, in places, as amounting to ethnic cleansing. All major parties to the conflict, including federal forces, Eritrean troops, Amhara militias, and Tigrayan forces, were found to have committed serious war crimes.

The Pretoria Agreement, signed November 2, 2022, ended formal hostilities through a negotiated settlement establishing a Tigray Interim Administration (TIA) to govern the region pending elections, alongside commitments to TDF disarmament, withdrawal of Amhara and Eritrean forces from Tigrayan territory, restoration of federal services, and return of displaced populations — a comprehensive framework whose incomplete implementation over the following four years has become the central driver of renewed instability.

Current Situation

The TPLF's Internal Fracture

The single most consequential recent development reshaping Tigray's trajectory is not federal-Tigrayan conflict directly, but an internal Tigrayan political rupture. Following the Pretoria Agreement, Getachew Reda, a relative moderate within TPLF ranks, was appointed to lead the Tigray Interim Administration and worked, with varying success, to implement the peace framework's terms — an approach hardline TPLF elements increasingly viewed as capitulation, derisively labeling the Pretoria Agreement a "surrender document."

That internal grievance culminated in March 2025, when a faction loyal to TPLF chairman Debretsion Gebremichael seized control of government offices in Mekelle in what was widely characterized as an internal coup, deploying armed men to patrol the city and check civilian identification while Getachew fled to Addis Ababa. Credible reporting, including from The Guardian, suggested Eritrean intelligence had provided assistance enabling Debretsion's faction to consolidate power — a detail that, if accurate, illustrates how directly Eritrea remains embedded in Tigray's internal political dynamics even years after the war's formal end.

Debretsion's faction installed Tadesse Worede as the new TIA head in April 2025, and Tadesse has subsequently aligned closely with Debretsion's hardline positioning, sharply criticizing the federal government for failing to enforce Amhara militia withdrawal from Western Tigray or facilitate the return of displaced Tigrayans — both core, unimplemented Pretoria commitments. The TPLF leadership has used these legitimate grievances to justify its own non-compliance with the agreement's disarmament and demobilization provisions, and in June 2025, reinstated formal military command over the Tigray Defense Forces for the first time since the war's end — a direct, deliberate reversal of the demilitarization process Pretoria was designed to achieve.

The federal government's response has been to escalate in turn. In May 2025, Addis Ababa formally revoked the TPLF's legal standing as a political party, a move that leaves Tigray's dominant political and military force — the entity that actually controls the region on the ground — operating entirely outside any recognized Ethiopian institutional framework. This is a genuinely unusual and unstable arrangement: the federal government continues funding and nominally overseeing the Tigray Interim Administration, even as that administration is now led by figures aligned with a party Addis Ababa has stripped of all legal recognition.

The TIA Mandate Crisis and Frozen Elections

Tigray's governance crisis reached a genuine flashpoint in April 2026. The TIA's mandate was set to expire April 8, and under Ethiopian law, the federal government could not extend it a second time, having already done so once previously. With TPLF's legal party status revoked and no credible alternative political structure available to contest regional elections, Addis Ababa faced an acute dilemma: hold elections in Tigray that TPLF would likely dominate despite lacking legal recognition, risk a power vacuum by allowing the TIA's mandate to simply lapse, or find some other mechanism to extend interim governance.

Prime Minister Abiy met with TIA head Tadesse Worede on April 7, and the federal government extended the TIA's mandate by one year the following day — a move analysts characterized as averting an immediate flashpoint for renewed war, but one that resolves nothing structurally. The TPLF formally rejected the extension as a violation of the Pretoria Agreement and Tigray's own pre-war legal framework, characterizing it as unilateral federal imposition. Compounding the dispute, the federal government has separately indicated plans to hold parliamentary elections in some disputed areas of Tigray in June 2026 over explicit TPLF objections — elections most regional observers, including Tigrayan political analysts, consider effectively impossible to conduct credibly given the depth of ongoing political division and the absence of functioning, internationally recognized political party structures representing the region's dominant political force.

January 2026 Clashes: The Closest Call Yet

The most serious direct military escalation since the war's formal end occurred in late January 2026. Tensions had been building for months: in November 2025, Ethiopia's Afar Regional government accused TPLF elements of crossing the Tigray-Afar border and attacking civilians, threatening retaliation if TPLF forces did not withdraw — accusations TPLF denied, instead alleging the attacks were orchestrated by Ethiopian-backed militants. The following day, TPLF accused federal forces of conducting a drone strike on Raya Azebo that killed Tigrayan forces and civilians, characterizing it as a direct violation of the Pretoria ceasefire.

These accusations erupted into actual clashes on January 29, 2026, in Mai Degusha, a contested area of Tselemti district in western Tigray, pitting Tigrayan fighters against federal forces backed by Amhara militias. Ethiopian Airlines responded by canceling flights between Addis Ababa and Tigrayan cities — a telling, concrete indicator of how seriously authorities assessed the security deterioration. Getachew Reda, the ousted former TIA head now operating from Addis Ababa, issued a pointed warning that "power-hungry individuals within the TPLF" were "trying to drag Tigray into another round of war," a striking public break between Tigray's former and current leadership that underscores how deeply the region's own political class remains divided over strategy.

The clashes did not escalate into full renewed war, but the underlying triggers — disputed western Tigrayan territory still occupied by Amhara militias four years after Pretoria mandated their withdrawal, and unresolved accusations of cross-border drone strikes and militia coordination — remain entirely unresolved, meaning the conditions that produced January's flashpoint persist largely unchanged into the second half of 2026.

The Ethiopia-Eritrea Dimension: Red Sea Access as National Cause

Running parallel to, and increasingly intertwined with, the Tigray crisis is a sharply deteriorating Ethiopia-Eritrea relationship centered on Abiy Ahmed's escalating demand for Red Sea maritime access. Ethiopia, the world's most populous landlocked country, has depended on Djibouti for roughly 95 percent of its seaborne trade since losing its own coastline when Eritrea gained independence in 1993 — a dependency Abiy's government estimates costs Ethiopia approximately $1.5 billion annually in logistics and port fees.

Abiy's rhetoric on this question has escalated dramatically through late 2025 and into 2026. In September 2025, he characterized regaining access to Eritrea's port of Assab as merely "a matter of time," explicitly calling the 1993 loss of the port a historical "mistake." By October 28, he was calling for international mediation, describing maritime access as "a matter of survival" for Ethiopia. In a February 2026 parliamentary address, he declared that "the Red Sea and Ethiopia cannot remain separated forever," while a subsequent military parade in southern Ethiopia featured special forces marching beneath banners reading, in Amharic, that Ethiopia would not remain landlocked "whether you like it or not" — imagery that included a soldier symbolically breaching a door toward a seaport.

Ethiopia's Foreign Affairs Minister Gedion Timothewos sharpened the confrontation further in October 2025, accusing Eritrea and the TPLF of entering a coordinated pact to "wage" conflict against the federal government — an accusation that directly links the Red Sea dispute to the Tigray crisis, with Addis Ababa effectively framing Eritrea's alleged support for TPLF hardliners and its resistance to Ethiopian maritime ambitions as two fronts of a single strategic threat. Eritrea has firmly rejected these accusations as "patently false and fabricated," while itself accusing Ethiopia of military preparations along the shared border. In February 2026, Ethiopia formally demanded Eritrean troop withdrawal from Ethiopian territory in a diplomatic letter — a demand Eritrea denied had any basis.

Despite this escalatory spiral, Abiy has repeatedly and explicitly denied any intention to pursue Red Sea access through military force, stating Ethiopia has "no intention of invading or attacking others" while affirming continued pursuit of maritime access through diplomatic and commercial channels. Most regional security analysts, including former US Ambassador to Ethiopia David Shinn, view an actual Ethiopian invasion of Eritrea to seize Assab as highly improbable given Eritrea's heavily fortified southern border, its large standing military relative to population, and the catastrophic economic and diplomatic costs Ethiopia would incur — including likely jeopardizing its critical Djibouti port relationship and broader foreign investment climate, with the IMF projecting 7.1 percent real GDP growth for Ethiopia this year that any major conflict would directly threaten.

Saudi Arabia's Quiet Counterweight

An important and underappreciated dimension of the Eritrea standoff involves Saudi Arabia's alignment with Asmara, driven substantially by Riyadh's concern over the United Arab Emirates' growing influence across Ethiopia and the wider Horn of Africa — a dynamic that mirrors the broader Saudi-UAE rivalry Global Chanakya has tracked extensively in the context of both Yemen and Sudan. Some regional analysts have specifically suggested that any Ethiopian move into Eritrea could risk drawing a Saudi aerial response in Eritrea's defense, though the outbreak of the Iran-Israel-US conflict in early 2026 has complicated this calculus by potentially requiring Riyadh to retain greater military capability closer to its own borders rather than projecting power into the Horn of Africa.

Strategic Analysis

Abiy's Political Calculus: A Unifying Cause Amid Fragmentation

Understanding Abiy Ahmed's escalating Red Sea rhetoric requires understanding the extraordinary breadth of domestic challenges his government currently faces simultaneously. Beyond the Tigray crisis, Ethiopia continues grappling with ongoing insurgencies involving Amhara Fano militias and the Oromo Liberation Army, alongside the unresolved al-Fashaga border dispute with Sudan and the diplomatic fallout from his controversial 2024 Somaliland port access memorandum, which alienated Somalia and led Mogadishu to threaten expulsion of Ethiopian peacekeeping troops.

With national elections scheduled for June 2026 and Abiy's broader legacy — including his 2019 Nobel Peace Prize, awarded specifically for reconciliation with Eritrea — increasingly under strain from this accumulation of internal conflicts, Red Sea access functions as a rare unifying nationalist cause capable of generating support across Ethiopia's deeply fractured ethnic-political landscape. Few issues command the kind of cross-ethnic consensus that the loss of Ethiopia's coastline does; many Ethiopians genuinely view landlocked status as a historical injustice warranting correction, giving Abiy's rhetoric authentic domestic resonance beyond pure political calculation, even as analysts increasingly characterize it as a calculated diversion from internal instability rather than a serious military program.

Eritrea's Defensive Opportunism

Isaias Afwerki's calculus reflects a pattern consistent with Eritrea's broader regional strategy over the past several decades: cultivating relationships with armed factions opposed to whichever government in Addis Ababa it currently views as threatening, as a low-cost deterrent and leverage mechanism against a historically much larger and more powerful neighbor. Eritrea's alleged support for hardline TPLF elements — a striking reversal given Eritrea's direct military role fighting against the TPLF during the 2020-2022 war itself — illustrates this opportunism clearly: Asmara's strategic interest is not in any particular Tigrayan faction's success, but in maintaining persistent internal Ethiopian instability that constrains Addis Ababa's capacity to project power against Eritrea, whether over Assab specifically or more broadly.

This creates a genuinely dangerous dynamic the International Crisis Group has explicitly flagged: Eritrea's strategy of partnering with multiple Ethiopian opposition groups simultaneously — Fano, TPLF hardliners, and others — risks backfiring catastrophically if Addis Ababa eventually concludes Eritrean interference has crossed an intolerable threshold, providing genuine casus belli for the kind of confrontation most analysts currently view as unlikely but not impossible.

The Sudan-Ethiopia-RSF Connection

Ethiopia's regional positioning carries direct relevance to the broader Sudan conflict Global Chanakya has analyzed separately. Ethiopia has reportedly provided direct backing to Sudan's Rapid Support Forces since 2025, a calculated hedge against Egypt and a response to years of tension with the Sudanese Armed Forces stemming from SAF's historical ties to the TPLF and the unresolved al-Fashaga border dispute. Ethiopia has reportedly allowed UAE weapons transfers to the RSF to transit its territory and permitted RSF training camp establishment in the Benishangul-Gumuz region, from which RSF-aligned forces have launched operations into Sudan's Blue Nile state — with drone strikes from this infrastructure surging since Ethiopia completed what regional monitoring describes as dedicated "drone support infrastructure" in late 2025.

This places Ethiopia squarely within the broader Saudi-UAE proxy dynamic shaping Sudan's war, and illustrates how Horn of Africa conflicts increasingly interlock: Ethiopia's tensions with Egypt over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, its alignment with the UAE against Saudi-backed Sudanese and Eritrean interests, and its own internal Tigray crisis are not separate files but components of a single, increasingly interconnected regional power competition.

Global Impact

Red Sea Shipping and Maritime Security Compounding

Any significant escalation in the Ethiopia-Eritrea dispute would add yet another variable to an already severely stressed Red Sea security picture, layering onto the Houthi-driven Bab al-Mandab disruption Global Chanakya has extensively documented and the broader Sudan conflict's own Red Sea coastline implications. Eritrea's strategic position along the Red Sea's western shore, combined with its historically close relationship with both Russia — which has periodically explored naval basing arrangements in the region — and now its alignment with Saudi Arabia against UAE-aligned interests, means renewed Ethiopia-Eritrea conflict carries genuine potential to further destabilize one of the world's most consequential maritime chokepoints at a moment when it can least afford additional disruption.

Humanitarian Funding Strain

Tigray's recovery from the 2020-2022 war has been directly and severely affected by reductions in US foreign assistance funding, with the region — already reliant heavily on USAID support, historically Ethiopia's largest humanitarian donor — suffering acute strain from the Trump administration's funding cuts. This compounds an already dire underlying humanitarian picture: the original war's reconstruction costs alone were estimated at roughly $20 billion, a figure that has only grown given the subsequent years of incomplete recovery, continued displacement, and now renewed instability threatening to reverse what limited progress has occurred.

A Test Case for African Union Conflict Resolution

The Pretoria Agreement represented one of the African Union's most significant independent conflict-mediation achievements in recent memory, ending one of the continent's deadliest contemporary wars without primary reliance on Western or UN mediation architecture. Its incomplete implementation, and the genuine risk of renewed conflict despite the agreement's formal continued existence, represents a consequential test of the AU's capacity to enforce, rather than merely broker, conflict resolution — with direct implications for the institution's credibility in addressing the simultaneous, overlapping crises across Sudan, the broader Horn of Africa, and beyond that increasingly demand exactly this kind of sustained regional mediation capacity.

Risk Assessment

High-Probability Risks

  • Continued localized clashes in western Tigray: Given the persistent, unresolved Amhara militia occupation of contested territory and the precedent of January 2026's Mai Degusha clashes, further localized confrontations between Tigrayan forces and federal/Amhara forces remain highly likely through the remainder of 2026.
  • Continued TPLF-federal government institutional standoff: Given the TPLF's revoked legal status and rejection of the TIA mandate extension, continued institutional paralysis and mutual delegitimization between Tigray's de facto leadership and Addis Ababa is highly probable, regardless of whether June elections proceed in any form.
  • Escalating but contained Ethiopia-Eritrea rhetoric: Continued sharp diplomatic exchanges, accusations, and military posturing between Addis Ababa and Asmara, without full-scale conflict, represents the most probable near-term trajectory given both sides' demonstrated rhetorical escalation alongside consistent denial of war intentions.

Moderate-Probability Risks

  • Election-related crisis in June 2026: Given near-universal regional assessment that credible elections in Tigray are currently impossible, a moderate-probability risk exists of a serious political crisis if the federal government proceeds with elections in disputed areas over TPLF objections, potentially triggering exactly the kind of confrontation the April 2026 TIA mandate extension was designed to avert.
  • Direct but limited Ethiopia-Eritrea border clashes: Given troop mobilizations on both sides and the documented pattern of escalating accusations, a moderate-probability risk exists of limited border confrontations or proxy clashes, even without a full-scale invasion of Eritrean territory.
  • Further TPLF internal fragmentation: Given the depth of division between Debretsion's hardline faction and more moderate figures like the ousted Getachew Reda, continued internal Tigrayan political fragmentation — potentially producing competing claims to legitimate Tigrayan leadership — remains a real possibility.

Lower-Probability but High-Impact Risks

  • Renewed full-scale Tigray war: While individual triggers for renewed large-scale conflict exist, the catastrophic toll of the 2020-2022 war, the continued (if frayed) existence of the Pretoria framework, and the absence of clear appetite from any major external patron for a fresh full-scale conflict make a complete return to 2020-level warfare a lower-probability, though not negligible, outcome.
  • Full-scale Ethiopia-Eritrea invasion over Assab: Despite escalating rhetoric, the near-universal assessment among regional security analysts is that actual large-scale Ethiopian military action to seize Assab remains unlikely given the prohibitive costs, Eritrea's defensive fortifications, and the absence of any plausible scenario in which Ethiopia could hold seized territory without sustained, economically devastating conflict.
  • Direct Saudi-UAE military confrontation via Horn of Africa proxies: While both powers back opposing sides across multiple Horn of Africa files including Eritrea-Ethiopia and Sudan, direct military confrontation between Saudi and Emirati forces remains a low-probability outcome given both states' overriding interest in avoiding open rupture.

Future Scenarios

Scenario Analysis — the following projections are illustrative simulations based on current trajectories, not confirmed events.

Scenario One: Prolonged Frozen Instability (Most Likely)

Tigray continues operating under an extended but contested TIA mandate, with the TPLF's legal status remaining unresolved and periodic, contained localized clashes continuing in western Tigray without escalating to renewed full-scale war. Ethiopia-Eritrea tensions persist at an elevated rhetorical level, with Abiy continuing to invoke Red Sea access as a unifying domestic theme without pursuing actual military action against Assab. June 2026 elections proceed in most of Ethiopia but remain effectively impossible to credibly hold in Tigray, generating continued institutional ambiguity without acute crisis.

Scenario Two: Renewed Tigray Conflict

Continued non-implementation of Pretoria's territorial and disarmament provisions, combined with TPLF's reconstituted military command structure and ongoing Amhara militia occupation of contested western territory, produces an escalation beyond January 2026's contained clashes into a broader, sustained military confrontation between federal forces and Tigrayan forces — potentially drawing in Eritrean involvement given documented historical patterns and current allegations of coordination with TPLF hardline elements.

Scenario Three: Ethiopia-Eritrea Border Crisis

Continued mutual accusations and troop mobilizations along the Ethiopia-Eritrea border eventually produce a serious, if geographically contained, military confrontation — falling short of full invasion but involving significant clashes and casualties — driven either by deliberate escalation from one side or by miscalculation amid the current high-tension standoff, potentially triggering broader African Union and international mediation efforts under significant time pressure.

Scenario Four: Negotiated De-escalation

Sustained African Union, Gulf state, and international pressure — building on the precedent of successful crisis management around the April 2026 TIA mandate extension — produces genuine progress on Pretoria's outstanding implementation gaps, including actual Amhara militia withdrawal from contested territory and a credible pathway toward TPLF's reintegration into formal Ethiopian political structures, alongside parallel Ethiopia-Eritrea dialogue addressing both maritime access aspirations and Eritrean sovereignty concerns. This remains a less probable but genuinely achievable outcome given that both Abiy and Isaias have repeatedly signaled, even amid escalatory rhetoric, that neither actively seeks full-scale war.

Intelligence Forecast

Based on current trajectories, Global Chanakya's assessment for the next twelve to eighteen months centers on four core judgments.

First, Tigray's internal political fragmentation — not direct federal-Tigrayan military confrontation — will remain the most immediate driver of instability, given the TPLF's unresolved legal status, the unresolved rift between Debretsion's hardline faction and more moderate figures, and the practical impossibility of credible regional elections under current conditions.

Second, Abiy Ahmed's Red Sea rhetoric will likely continue intensifying through the run-up to and aftermath of June 2026 elections, functioning primarily as a domestic political unifying tool rather than genuine military preparation, though the risk of miscalculation or unintended escalation along the Eritrea border will rise correspondingly as rhetoric on both sides continues hardening.

Third, the interconnection between Ethiopia's internal conflicts, the Eritrea standoff, and the broader Sudan war will continue deepening, with Ethiopia's RSF backing and Saudi-Eritrea alignment against UAE-aligned interests representing a structural feature of regional competition unlikely to resolve independently of the broader Saudi-UAE Horn of Africa rivalry.

Fourth, the African Union's capacity to prevent renewed large-scale Tigray conflict will face its most serious test since the original Pretoria Agreement, given the accumulating, unresolved implementation gaps and the absence, thus far, of any credible enforcement mechanism beyond continued diplomatic engagement.

Final Strategic Takeaway

Ethiopia's Tigray crisis illustrates a pattern increasingly visible across multiple conflicts Global Chanakya tracks: a peace agreement that successfully halted active fighting without resolving the underlying political, territorial, and security questions that caused the war in the first place. Pretoria stopped the killing in 2022, but it did not return displaced Tigrayans home, did not remove Amhara militias from contested territory, did not achieve genuine TDF disarmament, and did not produce a stable, internationally recognized political structure capable of representing Tigrayan interests within Ethiopia's federal system. Four years later, every one of those unresolved gaps has become an active source of renewed tension.

What makes 2026 particularly dangerous is the simultaneous convergence of multiple, mutually reinforcing pressures: a fractured Tigrayan leadership with genuine internal incentive toward confrontation, a federal government extending interim rule by decree rather than addressing underlying grievances, an Eritrean regime with demonstrated historical willingness to exploit Ethiopian internal divisions, and a prime minister facing electoral pressure who has found Red Sea nationalism a uniquely effective unifying cause.

None of these pressures individually guarantees renewed war. Most regional analysts, weighing the catastrophic costs of the 2020-2022 conflict against the current balance of incentives, still consider continued frozen instability more likely than a full return to large-scale fighting. But frozen instability in the Horn of Africa has proven, repeatedly, to be a precarious equilibrium rather than a stable one — and the specific combination of unresolved Tigrayan political fragmentation, hardening Ethiopia-Eritrea rhetoric, and approaching elections that cannot credibly proceed in the region at the center of this entire dispute means the window for genuine diplomatic intervention may be narrower than comfortable assumptions about post-2022 peace would suggest. The African Union, Gulf mediators, and the broader international community would be wise to treat 2026 not as a year to monitor Tigray from a comfortable distance, but as the year the Pretoria framework either gets genuinely reinforced, or genuinely begins to unravel.

title: Serbia-Kosovo Tensions: The Balkans' Live Fault Line
content:
Serbia-Kosovo Tensions: The Balkans' Live Fault Line

Europe likes to believe the Balkans are a finished project — a region that fought its wars in the 1990s, made its peace, and settled into the slow, bureaucratic rhythm of EU accession queues. Serbia and Kosovo are the standing rebuttal to that comfortable assumption. More than a quarter-century after NATO bombs forced Belgrade out of Kosovo, the two remain locked in an unresolved sovereignty dispute that periodically produces real violence, real casualties, and real fear of wider escalation — most recently visible in the 2023 Banjska attack, the ongoing integration battles over Serb-majority institutions in the north, and a Serbian president who is simultaneously fighting for his political survival at home and accused of orchestrating instability across the border.

What makes 2026 a particularly important moment to examine this conflict is the convergence of several volatile threads at once: Aleksandar Vucic's government is weaker domestically than at any point in his rule, having spent over a year battling sustained student-led protests; Kosovo's Albin Kurti has emerged from a year-long political deadlock with a fresh mandate and an explicitly assimilationist integration agenda for the north; a new trilateral military partnership between Kosovo, Albania, and Croatia has alarmed Belgrade in ways that echo Cold War-style bloc anxieties; and the EU-facilitated dialogue between the two sides remains, by its own mediator's admission, in a state of "no meaningful progress." This report examines why Serbia-Kosovo tensions deserve far more sustained global attention than they currently receive.

Executive Summary

The Serbia-Kosovo dispute, rooted in Kosovo's 2008 declaration of independence following the 1998-99 war and NATO's intervention, remains one of Europe's most durable unresolved sovereignty conflicts. Kosovo has been recognized by roughly 100 countries, including the United States and most Western states, but not by Serbia, Russia, China, or five EU member states — a split recognition status that keeps Kosovo locked out of the United Nations and most international bodies, and keeps the underlying dispute permanently unresolved rather than merely dormant.

Tensions have escalated repeatedly since 2022, most seriously in the September 2023 Banjska attack, when a heavily armed Serb paramilitary group linked to Serbian-backed politician Milan Radoičić killed a Kosovo police officer in a fortified assault that Kosovo's government, the EU, and the United States have all characterized as state-linked aggression — an accusation Belgrade has never genuinely answered, with Radoičić remaining unprosecuted in Serbia to this day. Since then, Prime Minister Albin Kurti, reelected through a turbulent process culminating in a new government in February 2026, has pursued an accelerating integration agenda aimed at folding Serbia-funded parallel institutions — schools, hospitals, and administrative bodies operating in Serb-majority areas under Belgrade's financing — into Kosovo's formal state structure, moves Serbian officials describe as an assault on Kosovo Serb identity and survival, and which Kosovo frames as the unavoidable consolidation of sovereign statehood within its own recognized territory.

Layered onto this bilateral dispute is a domestic Serbian crisis that has fundamentally reshaped Vucic's room for maneuver: sustained, nationwide student-led protests, triggered by the November 2024 Novi Sad railway station canopy collapse that killed sixteen people, have continued for over eighteen months, with tens of thousands rallying as recently as May 2026 demanding early elections — elections Vucic has now signaled could occur between September and November 2026. A president fighting for domestic survival, simultaneously accused of regional destabilization and increasingly reliant on Russian diplomatic backing, makes for an unusually combustible combination heading into what is likely to be a consequential year for both Belgrade and Pristina.

Background

Kosovo's dispute with Serbia traces directly to the violent breakup of Yugoslavia. Kosovo, an autonomous province within Serbia under Tito-era Yugoslav federalism, lost that autonomy in 1989 under Slobodan Milosevic, triggering a decade of escalating repression against its overwhelmingly ethnic Albanian, Muslim-majority population. The Kosovo Liberation Army's 1998 insurgency against Serbian rule prompted a brutal Yugoslav counterinsurgency campaign, including mass killings and ethnic cleansing of Kosovo Albanians, which in turn triggered NATO's 78-day bombing campaign in 1999 — conducted without UN Security Council authorization, a fact Russia has cited repeatedly in the years since, including explicitly as partial justification for its own 2014 annexation of Crimea and 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

NATO's intervention forced Serbian withdrawal and placed Kosovo under UN administration via UNMIK, with NATO's KFOR mission providing security — a peacekeeping presence, still numbering around 4,500 troops, that remains in place today, over a quarter-century later. Kosovo declared independence unilaterally in February 2008, a move the International Court of Justice subsequently found did not violate international law, but one Serbia has never accepted, treating Kosovo constitutionally and politically as the autonomous province of "Kosovo and Metohija" rather than a sovereign state.

The two sides entered EU-facilitated dialogue in 2011, producing a series of partial agreements without ever resolving the core recognition question. The most significant of these, the 2013 Brussels Agreement, committed Kosovo to establishing an Association/Community of Serb-majority Municipalities (ASM) — granting Kosovo's Serb-majority municipalities defined collective powers over education, healthcare, and local economic development — in exchange for Serbia's acceptance of Kosovo's governing authority over the north. That agreement has never been implemented. Kosovo's government has consistently delayed submitting the ASM's draft statute for constitutional review, citing concerns that a sufficiently empowered Serb association would function as a Republika Srpska-style autonomous bloc capable of obstructing Kosovo's central governance — a concern reinforced, in Pristina's view, by Republika Srpska's own history of secessionist agitation within Bosnia and Herzegovina.

A further attempt at resolution came via the 2023 Ohrid Agreement, brokered under EU mediation in North Macedonia, under which both sides verbally endorsed a framework for normalized relations without Serbia extending formal recognition. Like its predecessors, the Ohrid deal remains unsigned and largely unimplemented, with both sides accusing the other of bad faith over sequencing — Kosovo insisting Serbia must demonstrably end its obstruction before further concessions, Serbia insisting the ASM must be implemented before any further normalization steps.

Current Situation

The Banjska Shadow

No single event has shaped the trajectory of Serbia-Kosovo relations over the past three years more than the September 2023 attack in Banjska, a Serb-majority village in northern Kosovo. A heavily armed group of roughly thirty men, equipped with military-grade weapons and operating from a fortified monastery compound, ambushed Kosovo police, killing one officer before a tense standoff ended in a gun battle that left several attackers dead. Kosovo's government identified the group's leader as Milan Radoičić, a Kosovo Serb businessman and politician with extensive documented ties to Belgrade's security establishment, and characterized the assault as a state-sponsored attempt at territorial seizure rather than a spontaneous local uprising.

The aftermath has become its own enduring source of friction. Radoičić, despite admitting organizational responsibility in a statement shortly after the attack, has never been meaningfully prosecuted inside Serbia — a failure cited repeatedly by EU institutions, Carnegie Endowment analysts, and the Jacques Delors Institute as conclusive evidence that Belgrade's commitment to accountability and de-escalation cannot be taken at face value. Kosovo's own judicial process has moved forward independently: as recently as May 2026, a Kosovo court jailed three Serb individuals connected to the Banjska attack, continuing a prosecution track that has proceeded entirely without reciprocal Serbian cooperation.

Banjska legitimized a more assertive Kosovo security posture in the north that persists today — the regular deployment of Kosovar special police units in Serb-majority areas, a presence Kosovo Serb communities and civil society groups describe as heavy-handed and frequently provocative, including raids on Serb-majority villages such as the operations conducted in Banovë and Prevlak in April 2026 based on information from civilian sources.

Kurti's Integration Agenda and the Institutional Battle

The dominant current flashpoint is Prime Minister Kurti's accelerating effort to dismantle Serbia-funded parallel institutions operating inside Kosovo's recognized territory. On January 16, 2026, Kurti announced plans to gradually integrate Serbia-supported health and education institutions in Serb-majority areas into Kosovo's formal state system — institutions that have, since the 1999 war, continued operating under Belgrade's financing and administrative oversight as a parallel structure Kosovo has historically tolerated but never formally recognized as legitimate.

This is, in the most literal sense, a sovereignty consolidation move: Kosovo asserting exclusive administrative authority over services within its own recognized borders. It is also, predictably, deeply destabilizing to the Kosovo Serb community's daily life and sense of security, given that these Serbian-funded institutions have functioned for over two decades as the practical infrastructure through which Kosovo Serbs access healthcare and education in a language and curriculum aligned with Belgrade rather than Pristina. EU Special Representative Peter Sørensen has pushed for the integration process to proceed inclusively and with structured consultation of Kosovo Serb community representatives, securing an agreement on implementation modalities in March 2026 covering residence permits and identification documents — but the underlying tension between Kosovo's sovereign prerogative and Kosovo Serb communities' practical dependence on Belgrade-funded services remains fundamentally unresolved.

A parallel flashpoint involves Kosovo's Law on Foreigners and Law on Vehicles, which entered force March 15, 2026, introducing registration requirements for non-residents and vehicles not registered with Kosovo institutions. Kosovo Serb civil society organizations and the Serbian Orthodox Church have warned these measures could disrupt Serbia-administered services and create severe difficulties for residents lacking Kosovo-issued documentation — concerns serious enough that Sørensen negotiated additional implementation accommodations specifically to mitigate disruption, an indication of how even seemingly technical bureaucratic measures in this conflict carry the potential to ignite broader unrest.

Kosovo's Political Recovery and the New Kurti Government

Kosovo spent much of 2025 in genuine political paralysis. Parliamentary elections in February 2025 produced no clear governing majority, triggering a deadlock that persisted for nearly a year. President Vjosa Osmani ultimately called snap elections for December 28, 2025, after Kurti's Vetëvendosje party again failed to secure sufficient parliamentary support to form a government from the initial February result.

The December snap election delivered Vetëvendosje a stronger mandate — roughly 51 percent of the vote and 57 of 120 assembly seats — though the post-election process was complicated by a nationwide recount and a vote-tampering investigation that saw authorities detain more than 100 people, ultimately without altering the result. Parliament finally approved a new Kurti-led government on February 11, 2026, ending more than a year of deadlock with 66 votes in favor.

One quietly significant element of this electoral cycle deserves particular attention: municipal elections held in October-November 2025 saw Srpska Lista (Serbian List), the dominant Kosovo Serb political party, win mayoral races in all ten Kosovo Serb-majority municipalities, with Kosovo Serb mayors assuming office for the first time since their 2022 mass resignation from Kosovo institutions. This represents a genuine, if fragile, normalization signal — Kosovo Serb political participation returning to formal institutional channels after years of boycott — even as the broader integration disputes over health, education, and documentation continue generating friction at the community level.

The Trilateral Military Partnership: A New Source of Belgrade Anxiety

A development that has measurably escalated Serbian threat perception over the past year is the deepening defense cooperation between Kosovo, Albania, and Croatia, formalized through a March 2025 memorandum and increasingly operationalized through 2026. February 2026 saw a meeting of the three countries' military chiefs of staff in Shkodra, Albania, followed by a Munich Security Conference sideline meeting between Kurti and Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenković, and the announcement of a full 2026 joint training schedule — two exercises in Zagreb, one in Tirana — alongside what Albanian officials describe as deepening operational coordination beyond simple joint exercises.

Belgrade's response has been sharp and consistent. Serbia's Ministry of Defense has characterized the trilateral framework as a direct violation of both the 1996 subregional arms control agreement and UN Security Council Resolution 1244, which designates KFOR as the sole legitimate armed force operating in Kosovo. Vucic himself, after observing Kurti and Plenković meeting at the Munich conference, remarked pointedly that "if their goal was to worry us, they worried us" — an unusually candid acknowledgment of genuine strategic anxiety, later softened somewhat by his account of direct conversations with Plenković in which the Croatian leader stressed the cooperation was not directed against Serbia. Kosovo and Albanian officials, including Kosovo policy analyst Ramadan Ilazi, have characterized the framework as legitimate NATO-aligned defense cooperation between member and aspirant states rather than any form of anti-Serbian bloc-building — though the framing does little to dispel Belgrade's underlying concern about strategic encirclement by a coordinated Albanian-Croatian-Kosovo axis.

Vucic's Domestic Crisis: A Weakened Counterpart

Understanding Serbia's current posture toward Kosovo requires understanding the extraordinary domestic pressure Vucic has faced since November 2024, when the collapse of a railway station canopy in Novi Sad killed sixteen people — a tragedy widely attributed by the Serbian public to corruption-linked construction shortcuts and inadequate safety oversight under Vucic's governing system. What began as anticorruption protests evolved into the most sustained, broadly supported challenge to Vucic's authority since he took power, drawing in university students, opposition politicians, and ordinary citizens across the country in a movement explicitly demanding accountability and early elections.

These protests have continued for well over eighteen months with no sign of organic resolution. Tens of thousands rallied again in Belgrade as recently as May 23, 2026, with sporadic clashes between protesters and police near the presidential building, and reports indicating more than 60 percent of Serbian citizens now vocally disapprove of the government. Vucic has responded with a combination of repression — Human Rights Watch has documented excessive force, arbitrary arrest, and sustained attacks on independent journalists and civil society — and tactical concession, eventually signaling that elections could be held between September and November 2026, a major shift from his earlier resistance to any early vote.

This domestic vulnerability matters enormously for the Kosovo dynamic in two distinct ways. First, a weakened Vucic has stronger incentive to use Kosovo-related nationalism as a unifying distraction and legitimacy tool, a pattern visible in his framing of regional security cooperation among Kosovo, Albania, and Croatia as an existential threat warranting heightened alert. Second, his deepening reliance on Russian diplomatic and political backing amid the protests — Putin has openly supported Vucic's framing of the demonstrations as a Western-orchestrated "colour revolution," and Serbia introduced arms export restrictions in mid-2025 reportedly under direct Russian pressure — further complicates Belgrade's relationship with the EU at precisely the moment its Kosovo policy is under the most international scrutiny it has faced in years.

The EU Dialogue: Stalled, Not Dead

The EU-facilitated Belgrade-Pristina dialogue, under Special Representative Peter Sørensen, has continued functioning through 2026 at a technical level — including the first meeting of a trilateral Joint Commission on Missing Persons in January, convened alongside the International Committee of the Red Cross — but has produced no meaningful movement on the core normalization questions. Sørensen's own assessment, delivered to the UN Security Council in April 2026, was blunt: there has been no meaningful progress in the dialogue on Belgrade-Pristina normalization, even as the security situation in northern Kosovo remains, in his characterization, "calm but fragile."

The EU has applied carrot-and-stick pressure with limited apparent effect. Brussels moved forward with lifting measures imposed on Kosovo in 2023 over the northern tensions, programming €216 million in financial assistance following gradual governance improvements in the north — a genuine reward for Kosovo's progress. Simultaneously, the EU's enlargement commissioner has warned that Serbia's democratic backsliding could cost Belgrade roughly €1.5 billion in EU funding, while European Parliament resolutions have called on Vucic to halt repression and demonstrate genuine accession seriousness. Yet senior EU figures — von der Leyen, European Council President António Costa, and Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos among them — have continued traveling to Belgrade to publicly affirm support for Vucic's government even amid the crackdowns, a pattern critics describe as a "masochistic" unwillingness to abandon the stability-through-strongman approach that has defined EU Balkans policy for over a decade.

Strategic Analysis

The Core Strategic Asymmetry: Recognized Statehood vs. Practical Control

The fundamental strategic logic driving this conflict's persistence is a deep asymmetry between legal status and practical reality. Kosovo possesses recognized statehood from the world's most powerful states — the US, most of the EU, and the broader Western alliance system — but lacks UN membership and remains unrecognized by Serbia itself, leaving its sovereignty permanently contested in ways that shape virtually every policy decision Pristina makes regarding its own Serb minority.
