Continued cross-border dynamics in Blue Nile, combined with deepening Chad-Sudan rupture and unresolved Ethiopia-Egypt Nile tensions, produce a broader regional conflict drawing in South Sudan, Chad, and potentially direct Ethiopian military involvement beyond alleged covert support — transforming a Sudanese civil war into a genuine multi-state Horn of Africa crisis with implications extending well beyond Sudan's borders.

Intelligence Forecast

Based on current trajectories, Global Chanakya's assessment for the next twelve to eighteen months centers on four core judgments.

First, the battle for El Obeid will be the single most important near-term military indicator to track. Its outcome will determine whether the current stalemate persists or whether the war enters a new, more dangerous phase favoring RSF momentum into central Sudan.

Second, the Saudi-UAE proxy dynamic will continue shaping the conflict's trajectory more decisively than any UN or multilateral diplomatic process, meaning genuine de-escalation is unlikely to emerge from Quad or Quintet declarations alone without a parallel, harder-to-achieve recalibration of Gulf state behavior.

Third, humanitarian conditions will continue deteriorating absent a dramatic, currently unlikely, funding and access breakthrough, with famine indicators likely to worsen further across both RSF and SAF-controlled territories given persistent aid obstruction by both parties.

Fourth, regional spillover risk — particularly involving Chad, Ethiopia, and South Sudan — will continue rising incrementally rather than dramatically, meaning the war's most dangerous escalation pathway is gradual normalization of cross-border involvement rather than any single dramatic trigger event.

Final Strategic Takeaway

Sudan's tragedy is compounded by a second, quieter failure: the failure of the international system to treat it with anything approaching the urgency its scale demands. A war that has displaced more people than any other active conflict on the planet, produced credible genocide findings, and pulled in at least five external states through direct or alleged proxy involvement continues to receive a fraction of the diplomatic energy, media coverage, and humanitarian funding directed toward conflicts of comparable or even lesser scale elsewhere.

Sudan is not a humanitarian crisis with geopolitical side effects. It is a geopolitical crisis — a live proxy contest between rival Gulf patrons, layered onto unresolved Nile basin rivalries and Horn of Africa power competition — that happens to be generating humanitarian consequences of almost unprecedented scale.

For India, the Gulf states, and the wider international community, Sudan carries lessons that extend well beyond its borders. It demonstrates how quickly an intra-alliance rivalry between ostensibly aligned partners can metastasize into a devastating proxy war when neither party faces meaningful consequences for their support. It demonstrates how unregulated drone proliferation is changing the character of conflict in regions with weak governance and limited oversight. And it demonstrates, perhaps most uncomfortably, how selective global attention can be — how a war this consequential can unfold for years with comparatively muted international response, simply because it lacks the geopolitical proximity to major power capitals that other conflicts command. Until that changes, Sudan will remain what it has tragically become: the clearest available proof that scale of suffering and scale of global attention are not the same thing.

title: Syria's Power Map 2026: Sharaa's Fragile Republic
content:
Syria's Power Map 2026: Sharaa's Fragile Republic

Eighteen months ago, Syria did not have a power map. It had a frozen civil war, a dictator hiding behind Russian and Iranian guarantees, and four separate authorities pretending the others did not exist. Then, in the space of eleven days in late 2024, the entire architecture collapsed. Bashar al-Assad fled to Moscow. Fifty-four years of Baath Party rule ended. And a former al-Qaeda affiliate commander who had spent the previous seven years quietly building a functioning mini-state in Idlib walked into Damascus and declared himself president.

What has happened since is one of the most consequential, least understood state-formation experiments in the modern Middle East. Ahmed al-Sharaa has gone from insurgent commander to head of state recognized by Washington, Brussels, and most of the Arab world. He has crushed the Kurdish autonomous project in the northeast, absorbed the country's largest oil fields, and secured the lifting of American sanctions. But underneath that headline consolidation sits a country still bleeding from sectarian massacres, still hosting an Israeli-backed breakaway enclave in the south, still haunted by a resurgent Islamic State, and still governed under emergency constitutional powers with no real elections in sight until the end of the decade. This is the actual power map of Syria in 2026 — not the simplified one, the real one.

Executive Summary

Syria today is best understood as a state with one dominant, internationally recognized center of gravity — the Damascus-based Syrian Transitional Government (STG) under President Ahmed al-Sharaa — surrounded by a shrinking but still meaningful periphery of contested, semi-autonomous, or externally-protected zones. Following a stunning January 2026 military and political campaign, the STG dismantled the Kurdish-led Autonomous Administration of North and East Syria (AANES) and absorbed its territory, oil fields, and security infrastructure, formalized through a January 30 ceasefire and integration deal. This single development reshaped more of Syria's map in five weeks than the previous year of diplomacy had managed.

Yet consolidation has not meant reconciliation. In the south, the Druze-majority province of Sweida operates as a de facto Israeli protectorate, governed by a "National Guard" militia loyal to Sheikh Hikmat al-Hijri that flies Israeli flags in its town squares and has become, by multiple independent accounts, a significant narcotics-trafficking node destabilizing neighboring Jordan. Identity-based massacres against Alawites and Druze in 2025 killed well over three thousand civilians combined and remain unaddressed by any credible transitional justice mechanism. The Islamic State has exploited the chaos of the SDF-to-government detention camp handover to stage a quiet resurgence. And Israel continues to occupy Syrian territory beyond the 1974 disengagement line in Quneitra and Dara'a, conducting strikes deep into Syrian territory whenever it judges its red lines crossed.

The deeper strategic story is the dramatic reordering of external patronage. Russia and Iran — Assad's two indispensable guarantors for over a decade — have been almost entirely displaced. Turkey and Qatar now enjoy outsized influence over Damascus's decision-making, while the United States, under President Donald Trump, has pursued a policy of conditional but increasingly personal backing for Sharaa, even as it abandoned its longtime Kurdish partners with striking speed. Syria has, in effect, swapped one set of external patrons for another — and the question now is whether Sharaa's government can convert military consolidation into genuine national legitimacy before the next sectarian fault line cracks open.

Background

To understand Syria's current map, it helps to remember how fast the old order actually fell. For most of 2024, Syria's civil war looked frozen — Assad controlled roughly two-thirds of the country with Russian air support and Iranian-aligned militia backing, the Kurdish-led SDF held the oil-rich northeast with American support, Turkish-backed factions controlled a strip along the northern border, and Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham (HTS) governed an Islamist mini-state in Idlib province under Sharaa's leadership, having formally broken from al-Qaeda in 2016.

That frozen picture shattered in late November 2024, when HTS launched a surprise offensive codenamed "Deterrence of Aggression" out of Idlib. What followed stunned virtually every regional intelligence service. Assad's army, hollowed out by years of corruption, low morale, and an economy in freefall, simply did not fight. Aleppo fell within days. Hama and Homs followed within two weeks. On December 8, 2024, opposition forces entered Damascus essentially unopposed, and Assad fled to Moscow, ending over fifty years of Assad family rule that began when his father Hafez seized power in a 1970 coup.

The speed of the collapse mattered as much as the outcome. Russia, consumed by its war in Ukraine, could not mobilize the kind of intervention that had saved Assad in 2015. Iran's regional network was already reeling — Israel's campaign against Hezbollah had killed much of its senior leadership through 2024, and Tehran simply did not have the capacity or appetite to rescue a third front. Assad's fall was, in many respects, collateral damage from the broader unraveling of Iran's regional axis rather than a Syria-specific military defeat.

What came next was Sharaa moving with remarkable discipline to consolidate sole authority. He declared the dissolution of all armed factions — including HTS itself — and called for their integration into new state institutions. He suspended the 2012 constitution, dissolved the Baath Party and Assad-era legislature, and on January 29, 2025, was formally declared president for a transitional period. A provisional Constitutional Declaration, ratified in March 2025, established a five-year transition running through 2030, concentrating executive power heavily in the presidency, with no prime minister position and direct presidential authority over judicial and legislative appointments — a structure Human Rights Watch and other observers have criticized for lacking meaningful checks or oversight, justified by transitional authorities as a temporary necessity.

Current Situation

The map of Syria today divides into five distinct zones of authority, each with a different trajectory, external patron, and risk profile.

Zone One: The Damascus Core — Consolidated STG Authority

The Syrian Transitional Government, formally established on March 29, 2025, now governs the large majority of Syrian territory, including Damascus, Aleppo, Homs, Hama, and — as of January 2026 — most of the former Kurdish-administered northeast. Sharaa retained key wartime allies in central positions: Asaad al-Shaibani as Foreign Minister and Murhaf Abu Qasra as Defense Minister, while building a cabinet that, on paper, reflects genuine sectarian diversity — including an Alawite, a Druze, a Christian, and a Kurdish minister among the technocratic appointees unveiled in March 2025.

Institutionally, the government has moved toward a managed, indirect electoral process rather than genuine competitive elections. A People's Assembly was partially seated in October 2025 through indirect voting, with seats in Raqqa, Hasakah, Suweida, and Kobane postponed due to security conditions at the time. Indirect elections for remaining Raqqa seats were completed by March 2026, with further voting in Hasakah and Kobane following. President Sharaa retains the authority to directly appoint a further 70 members of the Assembly himself — meaning the legislature that eventually convenes will be substantially shaped by presidential discretion rather than popular mandate, a structure that critics argue undermines the credibility of any claim to democratic transition.

On the international front, Sharaa's diplomatic rehabilitation has been extraordinarily fast by any historical standard for a former insurgent commander. The Trump administration lifted a wide range of US sanctions on May 23, 2026, following a meeting between Foreign Minister al-Shaibani and Secretary of State Marco Rubio in Antalya. President Trump has met Sharaa twice and has spoken approvingly of his consolidation efforts. The European Union followed with substantial financial commitment: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen visited Damascus on January 9, 2026, announcing approximately €620 million in assistance to be disbursed through 2026 and 2027. This combination of sanctions relief and reconstruction financing represents the most significant external validation any Syrian government has received in over a decade — though it sits uneasily against the World Bank's estimate that Syria's actual reconstruction needs approach $216 billion, a figure that dwarfs everything pledged so far.

Zone Two: The Former Kurdish Northeast — A Rapid, Contested Absorption

The single most dramatic shift in Syria's power map over the past six months has been the collapse of Kurdish autonomy in the northeast. The Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), commanded by Mazloum Abdi, had controlled roughly a quarter of Syrian territory east of the Euphrates since 2019, including the country's largest oil fields, the Tabqa hydroelectric dam, and detention facilities holding tens of thousands of Islamic State fighters and family members — a position built on its role as Washington's primary ground partner in the anti-ISIS campaign.

That leverage evaporated with stunning speed in January 2026. Talks on full SDF integration into a unified Syrian armed force, originally targeted for completion by the end of 2025, stalled — prompting Turkey to reportedly threaten direct military action, given Ankara's longstanding position that core SDF elements are functionally an extension of the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK), a group proscribed as terrorist by Turkey, the United States, and the United Kingdom. US envoy Tom Barrack publicly assessed that the SDF's original anti-ISIS purpose had "largely expired," and the Trump administration showed little interest in defending Kurdish political autonomy once the immediate counter-ISIS mission was judged complete.

Damascus moved decisively. Government forces seized swathes of northern and eastern Syria from Kurdish control, capturing the country's largest oil fields, the hydroelectric dam, and ISIS detention facilities. The SDF fell back toward Kurdish-majority core areas, and on January 30, 2026, signed a ceasefire and integration agreement that, by any honest reading, represented capitulation framed as negotiation. Under the deal's subsequent 14-point elaboration on January 18 (refined further through the spring): the SDF ceded territorial control over Deir al-Zour and Raqqa provinces outright; Hasakah province was retained nominally by SDF-linked local forces but integrated administratively into the central government; oil fields and external borders reverted to interim authority control; Kurdish fighters would join the new national army as individuals rather than as intact units (eliminating the SDF as a coherent independent force); and all non-Syrian PKK fighters were required to leave the country.

Implementation has not been clean. Local groups linked to the SDF stormed government internal security headquarters in Qamishli in March 2026, tearing down the Syrian flag at the city's airport, which triggered retaliatory attacks on Kurdish civilians in Aleppo — a pattern of low-level friction that suggests genuine integration, as opposed to managed subjugation, remains incomplete. Iraq's Kurdistan Democratic Party intervened to mediate between the SDF and Damascus, while the rival Kurdish National Council — long opposed to PKK-linked YPG dominance of Kurdish politics — has resurfaced as an alternative Kurdish political voice more amenable to Damascus.

The broader lesson of the northeast collapse is structural: the SDF's entire strategic position for nearly a decade rested on serving as Washington's indispensable partner against ISIS. Once Washington judged that mission complete, Kurdish political leverage essentially vanished overnight, despite years of SDF promises to Western audiences about building a pluralistic, democratic model of governance in northeast Syria.

Zone Three: Sweida — An Israeli-Protected Druze Enclave

If the northeast represents successful government consolidation, southern Syria's Druze-majority Sweida province represents its mirror opposite: a province Damascus does not control and, for now, cannot retake.

The roots of the rupture trace to escalating violence through 2025. Identity-based killings of Druze civilians by government-aligned forces occurred in April 2025, but the decisive break came in July 2025, when a kidnapping dispute between Bedouin tribes and Druze factions spiraled into a full government and allied-tribal assault on Sweida that killed at least 1,400 to 2,000 civilians according to UN and human rights documentation — violence the UN Commission of Inquiry assessed may have amounted to war crimes, carried out, according to joint investigation by Human Rights Watch and Syrian monitoring groups, under centrally coordinated direction from the Ministry of Defense.

Israel intervened directly, launching strikes on more than 160 sites across four Syrian provinces — including direct strikes on Damascus itself — forcing government forces to withdraw from Sweida. In the aftermath, Druze factions consolidated into the National Guard, a unified militia announced August 23, 2025, bringing together roughly forty local armed groups under the spiritual authority of Sheikh Hikmat al-Hijri, one of three senior Druze religious leaders in Syria and by far the most hardline on the question of relations with Damascus. A parallel civilian structure, the "Supreme Legal Committee," now functions as a de facto autonomous administration across central, southern, and eastern Sweida.

What makes Sweida strategically distinct from every other contested zone in Syria is the open, symbolic nature of its alignment with Israel. National Guard uniforms reportedly feature a Star of David. Demonstrations in Sweida's central Karama Square have featured Israeli flags and portraits of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. A senior National Guard commander has publicly described Israel as the force's "closest ally." Analysts broadly agree this reflects a genuine — if pragmatically calculated — Israeli strategy of using minority protection as a vehicle to constrain the Islamist-led government in Damascus and secure Israel's northern border region, rather than a vision of formal Druze statehood, which most Syrian Druze leaders, even within the National Guard's orbit, openly acknowledge could not survive as an independent entity.

The human cost of this standoff has compounded over time. Eagle Eye, a feared internal security apparatus reportedly established with Israeli assistance under al-Hijri's authority, has been linked to the detention of at least thirty Druze figures accused of communicating with Damascus. US-mediated talks between al-Hijri and the government, focused initially on prisoner exchanges, have continued intermittently through 2026 without producing a comprehensive settlement. And perhaps most damaging to the National Guard's claimed legitimacy, independent reporting through 2026 has documented a more than 325 percent surge in narcotics trafficking from Sweida toward Jordan since the militia consolidated control in July 2025 — a trend serious enough that Jordan's air force has launched five separate strikes on trafficking infrastructure inside Sweida province since Assad's fall, including a six-target operation on May 3, 2026, explicitly aimed at smuggling networks operating under the cover of the autonomous zone's security vacuum.

Zone Four: The Alawite Coast — Suppressed but Unresolved Grievance

Western coastal Syria, the historic Alawite heartland and Assad family power base, represents a quieter but no less serious fault line. In March 2025, insurgent attacks on government forces in Latakia, Tartous, and Hama triggered a wave of identity-based violence in which government forces, affiliated armed groups, and armed volunteers killed at least 1,400 people in Alawite-majority areas — mass graves, summary executions, and torched homes documented in a centrally coordinated military operation, according to investigation findings.

Unlike Sweida, the Alawite community has no equivalent external patron. Russia and Iran, the two powers historically aligned with the Assad-era Alawite establishment, have both been effectively displaced from Syria — Russia's position reduced to negotiations over the future status of its Hmeimim airbase and the Tartous naval facility (whose lease the transitional government has reportedly already terminated), and Iran's regional network shattered by the Hezbollah leadership losses of 2024. This leaves Syria's Alawite minority in the most precarious position of any major community: targeted by serious documented violence, without the leverage that Kurdish military utility or Druze-Israeli alignment has provided to other minorities, and almost entirely dependent on whatever genuine reconciliation Damascus chooses to offer.

Zone Five: The Resurgent Islamic State and Residual Foreign Presence

Beneath the headline territorial consolidation, the Islamic State has found renewed operating space. The chaotic handover of SDF-run detention camps — holding an estimated 7,000 to 9,000 ISIS-linked detainees, with roughly 2,000 remaining under joint arrangements in the northeast — created documented gaps that allowed escapes; US officials warned up to 200 detainees escaped during the January 2026 fighting alone. Roughly 7,000 detainees are now intended for transfer to Iraq under US supervision, while UN agencies have been asked to take over management of camps housing ISIS-linked family members. ISIS has used the resulting security vacuum to intensify operations against both government forces and remaining Kurdish security elements, with monitoring data showing renewed activity zones outside the group's formal territorial control.

The American military footprint, meanwhile, has shrunk dramatically and rapidly. The US withdrew from the Tanf garrison in southern Syria — long a strategically significant position interdicting the Iran-to-Lebanon land corridor — as part of the broader drawdown that accompanied Washington's tilt toward backing Damascus over the SDF. Russia, by contrast, has maintained its core bases, even as the broader scope of its post-Assad role in Syria remains genuinely unresolved.

The Israeli Factor Beyond Sweida

Israel's involvement in Syria extends well past its patronage of the Druze National Guard. Within days of Assad's fall, Israeli forces moved beyond the 1974 UN-patrolled buffer zone in the Golan Heights into Quneitra and southwest Dara'a, territory it continues to occupy. Israel also conducted hundreds of airstrikes in the weeks following Assad's collapse aimed at destroying weapons stockpiles and military infrastructure across Syria, concentrated heavily in Dara'a, Damascus, Rural Damascus, and Latakia governorates — a campaign explicitly designed to prevent advanced weaponry from falling into the hands of the new Islamist-led authorities, regardless of how moderate Sharaa's public posture has been.

The regional escalation triggered by the February 28, 2026, Israeli-US strikes on Iran further complicated Syria's position. Both Israeli and Iranian strikes targeting each other's regional assets have repeatedly violated Syrian airspace, with missile debris causing deaths and injuries inside Syrian territory. Syria reported one of its military bases in Hasakah governorate was struck by missiles launched from Iraq, attributed to pro-Iranian Iraqi militia groups retaliating against US regional assets. Sharaa has characterized this broader regional escalation as an existential threat to the Middle East and has reinforced Syria's border with Lebanon with thousands of troops, citing concerns over Hezbollah infiltration and arms smuggling — notable given Sharaa has also expressed public support for Lebanon's efforts to disarm Hezbollah entirely, a significant reversal from Assad-era alignment.

Strategic Analysis

Sharaa's Calculated Bet: Centralization Over Power-Sharing

The defining strategic choice Sharaa has made since December 2024 is centralization over federalism, even where federalism might have produced faster, less costly stability. US envoy Tom Barrack has publicly suggested Syria might need something short of full federalism — a system protecting community autonomy, culture, and language without the structural fragmentation federalism implies. Sharaa has consistently rejected this framing, pursuing instead a model that more closely resembles pre-war centralized Syrian statehood, just with different leadership and a different ideological coloring.

This bet carries genuine logic. A federal Syria risks permanent fragmentation along the same lines that have made Iraq and Lebanon difficult to govern for decades, and centralization has demonstrably worked faster than negotiation in the Kurdish case — Damascus achieved more through the threat and application of force in five weeks than years of diplomacy had produced. But the same playbook has visibly failed against the Druze, where superior Israeli airpower neutralized the government's military advantage entirely, and the same instinct toward forceful consolidation is precisely what triggered the Alawite coastal massacres in the first place. Sharaa's government has not yet demonstrated it can distinguish between situations where centralization is achievable and situations where it will simply generate the next massacre.

The Patron Swap: From Moscow-Tehran to Ankara-Doha-Washington

Syria's external alignment has undergone one of the most complete reversals of any state in the modern Middle East within an eighteen-month window. Assad's Syria depended entirely on Russian airpower and Iranian-aligned ground forces for survival. Sharaa's Syria now depends on a fundamentally different coalition: Turkey, which backed the Syrian National Army factions that helped topple Assad and retains powerful leverage through its proximity, troop presence, and the PKK question; Qatar, which has provided significant financial and diplomatic backing; and the United States, which has extended sanctions relief and direct presidential engagement despite Sharaa's al-Qaeda-linked past.

This reordering reflects a broader regional pattern Global Chanakya has tracked across multiple files: the contraction of Iran's "Axis of Resistance" following the degradation of Hezbollah's leadership and the broader pressure campaign against Tehran, opening space that Turkey and the Gulf states — rather than Western powers in any traditional sense — have moved fastest to fill. Russia's residual presence, centered on its airbases, persists less because of genuine leverage and more because no other actor has yet forced the question of full withdrawal.

The Israel Variable: Containment Through Minority Patronage

Israel's Syria strategy under Prime Minister Netanyahu reflects a consistent doctrine applied across multiple post-Arab Spring contexts: where a hostile or unpredictable Islamist-led central government cannot be prevented from forming, cultivate minority autonomy along the border to create strategic depth and deniable leverage. This is precisely the model Israel has applied to Sweida — and it has worked, in the narrow sense that Damascus genuinely cannot project force into the province without risking another devastating Israeli air campaign.

The strategic cost of this approach, however, is becoming clearer over time. The National Guard's transformation into a documented narcotics-trafficking hub destabilizing Jordan — a core US and Western security partner — illustrates the risk inherent in this kind of patronage: protected ungoverned spaces tend to attract exactly the kind of criminal and security pathologies that eventually generate blowback against the patron itself. Israel's calculation appears to be that the strategic value of a friendly buffer outweighs these costs, but Jordan's repeated unilateral strikes inside Sweida — now five separate operations — suggest Amman is losing patience with an arrangement it had no role in designing.

Reconstruction Financing as Geopolitical Leverage

The gap between pledged reconstruction assistance and Syria's actual estimated needs — roughly $620 million in EU commitments and partial American sanctions relief against a World Bank estimate of $216 billion required — means external financing will function as a powerful, long-running lever over Damascus's behavior for years to come. Every government considering further investment, from Gulf sovereign wealth funds to European development institutions, will calibrate disbursement against Sharaa's handling of minority rights, transitional justice, and the credibility of the eventual electoral process. This gives outside powers, particularly the Gulf states and the EU, sustained influence over Syria's internal trajectory without requiring military presence — a more sustainable form of leverage than the coercive patronage Russia and Iran once exercised.

Global Impact

The Refugee and Reconstruction Equation

Syria's post-Assad stabilization carries direct implications for the millions of Syrian refugees hosted across Turkey, Lebanon, Jordan, and Europe. European governments, Germany prominent among them, have closely tied their willingness to support large-scale return programs to demonstrable security improvements inside Syria — improvements that remain inconsistent given the continued violence in Sweida and the unresolved Alawite reconciliation question. The €620 million EU package reflects Brussels' calculated bet that supporting Sharaa's government, even with reservations about its Islamist origins, offers a faster path to reducing the refugee burden than continued instability would.

Counterterrorism Stakes for the Broader International System

The Islamic State's resurgence amid the chaotic SDF-to-government detention transition is not a peripheral concern — it is a direct continuation of the exact threat that originally drew a global coalition into Syria a decade ago. Western governments that have spent years urging the repatriation of their own citizens from Syrian detention camps now face the same question under a transitional government with far less operational capacity and far less international scrutiny than the SDF's American-backed structure provided. Any significant ISIS resurgence inside Syria would have immediate implications well beyond the country's borders, given the group's demonstrated capacity to inspire and direct attacks internationally.

Turkey's Expanded Regional Position

Turkey emerges from Syria's transition as perhaps the single biggest strategic winner among external powers. Ankara's longstanding objective — preventing the consolidation of an autonomous, PKK-linked Kurdish entity along its southern border — has been achieved largely through Damascus's own military and political action rather than direct Turkish intervention, a far more sustainable outcome than years of unilateral cross-border operations had produced. Turkey's parallel peace process with the PKK domestically, paired with the SDF's effective dissolution in Syria, represents a genuine strategic convergence that strengthens President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's position both regionally and domestically.

Implications for the Iran-Israel Strategic Balance

Syria's loss as a reliable Iranian client state represents one of the most significant blows to Tehran's regional position in over a decade, compounding the degradation of Hezbollah and reinforcing the broader pattern of Iranian strategic contraction that has defined the regional landscape since 2024. The closure or contested status of the historic Iran-to-Lebanon overland supply corridor through Syria — long essential to sustaining Hezbollah's arsenal — represents a structural, not merely tactical, setback for Iran's regional deterrence architecture, one unlikely to be reversed even if broader US-Iran tensions eventually ease.

Risk Assessment

High-Probability Risks

  • Continued low-level Kurdish-government friction: Despite the January 2026 integration deal, incidents like the Qamishli flag confrontation suggest genuine reconciliation remains incomplete; sporadic clashes and localized unrest in the northeast are likely to continue through the integration process.
  • Sweida remaining outside effective central government control: Absent a fundamental shift in Israeli policy or a genuine political breakthrough in US-mediated talks, the National Guard's de facto autonomy is likely to persist, with continued narcotics-related friction with Jordan.
  • Slow, contested progress on the electoral and constitutional track: Given the postponements already seen in Suweida, Raqqa, Hasakah, and Kobane, further delays in completing the People's Assembly and any subsequent steps toward a permanent constitution are highly likely.

Moderate-Probability Risks

  • Renewed large-scale sectarian violence: Given the documented pattern of 2025 — Alawite, Druze, and intercommunal violence occurring roughly every few months — further serious incidents remain a real possibility absent credible transitional justice mechanisms addressing prior atrocities.
  • Further Israeli strikes inside Syrian territory: Given Israel's demonstrated willingness to intervene militarily whenever it judges Druze security or its own strategic interests threatened, additional strikes — potentially including against Damascus directly — remain plausible if government forces move against Sweida again.
  • ISIS resurgence escalating beyond current insurgent-level activity: Continued gaps in detention facility security and reduced international counterterrorism coordination could allow for a more significant operational rebound.

Lower-Probability but High-Impact Risks

  • Formal Sweida secession or Israeli annexation: While rhetoric exists on both sides, most Druze leadership — even within the National Guard's orbit — recognize an independent Druze polity is not viable, making formal secession unlikely absent a much larger regional reconfiguration.
  • Collapse of the Sharaa government itself: Despite the fragility of the underlying social contract, Sharaa's combination of international recognition, financial backing, and demonstrated military capability against the Kurds makes any near-term internal collapse of the STG unlikely, barring a major external shock.
  • Direct Turkey-Israel friction over Syria: Both powers have significant, sometimes contradictory interests inside Syria — Turkey backing Damascus's centralization, Israel backing fragmentation in the south — creating a structural friction point that could sharpen if either side's position hardens further.

Future Scenarios

Scenario Analysis — the following projections are illustrative simulations based on current trajectories, not confirmed events.

Scenario One: Managed Consolidation with Persistent Friction (Most Likely)

Sharaa's government continues gradually extending nominal authority across most of Syria, completing the People's Assembly process and moving toward eventual elections on its extended multi-year timeline, while Sweida remains a semi-permanent exception under Israeli protection and the Kurdish integration process proceeds unevenly with periodic local flare-ups. International reconstruction financing arrives in increments tied to incremental governance improvements. This scenario essentially extends the current trajectory: real progress on territorial consolidation, persistent failure on genuine national reconciliation.

Scenario Two: Renewed Sectarian Crisis

A new triggering incident — whether in Sweida, the Alawite coast, or among the integrating Kurdish population — produces another large-scale episode of identity-based violence comparable to July 2025. This would likely prompt renewed Israeli intervention if Druze communities are targeted, significant international condemnation, and could meaningfully slow the sanctions relief and reconstruction financing trajectory Damascus has worked to secure, given the conditionality increasingly attached by European and Gulf donors.

Scenario Three: Sweida Negotiated Settlement

US-mediated talks between al-Hijri and Damascus, building on the prisoner exchange framework, eventually produce a formal autonomy arrangement for Sweida — something short of federalism but offering genuine administrative and security guarantees, similar in structure though not necessarily generosity to the Kurdish integration model. This would require Israel's tacit acceptance of reduced direct involvement, a non-trivial concession given Jerusalem's demonstrated investment in the current arrangement, but would address the most acute narcotics-trafficking concerns driving Jordanian frustration.

Scenario Four: ISIS Resurgence Forces International Re-engagement

Continued security gaps in former SDF-administered detention facilities and reduced coalition counterterrorism coordination allow ISIS to mount a significant operational comeback, potentially including attacks beyond Syria's borders. This would likely force renewed direct US and international military engagement inside Syria, reversing the current drawdown trajectory and complicating Damascus's broader sovereignty narrative just as it has worked to demonstrate full territorial control.

Intelligence Forecast

Based on current trajectories, Global Chanakya's assessment for the next twelve to eighteen months centers on four core judgments.

First, Damascus's territorial consolidation will continue but will not translate into uniform national legitimacy. The Kurdish integration model — overwhelming force followed by negotiated capitulation — worked because the SDF lost its essential external patron. It cannot simply be replicated against Sweida, where Israeli backing provides exactly the kind of external protection the Kurds lost, meaning the south will likely remain Syria's most durable contested zone.

Second, Turkey's influence over Syria's trajectory will continue expanding, increasingly at the expense of any residual Russian role, while the Gulf states — particularly Qatar — deepen their financial and political stake in Sharaa's success as a demonstration that post-Islamist governance models can achieve international legitimacy.

Third, the absence of meaningful transitional justice for the 2025 sectarian massacres will remain a persistent vulnerability for the Sharaa government, one likely to be exploited rhetorically by international human rights bodies, by minority communities seeking leverage, and potentially by Israel as continued justification for its Sweida policy.

Fourth, Syria's trajectory will remain unusually exposed to spillover from the broader Iran-Israel confrontation given its shared borders with both Lebanon and Iraq and its position directly beneath the missile and drone corridors connecting the two. Sharaa's deployment of thousands of troops to the Lebanese border reflects a government already treating this exposure as a near-term operational reality rather than a distant risk.

Final Strategic Takeaway

Syria in 2026 is a genuinely unusual case in modern state formation: a country where the central government has won, decisively, against its most organized internal rival, and yet still does not control its own territory in any uniform sense. Ahmed al-Sharaa has accomplished something few insurgent leaders manage — converting battlefield victory into international legitimacy, sanctions relief, and reconstruction financing within eighteen months. That is a genuine, significant achievement, and one that has reshaped the broader regional balance against Iran in ways that will likely outlast the current Syrian government itself.

But consolidation built on superior force against a weakened rival is not the same as a durable national settlement — and Syria's remaining fault lines, Sweida above all, are precisely the ones that cannot be resolved through the same playbook that worked against the Kurds.

The honest assessment is that Syria has traded one kind of fragility for another. Under Assad, the country was frozen but predictable, propped up by external guarantors with clear, stable interests. Under Sharaa, Syria is dynamic and rapidly consolidating, but its stability now depends on a far more complicated set of variables: whether Damascus can extend genuine inclusion rather than coerced submission to its minorities, whether Israel eventually accepts a reduced role in the south, whether Turkey's interests and Damascus's centralizing instincts remain aligned, and whether the broader Iran-Israel confrontation stays contained enough that Syria does not become collateral damage in someone else's war. For now, the map favors Damascus more than at any point since 2011. Whether that map holds depends entirely on choices Sharaa's government has not yet had to make.

title: Yemen's Strategic Chokehold: Why the World Cannot Look Away
content:
Yemen's Strategic Chokehold: Why the World Cannot Look Away

There is a particular kind of war that the world only notices in fragments — a missile here, a sunken ship there, a famine statistic that flashes across a screen and disappears. Yemen has been that war for more than a decade. But in 2026, something has shifted. What was once dismissed as the Arab world's "forgotten conflict" has quietly become one of the most consequential flashpoints on the planet, sitting astride a maritime chokepoint that carries a meaningful share of global trade, hosting the most battle-hardened Iranian proxy force outside Lebanon, and now functioning as a live pressure valve for the wider Iran-Israel-Gulf confrontation. Yemen is no longer a sideshow. It is a control panel.

This report examines why Yemen's civil war, despite eleven years of grinding stalemate, has become strategically indispensable to understanding the Middle East's trajectory — and why every major power, from Washington to Beijing to New Delhi, now has skin in this game.

Executive Summary

Yemen in mid-2026 is a country fractured into three competing centers of power, sitting on top of one of the world's most sensitive maritime arteries, the Bab al-Mandab Strait. The Iran-backed Houthi movement (Ansar Allah), led by Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, controls Sana'a and the bulk of the population in the north. The Saudi-backed Presidential Leadership Council (PLC), chaired by Rashad al-Alimi, holds the internationally recognized government's seat in Aden. And a once-ascendant secessionist project, the Southern Transitional Council (STC), has just been militarily crushed and expelled from power after a failed bid to seize Yemen's eastern oil provinces in December 2025 — a move that triggered direct Saudi intervention against the very faction the UAE had spent eight years building up.

That single episode — Saudi Arabia bombing an Emirati-backed force inside Yemen — tells you everything about how far this conflict has evolved beyond its original Houthi-versus-government framing. Riyadh and Abu Dhabi, nominal partners in the original 2015 coalition, are now operating from visibly divergent threat perceptions inside the same battlespace.

Layered on top of this intra-coalition rupture is the bigger story: the Houthis' transformation from a domestic insurgency into a forward-deployed arm of Iran's "Axis of Resistance," capable of striking Israeli territory, throttling Red Sea shipping, and absorbing American and Israeli airstrikes while remaining functionally undefeated. Following the February 2026 Israeli-US strikes on Iran, the Houthis fired missiles at Israel for the first time since the broader regional war began, and UN officials have repeatedly warned that Yemen risks being "dragged" into a war it did not start. A US-Iran de-escalation track and the release of roughly 1,600 long-held Yemeni war prisoners in mid-2026 have created a fragile diplomatic opening — but Special Envoy Hans Grundberg has been blunt: what Yemen has now "is not peace."

For India and the wider Indo-Pacific trading world, Yemen's coastline is not an abstraction. It sits directly on the route connecting the Suez Canal to the Indian Ocean, meaning instability here has already reshaped shipping insurance costs, freight times, and energy flows for economies thousands of kilometers away. This is the strategic core of why Global Chanakya is tracking Yemen as a Tier-1 conflict, not a peripheral one.

Background

Yemen's war formally began in September 2014, when Houthi forces — a Zaydi Shia movement rooted in the mountainous Sa'dah governorate near the Saudi border — swept into Sana'a and forced the internationally recognized government to flee. By March 2015, with the Houthis allied to forces loyal to former president Ali Abdullah Saleh and advancing on Aden, Saudi Arabia assembled a multinational coalition and launched Operation Decisive Storm, framing the intervention as a defense against an Iranian-aligned takeover on its southern border.

What followed was a decade-long demonstration of how difficult it is to defeat a deeply entrenched, ideologically motivated insurgency through airpower alone. The Saudi-UAE coalition conducted more than twenty-five thousand airstrikes, generated catastrophic civilian casualties, and triggered the imposition of a naval blockade that has been at the very center of Yemen's humanitarian collapse. The Houthis, far from being dislodged, consolidated control over the most populous parts of the country, including the capital and the critical Red Sea port of Hodeidah.

Three structural fractures have defined this war since its inception, and all three remain live today:

  • The Houthi-versus-Republic fracture — the core ideological and sectarian struggle between Zaydi revivalism in the north and the internationally recognized government structure in the south.
  • The Saudi-Emirati fracture — two Gulf monarchies that entered the war as allies but built rival client networks, Riyadh backing the PLC's mainstream factions and Abu Dhabi cultivating the separatist STC, producing a coalition that has periodically fought itself as much as it fought the Houthis.
  • The Iran-Saudi proxy fracture — the broader regional contest in which Yemen became one battlefield among several (alongside Syria, Lebanon, and Iraq) for influence between Tehran and Riyadh.

A landmark moment came in March 2023, when China brokered a surprise rapprochement between Iran and Saudi Arabia, under which Tehran reportedly agreed to curb military support to the Houthis and respect the UN arms embargo. That deal, alongside a UN-brokered nationwide truce that began in April 2022 and was never formally renewed but has largely held on the ground, froze Yemen's internal frontlines for the first time in years. Direct Houthi-versus-PLC/STC combat has been largely suspended since, even as the truce's architecture officially lapsed in October 2022.

But "frozen frontlines" did not mean "frozen conflict." Beginning in November 2023, in the wake of the Israel-Hamas war, the Houthis discovered something far more strategically valuable than territorial conquest: the ability to hold global shipping hostage from a position of near-total external impunity. This pivot — from a localized insurgency to a transnational maritime-disruption actor — is the single most important development in understanding why Yemen now matters to the entire world, not just to its neighbors.

Current Situation

The map of Yemen today reflects a conflict that has stopped converging toward resolution and instead splintered into three distinct, semi-autonomous zones of authority, each with a different external patron and a different strategic logic.

The Houthi North: Iran's Forward Operating Base

The Houthis, under Abdul-Malik al-Houthi and the political leadership of Mahdi al-Mashat's Supreme Political Council, control Sana'a and virtually all of former North Yemen barring eastern Marib governorate. This territory holds the majority of Yemen's roughly 42 million people. Critically, Houthi control extends along the Red Sea coastline, including the strategic port of Hodeidah, giving the group direct leverage over traffic transiting the Bab al-Mandab Strait — one of the most consequential chokepoints in global trade.

The Houthis have spent the past two and a half years converting that geographic leverage into a genuine strategic asset for Iran's regional axis. From November 2023 they launched sustained attacks against commercial and naval shipping in the Red Sea, framed as solidarity with Hamas during the Gaza war. They sank vessels, killed crew members, seized ships including the Galaxy Leader, and forced a meaningful share of global container traffic to reroute around the Cape of Good Hope. A US-led international naval coalition was assembled to protect shipping, and Washington and London conducted direct strikes against Houthi military infrastructure.

The pattern since has been one of escalation, pause, and re-escalation, tracking almost exactly with the wider regional temperature:

  • Houthi attacks on shipping continued intermittently through 2024 into 2025.
  • From March to May 2025, expanded US strikes under the Trump administration targeted Houthi capabilities directly, ending in an Oman-brokered ceasefire in which the Houthis agreed to stop targeting American vessels in exchange for a halt in US strikes.
  • Houthi attacks on non-US shipping resumed in July 2025, alongside continued long-range strikes on Israel.
  • The Houthis suspended these attacks following the October 2025 Gaza ceasefire — but explicitly signaled they would resume if that ceasefire collapsed.
  • Following the February 28, 2026, Israeli-US strikes on Iran, the Houthis crossed a new threshold: on March 27-28, they launched their first direct missile attacks on Israel since the wider regional war erupted, explicitly acting in support of Tehran rather than purely in the Gaza-solidarity framing they had used since 2023.

This is the single most important strategic data point in the entire Yemen file: the Houthis have demonstrated, repeatedly, that they can be switched on and off as a regional pressure instrument depending on Iran's calculus. They are no longer a Yemen-specific armed faction. They are functionally what one senior diplomat described to the UN Security Council as the "military arm of the Iranian Revolutionary Guard," using Yemeni sovereign territory as a launch platform for a cross-border regional agenda — a characterization Russia notably did not echo, instead framing the Houthi question as downstream of broader US-Iran dynamics.

Domestically, Houthi governance has hardened into an increasingly closed, securitized system. The group has arbitrarily detained dozens of United Nations staff, NGO workers, and diplomatic personnel — 73 UN personnel remain detained as of mid-2026, with three referred to a Houthi-run "special criminal court." This systematic targeting of humanitarian actors triggered a watershed moment in January 2026, when the World Food Programme terminated contracts for all 365 of its staff in Houthi-controlled northern Yemen — the area accounting for roughly 70 percent of the country's total humanitarian need — citing the insecure operating environment and Houthi obstruction as the decisive factors. When the organization feeding millions of starving people concludes it can no longer safely operate, that is not a humanitarian footnote. It is a strategic indictment of how the Houthis have chosen to govern.

The Southern Collapse: STC's Rise and Sudden Fall

The most dramatic shift inside the anti-Houthi camp over the past six months has been the implosion of the Southern Transitional Council's independence project — and it is a case study in how quickly Gulf patron rivalries can detonate an entire coalition structure.

The STC, founded in 2017 and long backed militarily and financially by the UAE, had been formally absorbed into the PLC's eight-member governing structure in 2022 as part of the effort to unify anti-Houthi forces. But the marriage was always one of convenience. In December 2025, STC forces moved to seize Yemen's eastern oil-producing governorates and the port of Mukalla — an aggressive bid to establish a fait accompli ahead of a planned independence referendum the group hoped to hold within two years.

Saudi Arabia's response was swift and unambiguous. On December 30, the Royal Saudi Air Force struck STC-controlled Mukalla, targeting what it described as a weapons shipment that had arrived from the UAE — an accusation Abu Dhabi denied. The internationally recognized government then ordered all UAE forces out of Yemen within 24 hours, imposed a blockade, and declared a 90-day state of emergency. By January 2, 2026, Saudi-backed government forces launched a counteroffensive that recaptured Seiyun on January 3 and Mukalla on January 4, fully reversing the STC's territorial gains within days. STC leader Aidarous al-Zubaidi was accused of treason, expelled from the PLC, and fled the country — reportedly via Somaliland to the UAE — while the UAE formally withdrew its remaining forces from Yemen entirely.

This episode matters far beyond Yemen's borders for three reasons. First, it confirms Saudi Arabia has decisively repositioned itself as the principal — arguably sole — external security guarantor of the Yemeni government, a role it had previously shared uneasily with the UAE. Second, it exposes a genuine and significant rupture in Saudi-Emirati strategic alignment, two states that are framed internationally as a unified "Gulf bloc" but that, in practice, have been running parallel and sometimes contradictory Yemen policies for years. Third, it removes — at least for now — the secessionist variable that many analysts viewed as the second-most-likely trigger for renewed full-scale civil war, even as STC structures and grievances persist on the ground and government forces have used force against pro-STC protests in Aden and Mukalla in subsequent months.

The Government in Aden: Consolidation Without Capacity

The PLC under Rashad al-Alimi now finds itself, on paper, stronger than at any point since 2022 — having absorbed the STC's territory and forces, with Saudi Arabia firmly established as its "principal sponsor and security partner." But analysts continue to describe the PLC as structurally fractured, and the harder test — actually integrating disparate armed factions including the National Resistance Forces into a unified national military — has barely begun.

The government's authority remains thin on the ground in parts of the south. Pro-STC demonstrations have continued in Aden and Mukalla, and government-aligned forces have responded with lethal force on at least two documented occasions in early 2026, drawing direct criticism from Human Rights Watch for excessive force and arbitrary detention of protesters. This is the paradox of the post-STC order: Riyadh has eliminated a rival power center, but has not yet built a government capable of governing the territory it formally controls.

The Diplomatic Track: Cautious, Fragile Momentum

Underneath the military picture, 2026 has also produced the most tangible diplomatic movement Yemen has seen in years. A US-Houthi ceasefire, brokered by Oman and effective from May 6, ended the intense American bombing campaign that had run since mid-March. Conflict-related detainee negotiations under the Stockholm Agreement framework resumed in December 2025 and continued in Amman through the spring. In a genuinely significant development, roughly 1,600 long-held Yemeni war prisoners were released in mid-2026, generating what UN Special Envoy Hans Grundberg called fresh momentum, compounded further by the broader US-Iran de-escalation track that followed the February 2026 conflict.

Grundberg has structured his renewed push for an inclusive political process around three guiding principles: that any process must reflect Yemen's current, more complex reality rather than relying on outdated 2015-era assumptions; that Yemen's political, economic, and security tracks must be negotiated simultaneously rather than sequentially; and that the process must be genuinely Yemeni-owned even as it requires sustained regional and international buy-in. His shuttle diplomacy has taken him to Moscow, Washington, and Riyadh in recent months — itself a signal of how many external capitals now consider themselves stakeholders in Yemen's outcome.

Yet Grundberg's own language has been carefully unsentimental. "What Yemen has now is not peace," he told the Security Council, pointing to continued mistrust between the parties, reports that some factions are still actively preparing for renewed war, and an economy on the verge of collapse. That sober assessment is the most accurate one-line summary of Yemen's strategic condition available today.

Strategic Analysis

Yemen as a Geographic Force Multiplier

Strip away the politics for a moment and look purely at the map. Yemen controls the eastern shore of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the narrow chokepoint connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and onward to the Indian Ocean. Roughly twelve percent of global trade volume has historically transited this corridor, including a substantial share of containerized goods moving between Asia and Europe, and significant energy flows from Gulf producers toward Western markets. Whoever controls Yemen's western coastline controls a lever that can be pulled to impose costs on the entire global trading system without needing a navy capable of contesting open water — a classic example of what military strategists call "sea denial" achieved through asymmetric, land-based missile and drone capability rather than a conventional fleet.

This is precisely the capability the Houthis have built and demonstrated since late 2023. They do not need to sink every ship; they only need to make insurance underwriters and shipping conglomerates believe that any given transit carries elevated risk. That perception alone has been sufficient to push a meaningful share of Asia-Europe container traffic around the Cape of Good Hope — adding roughly ten to fourteen days and significant fuel costs to each voyage — even during periods when actual attack frequency has been low. Sea traffic through the Red Sea has not recovered to pre-2023 levels, and some shipping lines have continued avoiding the route even amid the broader 2026 Israel-US-Iran conflict, reflecting how durably the Houthis have damaged confidence in the corridor's security.

Iran's Calculated Use of an Expendable Proxy

From Tehran's perspective, Yemen offers something none of its other regional proxies can fully replicate: deniability combined with reach. Hezbollah is geographically constrained and has absorbed devastating losses from Israeli operations against its senior leadership. Iraqi militias operate under closer scrutiny given the US troop presence nearby. The Houthis, by contrast, sit at the edge of the Arabian Peninsula, beyond easy reach of a sustained Israeli ground or even consistent air campaign, while still possessing the missile and drone range to strike both Israeli territory and shipping lanes vital to the global economy.

This is precisely why Iran has been willing to absorb the political cost of the Houthis activating against Israel even while broader Tehran-Washington de-escalation talks are underway — it is a controllable pressure valve that can be opened or closed with minimal direct exposure for the Iranian state itself, and one that has proven remarkably resilient to both Saudi airpower since 2015 and direct American strikes since 2025. The Houthi calculation, meanwhile, is not purely subordinate to Iran. The group has its own domestic legitimacy incentives — striking Israel plays well with a Yemeni public that has been saturated with Gaza-war imagery for over two years, giving al-Mashat and Abdul-Malik al-Houthi a populist justification independent of any direct Iranian instruction.

The Saudi Dilemma: Exit Fatigue Meets Renewed Entanglement

Saudi Arabia's trajectory in Yemen over the past three years has been a study in contradiction. Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has spent enormous political and financial capital trying to extract the kingdom from a war that has cost an estimated $265 billion and consistently undermined the investor confidence central to Vision 2030. Riyadh pursued direct backchannel diplomacy with the Houthis through 2023, hosted Houthi delegations, and worked to position itself as a facilitator rather than a combatant.

Yet 2026 has forced Saudi Arabia back into a far more direct and assertive military and political role than it had hoped to play — first through the December 2025-January 2026 intervention against the STC, and now through its central position as the primary backer of a PLC government still working to consolidate authority. The kingdom's core strategic interest has not changed: it wants a stable, non-hostile southern border that does not host missile and drone platforms capable of striking Saudi territory, and it wants an end to a war that has become a permanent drag on its broader economic transformation agenda. What has changed is Riyadh's apparent recognition that achieving that outcome now requires more direct intervention against its own erstwhile allies, not less.

The UAE's Quiet Recalibration

The UAE's full withdrawal from Yemen in January 2026, following the collapsed STC gambit, marks the formal end of an eight-year Emirati strategy built around cultivating southern separatism as a hedge against both Houthi expansion and excessive Saudi dominance of the post-war order. Abu Dhabi's calculation appears to have shifted toward accepting that an independent or autonomous south was never going to be tolerated by Riyadh, and that continued investment in the STC risked a far more damaging open rupture with Saudi Arabia than the marginal benefits of a southern client were worth. This recalibration likely reflects the UAE's broader regional posture of prioritizing economic and diplomatic flexibility — including its own engagement with Israel under the Abraham Accords framework and its careful balancing act with Iran — over open-ended military entanglement in a conflict with diminishing returns.

The United States: Transactional Engagement, Not Resolution

Washington's Yemen policy under the Trump administration has been characterized by sharp, reactive military escalation followed by equally sharp disengagement once core American interests — specifically, the safety of US naval and commercial shipping — were addressed. The March-May 2025 bombing campaign, redesignation of the Houthis as a Foreign Terrorist Organization, and subsequent Oman-brokered ceasefire reflect a transactional logic: protect American assets, then exit. Notably, the May 2025 deal did not require the Houthis to halt attacks on Israel, a detail that drew criticism but that aligns with the administration's narrower framing of US interests in Yemen.

This pattern has continued into 2026. The administration has supported sunsetting UN mechanisms like UNMHA, arguing such mission have "outlived their usefulness," while simultaneously authorizing the military to repurpose intercepted Houthi-bound weapons shipments for its own drawdown purposes under the 2026 National Defense Authorization Act. The consistent thread is a US posture focused on threat suppression and resource denial rather than sustained investment in Yemen's underlying political settlement — leaving the harder diplomatic lifting disproportionately to the UN, Oman, and Saudi Arabia.

China's Quiet but Consequential Footprint

China's role in Yemen is rarely framed in dramatic terms, but it is structurally significant. Beyond brokering the 2023 Iran-Saudi rapprochement that initially constrained Iranian arms flows to the Houthis, Chinese-origin dual-use goods have continued reaching Houthi-controlled territory in volumes serious enough that US officials told the Security Council in 2026 that more than 70 percent of prohibited or restricted dual-use items intercepted under UN verification mechanisms between January 2025 and April 2026 originated in China. Whether this reflects deliberate state policy, weak export enforcement, or private commercial networks operating with limited oversight is genuinely contested — but the practical effect is the same: a steady trickle of components sustaining Houthi missile and drone production capacity, even amid official Chinese rhetoric supporting Yemeni stability and freedom of navigation.

Global Impact

Maritime Trade and the Reordering of Global Shipping

The most immediate and measurable global consequence of Yemen's instability has been the structural disruption of Red Sea shipping patterns. Major container lines diverted significant volumes around the Cape of Good Hope from late 2023 onward, and that diversion has proven stickier than many analysts initially expected — sea traffic through the Red Sea still has not recovered to pre-2023 levels even amid periods of relative Houthi quiet. This has compounded shipping costs, lengthened delivery timelines for goods moving between Asian manufacturing hubs and European consumer markets, and forced energy companies to periodically pause transits altogether during acute escalation periods.

For India specifically, this matters directly. A significant share of Indian trade with Europe and the Mediterranean transits via the Suez-Red Sea corridor; sustained disruption raises freight costs for Indian exporters and importers alike and adds strategic weight to New Delhi's parallel investment in alternative connectivity corridors, including its participation in the International North-South Transport Corridor and growing interest in the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor framework discussed alongside the G20.

Energy Security Implications

While Yemen itself is not a major energy producer, its coastline borders the approach routes to both the Suez Canal and the Strait of Hormuz region's broader maritime architecture. Sustained Houthi disruption capability raises the specter — explicitly flagged by UN officials — of Yemen's waters becoming "another commercial shipping chokehold, akin to Iran's strategy in the Strait of Hormuz," effectively giving Tehran's regional network two pressure points rather than one through which to threaten global energy and trade flows simultaneously during periods of acute crisis.

Humanitarian Catastrophe as Geopolitical Liability

Yemen's humanitarian crisis is not a side effect of the geopolitical contest — it has become a strategic factor in its own right. More than 18 million Yemenis, over half the population, are now acutely hungry, with over 2.2 million children under five acutely malnourished. The 2026 Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan calls for $2.16 billion, yet Yemen's 2025 appeal was funded at only 29 percent, forcing systematic cuts to life-saving programs precisely as needs intensified. This is a crisis any external actor seeking influence in Yemen must eventually reckon with, and it provides Houthi authorities a recurring tool of leverage — controlling access to a starving population gives them negotiating weight disproportionate to their formal diplomatic standing.

Precedent for Asymmetric Maritime Warfare

Perhaps the most underappreciated global implication of the Yemen conflict is doctrinal. The Houthis have demonstrated, in real time, that a non-state actor with limited resources can impose meaningful costs on global trade using relatively low-cost missile, drone, and naval mine technology against a chokepoint, without needing to defeat any conventional navy in open battle. This is now studied seriously by naval planners worldwide — including in the Indo-Pacific, where the same logic applies with even greater force to scenarios involving the Strait of Malacca, the South China Sea, and the Taiwan Strait. China's own People's Liberation Army Navy doctrine around anti-access/area-denial draws on related principles; Yemen has become an unintended live-fire laboratory for how such strategies perform against a determined international naval response.

Risk Assessment

High-Probability Risks (12-18 Month Horizon)

  • Renewed Houthi-Israel exchanges: Given the precedent set in March 2026 and the group's demonstrated willingness to activate in solidarity with Iran or Gaza-linked triggers, further Houthi missile or drone strikes on Israel remain highly likely if regional tensions resurge, with corresponding Israeli retaliatory strikes on Hodeidah port, Sana'a airport, or power infrastructure.
  • Continued humanitarian deterioration: With funding chronically short and WFP operations curtailed across Houthi territory, further deterioration in malnutrition indicators is near-certain absent a dramatic funding and access breakthrough.
  • Localized southern instability: Pro-STC sentiment in Aden, Mukalla, and surrounding governorates has not disappeared simply because the STC's leadership was expelled. Further protests, and further heavy-handed government responses, are likely.

Moderate-Probability Risks

  • Resumption of Red Sea shipping attacks: Should the Gaza ceasefire collapse or the broader Iran-Israel-US confrontation reignite, the Houthis have signaled clear intent to resume attacks on commercial shipping, a capability they have paused but never relinquished.
  • Stalled detainee and political negotiations: The Amman talks and prisoner releases represent genuine progress, but the underlying mistrust Grundberg describes — including reports that factions are still preparing for war — means formal political negotiations could stall or collapse without warning.
  • UN operational withdrawal: Continued Houthi detention of UN personnel and obstruction of humanitarian access could trigger further agency withdrawals beyond WFP, deepening the access vacuum in northern Yemen.

Lower-Probability but High-Impact Risks

  • Full collapse of the north-south truce: A return to direct large-scale Houthi-versus-PLC ground combat would represent a genuine rupture of the de facto ceasefire that has held in various forms since April 2022 — possible but currently contradicted by the interests of all major external patrons, none of whom want to fund renewed full-scale war.
  • Saudi-UAE open rupture: While the STC episode exposed real friction, both kingdoms have far greater shared interests — regional stability, economic diversification, and counterbalancing Iran — than the Yemen file alone would suggest is worth jeopardizing through open confrontation.
  • AQAP resurgence: Al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula has shown renewed activity amid the broader chaos and reduced counterterrorism focus from external actors distracted by the Houthi-Israel-Iran dimension; a security vacuum in contested areas could allow further entrenchment.

Future Scenarios

Scenario Analysis — the following projections are illustrative simulations based on current trajectories, not confirmed events.

Scenario One: Managed Fragmentation (Most Likely)

Yemen continues as a de facto partitioned state for the foreseeable future — Houthi north, Saudi-backed government south — with the current uneasy truce holding in fits and starts. Periodic Houthi-Israel exchanges occur whenever regional tensions spike, met by proportionate Israeli retaliation, without escalating into full reconquest attempts on either side. Diplomatic talks under Grundberg continue incrementally, producing further detainee exchanges and possibly a renewed economic and salary-payment framework, but no comprehensive political settlement materializes within the next two years. This scenario essentially extends the post-2022 status quo indefinitely, with Yemen remaining a persistent but contained source of regional friction.

Scenario Two: Regional Conflagration Spillover

Should the broader Iran-Israel-US confrontation reignite at scale — whether through renewed strikes on Iranian nuclear or military infrastructure, or a collapse of the current de-escalation track — the Houthis activate fully as Iran's forward platform, resuming sustained attacks on both Israel and Red Sea shipping simultaneously. This would likely trigger a renewed, larger-scale US and Israeli air campaign against Houthi infrastructure, push global shipping insurance costs sharply upward, and risk drawing Saudi Arabia and the UAE — despite their reluctance — into providing at least logistical or basing support to US operations, reigniting the very entanglement both kingdoms have spent years trying to exit.

Scenario Three: Negotiated De-Escalation Breakthrough

Building on the May 2026 US-Houthi ceasefire, the prisoner releases, and the broader Iran-US diplomatic track, a more durable Saudi-Houthi bilateral framework emerges — addressing border security, reconstruction financing, and a phased normalization of north-south economic relations, even without full Houthi disarmament. This would not resolve Yemen's internal political legitimacy questions but could meaningfully reduce both humanitarian suffering and external escalation risk. Given Saudi Arabia's demonstrated economic incentive to exit the conflict and the genuine diplomatic momentum visible in 2026, this scenario is plausible but contingent on Iran's continued willingness to restrain — not just pause — Houthi external operations.

Scenario Four: Southern Re-Fragmentation

Continued government mishandling of pro-STC sentiment in Aden and the eastern governorates — particularly further use of lethal force against protesters — triggers a renewed, more diffuse southern uprising, this time without unified STC leadership but potentially more difficult to suppress precisely because it lacks a single addressable command structure. Saudi Arabia would face the uncomfortable choice of deeper direct military administration of southern Yemen or risking a second secessionist wave, this time without UAE backing to negotiate against.

Intelligence Forecast

Based on current trajectories, Global Chanakya's assessment for the next twelve to eighteen months centers on five core judgments:

First, the Houthi movement will remain functionally undefeated and increasingly normalized as a permanent regional security variable rather than a temporary insurgency awaiting resolution. Neither Saudi airpower since 2015 nor American strikes since 2025 have meaningfully degraded its core missile and drone capability or its political control over northern Yemen.

Second, Saudi Arabia's direct military and political re-engagement, triggered by the STC collapse, is likely to deepen rather than reverse in the near term, as Riyadh works to consolidate a PLC government that currently lacks the institutional capacity to govern independently of Saudi backing.

Third, the Red Sea will remain a contested, elevated-risk corridor for global shipping for the foreseeable future, with traffic volumes unlikely to return to pre-2023 levels even during quiet periods, given the persistent underlying capability — not just intent — that the Houthis have demonstrated.

Fourth, the humanitarian crisis will continue to deteriorate on its current trajectory absent a dramatic funding and access breakthrough, and will increasingly function as a Houthi leverage tool in any political negotiation rather than purely a tragedy requiring outside intervention.

Fifth, Yemen's trajectory will remain tightly coupled to the broader Iran-Israel-US relationship rather than driven primarily by its own internal dynamics — meaning the single most important variable to watch is not anything happening inside Yemen itself, but the state of negotiations and tensions between Tehran, Washington, and Jerusalem.

Final Strategic Takeaway

Yemen has spent over a decade being misread by the outside world — first as a simple proxy battlefield between Saudi Arabia and Iran, then as a humanitarian catastrophe demanding aid rather than analysis, and more recently as a shipping-lane nuisance to be managed through periodic airstrikes. Each of these framings captured something real and missed the larger picture.

What Yemen actually represents in 2026 is a live demonstration of a new kind of strategic geography — one where a fractured, impoverished state with no functioning central government can nonetheless impose costs on the global economy, host a forward-deployed proxy force capable of striking a nuclear-armed regional power, and force three Gulf monarchies, two global superpowers, and the United Nations Security Council into sustained, anxious engagement. Population size and GDP no longer determine strategic relevance the way they once did. Geography, asymmetric capability, and the willingness to absorb punishment without collapsing now matter just as much.

The lesson radiating outward from Yemen is uncomfortable but increasingly undeniable: in the contemporary security environment, a determined non-state actor sitting on the right strip of coastline can hold more leverage over the global trading system than most mid-sized states possess through conventional means.

For India, the Gulf states, and the wider Indo-Pacific trading community, the message is clear. Yemen is not a problem that will resolve itself through patience, nor one that can be permanently solved through airpower. It requires sustained, multilateral, economically serious engagement — the kind that addresses Saudi Arabia's genuine desire to exit, the Houthis' entrenched governance reality, the south's unresolved political identity, and Iran's calculated use of Yemeni territory as a regional pressure valve, simultaneously rather than sequentially, exactly as Special Envoy Grundberg has argued. Until that happens, Yemen will remain what it has become: not a forgotten war, but a strategic chokehold the world cannot afford to ignore.

title: Iran-Israel Proxy War Explained: From Shadow War to Open War
content:
Iran-Israel Proxy War Explained: From Shadow War to Open War

For nearly four decades, Iran and Israel fought a war neither country officially declared. It was waged through intermediaries — Hezbollah rockets fired from southern Lebanon, Hamas tunnels dug beneath Gaza, Houthi missiles launched at Red Sea shipping, militia attacks on American bases in Iraq and Syria — a careful architecture of deniability that allowed Tehran to bleed Israel and its allies without ever putting the Islamic Republic's own territory or leadership directly in the crosshairs. That architecture, built across the careers of multiple Iranian supreme leaders and sustained through billions of dollars in funding, weapons transfers, and training programs across what Tehran called its "Axis of Resistance," collapsed entirely on the morning of February 28, 2026.

At 06:45 UTC that day, Israeli warplanes struck a residential compound in Tehran where Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei was meeting with senior officials. He died in the strike, along with members of his family and several of his most senior commanders. Within minutes, American B-2 bombers and Tomahawk-armed warships joined the assault, targeting Iran's fortified ballistic missile facilities under an operation Washington called Epic Fury and Israel called Roaring Lion. The proxy war was over. What replaced it was the most direct, most destructive confrontation between Iran, Israel, and the United States in the Islamic Republic's history — a war that, even after a ceasefire and a formal memorandum of understanding, has left every element of the old proxy architecture either shattered, mutating, or fighting on regardless of what any document in Switzerland says.

Executive Summary
