The strategic calculation is generational rather than immediate — Beijing is betting that technological sovereignty, even at a near-term performance cost, provides more durable long-term security than continued dependence on American-controlled technology inputs that Washington has demonstrated repeatedly it is willing to restrict for strategic leverage.

The May 2026 Trump-Xi summit in Beijing produced a ninety-day trade truce following tariffs that had reached as high as 145% on certain goods, illustrating both the severity of the underlying confrontation and the mutual recognition that unconstrained escalation serves neither side's interests. But beneath the diplomatic theater, the structural trajectory toward bifurcated technology ecosystems continues largely unabated, with both Washington and Beijing treating periodic truces as tactical pauses rather than genuine resolution of the underlying strategic competition.

Strategic Analysis: The Architecture of Integrated Leverage

Why China's Strategy Is More Coherent Than Western Commentary Often Acknowledges

Western analysis of Chinese expansion frequently treats Belt and Road infrastructure, rare earth policy, military basing, and technology competition as separate analytical categories, assessed by different expert communities using different frameworks. This compartmentalized analysis, while methodologically convenient, obscures the most important strategic feature of China's approach: its deliberate integration across domains.

Consider how these elements reinforce each other in practice. BRI infrastructure investment creates the physical and diplomatic foundation for expanded rare earth and critical mineral access, since many of the resource-rich countries where China has built mining and processing partnerships — across Africa, Central Asia, and Latin America — are also major BRI recipients whose governments have accumulated both financial obligations and diplomatic goodwill toward Beijing. That mineral processing dominance, in turn, provides the coercive leverage Beijing has demonstrated it is willing to deploy against specific strategic rivals during moments of geopolitical tension, as the Japan case illustrates concretely. And the dual-use port infrastructure built through BRI financing provides the physical network through which Chinese naval power could eventually be projected to protect these accumulated economic interests, should circumstances require it.

This is not a series of disconnected initiatives pursued by different bureaucratic constituencies within the Chinese state — though Chinese policy implementation certainly involves genuine inter-agency competition and coordination challenges, as it does in any large bureaucracy. It is, at the level of strategic intent articulated by Xi Jinping's leadership, a coherent architecture aimed at constructing Chinese global influence that is resilient to any single point of Western counter-pressure, because no single American or allied policy response — whether sanctions, tariffs, military deterrence, or diplomatic isolation — can simultaneously address infrastructure dependency, resource leverage, technological dependence, and military access constraints all at once.

The Calculated Restraint Beneath the Aggressive Headlines

Despite the genuinely aggressive instruments China has demonstrated a willingness to deploy — extraterritorial export controls, operational rare earth coercion against treaty allies, dual-use military infrastructure — Beijing's overall expansion strategy remains characterized by calculated restraint rather than reckless overextension. China has not, even amid the Japan rare earth episode, moved to fully weaponize its mineral dominance against the broader Western economy in a manner that would trigger the kind of comprehensive decoupling response that would accelerate the very alternative supply chain development Beijing's strategy is designed to forestall.

This restraint reflects sound strategic logic rooted in China's own economic vulnerabilities. Beijing's export-dependent industrial model, still grappling with a multi-year property sector contraction and persistent deflationary pressure, cannot afford the comprehensive Western economic isolation that maximalist coercion would invite. The calibrated, targeted nature of Chinese leverage — deployed against specific allies regarding specific contingencies, rather than indiscriminately against the entire Western alliance system — reflects a strategic culture that prizes patient, sustainable pressure over dramatic but potentially self-defeating confrontation.

The Counter-Coalition Response and Its Limits

China's expansion strategy has triggered, as any sufficiently successful expansion strategy eventually does, a coordinated allied counter-response that is itself worth examining closely. The early-2026 G7 ministerial meeting in Washington focused specifically on rare earth supply chain resilience, exploring measures including price floors and coordinated international incentives to reduce collective Western dependence on Chinese mineral processing. The United States has accelerated funding and expanded cooperation with Australia, Japan, and Southeast Asian partners including Malaysia and Thailand, treating supply chain diversification as a structural priority rather than a response to episodic disruption.

The Japan-specific response is particularly significant given Tokyo's position as the most immediate target of Chinese rare earth coercion. Japan and the United States have developed a bilateral critical minerals framework identifying strategic co-investment projects, alongside a February 2026 action plan exploring border-adjusted price floors and trade policy coordination, and a March 2026 memorandum on deep-sea mining cooperation specifically targeting extraction of Japan's own rare earth deposits located in seabed muds off Minamitorishima Island. This represents a serious, well-resourced effort to deny Beijing exactly the kind of coercive leverage it has already demonstrated a willingness to use.

Yet the structural reality remains sobering for the alternative supply chain project: despite a genuine surge in Western innovation around extraction and processing technology, commercial scalability at the volumes required to meaningfully displace Chinese dominance remains unproven. Many promising alternative approaches have demonstrated viability only at pilot or demonstration scale, and the gap between technological proof-of-concept and reliable, cost-competitive industrial production at the scale China has built over decades is likely to persist for years, not months. China's strategic planners understand this timeline advantage clearly, and it shapes their calculated confidence in continuing to deploy mineral leverage even as Western counter-investment accelerates.

Global Impact: How China's Expansion Reshapes Regional Orders

Africa: From Resource Extraction to Institutional Influence

China's expansion strategy in Africa has evolved well beyond the resource-extraction characterization that dominated early Western commentary. Beijing's current approach combines continued infrastructure and energy investment with deliberate efforts to shape African collective diplomatic positions through influence over the African Union and individual governments' voting behavior in UN and other multilateral forums. This institutional dimension matters enormously for China's broader multipolarity project: African votes within UN bodies, frequently aligned with Chinese positions on issues ranging from human rights resolutions to Taiwan's international status, represent a meaningful accumulated diplomatic asset that pure economic analysis of BRI investment often underweights.

Latin America: Quiet Expansion Into America's Traditional Sphere

China's deepening energy and infrastructure investment across Brazil, Argentina, and Venezuela represents a particularly pointed strategic development given the Trump administration's explicit 2026 National Security Strategy prioritization of Western Hemisphere primacy through its "Trump Corollary" to the Monroe Doctrine. Chinese expansion into precisely the geography Washington has designated its highest strategic priority creates a direct, if largely indirect and economically-mediated, test of competing claims to hemispheric influence — one that China is pursuing through patient infrastructure and energy investment rather than the kind of confrontational posture that would invite direct American countermeasures.

The Indo-Pacific: Where Expansion Meets Maximum Resistance

China's expansion strategy faces its most organized and well-resourced resistance within the Indo-Pacific, where American alliance structures, QUAD coordination, and AUKUS military cooperation collectively represent the most sophisticated counter-balancing architecture Beijing confronts anywhere globally. The rare earth coercion deployed against Japan specifically illustrates how China's economic leverage tools are being tested directly against the alliance structure most capable of constraining Chinese regional ambitions, particularly regarding Taiwan.

Risk Assessment

The Overextension Risk

China's expansion strategy, for all its demonstrated sophistication, carries genuine overextension risk that Beijing's own strategic planners openly debate. Maintaining dual-use military infrastructure across more than a dozen countries, managing the debt distress consequences of BRI lending across dozens of recipient economies, and sustaining the rare earth coercion campaign against treaty allies of the world's most powerful military, all simultaneously, requires sustained resource commitment that China's own slowing domestic economic growth makes increasingly difficult to guarantee indefinitely.

The Counter-Coalition Acceleration Risk

Beijing's most operationally aggressive moves — particularly the extraterritorial rare earth controls and the explicit coercion deployed against Japan — carry a meaningful risk of accelerating exactly the kind of coordinated allied supply chain diversification that would, if successful at scale, permanently erode the mineral leverage China has spent decades accumulating. The G7's 2026 rare earth coordination and the Japan-US-Australia trilateral investment architecture represent early evidence that Chinese coercion, deployed too visibly or too aggressively, can catalyze precisely the alternative supply chain investment that patient, less confrontational Chinese strategy might otherwise have continued to forestall.

Future Scenarios

Scenario Analysis: China's Expansion Trajectory Through 2030

Scenario One: Sustained Integrated Expansion (Probability: 40%)

China continues successfully integrating its BRI, rare earth, military basing, and technology strategies into a mutually reinforcing architecture, managing the overextension risks through continued selective, calibrated deployment of coercive tools rather than maximalist confrontation. Beijing's regional influence, particularly across Africa, Central Asia, and parts of Latin America, continues deepening, while the Indo-Pacific remains the primary zone of effective Western counter-balancing.

Scenario Two: Accelerated Counter-Coalition Response (Probability: 35%)

Western allied supply chain diversification, accelerated specifically by the visibility of Chinese coercion against Japan and other allies, achieves meaningful scale faster than current technological and commercial timelines suggest, eroding Chinese mineral leverage materially by 2029-2030. This scenario requires sustained, well-coordinated Western investment commitment that historical patterns of allied coordination on long-horizon industrial policy have not always reliably demonstrated.

Scenario Three: Domestic Constraint Forces Recalibration (Probability: 25%)

China's own domestic economic challenges — continued property sector weakness, demographic decline, and youth unemployment pressures — force a meaningful scaling back of overseas expansion ambitions, prioritizing domestic economic stabilization over continued global infrastructure and military footprint expansion. This would represent a significant, though not necessarily permanent, recalibration of the patient, multi-decade expansion strategy Xi Jinping has pursued since 2013.

Intelligence Forecast

  • China will continue selective rare earth coercion calibrated to specific strategic contingencies rather than broad-based weaponization, with Taiwan-related deterrence against Japan and other potential allied military supporters remaining the primary operational use case.
  • Additional dual-use port and basing arrangements will continue developing across the Indian Ocean littoral and parts of Africa, with Pakistan's Gwadar and Cambodia's Ream Naval Base remaining the most strategically significant facilities to monitor for eventual formalized military access agreements.
  • Western alternative supply chain investment will continue accelerating but will not achieve commercial scale sufficient to materially reduce Chinese rare earth leverage before approximately 2029-2030, given current technology readiness levels for alternative extraction and processing approaches.
  • BRI lending will remain selective and strategically targeted rather than returning to the volume-driven approach of 2013-2018, with Africa and Latin America remaining priority geographies and continued careful debt-distress management to avoid reputational costs comparable to the Hambantota precedent.
  • The technology bifurcation between American and Chinese ecosystems will deepen regardless of periodic tariff truces, as both sides continue treating diplomatic de-escalation as tactical rather than addressing the underlying structural competition over semiconductor and AI technological sovereignty.

Final Strategic Takeaway

China's long-term global expansion strategy succeeds precisely because it refuses to be reduced to any single headline-generating confrontation. There is no equivalent of a Cuban Missile Crisis moment in Beijing's approach — no single dramatic event that crystallizes the entire strategy for global publics and forces a unified, urgent Western response. Instead, there is a port financed here, a mineral processing license secured there, a logistics facility quietly expanded, an export control regulation issued, each individually defensible as ordinary statecraft, but collectively constituting the most ambitious and architecturally coherent expansion of global influence any single power has attempted since the height of American Cold War alliance-building.

What should concern Western strategists most is not any individual element of this strategy but its demonstrated integration and adaptability. China has shown the capacity to learn from early mistakes — recalibrating BRI lending practices after the Hambantota reputational damage, developing increasingly sophisticated extraterritorial regulatory tools modeled explicitly on American precedents, and deploying coercive leverage with calculated restraint rather than reckless overreach. This is not the behavior of a rising power stumbling opportunistically from one tactical advantage to the next. It is the behavior of a state executing a patient, multi-decade strategic architecture with remarkable institutional discipline.

The countervailing reality, and the genuine source of strategic hope for those concerned about unchecked Chinese global influence, lies in the structural vulnerabilities Beijing's own economic trajectory presents, and in the increasingly coordinated, if still incomplete, allied response taking shape across the G7, QUAD, and AUKUS architectures. China's expansion strategy is formidable, but it is not invincible, and it is not operating in a vacuum of Western strategic response. The next five years will determine whether patient Chinese architecture-building outpaces increasingly urgent allied counter-investment, or whether the very visibility of Chinese coercion — demonstrated starkly in the Japan rare earth case — has already triggered the kind of sustained, well-resourced Western response that could meaningfully constrain Beijing's long-term ambitions.

Global Chanakya Intelligence Assessment: China's expansion strategy is not a series of opportunistic moves — it is integrated architecture built over a decade and designed to outlast any single American administration's policy response. Understanding it as a coherent system, rather than a collection of separate headlines, is the only way the democratic world can build a response equal to its ambition.

title: The Decline of Unipolarity: Is American Dominance Really Fading in 2026?
content:
The Decline of Unipolarity: Is American Dominance Really Fading in 2026?

Executive Summary

For the first time in a generation, the question of whether American dominance is fading is no longer being asked primarily by Washington's rivals or by academic theorists. It is being asked, with striking candor, by the United States government itself. In May 2025, Vice President JD Vance stood before the Naval Academy and told graduating officers that "the era of uncontested US dominance is over." Secretary of State Marco Rubio has built an entire framework around the premise that unipolarity was a post-Cold War anomaly rather than a natural or permanent state of affairs, and that the multipolar world now emerging requires Washington to prioritize narrow national interests over the costly maintenance of the liberal international order it spent eighty years constructing.

This is not decline by stealth. It is decline acknowledged, in some quarters even embraced, as a starting premise for a new American grand strategy. The 2026 National Security Strategy, released under the Trump administration, abandons the great-power-competition framework that defined American strategic thinking since at least 2017 in favor of a highly ideological document that elevates the Western Hemisphere as America's highest priority, invokes a "Trump Corollary" to the Monroe Doctrine, and reserves its sharpest criticism not for China or Russia but for European allies and the foreign policy establishment Trump considers responsible for America's strategic overextension.

Yet the picture is more complicated than a simple narrative of collapse. The United States retains the world's largest economy, its most powerful military by a wide margin, the deepest and most liquid capital markets on earth, and a technological edge in artificial intelligence and advanced computing that no rival has matched. What is genuinely declining is not American capability but American willingness to convert that capability into global public goods — security guarantees, open markets, multilateral leadership — without direct, often transactional, compensation. This distinction between hegemonic capacity and hegemonic will is the single most important analytical key to understanding what is actually happening to American power in 2026, and it has consequences that will outlast any single administration.

Background: The Long Arc From Unipolar Moment to Multipolar Reality

The phrase "unipolar moment" was coined by columnist Charles Krauthammer in a 1990 essay, written even before the Soviet Union's formal dissolution, anticipating a world in which American power would face no peer competitor. For roughly a decade and a half, that prediction held with striking accuracy. The 1990s saw the United States preside over NATO expansion, the Gulf War coalition, the Balkans interventions, and the early architecture of post-Cold War globalization, largely on its own terms.

The first serious cracks appeared not from external challenge but from self-inflicted strategic overextension. The 2003 invasion of Iraq, conducted over the objections of key allies and without UN Security Council authorization, revealed both the extent of American military power and the limits of what that power could accomplish absent broader international legitimacy and sound strategic judgment. The subsequent insurgency, the 2008 financial crisis that originated in American mortgage markets and metastasized globally, and the protracted, ultimately unsuccessful nation-building efforts in Afghanistan collectively eroded both American material capacity and, more importantly, the global perception of American competence and reliability that unipolarity had depended upon as much as raw power.

China's economic rise during this same period transformed the structural foundation of the international system more thoroughly than any single American policy failure. Beijing's economy grew from roughly one-tenth the size of America's in 1990 to near-parity on a purchasing power parity basis by the mid-2020s. This growth funded military modernization, the Belt and Road Initiative's global infrastructure footprint, and a foreign policy posture under Xi Jinping that increasingly positioned China as a legitimate alternative pole of global power rather than merely a regional actor managing its own development.

Russia's trajectory has been different but complementary to this multipolar drift. Stripped of much of its Soviet-era economic weight, Moscow under Vladimir Putin has pursued a strategy of asymmetric disruption — using energy leverage over Europe, military intervention in Georgia, Syria, and Ukraine, and active measures against Western democratic processes to demonstrate that American-led order could be contested and degraded even by a power with a GDP smaller than Italy's. Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 became, paradoxically, both a demonstration of the costs major powers will still bear to challenge the post-Cold War settlement and a catalyst that accelerated exactly the kind of multipolar coalition-building — between Russia, China, Iran, and North Korea — that American strategists had spent decades trying to prevent.

By the time Trump returned to office in January 2025, the structural conditions for declining American unipolarity were already firmly established. What changed with his return was something different and, in important respects, more consequential: an American president and administration willing to explicitly acknowledge and, in some respects, accelerate that decline rather than resist it.

Current Situation: Washington's Own Acknowledgment of a Changed World

The Rhetorical Turn: Multipolarity as Official Doctrine

What distinguishes 2025-2026 from previous periods of debate about American decline is the degree to which senior US officials have stopped contesting the premise and started building policy around it. Secretary of State Rubio's framing — that unipolarity was a "post-Cold War anomaly" rather than a natural state, and that the world has simply returned to its historically normal multipolar condition — represents a genuine doctrinal shift. This is not the language of an administration in denial about declining relative power. It is the language of an administration that has concluded resistance to multipolarity is futile and that American interests are better served by managing the transition on favorable terms than by exhausting national resources trying to prevent it.

Vice President Vance's Naval Academy speech in May 2025 made this explicit in front of the next generation of American military officers: the United States was a superpower without peer for a brief historical window following the Soviet collapse, but that window has closed, and American strategy must now operate in a world with genuine competitors. This is a remarkable thing for a sitting vice president to tell military graduates — not a warning about future risk, but a statement of present reality that fundamentally reframes what American military power is meant to accomplish.

The 2026 National Security Strategy: Abandoning Great-Power Competition for Hemispheric Primacy

The clearest institutional expression of this shift is the 2026 National Security Strategy itself, which the Council on Foreign Relations has characterized as a striking departure from every predecessor document since the concept of great-power competition became the organizing framework of American strategic thinking. Rather than centering China and Russia as the primary threats requiring sustained, resourced global engagement, the 2026 NSS elevates the Western Hemisphere as America's highest strategic priority, framed around stopping migration, combating drug trafficking networks the document labels "narco-terrorists," and securing what the strategy calls a "Trump Corollary" to the nineteenth-century Monroe Doctrine.

This represents a fundamental reordering of strategic priorities with profound implications. A National Security Strategy that elevates hemispheric primacy above global great-power competition is, definitionally, a document that accepts reduced American engagement and resource commitment in the Indo-Pacific, Europe, and the Middle East relative to the framework that has governed American strategy since at least the Obama administration's "pivot to Asia." The CFR's assessment that the document reserves its sharpest criticism for European allies and domestic foreign policy elites — rather than for China or Russia, the traditionally identified strategic competitors — is perhaps the most telling detail of all. An American security strategy more animated by grievance against its own allies than concern about its adversaries is a document describing a superpower turning inward.

The Institutional Withdrawal: Counting the Departures

The Trump administration's institutional disengagement from the architecture of American-led global order has been systematic and extensive. The United States formally withdrew from the World Health Organization and the Paris Peace Accords framework, shut down the United States Agency for International Development entirely, and substantially reduced funding for numerous United Nations agencies. The Chicago Council on Global Affairs' assessment of 2025 as "highly disruptive, tumultuous, and chaotic" for the international order, with the United States as "a major, if not the only, driver" of that disruption, reflects a consensus among foreign policy analysts across the ideological spectrum that something qualitatively different is occurring compared to previous episodes of American skepticism toward multilateralism.

The international trade order has been thrown into comparable disarray. Trade relationships built over decades have been explicitly subordinated to national security framing, with tariffs deployed not as part of coordinated, congressionally consulted strategy but — in the Center for American Progress's characterization — as blunt instruments wielded impulsively, damaging long-standing partnerships in ways that are proving difficult to repair even when individual disputes are eventually resolved. Nearly 70% of Americans, according to polling cited by domestic policy analysts, now believe 2026 will be a year of economic difficulty — a remarkable erosion of public confidence that constrains the administration's room to pursue costly global commitments even if its strategic preferences shifted.

The State Department itself has undergone significant internal transformation, with career diplomats and national security professionals replaced or sidelined in favor of personnel selected primarily for political loyalty rather than regional expertise or institutional continuity. This matters enormously for the practical exercise of American global influence: diplomatic effectiveness depends substantially on accumulated relationships, country-specific knowledge, and institutional memory that cannot be rebuilt quickly once dispersed.

NATO and the Unresolved Question of European Security

Nowhere is the ambiguity of American retrenchment more consequential than in the alliance architecture governing European security. The Stiftung Wissenschaft und Politik's February 2026 analysis identifies the core contradiction precisely: the 2026 National Defense Strategy provides no details about the size, orientation, deployment, or stationing of US troops and equipment in Europe, leaving allies in a state of structural uncertainty about Washington's actual alliance commitments even as official documents continue to affirm NATO's importance in general terms.

This is not simple abandonment — American forces remain in Europe, and the administration has not formally signaled NATO withdrawal. But the security strategy documents simultaneously contain what SWP's analysts describe as a sweeping verbal attack on liberal Europe, directed primarily at the European Union but implicitly questioning the values underpinning NATO itself. The practical message to Berlin, Paris, and other European capitals is unmistakable: the alliance commitments that defined transatlantic security since 1949 can no longer be assumed to operate on the predictable, broadly bipartisan basis that characterized even periods of American skepticism toward European burden-sharing in previous decades. German and European decision-makers, the analysis concludes bluntly, should not fall victim to the false hope that NATO in its current form survives Trump's second term unchanged.

This uncertainty has already produced concrete behavioral changes among European allies, as documented across multiple analyses: NATO European members and Canada increased defense spending by 20% in 2025, and alliance members have agreed to move toward a 5% of GDP defense spending framework by 2035. These are not the actions of allies confident in unconditional American protection — they are the actions of governments hedging against a genuine possibility of reduced American commitment, accelerating precisely the kind of European strategic autonomy that successive American administrations have rhetorically encouraged but rarely actually wanted to see fully realized, since a genuinely autonomous Europe is also a Europe less dependent on American leadership and more capable of pursuing its own, sometimes divergent, strategic preferences.

Strategic Analysis: Capability Versus Will — The Central Distinction

What Hasn't Declined: The Hard Power Foundations

Before accepting any narrative of American collapse, the analytical discipline required of serious strategic assessment demands an honest accounting of what remains extraordinarily, even overwhelmingly, in America's favor. The United States retains defense spending exceeding the next several highest-spending nations combined, a global network of military bases and access agreements that no rival power can replicate, and decisive technological advantages in critical domains including artificial intelligence model development, advanced semiconductor design (even where manufacturing has shifted overseas), aerospace, and biotechnology.

American capital markets remain unmatched in depth, liquidity, and legal predictability — features that continue to attract global investment even amid policy uncertainty, because the alternative options (Chinese capital markets with capital controls and political risk, European markets fragmented across national jurisdictions, emerging market alternatives lacking comparable scale) simply do not offer comparable characteristics. The dollar, despite genuine erosion at the margins documented in BRICS de-dollarization efforts, remains the dominant global reserve currency by an enormous margin, with no credible alternative positioned to displace it within any realistic medium-term horizon.

The United States also retains something less tangible but strategically significant: a network of alliance relationships built over eight decades that, even under current strain, represents an asset no rival power possesses at comparable scale. China's alliance network is essentially limited to North Korea and an increasingly dependent Russia. Even a damaged American alliance system — with allies hedging, diversifying, and increasingly skeptical — still vastly outweighs anything Beijing or Moscow can claim.

What Has Genuinely Declined: Strategic Will and Institutional Coherence

What is declining, and declining sharply, is not American capability but American strategic coherence and the political will to deploy capability in the sustained, predictable, costly manner that genuine global leadership requires. This distinction is not merely semantic — it has profound practical consequences, because allies and adversaries alike calibrate their behavior based on perceived reliability and predictability, not merely raw capability that might or might not be deployed.

The internal contradictions documented across multiple 2026 strategic assessments are not incidental flaws in otherwise coherent policy — they reflect a deeper, unresolved tension within American strategic thinking about what role the United States should play in a world it can no longer unilaterally dominate. The administration's own strategy documents affirm alliance importance in general terms while simultaneously attacking allies rhetorically and providing no operational clarity about force posture commitments. This is not strategic ambiguity deployed deliberately as a tool of statecraft, in the manner Washington has historically used calculated ambiguity over Taiwan, for instance. It is, per SWP's assessment, the product of an unresolved internal debate about how the United States should deal with the loss of global dominance — a debate that has been ongoing for a quarter century but has never been definitively resolved by any administration, Democratic or Republican.

The result is what Foreign Policy magazine's January 2026 cover essay described starkly as "The World Minus One" — a global order increasingly forced to function and adapt around the assumption that American participation and leadership cannot be reliably counted upon, even as the United States remains far too powerful and consequential to simply be excluded from global affairs. This is an unprecedented condition in the post-1945 international system: not American absence, but American unpredictability functioning as a structural feature that the rest of the world must now plan around.

The Paradox of Self-Inflicted Decline

Perhaps the most analytically significant feature of America's current trajectory is how much of the erosion in global influence appears self-inflicted rather than imposed by external competitors. China's military modernization and economic rise are real and consequential, but the acceleration of skepticism toward American reliability among traditional allies — in Europe, in parts of the Indo-Pacific, even within the Western Hemisphere the 2026 NSS prioritizes — stems substantially from Washington's own policy choices rather than from any single Chinese or Russian action.

The SAIS Review's analysis of the relationship between Trump's foreign policy and Russia's multipolar vision identifies a genuinely troubling dynamic: Washington's implicit recognition of Russian dominance in its "near abroad," pursued seemingly in service of disentangling America from costly European security commitments, has not secured reciprocal American advantages elsewhere in Europe. Instead, this asymmetric concession risks reshaping international power configurations in favor of precisely the rival powers — a Sino-Russian strategic partnership well-positioned to challenge American-led order even from within structures like NATO that were originally built to contain such challenges. In other words, American retrenchment pursued in the name of prioritizing narrow national interest may be inadvertently accelerating the very multipolar erosion of American influence that more sustained engagement might have better managed, even if at higher near-term cost.

This is the central strategic question hanging over the entire decline-of-unipolarity debate: is the United States adapting intelligently to genuinely changed structural conditions that made the unipolar moment unsustainable regardless of policy choices, or is it accelerating and mismanaging a transition that more skillful, less domestically-driven statecraft could have navigated with substantially better outcomes for long-term American interests? The honest answer, based on the available evidence, leans toward the latter — the structural drivers of multipolarity (Chinese economic rise, the diffusion of military technology, the limits of unilateral power projection) were real and would have eroded American unipolarity under any administration. But the speed, manner, and self-inflicted institutional damage of the current transition reflects policy choices, not strategic inevitability.

Global Impact: How the World Is Adapting to American Unpredictability

Allied Hedging Becomes the Default Strategic Posture

The defining global response to declining confidence in American reliability has been a broad-based, geographically dispersed turn toward strategic hedging among traditional American allies and partners. This is not formal realignment away from the United States — most allies retain no viable, comparably attractive alternative security guarantor — but a systematic diversification of relationships designed to reduce vulnerability to any single point of American policy volatility.

Europe's defense spending acceleration, discussed earlier, represents the most visible manifestation of this hedging. But the pattern extends globally: Indo-Pacific allies deepening minilateral arrangements like the QUAD and trilateral frameworks that do not depend exclusively on bilateral American guarantees; Gulf states diversifying economic and security relationships across Washington, Beijing, and Moscow simultaneously; even traditionally America-aligned Latin American governments exploring expanded engagement with China's Belt and Road Initiative and BRICS-adjacent financial architecture, despite the 2026 NSS's explicit prioritization of hemispheric primacy designed specifically to prevent exactly this kind of regional drift.

China and Russia: Calibrated Exploitation Rather Than Triumphant Advance

Both Beijing and Moscow have responded to perceived American retrenchment with calibrated, often cautious exploitation rather than the kind of triumphant, accelerated advance that simpler declinist narratives might predict. China's restraint, as documented extensively in Indo-Pacific analysis, reflects Beijing's own domestic economic constraints and a calculated judgment that overextension risks accelerating exactly the kind of broad coalition-building against Chinese interests that more patient strategy can avoid. Russia, deeply enmeshed in its costly Ukraine war and structurally dependent on Chinese economic and diplomatic support, lacks the independent capacity to rapidly exploit American retrenchment even where opportunities present themselves.

The Sino-Russian strategic partnership, formalized further through the May 2026 Xi-Putin joint declaration on multipolarity, represents the most coherent organized response to American retrenchment — but even this partnership operates more as parallel, mutually reinforcing pressure on American-led order than as a unified bloc with fully aligned strategic objectives. Russia's interest in disrupting the post-Cold War European settlement and China's interest in establishing regional preeminence in the Indo-Pacific are complementary but distinct projects, unified primarily by shared opposition to American-led constraints rather than by a genuinely common positive vision of global order.

Risk Assessment

The Predictability Deficit as Systemic Risk

The single greatest risk emerging from America's current strategic posture is not decline itself but the unpredictability accompanying it. Alliance systems, deterrence architecture, and international economic stability all depend substantially on predictable behavior patterns that allow other actors to calibrate their own decisions with reasonable confidence. An America that retains overwhelming capability but exercises it unpredictably — sometimes disengaging, sometimes asserting hemispheric primacy aggressively, sometimes threatening tariffs against allies and adversaries alike without clear strategic logic — creates exactly the kind of miscalculation risk that stable deterrence architecture is designed to prevent.

The Domestic Political Sustainability Question

With nearly 70% of Americans anticipating economic difficulty in 2026 and bipartisan congressional checks on executive foreign policy action notably diminished compared to Trump's first term, the domestic political sustainability of current American strategic posture remains genuinely uncertain. The 2026 midterm elections represent a significant variable: a substantial shift in congressional composition could reintroduce institutional friction that has been largely absent, while continued alignment would further entrench the current trajectory's institutional momentum.

Future Scenarios

Scenario Analysis: American Power Through 2030

Scenario One: Managed Adaptation (Probability: 30%)

The United States successfully transitions from unipolar hegemon to "first among equals" within a managed multipolar order, retaining decisive influence in critical domains (technology, finance, military power projection) while accepting reduced direct management of regional security architectures in Europe and parts of the Indo-Pacific. This requires the current strategic incoherence to resolve into a more consistent doctrine — whether through 2026 midterm-driven institutional correction or through the administration's own strategic learning — that allows allies to rebuild confidence in calibrated, if reduced, American commitments.

Scenario Two: Continued Strategic Drift (Probability: 45%)

The most probable trajectory involves continued internal contradiction between rhetorical multipolar acceptance and episodic assertions of primacy, producing an extended period of allied hedging, gradual institutional erosion, and incremental loss of American agenda-setting capacity across multiple regions simultaneously. The United States remains the single most powerful country in the world throughout this period but increasingly operates as one significant actor among several rather than as the organizing center of the international system.

Scenario Three: Sharp Correction (Probability: 25%)

A significant external shock — a Taiwan crisis demonstrating the costs of accumulated ambiguity, a European security crisis exposing the consequences of NATO uncertainty, or a domestic political shift following the 2026 midterms — forces a more decisive American strategic recalibration in either direction: either a renewed, more coherently resourced commitment to global leadership, or an accelerated, more deliberate embrace of restrained hemispheric primacy. Either outcome would resolve current ambiguity but carries its own substantial risks and adjustment costs for the broader international system.

Intelligence Forecast

  • American strategic incoherence will likely persist through 2026 absent a major external shock, with continued gaps between rhetorical alliance affirmation and operational force posture clarity, particularly regarding European troop levels and Indo-Pacific commitment depth.
  • European defense autonomy will continue accelerating regardless of any partial American course correction, as the credibility damage from 2025-2026 uncertainty has already triggered structural European investment decisions that will not reverse even if Washington's posture moderates.
  • China and Russia will continue calibrated, cautious exploitation of American retrenchment rather than aggressive advance, constrained by their own domestic economic limitations and the risk of triggering broader counter-coalition responses.
  • The 2026 midterm elections will be a critical inflection variable, with outcomes shaping whether institutional checks on executive foreign policy authority meaningfully reassert themselves or whether current trajectory continues largely unconstrained through the remainder of the administration's term.
  • Dollar dominance and core American financial primacy will persist through this period despite continued marginal erosion from BRICS de-dollarization efforts, as no credible alternative reserve currency architecture exists at comparable scale and liquidity.

Final Strategic Takeaway

The decline of American unipolarity is not a hypothesis requiring further proof in 2026 — it is an acknowledged reality, stated openly by the vice president of the United States and embedded explicitly in the nation's own strategic doctrine. What remains genuinely contested, and what will determine the actual trajectory of American global influence over the coming decade, is not whether unipolarity has ended but how skillfully or chaotically the transition away from it is managed.

The evidence assembled across America's own strategic documents, allied behavior, and rival power responses points toward a sobering conclusion: the United States retains, by a considerable margin, more raw capability than any other single power on earth, but is currently deploying that capability with a degree of strategic incoherence that is actively accelerating the erosion of the predictability, institutional leadership, and alliance cohesion that translated raw capability into durable global influence for eight decades. Capability without coherent strategic will does not produce hegemony — it produces exactly the kind of "world minus one" condition that allies and adversaries alike are now learning to navigate around rather than depend upon.

This need not be a permanent condition. American institutions retain significant capacity for self-correction, and the structural advantages underpinning American power — its economy, its technology base, its demographic and innovation ecosystem relative to an aging China — remain genuinely formidable. But the window for managing this transition skillfully, rather than chaotically, is not unlimited. Every month of continued strategic ambiguity further entrenches allied hedging behaviors and rival power confidence that, once established, prove difficult to reverse even if Washington's posture eventually stabilizes. The question that will define the next phase of global power is not whether American dominance is fading — it plainly is — but whether the United States can still shape the multipolar order succeeding it, or whether it has already ceded that shaping role to the very dynamics of fragmentation its own retrenchment has helped unleash.

Global Chanakya Intelligence Assessment: The United States has not lost its power — it has lost its strategic clarity about how to use it. That distinction, more than any single policy decision, will determine whether America remains the indispensable anchor of a reformed global order or becomes merely its largest, most unpredictable participant.

title: How BRICS Is Reshaping Global Power in 2026: Inside the Quiet Revolution
content:
How BRICS Is Reshaping Global Power in 2026: Inside the Quiet Revolution

Executive Summary

There is a peculiar irony at the heart of the BRICS story in 2026. The bloc that Western commentators spent two decades dismissing as an acronym in search of a purpose has become, almost without anyone agreeing on exactly when it happened, the most consequential economic coalition operating outside the G7 system. BRICS — now an eleven-member grouping spanning Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Indonesia, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates, with roughly ten additional partner countries orbiting its institutions — represents close to 40% of global GDP on a purchasing power parity basis and nearly half of the world's population.

What makes 2026 a genuine inflection point is not the bloc's size, which has been substantial for several years, but its functional maturation. Under India's fourth BRICS presidency, the grouping is shifting from a forum that produces declarations into an architecture that produces infrastructure. The New Development Bank has now deployed over $42.9 billion across 139 projects and recently secured an additional AAA credit rating from China Chengxin International, layering onto an existing top-tier rating from Japan's JCR — a signal that the institution is being treated by serious financial markets as a credible alternative lender, not a political vanity project. BRICS Pay, the bloc's decentralized payment-linking system, has reportedly cut dollar usage in intra-bloc trade by roughly two-thirds in certain corridors. Intra-BRICS trade crossed $500 billion in 2025, with some bilateral corridors now running 90% non-dollarized.

Yet the most important story about BRICS in 2026 is not the headline statistics — it is the internal contest over what the bloc is actually for. India, hosting the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi on September 12-13, 2026, under the theme "Building Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation, and Sustainability," is fighting to keep BRICS a development-and-governance-reform platform rather than allow it to calcify into the anti-Western bloc that Russia and, to a lesser degree, China would prefer it to become. This internal tension — between India's vision of negotiated multipolarity and the more confrontational instincts of Moscow and parts of Beijing's foreign policy establishment — is the single most important dynamic determining whether BRICS becomes a genuine pillar of a reformed global order or fractures under the weight of its own contradictions.

Background: From Acronym to Architecture

BRICS began as an investment thesis, not a geopolitical project. Goldman Sachs economist Jim O'Neill coined the term in 2001 to describe Brazil, Russia, India, and China as the fast-growing emerging economies that would reshape global GDP distribution over coming decades. The four countries themselves did not hold their first formal summit until 2009, in Yekaterinburg, Russia — a meeting driven substantially by Moscow's interest in creating a diplomatic platform that did not run through Washington or Brussels. South Africa joined in 2010, completing the acronym and giving the grouping a foothold on the African continent.

For its first decade, BRICS was widely — and not unfairly — dismissed as a talking shop. The five founding members had wildly divergent political systems, economic models, and strategic interests. China and India share a disputed Himalayan border and fought a war in 1962 whose legacy still shapes their bilateral relationship. Russia and India have a deep historical defense relationship rooted in Cold War-era Soviet support, while Brazil and South Africa have comparatively peripheral strategic stakes in either US-China or Russia-West tensions. The one institutional achievement of the bloc's first decade — the establishment of the New Development Bank in 2014, headquartered in Shanghai — was significant but modest in scale relative to the World Bank and IMF.

The transformation began in earnest with the 2023 Johannesburg Summit, where BRICS announced its first major expansion, inviting Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE to join (Argentina was also invited but declined under President Javier Milei). This expansion — sometimes called "BRICS+" — was a deliberate response to two converging pressures: the West's use of financial sanctions as a primary tool of coercive statecraft, dramatically demonstrated by the freezing of Russian central bank assets after the 2022 Ukraine invasion, and the accumulating frustration among Global South economies that the IMF, World Bank, and UN Security Council structure no longer reflected actual twenty-first century power distributions.

The accession of Indonesia in January 2025 — the first new full member added after the initial 2024 expansion wave — pushed BRICS membership into a genuinely civilizational scale: the bloc now includes the world's most populous country (India), its second-largest economy (China), its largest Muslim-majority democracy (Indonesia), the custodian of roughly a fifth of global oil reserves through Saudi Arabia and the UAE, and Africa's two most consequential rising economies in Egypt and Ethiopia. This is no longer an acronym. It is a parallel architecture.

Current Situation: India's Presidency and the Battle for BRICS' Soul

The Handover and the Stakes

India officially assumed the BRICS presidency from Brazil on January 1, 2026 — its fourth tenure in the chair, following 2012, 2016, and 2021. External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar unveiled the presidency's official logo, theme, and roadmap in New Delhi, with the interlocking-gears symbolism deliberately chosen to project resilience and functional cooperation rather than ideological confrontation. The theme — "Building Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation, and Sustainability" — is calculated, almost defiantly technocratic language at a moment when other BRICS members, particularly Russia, would prefer sharper anti-Western framing.

The contrast with Brazil's 2025 presidency is instructive. At the July 2025 Rio Summit, President Lula da Silva explicitly positioned the gathering as a response to Trump's tariff escalation, framing BRICS as a platform for those who still believe in multilateralism — a direct rhetorical jab at Washington. Xi Jinping's conspicuous absence from that summit allowed Brazilian and Indian voices to dominate the narrative, and the New Development Bank approved nearly $7 billion in financing for Brazil, with India leading the bloc's total financing contributions. India is continuing this pattern of practical, delivery-focused leadership rather than escalatory rhetoric — a deliberate strategic choice given New Delhi's parallel commitments to the QUAD, its deepening defense relationship with the United States, and its determination not to be pulled into a bloc that reads as explicitly anti-American.

India's presidency faces an immediate and direct test of nerve. Donald Trump has repeatedly and explicitly threatened BRICS members with a 100% tariff if the bloc moves to replace the US dollar as a reserve or trade currency — a threat aimed squarely at deterring exactly the kind of financial architecture-building that BRICS has been pursuing. India's response has been carefully calibrated: Jaishankar stated unambiguously in March 2025 that India has "no policy on our part to replace the dollar," a position New Delhi has maintained into 2026 even as it simultaneously pursues de-dollarization measures for entirely separate reasons — namely, derisking Indian trade exposure to any single currency, rather than mounting an ideological challenge to dollar primacy.

The De-Dollarization Infrastructure: From Talk to Transactions

The most consequential operational development inside BRICS in 2026 is the maturation of its de-dollarization infrastructure — and the critical nuance here matters enormously. The bloc has explicitly and repeatedly shelved the idea of a single common BRICS currency, recognizing correctly that the economic and political prerequisites for a shared currency among countries with such divergent monetary policies, capital controls, and fiscal positions simply do not exist. What BRICS is building instead is something more modest and, paradoxically, more threatening to dollar primacy precisely because it is achievable: a set of interoperable mechanisms that reduce dependence on the dollar in bilateral and intra-bloc trade without requiring any single alternative reserve currency.

BRICS Pay, the bloc's decentralized payment-linking infrastructure, connects national payment networks directly, allowing member states to settle trade without routing transactions through dollar-denominated correspondent banking relationships. The reported reduction of roughly two-thirds in dollar usage within certain intra-bloc trade corridors represents a meaningful structural shift, not merely a symbolic one. The proposed "BRICS Unit" — a gold-backed settlement instrument under development — and ongoing work on central bank digital currency interoperability frameworks represent further steps toward an alternative settlement architecture that does not require any country to formally renounce the dollar but simply makes it easier, cheaper, and more politically comfortable to avoid it.

The strategic logic driving this push is not primarily ideological — it is defensive. The dollar's share of global reserves has fallen from a peak of approximately 88% around 2000 to roughly 58% today, a gradual but consistent decline that reflects genuine diversification motives among central banks worldwide, not merely BRICS coordination. The freezing of roughly $300 billion in Russian central bank reserves following the 2022 Ukraine invasion was the single most consequential event in accelerating this diversification, because it demonstrated definitively that dollar-denominated reserves are not neutral, apolitical assets — they are instruments that Washington can and will weaponize against states it considers adversarial. Every finance ministry and central bank in the Global South absorbed that lesson, regardless of their formal alignment with BRICS.

The New Development Bank: Building Credibility Through Delivery

The New Development Bank, headquartered in Shanghai and chaired since 2023 by former Brazilian president Dilma Rousseff, has become the most tangible proof point of BRICS' institutional seriousness. Having deployed over $42.9 billion across 139 projects since its 2016 launch, the NDB has methodically built the kind of track record that converts skeptics. Its receipt of an additional AAA credit rating from China Chengxin International in April 2026 — layering onto an existing top-tier rating from Japan's JCR — is a significant signal precisely because it comes from outside the BRICS political bloc itself, lending external credibility to claims that the institution operates on sound financial principles rather than purely political lending criteria.

The NDB's expansion of local-currency lending is a direct, practical complement to the broader de-dollarization push: by issuing loans denominated in members' own currencies rather than dollars, the bank reduces currency mismatch risk for borrowing governments and reinforces the broader architecture of alternative financial infrastructure. This is unglamorous, technical work — the kind that rarely generates headlines — but it is precisely the kind of institutional plumbing that determines whether an alternative financial system is real or merely rhetorical.

The Expansion Queue: Who Wants In, and Why It's Complicated

One of the more remarkable, underreported dynamics of 2026 is the sheer scale of international interest in BRICS membership and partnership. Reports suggest nearly 65 countries across Latin America, Asia, and Africa have expressed some form of interest in formal accession or partner status. India is using its presidency to push for clearer, more rigorous expansion guidelines rather than the somewhat ad hoc process that characterized the 2023-2024 expansion wave — a position that reflects New Delhi's concern that uncontrolled growth could dilute the bloc's coherence and complicate consensus-based decision-making, which BRICS, unlike the EU, relies upon entirely.

Nigeria has emerged as a leading candidate for the next round of African representation, with India explicitly describing Lagos as a "strategic partner" in bilateral discussions ahead of the New Delhi summit. Pakistan applied for BRICS membership in 2023 with Russian backing and has separately expressed interest in accessing New Development Bank financing as it grapples with persistent economic difficulties — a prospect that creates obvious friction given India's veto-equivalent influence within the bloc's consensus mechanisms and the near-impossibility of New Delhi accepting an expansion that elevates its primary regional rival.

This expansion dynamic illustrates a structural truth about BRICS that Western analysis frequently misses: the bloc is not simply an instrument of Chinese foreign policy, however much Beijing might prefer it to function that way. India's participation actively constrains Chinese dominance within BRICS decision-making, and Indian objections have already shaped — and in some cases blocked — expansion candidates that New Delhi views as strategically adverse. The bloc's consensus-based governance structure, which requires unanimity for major decisions including membership, means that BRICS expansion is fundamentally a negotiated outcome among genuinely competing national interests, not a unified geopolitical project executed by a single dominant power.

Strategic Analysis: What BRICS Actually Is — and Isn't

The Internal Fault Lines

The single most important analytical error in conventional discourse about BRICS is treating it as a coherent bloc with a unified strategic purpose. It is nothing of the sort. BRICS in 2026 contains American treaty-adjacent partners (Saudi Arabia, UAE) sitting alongside Russian client states (Belarus, as a partner country) and countries locked in active strategic competition with each other (India and China, India and Pakistan-aligned interests, Iran and the Gulf states with whom it shares membership). Managing this political heterogeneity is not a minor administrative challenge — it is the defining structural constraint on what BRICS can actually accomplish as an institution.

China's interests within BRICS center on using the bloc to advance yuan internationalization, deepen Belt and Road connectivity, and gradually erode the institutional dominance of Western-controlled multilateral bodies — objectives that align with Beijing's broader multipolarity project, as articulated in the May 2026 Xi-Putin joint declaration on a new type of international relations. Russia's interests are more straightforwardly defensive and confrontational: Moscow needs BRICS as a platform to demonstrate that Western sanctions have not achieved diplomatic isolation, and to build alternative financial channels that reduce the bite of the sanctions regime it continues to operate under because of the Ukraine war.

India's interests, by contrast, are fundamentally about institutional reform rather than institutional replacement. New Delhi wants a reformed UN Security Council that includes India as a permanent member, a reformed IMF and World Bank quota structure that reflects current GDP distribution rather than 1944 power configurations, and a financial architecture that reduces the structural vulnerability that comes from near-total dependence on dollar-denominated systems — without abandoning India's substantial and growing economic and security relationships with the United States, the European Union, and Japan. This is not a contradiction in Indian policy; it is the precise definition of strategic autonomy that has defined Indian foreign policy since independence, now applied at unprecedented scale and sophistication.

Brazil under Lula occupies a position closer to India's than to Russia's or China's — using BRICS as diplomatic leverage in Brasília's relationship with Washington rather than as an instrument of anti-Western confrontation. Indonesia, the bloc's newest major member, brings a similarly pragmatic, non-aligned sensibility shaped by its own long history of leading the Non-Aligned Movement. The Gulf states — Saudi Arabia and the UAE — are perhaps the clearest illustration of BRICS' essentially transactional character for many members: both countries maintain deep security relationships with Washington while simultaneously diversifying their economic and diplomatic portfolios through BRICS membership, treating bloc participation as risk management and optionality rather than ideological alignment.

BRICS as Hedging Infrastructure, Not Anti-Western Alliance

The most accurate framework for understanding BRICS' actual function in the international system is as collective hedging infrastructure for states that have concluded — independently and for varied reasons — that excessive dependence on any single power's financial and institutional architecture carries unacceptable strategic risk. This framing explains far more of observed BRICS behavior than the simpler "anti-Western bloc" narrative that dominates much Western commentary.

Consider the evidence: BRICS has not coordinated unified positions on most major geopolitical conflicts. Member states have taken divergent positions on Russia's invasion of Ukraine, on the Israel-Gaza conflict, on Taiwan, and on numerous other contested issues. The bloc has explicitly avoided developing into a military alliance, has shelved currency unification, and has focused its concrete institutional energy on financial infrastructure (NDB, BRICS Pay) and diplomatic platforming (summit declarations, working groups) rather than the kind of binding collective security or economic commitments that would characterize a genuine counter-alliance to the West.

What BRICS provides its members, instead, is optionality: an alternative set of financial rails, an alternative development financing source that comes without the political conditionality the IMF and World Bank traditionally attach to lending, an alternative diplomatic platform for voicing Global South grievances about underrepresentation in existing institutions, and collective negotiating leverage on issues like climate finance and debt relief where individual middle and developing economies have limited bargaining power against the G7. This is a fundamentally different — and in some ways more durable — strategic project than a traditional military or political alliance, because it does not require its members to align on contested geopolitical questions in order to derive value from participation.

The China Question Inside BRICS

No analysis of BRICS' reshaping of global power can avoid confronting directly the question of Chinese dominance within the bloc. China's economy is roughly five times the size of India's, the bloc's second-largest economy, and Beijing's Belt and Road Initiative has created deep infrastructure and debt relationships with a substantial proportion of BRICS' newer members, particularly across Africa and Central Asia. This raises a legitimate structural question: is BRICS simply an instrument through which Chinese economic weight translates into geopolitical influence under a multilateral veneer?

The honest answer is more nuanced than either Beijing's boosters or BRICS' Western critics suggest. China undoubtedly derives substantial strategic value from BRICS — it provides a platform for advancing yuan internationalization, a vehicle for expanding the NDB as an alternative to World Bank lending that comes without Western governance conditionalities, and crucially, diplomatic cover and company in Beijing's broader project of presenting an alternative to the US-led order. But India's structural position within BRICS — as the second-largest economy, the rotating co-leadership the bloc's consensus mechanism requires, and a country with every incentive to prevent Chinese dominance from becoming entrenched — functions as a genuine internal check.

India's deliberate choice to prioritize trilateral IBSAMAR naval exercises with Brazil and South Africa over BRICS-wide naval drills hosted in South Africa is a small but telling data point: New Delhi is consistently signaling that its BRICS engagement does not extend to military or security cooperation that could be read as aligning against the United States or its allies. This careful boundary-drawing is precisely how India is using its 2026 presidency to keep BRICS anchored as an economic and developmental platform rather than allowing it to drift, under Russian or Chinese preference, toward something resembling a security bloc.

Global Impact: How BRICS Is Reshaping the International System

Reshaping Development Finance

The most concrete and measurable way BRICS is reshaping global power is through development finance. The New Development Bank's $42.9 billion deployment across 139 projects represents real infrastructure, energy, and development financing flowing to countries that previously had limited alternatives to Western-dominated lending institutions with their associated political conditionalities. This matters enormously for recipient governments: NDB and Chinese-led financing typically come with fewer governance, human rights, or macroeconomic policy conditions than IMF or World Bank lending, a feature that some Western analysts criticize as enabling poor governance but that recipient governments frequently experience as a meaningful expansion of sovereign policy space.

This competitive pressure has already produced observable effects on Western multilateral institutions, which have faced increasing pressure to reform their own lending practices, expand voting weight for emerging economies, and accelerate disbursement timelines in response to the existence of a credible alternative. Institutional competition, in this sense, is functioning roughly as economic theory would predict: the presence of an alternative supplier disciplines the incumbent.

Reshaping Currency and Payment Systems

The de-dollarization infrastructure BRICS is building — even without a common currency — represents a genuine, if gradual, restructuring of global payment architecture. As intra-bloc trade increasingly settles outside dollar-denominated correspondent banking, and as BRICS Pay interoperability expands, the marginal transaction costs of avoiding the dollar continue to fall for an expanding set of bilateral trade relationships. This does not threaten the dollar's overall reserve currency status in any near-term sense — the depth, liquidity, and legal predictability of dollar-denominated capital markets remain unmatched, and no BRICS currency comes close to offering comparable characteristics. But it does represent meaningful erosion at the margins, and marginal erosion compounds over time in ways that matter for long-term financial architecture.

Reshaping Global Governance Debates

BRICS has fundamentally altered the terms of debate around global governance reform. UN Security Council expansion, IMF quota reform, World Bank governance restructuring — these issues, long discussed in essentially theoretical terms within Western policy circles, now carry the weight of a coordinated bloc representing 40% of global GDP actively demanding change, rather than individual developing countries petitioning for marginal adjustments. Whether or not BRICS achieves its specific institutional reform demands, it has permanently changed the political dynamics of these debates by demonstrating that a critical mass of non-Western economic weight can coordinate, however imperfectly, around shared grievances.

Risk Assessment

The Coherence Risk

The greatest internal risk to BRICS' continued relevance is the erosion of consensus-based decision-making as the bloc's membership grows more diverse and its internal contradictions multiply. The India-China relationship remains fundamentally adversarial despite cautious recent efforts at border de-escalation, and any serious deterioration — a renewed Himalayan border crisis, an intensified confrontation in the Indo-Pacific — would create immediate and severe strain on India's willingness to continue legitimizing a bloc in which China is the dominant economic power. Iran's domestic political instability and its complicated relationships with Gulf BRICS members (Saudi Arabia, UAE) represent another persistent source of internal friction that consensus-based governance struggles to manage.

The American Pressure Risk

Trump's explicit tariff threats against BRICS de-dollarization efforts represent a serious, credible risk to the bloc's economic cohesion. A 100% tariff threat, if actually implemented against major BRICS economies, would impose severe costs on members whose economic relationships with the United States remain substantial — including India, whose trade relationship with America is significant even as New Delhi pursues BRICS engagement. This creates a genuine deterrent effect that has already visibly shaped Indian rhetoric, with Jaishankar's explicit dollar-replacement denials reflecting calculated risk management rather than mere diplomatic politeness.

The Expansion Dilution Risk

The queue of nearly 65 countries expressing interest in BRICS membership or partnership creates a genuine institutional risk: rapid, poorly governed expansion could dilute the bloc's coherence to the point of strategic irrelevance, replicating some of the consensus-paralysis dynamics that limit the effectiveness of much larger multilateral bodies like the UN General Assembly. India's push for clearer expansion criteria during its 2026 presidency reflects a sophisticated recognition of this risk, but the pressure from China and Russia to expand rapidly — for their own strategic reasons of maximizing the bloc's nominal scale and diplomatic weight — creates ongoing tension over the pace and governance of further accession.

Future Scenarios

Scenario Analysis: BRICS Trajectories Through 2030

Scenario One: Institutional Consolidation (Probability: 40%)

BRICS successfully navigates its internal contradictions under India's stewardship, establishing clearer governance and expansion criteria at the September 2026 New Delhi summit. The New Development Bank continues expanding its lending base and credit credibility, BRICS Pay achieves meaningful interoperability with national payment systems beyond the core membership, and the bloc establishes itself durably as a genuine alternative development finance and diplomatic coordination platform — without becoming a military alliance or achieving a common currency. This outcome requires India to successfully balance its competing relationships with the US-led order and the BRICS framework, and requires China and Russia to accept a more pluralistic, less confrontational BRICS than their own preferences might otherwise dictate.

Scenario Two: Drift Toward Bifurcation (Probability: 35%)

Escalating US-China technology and trade competition, combined with continued American tariff pressure on de-dollarization efforts, gradually pushes BRICS toward a more explicitly bifurcated global economic architecture — not through deliberate strategic design but through the accumulated weight of individual defensive responses to Western economic pressure. India's careful balancing position becomes increasingly difficult to sustain, forcing New Delhi toward harder choices between its BRICS commitments and its QUAD and US bilateral relationships. The bloc retains its development finance and payment infrastructure functions but increasingly operates as one node within a genuinely bifurcated global economy.

Scenario Three: Fragmentation Under Internal Strain (Probability: 25%)

A serious India-China crisis — whether a renewed border confrontation or an Indo-Pacific flashpoint — combined with continued Iranian instability and unresolved Gulf-Iran tensions within the bloc's own membership, produces a genuine crisis of BRICS coherence. India's continued participation becomes politically untenable domestically, or New Delhi deliberately reduces its engagement to a minimal, transactional level while channeling its strategic energy more fully into QUAD and Western-aligned frameworks. BRICS persists nominally but loses much of its claim to represent a genuinely pluralistic Global South coalition, increasingly resembling a China-Russia-centered grouping with reduced broader credibility.

Intelligence Forecast

Based on current trajectories, Global Chanakya's assessment projects the following developments through the September 2026 New Delhi summit and beyond:

  • The 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi (September 12-13, 2026) will produce expansion guidelines rather than a large new membership cohort, reflecting India's push for governance discipline over rapid scale expansion. Nigeria is the most likely candidate for fast-tracked partner-to-full-member progression.
  • De-dollarization infrastructure will continue advancing incrementally through BRICS Pay expansion and NDB local-currency lending, without any formal move toward a common currency. Expect continued explicit denials from India and other members regarding dollar-replacement ambitions, even as practical de-dollarization measures proceed.
  • Trump administration tariff pressure on BRICS will likely escalate selectively rather than through a blanket 100% tariff implementation, targeting specific de-dollarization-linked trade measures while avoiding the kind of broad economic confrontation that would damage substantial US trade relationships with India and other BRICS members.
  • India-China tension within BRICS will remain a persistent but managed friction point, with New Delhi continuing to use bilateral and minilateral mechanisms (IBSAMAR, QUAD) to signal limits on its BRICS security cooperation while maintaining full economic and diplomatic engagement.
  • The New Development Bank's credit profile will continue strengthening, with additional rating agency endorsements likely as the institution's lending track record extends, gradually normalizing its position as a legitimate complement to — rather than simply a political alternative to — traditional multilateral development finance.

Final Strategic Takeaway

BRICS in 2026 is neither the anti-Western juggernaut that alarmist Western commentary sometimes portrays nor the toothless talking shop that dismissive critics long assumed it would remain. It is something more interesting and, in important respects, more consequential than either caricature: a genuinely novel form of international coordination among states with profoundly different political systems, strategic interests, and relationships to Western power, unified not by shared ideology but by a shared interest in reducing structural dependence on any single power's institutions.

The bloc's durability will be determined not by its rhetoric but by whether India can successfully continue performing the delicate balancing act that has defined its 2026 presidency — using BRICS to advance legitimate Global South interests in institutional reform and development finance diversification, while preventing the bloc from calcifying into the confrontational anti-Western instrument that Russia's strategic interests, and to a lesser degree China's, would prefer it to become. This is not a peripheral diplomatic challenge for New Delhi — it is now one of the central tests of Indian strategic autonomy on the world stage, conducted in full view of Washington, Beijing, Moscow, and every middle power watching to see whether genuinely independent, multi-vector foreign policy can succeed at scale in a fracturing global order.

What is beyond serious dispute is that BRICS has already permanently altered the architecture of global power. The New Development Bank exists and lends. BRICS Pay processes real transactions. The dollar's reserve currency dominance, while still overwhelming, is measurably eroding at the margins. And the diplomatic claim that any serious discussion of global governance reform must account for the preferences of a coalition representing 40% of world GDP and half its population is no longer contestable.
