Trump approval rating — domestic pressure mounting
21 hrs
Islamabad Talks — ended without Iran deal
4 yrs+
Russia-Ukraine war duration as of May 2026

The Context: Why May 2026 Is a Diplomatic Inflection Point

Trump and Putin at the 2017 G-20 Hamburg Summit — the diplomatic dynamic between the two leaders has defined much of global politics since.

To understand why the second week of May 2026 matters so much, you have to step back and look at the full picture of what Donald Trump inherited — or in many cases created — in his second term. The United States is currently involved in three overlapping geopolitical crises, each of which individually would dominate any other presidency's foreign policy agenda.

First, there is the Russia-Ukraine war — now over four years old, having begun with Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022. Second, there is the 2026 Iran war — started on February 28 when the US and Israel launched coordinated airstrikes on Iran, assassinating Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and triggering the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Third, there is the US-China relationship — simultaneously the world's most important economic partnership and its most dangerous geopolitical rivalry.

In ordinary times, a US president would handle one of these at a time. Trump, by personality and political necessity, is trying to resolve all three in the same month. The question is whether this is strategic genius or dangerous overextension — and the answer will likely define his second term.

The domestic pressure behind the diplomacy: Trump's approval rating has fallen to 36 percent. Rising gasoline prices linked to the Iran-Hormuz crisis are being felt at every American pump. Inflation is running hot. The midterm elections are approaching. Every foreign policy win Trump can manufacture becomes domestic political capital. This is the hidden engine behind the sudden flurry of diplomatic activity in May 2026.

Front One: The Russia-Ukraine Ceasefire — A Masterclass in Timing

On the evening of May 8, 2026, Trump posted to Truth Social with characteristic capitalisation: "I am pleased to announce that there will be a THREE DAY CEASEFIRE (May 9th, 10th, and 11th) in the War between Russia and Ukraine."

Within minutes, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed on X that a three-day truce had been arranged. Russian presidential aide Yuri Ushakov confirmed that an agreement had been reached through US-Russia telephone contacts. The ceasefire would include, Trump announced, a suspension of all kinetic activity and the exchange of 1,000 prisoners from each side — 2,000 human beings returning home from captivity, in one of the largest single prisoner swaps of the entire conflict.

The timing was deliberate. May 9 is Victory Day in Russia — the annual commemoration of the Soviet Union's defeat of Nazi Germany in World War II. It is the single most politically sacred day in the Russian calendar, the occasion when Putin has traditionally staged enormous military parades through Moscow's Red Square, flanked by tanks, missiles, and thousands of troops. For Trump, tying the ceasefire to Victory Day was elegant: it gave Putin a diplomatic face-saving narrative (the ceasefire as a gesture of peace befitting the day of victory), while simultaneously forcing a pause in hostilities. It also gave Zelenskyy something extraordinary to work with.

Zelenskyy's Savage Decree

Zelenskyy's response to the ceasefire announcement became one of the most darkly comic moments of the entire war. Rather than simply confirming Ukraine's agreement, he issued a formal presidential decree — complete with GPS coordinates — stating that Ukraine would "allow a parade to be held in Moscow." The decree specified that "for the duration of the parade (beginning at 10:00 a.m. Kyiv time on May 9, 2026), the territorial sector of Red Square shall be excluded from the operational use plan of Ukrainian weaponry."

The subtext was unmistakable and devastating: Ukraine now possesses the long-range drone and missile capability to strike Moscow. The decree was Zelenskyy publicly demonstrating that Ukraine could, in principle, disrupt the most important ceremony in the Russian political calendar — and was choosing not to, as a matter of strategic mercy, not military incapability.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov's response — that the decree was a "silly joke" and "we don't need anyone's permission to be proud of our Victory Day" — only confirmed how effectively the message had landed. It is difficult to dismiss a joke when the person making it has already hit your military infrastructure from 1,000 kilometres away.

Why this ceasefire is fragile: Before Trump's announcement, both sides had already declared and violated separate unilateral ceasefires. Ukraine declared a ceasefire on May 6 — Russia violated it 1,820 times by 10 a.m. the same morning, according to Zelenskyy. Russia had announced its own two-day ceasefire for May 8-9 — it quickly unraveled, with both sides blaming each other. The history of this conflict is littered with ceasefires that collapsed within hours. The Trump-brokered three-day truce is more likely to hold precisely because it has explicit US political investment in it — but that does not make it a peace deal.

The Scaled-Back Victory Day Parade — What It Reveals

This year's Victory Day parade in Moscow was notable for what was absent. For the first time in Vladimir Putin's era, no missiles, tanks, or armoured vehicles appeared in the Red Square parade. The Kremlin offered no explanation. But the military and intelligence community's explanation was obvious: Ukraine's ability to conduct deep strikes inside Russian territory has made moving heavy military hardware through Moscow a genuine security risk. The parade that was once Russia's most powerful annual display of military might has been quietly humbled by Ukrainian long-range capability.

Putin's speech at the parade was vintage aggression — targeting NATO, vowing victory in Ukraine, invoking the sacrifice of the Soviet generation. But even the most bellicose rhetoric cannot fully conceal the military reality: Russia has been fighting for over four years, absorbing enormous casualties, and has not achieved its stated war aims. The three-day ceasefire and prisoner exchange — brokered by the American president, not won by Russian arms — tells the deeper story.

What the Prisoner Exchange Means

The agreement to exchange 1,000 prisoners from each side is not just a humanitarian gesture. It is a diplomatic signal. Prisoner exchanges require detailed negotiations, verification mechanisms, and sustained back-channel communication. They do not happen between parties who have completely abandoned dialogue. The very existence of this exchange — the largest of the conflict — suggests that both Russia and Ukraine are maintaining channels that could eventually support a broader negotiation.

Trump's framing was characteristically optimistic but not entirely divorced from reality: "Hopefully, it is the beginning of the end of a very long, deadly, and hard fought War. Talks are continuing on ending this Major Conflict, the biggest since World War II, and we are getting closer and closer every day."

Front Two: The Beijing Summit — Trump Goes to China

On May 14-15, 2026, Donald Trump will land in Beijing — becoming the first sitting US president to visit China since November 2017, when Trump himself made his first presidential trip there. The fact that this visit represents a nearly decade-long absence from presidential China diplomacy underscores how dramatically the US-China relationship has deteriorated — and how significant this summit genuinely is.

The visit was originally scheduled for April, but was delayed by the Iran war. The connection is not coincidental: Trump is travelling to Beijing precisely because he needs Chinese help to resolve the Iran-Hormuz crisis. China has been quietly importing Iranian oil throughout the war, paying in yuan through IRGC-affiliated channels — effectively undermining the US economic blockade of Iran. If Beijing agrees to pressure Tehran to accept a ceasefire and reopen the strait, Trump gets an enormous geopolitical win. If China refuses, the strait remains effectively closed and global oil markets continue to suffer.

What Trump Needs from Xi

According to analysis from CSIS (Center for Strategic and International Studies), the Trump administration sees three primary objectives in Beijing. First and most immediately: Chinese cooperation in pressuring Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi made a high-profile visit to Beijing in the weeks before the summit — which observers interpret as China already beginning to position itself as having leverage with Tehran. The question is whether Xi will use that leverage on Trump's behalf, and at what price.

Second, Trump is looking for economic deliverables — new trade agreements, Chinese purchases of American goods, and potentially a breakthrough on the TikTok dispute that has lingered through Trump's second term. Previous talks in Madrid had produced "significant progress" on a framework, with Boeing aircraft purchases reportedly on the table. Third, there are broader strategic conversations about Taiwan, nuclear security, and the structure of the post-Hormuz-crisis global energy market.

🇺🇸

What Trump Wants

Chinese pressure on Iran to reopen Hormuz. Trade deals. TikTok resolution. Boeing aircraft purchases. A domestic political win before midterms.

🇨🇳

What Xi Wants

Tariff reductions. Technology transfer limits eased. Taiwan red lines respected. A "win-win" narrative for domestic audiences. Strategic stability with US.

🌍

What the World Wants

Strait of Hormuz reopened. Oil prices stabilised. Iran nuclear standoff resolved. Ukraine peace process back on track.

The Optics of Arriving in Beijing

As analysts at Modern Diplomacy have noted, when Trump lands in Beijing on May 14, "the optics will matter almost as much as the outcomes." A sitting US president arriving in Beijing — received by Xi Jinping with the full ceremonial weight of a Chinese state visit — sends a message to every other government in the world. It signals that despite everything — the trade wars, the technology controls, the Hormuz crisis, the mutual accusations — the two superpowers still talk. They still meet. They still have a relationship worth managing.

The contrast with the post-COVID period of frozen communication is striking. In January 2023, the Chinese spy balloon incident caused Beijing to cut off military-to-military communication entirely. The Biden era ended without a single presidential visit to China. Now Trump is arriving in the Forbidden City — the same venue where he received his famous "state plus" treatment in 2017 — for what the Chinese side views as a major diplomatic event that should yield substantive results for the remainder of Trump's second term.

The Risk of Expectations

Brookings Institution experts are urging low expectations. China is "confident enough to stand up to Trump on many key issues, including sanctions, technology controls, critical minerals, and Iran," according to CSIS analysis. Beijing's eagerness for the summit actually signals that China is less confident than it appears — a powerful economy under pressure from US tariffs and a global energy crisis partly of America's making is not in an ideal negotiating position. But that does not mean China will give Trump everything he wants. Iran is an important relationship for Beijing — Chinese companies buy Iranian oil, Chinese diplomats use Tehran as a strategic counterweight to US influence, and any agreement to "pressure Iran" must be carefully packaged to avoid looking like Beijing is subordinating itself to Washington.

"For Beijing, this should not be a usual head-of-state visit, but a major diplomatic effort that yields substantive results for the rest of the second Trump administration." — Brookings Institution analysis, April 2026

Front Three: The Iran Endgame — The Deal That Isn't There Yet

The third front — and in many ways the most consequential — is Iran. The Strait of Hormuz remains effectively closed. The International Energy Agency has described the ongoing situation as the "largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market." Brent crude peaked at $120 per barrel. Global jet fuel exports have fallen 30%. Countries from South Korea to India to Germany are managing energy emergencies.

The Islamabad Talks of April 11-12 — 21 hours of negotiations at the Serena Hotel, with a 300-member US team led by VP JD Vance and a 70-member Iranian team led by Parliamentary Speaker Ghalibaf — ended without a deal. Iran's Foreign Minister said they were "inches away from an MoU" but accused the US of "moving the goalposts." The main sticking points: Iran's nuclear programme, the future status of the Strait of Hormuz, and sanctions relief.

On May 4, Trump launched Operation Project Freedom — a US Navy mission to escort trapped merchant vessels through the strait. On May 6, he paused it, citing "great progress" toward a deal. On May 8, US forces disabled two Iranian tankers that tried to break the US naval blockade. The fragile ceasefire that exists is not a peace — it is a pause between escalations.

Breaking — May 10: Euronews reports that a "fragile truce holds as US awaits Iran's response to latest proposal." Iran has not yet formally rejected or accepted the most recent US framework. Pakistan's diplomatic back-channel remains active. The next 72 hours could determine whether talks restart or whether Trump resumes bombing.

Why Beijing Holds the Key to Tehran

Here is the hidden connection between Trump's three diplomatic fronts: the Beijing summit is not just about US-China trade. It is fundamentally about Iran. China's willingness to stop buying Iranian oil — or to use its relationship with Tehran to pressure Iran into a deal — is the single most powerful economic lever that could force Iran to the negotiating table on terms acceptable to the US.

Without Chinese pressure, Iran can survive the US economic blockade longer than America's domestic political patience allows. With Chinese pressure, Tehran loses its most important economic lifeline and its most important diplomatic cover. This is why Trump is going to Beijing. This is why Xi agreed to host him. And this is why Iran's Foreign Minister went to Beijing first — to make sure China heard Tehran's position before Trump arrived.

The diplomatic chess game unfolding in May 2026 is fundamentally triangular: Washington, Beijing, and Tehran — each managing the others, each seeking an outcome that it can present domestically as a victory.

Pakistan's Continuing Role

The unlikely hero of this diplomatic crisis remains Pakistan. A country that international analysts had been calling a "failed state" as recently as 2024 — with a collapsing economy, political chaos, and a reputation for sponsoring regional instability — has somehow become the indispensable mediator between the world's most powerful country and one of its most defiant adversaries.

Pakistan's PM Shehbaz Sharif and Field Marshal Asim Munir have maintained communication with both Washington and Tehran throughout the crisis. Pakistan brokered the April ceasefire. Pakistan is now trying to bring both sides back to a second round of the "Islamabad process." In exchange, Pakistan has extracted a significant trade deal with the United States — a remarkable diplomatic transaction for a country that was largely isolated on the world stage just eighteen months ago.

The Diplomatic Scorecard: Winners and Losers of May 2026

🇺🇸

Trump — Cautious Winner

Brokered Ukraine ceasefire and prisoner swap. Beijing summit locked in. Iran deal not yet closed. Domestic approval at 36% — needs wins urgently. Too early to declare victory.

🇷🇺

Russia — Quietly Losing

Victory Day parade scaled back due to Ukrainian strike threat. Ceasefire agreed on American terms. Four years of war has not delivered stated objectives. Isolated economically but still fighting.

🇺🇦

Ukraine — Strategic Resilience

Can now strike deep inside Russia including near Moscow. Zelenskyy's "parade permission" decree was a masterclass in information warfare. Receives 1,000 prisoners home. Cautiously hopeful but deeply distrustful of Russia's commitments.

🇨🇳

China — Positioned Carefully

Hosting the US president from a position of relative strength. Has leverage over Iran. Has leverage over trade. Wants stability — but on its own terms. The real kingmaker of May 2026.

🇮🇷

Iran — Defiant but Cornered

Created the Persian Gulf Strait Authority. Still refusing full capitulation. But losing $500M/day from US blockade. Sent FM to Beijing first — which tells you everything about how much Tehran needs Chinese backing.

🇵🇰

Pakistan — Surprising Winner

From "failed state" to global mediator in 90 days. Scored US trade deal. PM nominated Trump for Nobel. Hosting the "Islamabad process." The most remarkable diplomatic rehabilitation of the decade.

The NATO Question: What Happens to the Alliance?

One of the most significant but least-discussed consequences of Trump's diplomatic activity is its effect on NATO. The alliance was already under strain from Trump's repeated demands that European members increase defence spending and his suggestion that the US might not automatically defend NATO members who didn't pay their "fair share." The Iran war added a new dimension: Trump launched strikes on Iran without consulting NATO allies, leaving the alliance in the dark about a military action that fundamentally disrupted the energy supplies of every European member state.

European leaders have been forced to reckon with the reality that America under Trump is not a predictable ally. They are scrambling to secure alternative jet fuel supplies, diversify energy sources away from the Gulf, and develop military capabilities that don't depend on US protection. France's Macron has been particularly vocal — calling for European strategic autonomy, proposing joint France-UK maritime missions to secure the Strait of Hormuz, and asserting that Europe cannot simply wait for Washington to resolve every crisis.

Meanwhile, Trump has floated the possibility of moving US troops from Germany to Poland — another signal that the traditional architecture of European security is being renegotiated without European governments being primary participants in that negotiation.

The India Problem — Sidelined Again

India finds itself in an increasingly uncomfortable position. The world's most populous country, the fifth-largest economy, and a nation that has explicitly positioned itself as a rising geopolitical power — is absent from every significant diplomatic conversation of May 2026. The Russia-Ukraine ceasefire was brokered by the US. The Beijing summit is US-China. The Iran negotiations are US-Iran, mediated by Pakistan. India is not at any of these tables.

India's domestic energy crisis — driven by the Hormuz closure cutting off 90% of its LPG imports — has become a political liability for the Modi government. The opposition Congress party is pointing to Pakistan's diplomatic elevation as evidence of BJP foreign policy failure. India-US relations are at a low point due to Trump's tariffs, H1-B visa restrictions, and anger over India's continued purchase of Russian oil. India, which was supposed to be America's great Indo-Pacific partner, finds itself simultaneously alienated from Washington, outmanoeuvred by Islamabad, and watching its energy security unravel.

"India is experiencing some heartburn over Pakistan's visible role in negotiating the ceasefire between Iran and the US — a challenge to its own ambitions as the South Asian regional hegemon." — The Straits Times, April 2026

What to Watch in the Coming Days

MAY 10-11, 2026
Russia-Ukraine Ceasefire: Does It Hold?
Both sides have violated every previous truce. If this one holds through May 11, it will be the longest sustained ceasefire of the conflict and a genuine signal that broader negotiations are possible. If it collapses, Trump's diplomatic credibility takes a hit before he even lands in Beijing.
MAY 12-13, 2026
Iran's Response to Latest US Proposal
The fragile truce holds "as US awaits Iran's response." Tehran's answer — or lack of one — will determine whether Trump arrives in Beijing having already closed the Iran chapter, or whether he needs Xi to help him close it.
MAY 14-15, 2026
Trump Lands in Beijing — The Historic Summit
First US presidential visit to China in nine years. Trump will press Xi on Iran, trade, and energy markets. Xi will press Trump on tariffs, Taiwan, and technology controls. Both sides will claim victory regardless of what actually happens.
MAY 16+ 2026
Post-Summit Fallout — Does the Strait Reopen?
If Beijing and Washington align on Iran, Tehran faces an unprecedented squeeze. If China refuses to deliver, the strait stays closed and the global energy crisis deepens through summer. This is the fork in the road that determines the shape of the rest of 2026.

The Bottom Line

May 2026 is shaping up to be one of the most consequential months in post-Cold War diplomacy. Three interlocking crises — a four-year war in Europe, a Middle East oil shutdown, and the most important bilateral relationship in the world — are all reaching inflection points simultaneously. And at the centre of all three, by design or by accident, stands Donald Trump.

His critics will note that he started one of these crises himself (the Iran war), inherited another (Russia-Ukraine), and risks inflaming the third (US-China). His defenders will argue that only a leader willing to personally call Putin and Zelenskyy, fly to Beijing, and threaten to bomb Tehran could create the conditions for resolution on all three fronts at once.

Both things can be true. The question that history will eventually answer is whether Trump's May 2026 diplomatic sprint represents a genuine turning point toward peace — or simply the eye of a storm that is still gathering strength.

Three fronts. One president. Seventy-two hours that could define the next decade of global order.

title: The 2026 Strait of Hormuz Crisis: A Global Catastrophe
content:
Imagine a narrow strip of water — just 34 kilometres wide at its tightest point — and through it flows nearly 20% of the entire world's oil supply. Every day. Every hour. Now imagine that strip is on fire, mined, blockaded, and caught between two military superpowers pointing guns at each other.

That's the Strait of Hormuz in May 2026. And the International Energy Agency has already declared this the "largest supply disruption in the history of the global oil market."

20%
Global oil supply — blocked
32
Ships hit by missiles since Feb 28
$120
Brent crude price per barrel (peak)
71km²
Oil spill near Kharg Island
10.1mb/d
Global oil supply plummet in March
$500M
Daily cost to Iran from US blockade

Part 1: The Strait of Hormuz — A Geography Lesson the World Ignored

The Strait of Hormuz as seen from NASA satellite imagery — the world's most critical oil chokepoint.

The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow waterway connecting the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea. Iran lies to its north; Oman's Musandam Peninsula forms its southern boundary. At its narrowest point, it is approximately 34 kilometres wide — yet through this sliver of water passes the lifeblood of the modern global economy.

In 2024, oil flow through the strait averaged 20 million barrels per day — equivalent to roughly 20% of global petroleum consumption and about one-quarter of all seaborne oil trade worldwide. Additionally, 20% of the world's liquefied natural gas (LNG) passed through here, primarily from Qatar, which alone supplied over 112 billion cubic metres of LNG in 2025. Countries like Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Kuwait, UAE, Bahrain, and Qatar have no meaningful alternative to this single passage — their entire petroleum export infrastructure feeds into it.

About 84% of the crude oil and 83% of the LNG passing through the strait in 2024 was bound for Asia — primarily China, India, Japan, and South Korea. When analysts speak of Asia's "energy vulnerability," this is exactly what they mean: the entire continent's industrial supply chain, from steel mills in South Korea to petrochemical plants in India, runs through 34 kilometres of water governed by international maritime law — and partially by Iranian territorial waters.

Why there's almost no alternative: Only Saudi Arabia and the UAE have operational pipelines capable of bypassing the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi Aramco's East-West pipeline can carry up to 7 million b/d. The UAE's Fujairah pipeline manages 1.5 million b/d. Combined unused capacity from these bypass routes stands at roughly 3.5 to 5.5 million b/d — a fraction of the 20 million b/d that normally transits the strait. Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain, Iraq, and Iran have no bypass whatsoever.

A Chokepoint 35 Million Years in the Making

Geologically, the Strait of Hormuz was created roughly 35 million years ago through the collision of the Arabian and Eurasian tectonic plates. As Oxford professor of Earth Sciences Mike Searle explains, the same continental collision that formed this narrow waterway also tilted the Musandam Peninsula northward — creating the pinch point — while simultaneously trapping the vast oil and gas reserves beneath the Arabian plate that now lie under Iran, Iraq, and the Persian Gulf states. The geology that created the world's largest oil reserves also created the world's most dangerous bottleneck to export them.

The History of Control — From Marco Polo to the CIA

The Strait of Hormuz has been a centre of global power for centuries. By the 15th century, the island of Hormuz had become one of the great emporium-states of the medieval world — a hub where merchants from Egypt, China, Java, Bengal, Zanzibar, and Yemen converged. Marco Polo visited twice during his journeys. Chinese Admiral Zheng He made it the final destination of his famous treasure fleet during the Ming Dynasty.

In 1507, Portuguese Admiral Afonso de Albuquerque — understanding that whoever controls the strait controls everything between India and the Mediterranean — seized the port with just seven ships and 500 men. In 1622, Shah Abbas I recaptured it with English naval support. The British dominated it for centuries. In 1951, the British Navy imposed a blockade on the strait to pressure Iranian PM Mohammad Mosaddegh after he nationalised Iran's oil industry. That blockade lasted more than two years and contributed to the CIA-backed coup against Mosaddegh in 1953.

During the Iran-Iraq War of 1980-1988, the strait became a "Tanker War" battleground. The United States intervened in 1988 in Operation Praying Mantis — attacking Iranian naval targets after Iran mined international waters. The pattern is clear: every major power that rises must eventually reckon with the Strait of Hormuz.

Part 2: The War That Changed Everything — February 28, 2026

On February 28, 2026, the United States and Israel launched coordinated surprise airstrikes on Iran — targeting military installations, nuclear sites, and government infrastructure. In the strikes, Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei was assassinated, along with multiple senior Iranian officials. Iran immediately appointed Khamenei's son as his successor.

Iran's retaliation was swift, multi-directional, and devastating. Missile and drone attacks struck Israel, U.S. military bases across the region, and military and civilian locations in Gulf Arab states. The UAE was hit repeatedly. Saudi infrastructure came under threat. And then came the move that changed global economics in 72 hours: on March 4, 2026, the IRGC formally declared the Strait of Hormuz closed to all foreign shipping.

What the IRGC actually did: The Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps transmitted warnings via VHF radio to all vessels in the strait: "No ship is allowed to pass the Strait of Hormuz." They then backed these words with action — boarding and attacking merchant ships, laying sea mines throughout the strait, and launching drone strikes on vessels attempting transit. Commercial traffic through the strait dropped more than 90% within days.

Within 48 hours of the war starting, the world's largest marine insurance mutuals issued cancellation notices for war risk extensions covering the Gulf. Shipping giants suspended operations entirely. QatarEnergy declared force majeure on all LNG exports. Brent crude surged 10-13% to around $80-82 per barrel in the first two days alone — and it was just getting started.

Part 3: The Full Timeline — What Happened, When

FEB 28, 2026
US-Israel strikes Iran. Khamenei assassinated.
Coordinated airstrikes hit military, nuclear, and government targets across Iran. The 2026 Iran War begins. Iran launches counter-strikes on Israel, US bases, and Gulf states.
MARCH 4, 2026
Iran formally closes the Strait of Hormuz.
IRGC warns all vessels to leave. Ships boarded and attacked. Sea mines laid. Commercial traffic collapses by over 90%. Oil prices surge.
MARCH 19, 2026
US begins Strait of Hormuz aerial campaign.
US Air Force and Navy, joined by Israeli Air Force, begin striking Iranian naval vessels and drones in the strait. Goal: reopen passage to international shipping.
MARCH 25, 2026
Pakistan delivers US "15-point proposal" to Iran.
Pakistan begins its diplomatic shuttle role — delivering US ceasefire plan to Tehran. Iran rejects it. Issues a 5-point counter-proposal.
APRIL 7-8, 2026
Ceasefire agreed. Pakistan brokers the deal.
After nearly 6 weeks of conflict, the US and Iran agree to a conditional two-week ceasefire mediated by Pakistan's PM Shehbaz Sharif. Iran presents a 10-point plan. Trump calls it a "workable basis."
APRIL 11-12, 2026
Islamabad Talks — 21 hours, no deal.
A 300-member US team led by JD Vance, Steve Witkoff, and Jared Kushner meets a 70-member Iranian team led by Parliament Speaker Ghalibaf. After 21 hours across 3 rounds, delegations leave without agreement. Main sticking points: Iran's nuclear program, strait status, sanctions relief.
APRIL 13, 2026
US imposes naval blockade on Iranian ports.
Following the failed Islamabad Talks, Trump announces a full US naval blockade of Iranian ports — cutting off Tehran's oil revenue. The US estimates this costs Iran $500 million per day. Iran retaliates by seizing two cargo ships.
APRIL 17, 2026
Iran briefly announces strait open — then closes it again.
Due to Israel-Lebanon ceasefire, Iran announces strait open to commercial shipping. But with US blockade of Iranian ports still in place, Iran reimposed restrictions within days.
MAY 4, 2026
Trump launches "Operation Project Freedom."
US Navy mission to physically escort stranded merchant vessels out of the Gulf. Iran calls it a ceasefire violation. Over 100 US aircraft patrol the skies over the strait.
MAY 6, 2026
Trump pauses Project Freedom — "great progress" claimed.
Pakistan requests pause. Trump cites military success and progress toward a "complete and final agreement" with Iran. Only two US-flagged civilian ships have successfully transited the strait under escort.
MAY 8, 2026
US fires on two Iranian tankers. UAE struck again.
US forces disable two Iranian oil tankers attempting to breach the naval blockade. Iran creates the "Persian Gulf Strait Authority" to tax and vet shipping. UAE reports another missile and drone attack. Oil slick of 71 square kilometres detected near Kharg Island — 80,000 barrels spilled.

Part 4: The Economics of Catastrophe

The International Energy Agency has used language it has never used before. The head of the IEA described the situation as the "greatest global energy security crisis" ever recorded — worse than the 1973 Arab oil embargo, worse than the 1979 Iranian Revolution, worse than the 1991 Gulf War. Global oil supply plummeted by 10.1 million barrels per day in March alone — the largest single-month supply disruption in recorded history. The IEA now projects global oil demand will actually contract by 80,000 barrels per day in 2026, compared to growth of 730,000 b/d projected before the war.

Brent crude — the global benchmark — surged from $80 to $120 per barrel between March 2 and March 9 alone. Analysts who had previously predicted Brent could hit $150 in a worst-case scenario now consider that a realistic mid-case projection if the conflict extends through summer.

The fertiliser crisis nobody is talking about: The Persian Gulf accounts for roughly 30-35% of global urea exports and 20-30% of global ammonia exports. These nitrogen fertilisers are the foundation of global food production. As the strait remains closed, fertiliser prices are spiking globally — and analysts warn that less-wealthy food-and-fuel-importing nations could face acute stress if the conflict continues into the planting season.

The Jet Fuel Catastrophe of Summer 2026

Before the war, Persian Gulf exports represented the largest single source of jet fuel supply to the global market. Iran's blockade cut off those exports entirely. Global jet fuel exports plunged 30% in April — from 1.9 million barrels per day in April 2025 to just 1.3 million barrels per day in April 2026. Exxon Mobil CEO Darren Woods warned in a CNBC interview that commercial crude oil and refined product inventories "will eventually draw down to working minimums" — meaning the buffer that prevents a full shortage is depleting.

European airlines including Lufthansa and Ryanair have oil hedging contracts that provide some protection — but those run out. The EU is scrambling to secure alternative jet fuel from the United States, where refiners like Valero and Marathon Petroleum have maximised jet fuel production. US jet fuel exports to Europe surged over 400% in April compared to February. The concern is not just price — it's the possibility of actual flight cancellations for summer 2026 if alternative supplies cannot be secured in time.

Asian refineries are struggling even more acutely, having lost access to the crude feedstocks they depend on. As Kpler's director of commodity research Matt Smith told CNBC: "It's a slow motion car crash. We're just kind of sleepwalking through it."

Part 5: How the Crisis Hits Every Country Differently

🇮🇳

India

90% of India's LPG imports pass through Hormuz. Brent rising from $80 to $120 spiked household cooking fuel costs by 7%. LPG shortages triggered protests across India. Wheat prices also rising. India also lost diplomatic leverage as Pakistan emerged as the key mediator — a major strategic embarrassment for New Delhi.

🇨🇳

China

China has large strategic oil reserves providing short-term cushion — but continues secretly buying Iranian oil, paying in yuan through IRGC channels. However, China's 2026 growth outlook is under pressure: higher energy costs feed into steel, chemicals, and electronics production, squeezing export competitiveness during peak trade tensions with the US.

🇰🇷

South Korea

Gets over 60% of its crude through Hormuz. Activated a 100 trillion won ($68 billion) market-stabilisation programme. Began capping domestic petrol prices. One tanker that passed in mid-April with 1 million barrels arrived at South Korea's coast on May 8 — treated as major news.

🇯🇵

Japan

Nearly all of Japan's Middle Eastern oil imports come through Hormuz. Japan has activated emergency oil reserve protocols. LNG prices in Asia have surged significantly. Japan's energy security strategy — built on the assumption of a stable Gulf — is being fundamentally re-examined.

🇩🇪

Europe

Europe was the biggest importer of Middle Eastern jet fuel before the war. Now scrambling for alternatives. The EU is working to secure fuel from US refiners. Goldman Sachs economists project eurozone GDP growth could slow to just 0.5% year-on-year in the second half of 2026 if the crisis persists.

🇵🇰

Pakistan

The surprise winner diplomatically. Despite being a financially strained state, Pakistan emerged as the world's indispensable mediator — hosting the Islamabad Talks, brokering the ceasefire, and maintaining back-channel communications between Washington and Tehran "day and night." Its PM even nominated Trump for the Nobel Peace Prize — and Pakistan got a major trade deal in return.

Part 6: The Islamabad Talks — The 21-Hour Failure That Changed Everything

The most dramatic diplomatic event of the crisis occurred on April 11-12, 2026, at the Serena Hotel in Islamabad — a venue placed under complete city-wide lockdown to secure the delegations. The talks were attended by a 300-member US negotiating team led by Vice President JD Vance, alongside special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Iran sent a 70-member team led by Parliamentary Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi. Pakistan's PM Shehbaz Sharif, Field Marshal Asim Munir, and Deputy PM Ishaq Dar moderated.

In a moment of raw emotion, the Iranian delegation brought photographs and blood-soaked belongings of child victims killed in a US strike on a school in the town of Minab — a deliberate and powerful act of political testimony in the middle of diplomatic negotiations.

Three rounds of talks were held over 21 hours — the first indirect, the second and third direct. The talks collapsed without an agreement. The main unresolved issues: Iran's nuclear programme, the status of the Strait of Hormuz, sanctions relief, and Iran's frozen assets of $6 billion. Iran demanded comprehensive sanctions lifting as a precondition; the US insisted on phased relief tied to compliance. Iran's FM Araghchi said they were "inches away from an MoU" but accused the US of "moving the goalposts." JD Vance publicly stated that Iran had refused to rule out nuclear weapons development. Trump declared Iran had "knowingly failed."

"Iran will end the war when it decides to do so and when its own conditions are met." — Anonymous Iranian official, quoted by Press TV

Part 7: Iran's Audacious Power Grab — The Persian Gulf Strait Authority

While the war continued and negotiations stalled, Iran made a move that alarmed the entire world: it quietly created the Persian Gulf Strait Authority — a new government body specifically designed to vet, tax, and control ships seeking passage through the strait. Any vessel wishing to transit now faces Iranian bureaucratic approval and payment of fees — in Chinese yuan — to an IRGC-affiliated agency.

This is not a wartime improvisation. It is an attempt to permanently institutionalise Iranian control over an international waterway governed by UNCLOS — the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea — and used by the entire global community for centuries. Secretary of State Marco Rubio called it "unacceptable" and asked the question that now hangs over every diplomatic meeting: "Is the world going to accept that Iran now controls an international waterway? What is the world prepared to do about it?"

France's President Macron responded by calling for an immediate, unconditional reopening of the strait and proposing a joint France-UK multinational mission to secure the waterway — stating that "all parties must lift the blockade without delay and without conditions."

Part 8: India's Strategic Embarrassment

Perhaps the most significant geopolitical side-story of this crisis is India's diplomatic failure. India has long positioned itself as South Asia's dominant power and a critical US partner. Yet as the Iran war escalated, India found itself sidelined.

India maintained official neutrality — condemning strikes on American bases without mentioning Iran, while PM Modi spoke with Gulf leaders about sovereignty without specifically condemning the US-Israel strikes on Iran. The Indian National Congress called this position a "joke." Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi described Pakistan's growing global influence as a direct failure of BJP foreign policy.

The Straits Times noted that "India is experiencing some heartburn over Pakistan's visible role in negotiating the ceasefire — a challenge to its own ambitions as the South Asian regional hegemon." India-US relations are also at a low point due to Trump's tariffs on India, new H1-B visa barriers, and anger over India's purchases of Russian oil. India's once-dominant diplomatic position in the region has been quietly, systematically undercut.

India's energy crisis at home: 90% of India's LPG imports, and a massive share of its crude oil, pass through Hormuz. Brent going from $80 to $120 per barrel directly spiked household cooking fuel costs by 7%. LPG shortages led to protests across multiple states. The rupee came under pressure. Wheat prices rose. India, with thinner reserves than China and heavier reliance on Middle Eastern crude, is among the most vulnerable large economies to a prolonged disruption.

Part 9: The Environmental Catastrophe in Plain Sight

Beneath the headlines about blockades and tankers, a quiet environmental catastrophe is unfolding in the Persian Gulf. Satellite images taken on May 8, 2026 show an oil slick covering approximately 71 square kilometres — roughly the size of a small city — emanating from the western side of Kharg Island, Iran's main crude export terminal. According to maritime intelligence firm Windward AI, the equivalent of roughly 80,000 barrels of oil has spilled from Kharg Island since the slick was first detected by satellite on Tuesday, and images show it is still actively leaking.

The Persian Gulf's marine ecosystem — already one of the most stressed in the world due to high salinity, heat, and heavy shipping — faces consequences that will outlast any ceasefire by decades. Coral reefs, fish populations, and desalination infrastructure that Gulf states depend on for drinking water are all at risk. In the middle of the most consequential geopolitical standoff of the decade, the environment is losing quietly.

Part 10: What Happens Next?

As of May 9, 2026, the situation remains acutely unstable. The US blockade of Iranian ports remains in place. Iran's Persian Gulf Strait Authority continues to operate. Hundreds of commercial vessels remain bottled up inside the Gulf. Pakistan is intensifying efforts to bring both sides back to a negotiating table, referring to the broader engagement as the "Islamabad process" — suggesting a multi-round diplomatic framework rather than a one-off event.

Iran's ambassador to China has suggested that any long-term security guarantees could involve powers like China, Pakistan, Turkey, and Russia — a direct challenge to the US-led international order. Israel's PM Netanyahu has said that despite the ceasefire, "we still have goals to complete" — goals that include Iran's nuclear and ballistic missile programmes.

The IMO continues to urge ships to "exercise maximum caution," noting bluntly that "naval escorts are not a sustainable long-term solution." The ExxonMobil CEO warns that inventory buffers will run out. Jet fuel supplies for Asia and Europe are depleting. Some countries face critical shortages by June or July 2026 if alternative supplies cannot be secured.

Trump has threatened to resume full-scale bombing if Iran does not agree to a deal that includes reopening the strait and rolling back its nuclear programme. Iran's IRGC has responded that the strait "will not be opened to the enemies of this nation through the ridiculous spectacle by the president of the US."

The Bottom Line

The Strait of Hormuz was always described in policy papers as the world's most critical energy chokepoint — a theoretical vulnerability that experts warned about for decades. In 2026, that theory became brutal reality. The 34-kilometre pinch point between Iran and Oman has become the epicentre of the largest oil supply disruption in history, a diplomatic crisis involving every major global power, and an environmental catastrophe unfolding in slow motion.

A deal is theoretically close. Iran's FM said they were "inches away." Pakistan's diplomats are working around the clock. But "inches away" in diplomatic terms can mean weeks or months of continued disruption — and the global economy cannot afford months.

The world built its energy infrastructure around the assumption that the Strait of Hormuz would always be open. That assumption has been shattered. Whatever happens next, the lesson is permanent: when your civilisation's lifeline runs through 34 kilometres of contested water, geography is destiny.

One narrow strait. Two nuclear-threshold powers. Zero easy answers. And the entire world paying the price.

title: India's Strategic Awakening: Why Geopolitics Is No Longer Just for Diplomats
content:
The World Is Changing — Is India Ready?

Close your eyes and think about the last time you filled petrol at a pump. You probably noticed the price — maybe complained about it, maybe just accepted it and moved on. But did you wonder why it costs what it does? The answer is not in the refinery down the road or the government's tax policy alone. The real answer is in the Strait of Hormuz — a narrow strip of water between Iran and Oman, barely 33 kilometers wide at its narrowest point — through which nearly 20 percent of the world's oil flows every single day. When tensions rise in that strait, your petrol price rises with it. When a Houthi missile strikes a tanker in the Red Sea, freight costs spike globally, and Indian importers pay more. When OPEC+ nations — led by Saudi Arabia and Russia — decide to cut production in a Vienna conference room, Indian consumers feel it at the pump within weeks.

This is geopolitics. Not an abstract academic discipline. Not something reserved for retired generals and foreign service officers. Not the background noise of a 10 PM news debate. It is the invisible hand that reaches into your pocket, shapes your career opportunities, determines whether your city gets flooded with Chinese imports or benefits from a trade deal with Europe, and decides how safe the borders of your country will be in the decade ahead.

India, in 2025, stands at an extraordinary crossroads. It is the world's most populous nation. The fifth-largest economy by nominal GDP — and the third-largest by purchasing power parity. It has the second-largest army in the world. It is a nuclear power. It is a democracy of 1.4 billion people. And it sits at the geographic center of the most contested strategic theatre of the 21st century: the Indo-Pacific.

Every great power on earth — the United States, China, Russia, the European Union, Japan, the Gulf monarchies — has a position on India. They want something from India, or they want to prevent India from getting something. They are courting New Delhi, pressuring it, sanctioning its partners, offering it technology, or surrounding it with infrastructure debt. The world is not ignoring India. The world is intensely focused on India.

The question is: are Indians equally focused on the world?

That is the question that gave birth to Global Chanakya.

---

What Is Geopolitics — A Clear Definition for the Modern Indian Reader

The word "geopolitics" comes from two Greek roots — geo (earth) and politikos (of citizens, of the state). At its most fundamental level, geopolitics is the study of how geography shapes political power, and how political power reshapes geography.

The classical geopoliticians of the 19th and early 20th centuries — men like Halford Mackinder, Alfred Thayer Mahan, and Nicholas Spykman — built entire theories of world domination around geography. Mackinder argued that whoever controlled the "Heartland" of Eurasia (roughly modern Russia and Central Asia) would control the world. Mahan argued that naval power and control of sea lanes was the true key to global dominance. Spykman argued that it was the coastal "Rimland" — the littoral zones of Eurasia — that truly mattered.

These men wrote over a century ago. But look at a map of the world today and you will see their theories playing out in real time. China is building artificial islands in the South China Sea — attempting to control the Rimland sea lanes that Spykman identified. Russia's entire strategic anxiety is about controlling its Western approaches — the Heartland buffer that Mackinder described. The United States has spent 80 years building a network of naval bases across the Indo-Pacific — exactly the sea power projection that Mahan prescribed.

Modern geopolitics, however, has evolved far beyond pure geography. Today it encompasses:

  • Military strategy: Force postures, alliance systems, nuclear deterrence, grey-zone warfare
  • Economic statecraft: Trade policy, sanctions, technology controls, debt diplomacy
  • Energy security: Control of pipelines, shipping lanes, and resource supply chains
  • Technological competition: Semiconductors, AI, quantum computing, space, cyber
  • Information warfare: Influence operations, propaganda, narrative control
  • Demographic power: Population trends, migration, diaspora networks
  • Institutional power: Control of multilateral bodies — the UN, IMF, WTO, WHO

Every one of these dimensions directly affects India. And every one of them will be covered — rigorously, honestly, and from an Indian perspective — on Global Chanakya.

---

Chanakya: India's Original Grand Strategist

Before we discuss the world of today, it is worth spending a moment on the name we have chosen for this platform — because it is not chosen lightly.

Chanakya — also known as Kautilya or Vishnugupta — lived in the 4th century BCE. He was the prime minister and chief strategist of the Maurya Empire under Chandragupta Maurya. He is credited with writing the Arthashastra — a Sanskrit treatise on statecraft, economic policy, military strategy, and political philosophy that remains one of the most remarkable documents in human history.

What is extraordinary about the Arthashastra is how modern it feels. Chanakya wrote about intelligence networks and espionage — what we would today call signals intelligence and human intelligence. He wrote about economic warfare — using trade embargoes and financial pressure to weaken enemies. He wrote about the importance of a strong treasury as the foundation of military power. He wrote about the "Mandala theory" — a sophisticated model of how a state should manage relationships with its neighbors, neighbors' neighbors, and distant powers. He wrote about the use of propaganda and information to shape public perception.

Replace some of the Sanskrit terminology and the Arthashastra could pass as a modern geopolitical strategy document. The fundamentals of statecraft have not changed in 2,300 years, because human nature has not changed. States still seek security, resources, and dominance. Leaders still calculate interest and power. Alliances are still built on convenience, not friendship.

The name Global Chanakya is a declaration of intent: to bring that ancient Indian tradition of clear-eyed, unsentimental strategic analysis to bear on the complex world of the 21st century. We do not view international affairs through a lens of idealism or wishful thinking. We view it the way Chanakya did — asking always: where does real power lie, what are the genuine interests at stake, and what should India do?

---

The Five Geopolitical Forces Shaping India's World Right Now

To understand why geopolitics matters to India so urgently in this moment, consider five major forces that are simultaneously reshaping the international order.

1. The US-China Strategic Competition

The defining geopolitical contest of our era is the rivalry between the United States and China. This is not simply a trade dispute or a diplomatic disagreement. It is a systemic competition between two incompatible visions of world order — an American-led liberal international order built after 1945, and a China-led alternative order that Beijing has been patiently constructing for two decades.

China has built the world's largest navy by number of vessels. It has constructed a global infrastructure network through the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) spanning over 140 countries. It has become the world's largest trading nation. It has developed advanced capabilities in artificial intelligence, quantum computing, and hypersonic missiles. It has established military bases abroad — in Djibouti, and increasingly in the Indo-Pacific. And it has territorial claims against virtually every neighbor it has — including India.

The United States, meanwhile, has responded by building new military alliances (AUKUS, Quad), imposing sweeping technology export controls on China, reshoring semiconductor manufacturing, and dramatically increasing its naval presence in the Indo-Pacific.

India sits directly in the middle of this contest. Both Washington and Beijing want India on their side — or at least not on the other's side. This gives India remarkable diplomatic leverage, but it also creates genuine strategic dangers. Getting this balance wrong could be catastrophic. Getting it right could accelerate India's rise dramatically.

2. The Russia-Ukraine War and the End of the Post-Cold War Order

When Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, it did not just start a war in Eastern Europe. It shattered the foundational assumptions of the post-Cold War international order — the idea that territorial conquest was permanently off the table for major powers in Europe, that international institutions could prevent great power aggression, and that economic interdependence produced peace.

For India, this war created an immediate energy opportunity and a long-term strategic dilemma. India bought discounted Russian crude oil at scale — a pragmatic economic decision that saved billions of dollars. But India also had to navigate intense Western pressure, maintain its relationships with both Moscow and Washington simultaneously, and avoid being caught in secondary sanctions. India's "strategic autonomy" — its long-standing policy of non-alignment — was tested as never before.

The war also accelerated the fragmentation of the global economy into competing blocs — a trend with enormous implications for Indian trade, investment, and technology access.

3. The Indo-Pacific's Emergence as the World's Most Critical Theatre

The Indo-Pacific — broadly defined as the area stretching from the eastern coast of Africa to the western coast of the Americas, encompassing the Indian Ocean and Pacific Ocean — is now the undisputed center of global strategic competition. It contains the world's most important sea lanes, through which trillions of dollars of trade flows annually. It is home to the world's fastest-growing economies. It contains multiple unresolved territorial disputes — the South China Sea, the East China Sea, the Taiwan Strait. And it is where the US-China competition is most intense.

India is not a passive observer of the Indo-Pacific. India IS the Indo-Pacific. The Indian Ocean is named after India for a reason — it sits at the geographic heart of this region. India's coastline stretches over 7,500 kilometers. India has island territories — the Andaman and Nicobar Islands — that sit at the critical chokepoint between the Indian Ocean and the Pacific. India's navy is the seventh-largest in the world and growing rapidly.

The emergence of the Indo-Pacific as the world's most contested strategic theatre is, at its core, a story about India's rise — and India's choices about how to use its power.

4. The Technology Revolution and the New Arms Race

The 21st century has added entirely new dimensions to geopolitical competition. The battles of the future — and in many cases the battles of today — are being fought over semiconductors, artificial intelligence, quantum computing, space assets, undersea cables, and cyber infrastructure.

Semiconductors — the microchips that power everything from smartphones to missiles — have become the new oil. The United States has imposed sweeping export controls to prevent China from accessing advanced chips and the equipment to make them. Taiwan — which produces over 60 percent of the world's most advanced semiconductors at TSMC — has become arguably the most strategically important piece of territory on earth. A Chinese takeover of Taiwan would give Beijing control of the global chip supply, with catastrophic implications for every technologically advanced nation including India.

India is building its own semiconductor ambitions — with government incentives attracting chip manufacturers, and growing investment in AI and space technology. But India is also deeply dependent on foreign technology for its defence systems, telecommunications infrastructure, and digital economy. Managing these technology dependencies while building indigenous capability is one of the most complex strategic challenges India faces.

5. The Middle East Realignment

The Middle East has always been critical to India — as the source of most of India's oil and gas, as home to over 9 million Indian diaspora workers who send billions in remittances annually, and as a region whose instability directly threatens Indian energy security and the safety of Indian citizens abroad.

In recent years, the Middle East has undergone the most significant realignment in decades. The Abraham Accords normalized relations between Israel and several Arab states. The China-brokered Iran-Saudi Arabia détente signaled Beijing's growing role as a Middle East power broker. The Israel-Hamas war that began in October 2023 reignited regional tensions and drew in Hezbollah, the Houthis, and Iran directly. The ongoing civil conflicts in Yemen, Libya, and Sudan add further instability.

For India, this realignment creates both opportunities and risks. The India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC) — announced at the G20 summit in New Delhi — represents an attempt to build new trade connectivity linking India to Gulf states and Europe. But the same region's instability threatens the energy supplies and the safety of the Indian diaspora on which India's economy partially depends.

How Geopolitics Affects Your Daily Life as an Indian

If the above seems too grand — too distant from your daily reality — let us make it concrete. Here is how geopolitics directly touches the life of an ordinary Indian citizen.

Your Fuel Price

As discussed, oil prices are set by OPEC+ decisions, Middle East tensions, and the US dollar's exchange rate — all geopolitical variables. India imports over 85 percent of its crude oil. Every rupee of exchange rate depreciation and every dollar rise in crude prices costs India billions. The government's ability to subsidize fuel — or its inability to do so — is directly a function of global geopolitics.

Your Job Market

The global technology supply chain restructuring driven by US-China competition is creating enormous opportunities for India. Apple has shifted significant iPhone production to India. Samsung has expanded Indian manufacturing. Dozens of global companies are establishing India as an alternative to China. This is not charity — it is geopolitics creating economic opportunity. The jobs being created in Indian manufacturing today are a direct result of strategic decoupling from China.

Your Digital Security

The Indian government's ban on hundreds of Chinese apps — including TikTok — following the 2020 Galwan Valley clash was a geopolitical decision with direct consequences for every Indian smartphone user. The ongoing debate about Chinese equipment in Indian telecommunications networks (Huawei, ZTE) is a geopolitical debate with direct implications for the privacy and security of every Indian's digital life.

Your Food Prices

The Russia-Ukraine war disrupted global wheat and fertilizer supplies significantly — because both Russia and Ukraine are among the world's largest exporters of both. India, which had been importing fertilizer from Russia and wheat from the Black Sea region, had to scramble to find alternatives. The price of dal, wheat flour, and vegetables in Indian markets was partly determined by a war being fought 5,000 kilometers away.

Your Passport's Power

Whether you can travel visa-free to a country, how easily you can get a work visa, whether your professional qualifications are recognized abroad — all of these are determined by bilateral and multilateral agreements that are fundamentally geopolitical in nature. India's improving diplomatic relationships have gradually strengthened the Indian passport. Further progress depends on continued geopolitical engagement.

Why Most Indians Are Underserved by Existing Media

Given how profoundly geopolitics shapes Indian life, you might expect India to have a rich ecosystem of strategic analysis media. The reality is disappointing.

Television news — both English and Hindi — is almost entirely consumed by domestic political combat. Geopolitics appears on prime time only when there is a border incident or a diplomatic crisis, and even then it is typically framed through the prism of partisan politics rather than genuine strategic analysis. The quality of analysis is poor, the heat is high, the light is minimal.

English-language digital media covers geopolitics more seriously, but much of it imports frameworks and perspectives from Western outlets — The Economist, Foreign Policy, Foreign Affairs — that are sophisticated but are written for Western audiences with Western interests at heart. They are not asking what is best for India. They are asking what is best for the liberal international order as Washington or London conceives it.

Hindi-language digital media has grown enormously but has not yet developed a strong tradition of long-form strategic analysis. Speed dominates. Depth is rare.

Think tanks produce excellent research — organizations like the Observer Research Foundation (ORF), the Institute for Defence Studies and Analyses (IDSA), and the Takshashila Institution do genuinely rigorous work. But their output is largely academic, often behind institutional barriers, and rarely written in a style accessible to a general educated audience.

India's Grand Strategy: The Choices Ahead

What should India's grand strategy be in this complex, rapidly shifting world? This is the central question that Global Chanakya will return to again and again — examining it from every angle, debating different perspectives, and tracking how India's choices play out over time.

Here are the core strategic debates India faces:

Strategic Autonomy vs. Alliance Politics

India has maintained a tradition of "strategic autonomy" since the Nehruvian era — the policy of not formally aligning with any great power bloc. This served India reasonably well through the Cold War. But in today's world, where the US-China competition is forcing countries to choose sides, pure non-alignment may become increasingly untenable. India is already a member of the Quad — a security grouping with the US, Japan, and Australia that has a clear anti-China orientation, even if none of its members say so explicitly. India has also deepened defence ties with the US, signed key foundational defence agreements, and bought American weapons systems. At the same time, India continues to buy Russian weapons, refuses to condemn Russia's invasion of Ukraine in UN votes, and participates in BRICS and SCO alongside China and Russia. Can India sustain this balance? For how long? These are questions without easy answers — and they are questions Global Chanakya will examine rigorously.

Economic Integration vs. Strategic Decoupling

India's trade deficit with China is over $80 billion annually. India depends on Chinese imports for everything from electronics components to pharmaceuticals to solar panels. Yet China is India's primary strategic adversary, with active territorial disputes, a history of border aggression, and a demonstrated willingness to use economic coercion as a weapon. How does India reduce this dangerous dependency without cratering its own manufacturing sector? How does India attract the global supply chain diversification away from China without simply replacing one dependency with another? These are among the most difficult economic-strategic questions India faces.

Military Modernization vs. Fiscal Constraints

India's defence spending as a percentage of GDP has actually declined in recent years — hovering around 2 percent — even as China has dramatically increased its military capabilities and Pakistan has acquired new weapons systems. India's military faces aging equipment, indigenous development programs that run chronically over schedule and over budget, and a force structure designed for a different era. Modernizing Indian military power to the level required by India's strategic ambitions is a generational challenge that will require sustained political will and fiscal commitment.

Neighbourhood First vs. Great Power Ambitions

India's neighbourhood — Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Myanmar, the Maldives, and Afghanistan — is uniquely challenging. Every one of these countries has been, at some point in recent years, either in political crisis, under Chinese influence, or in direct conflict with Indian interests. India cannot become a great power if it cannot manage its own backyard. Yet India's neighbourhood policy has had significant failures — Sri Lanka's dramatic turn toward China under the Rajapaksas, Nepal's occasional diplomatic hostility, the Maldives' 2023 election of a president openly hostile to India. Getting South Asia right is a prerequisite for India's global ambitions.

The Indo-Pacific: India's Strategic Opportunity of the Century

Of all the geopolitical theatres that matter to India, none is more consequential than the Indo-Pacific. And in the Indo-Pacific, India has natural advantages that no amount of money or political will can manufacture for other countries — geography, history, and the fact that the ocean itself bears India's name.

The Indian Ocean handles approximately 80 percent of global seaborne oil trade and 50 percent of global container traffic. Nine of the world's ten busiest shipping lanes pass through the Indian Ocean. The critical chokepoints — the Strait of Hormuz, the Strait of Malacca, the Bab-el-Mandeb, the Mozambique Channel — are either in India's extended neighborhood or are directly relevant to Indian energy security.

China recognizes this. Beijing has invested heavily in what Indian strategic analysts call the "String of Pearls" — a network of Chinese-built or Chinese-financed ports and infrastructure projects stretching from the South China Sea through the Indian Ocean to the Arabian Sea and East Africa. Gwadar in Pakistan, Hambantota in Sri Lanka, Chittagong in Bangladesh, Kyaukpyu in Myanmar, and Djibouti on the Horn of Africa — this network represents a systematic Chinese effort to build influence and potential military access around India's maritime periphery.

India's response has been the development of its own "necklace of diamonds" strategy — building port partnerships, security relationships, and maritime domain awareness networks with island nations and coastal states across the Indian Ocean. India has developed strategic infrastructure in Mauritius, the Seychelles, Madagascar, and Oman. India's Sagarmala project is modernizing Indian ports. The Indian Navy is expanding rapidly.

The Indo-Pacific is where India's strategic future will be decided. Global Chanakya will cover every development in this theatre with the depth and consistency it deserves.

The Bigger Picture: Why a Strategically Literate India Matters

There is a reason that the most powerful nations in the world invest heavily in strategic education — not just for their elites, but for their broader populations. A citizenry that understands geopolitics makes better democratic choices about foreign policy. It is harder to manipulate with nationalist emotion when people understand the actual strategic trade-offs involved. It generates better political leaders, better diplomats, better military officers, better business leaders, and better civil servants.

India has produced extraordinary strategic thinkers — from Chanakya to Nehru to K. Subrahmanyam to Shivshankar Menon. But strategic literacy has not spread broadly enough through Indian society. Too many Indians learn about the world reactively — responding to crises rather than anticipating them, absorbing narratives rather than analyzing them, consuming emotion rather than generating thought.

As India rises — as it becomes the third-largest economy, as its military power grows, as its diplomatic weight increases — the quality of Indian strategic thinking becomes a matter of genuine national consequence. A great power needs a strategically literate population. The decisions India makes in the next two decades — about its alliances, its military posture, its technology policy, its neighbourhood relationships, its role in multilateral institutions — will shape the lives of Indians for generations.

Global Chanakya exists because we believe that better analysis leads to better decisions. And better decisions, compounded over years and decades, lead to a stronger, more secure, more prosperous India.
